en: Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
The Parāśara Saṃhitā, together with the commentary composed by Mādhavācārya.
Now begins the second chapter:
I bow to that elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa), by saluting whom Vāgīśa and the other wise ones become successful in their undertakings regarding all matters.

In the first chapter, among the common and uncommon duties of the four castes questioned by Vyāsa, the uncommon duty was explained in detail after briefly stating the common duty. Now, in the second chapter, that common duty which was previously stated in brief is explained in detail. Alternatively, the preceding chapter proceeded with an emphasis on duties pertaining to the next world (*āmuṣmika*), whereas this one proceeds with an emphasis on duties that are the cause of life in this world (*aihika*). Therein, at the outset, he declares the subject matter to be expounded in this chapter.
Henceforth, [I shall describe] the ritual conduct of the householder in the Kali age,
the common dharma according to one's capacity as it pertains to the four castes and stages of life.

I shall declare that first, according to the words of Parāśara. Following this brief exposition of the duties common to the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), it is now the appropriate occasion for a detailed exposition at a later time. For when the subject has been stated in brief for those of dull intellect who lack the capacity to study voluminous texts, it is fitting to explain it in detail for those capable ones of superior intellect, since such matters remain present to their minds. Therefore, the teachers have said:
"For by means of both summary and detail, [the law is taught] to men of dull and superior intellect respectively."
"The internal organ, being addressed as an object, is described by that [word].

Alternatively, "after this" means immediately following the exposition of the primary dharma pertaining to the hereafter; for when the dharma whose fruit is in the hereafter has been stated—by such passages as "devoted to the six duties" and "the twilight ablution"—and since the dharma whose fruit is in this world, such as agriculture and so forth, comes to mind, the occasion for its exposition is appropriate.

Intending to show that the duties such as agriculture (*kṛṣi*) which are about to be described are impossible for the student (*brahmacārin*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the ascetic (*yati*), he indicates the stage of life (*āśrama*) suitable for them: "of the householder" (*gṛhasthasya*). This means that in the *Kṛta*, *Tretā*, and *Dvāpara* ages, the entitlement to agriculture and so forth belongs only to the Vaiśya, and not to every householder, such as a Brāhmaṇa or others; therefore, he specifies "in the Kali age. The word *karman* (action/duty) is used in common parlance for any activity whatsoever, while the word *ācāra* (conduct) refers to scriptural activities in the form of Dharma. However, in other ages, agriculture and the like possess the nature of *karman*; in the Kali age, they possess the nature of *ācāra*. Thus, there is a dual nature. Likewise, in other stages of life, there is the nature of *karman*, whereas for the householder's state, there is the aforementioned nature of *ācāra*; with this intention, it is called "action-conduct" (*karmācāra*). Since for a householder in the Kali age, officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and so forth are difficult to obtain, agriculture and the like are prescribed as the means of livelihood, and thus their status as *ācāra* is established.

He establishes that agriculture and the like possess the nature of common duty (*sādhāraṇadharma*) by stating: "pertaining to the four castes and the stages of life" (verse 3). The term *cāturvarṇya* refers to the four castes themselves; this is well-known everywhere. The "stage of life" (*āśrama*) here refers to the state of the householder (*gārhasthya*). For even for a *śūdra*, there exist household duties such as marriage and the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). All of this will be clearly explained by us later on in the description of the stages of life. Because these are prescribed within that stage of life, they are common to all. By the word "Parāśara," one born in a past *kalpa* is intended. To make this very point clear, he says "formerly. I shall fully declare the words of Parāśara, established in a previous *kalpa*, exactly as they occurred regarding the duties of the Kali age, such as agriculture and so forth. Therefore, since these have come down through tradition, no dispute should be raised regarding the status of agriculture and the like as established practice (*ācāra*); this is the underlying intention. He said "I shall fully declare according to my ability" in order to teach the conduct of the learned that "humility must be observed toward weightier matters," and not to indicate his own incapacity regarding any duty, for it is impossible for Parāśara, who is proficient in the duties of the Kali age, to be incapable in that regard. (1)
He demonstrates the duty that has been promised:
"A Brahmin, while engaged in the six duties, may also perform the work of agriculture. (2)

The six duties previously mentioned—sacrificing and so forth, as well as the twilight prayers and so forth—with these, the Brahmin, accompanied by Śūdras who perform service, should carry out agriculture. Nor should it be argued: "Since sacrificing and the other duties are the means of livelihood, what is the use of this agriculture? For in the Kali age, sacrificing and the like are difficult to obtain in sufficient quantity for a livelihood. As for that which was stated by Manu: "Even if living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which consists mostly of violence and is dependent on others."
"They consider agriculture to be good, yet that livelihood is censured by the virtuous;
for the iron-tipped wood destroys the earth and the creatures dwelling in the earth. (MDh 10.83–84).
This expresses his own personal opinion, for otherwise it would contradict Manu's own statement, since agriculture was accepted by him as well.
"But if he cannot subsist by either of these two, how should it be?
He should subsist by adopting the livelihood of a Vaiśya, namely agriculture and cattle-rearing" (MDh 10.82).
Now, one might object: in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, agriculture performed by oneself is indeed accepted.
"One may either perform cultivation oneself or engage in trade or moneylending;
however, moneylending is a miserable and most sinful livelihood, so one should avoid it.
(Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.15.4) [5] Thus it is said.
That is not so, because this statement is intended for the purpose of censuring laziness. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"Even in the midst of dire calamities, a Brāhmaṇa must not engage in usury" (NSm 4.111).
Now, one might object that Bṛhaspati himself sanctioned agriculture performed by oneself.

"A twice-born man may engage in the activities of a lazy man—agriculture and trade—if they are not performed by himself; however, if he performs them himself in times of distress, he becomes joined with sin.
This is certainly so. For even one who is unable to cause others to perform [the work] is considered its agent, because of the specific qualification "in times of distress."

But surely, even the status of being a cause to have [work] done applies only to times of distress (*āpad*), since agriculture is the duty of a Vaiśya, whereas for a Brāhmaṇa, officiating at sacrifices and so forth are the primary means of livelihood. If that is so, let there be a systematic arrangement according to the degree of distress: having work done by others in minor distress, and performing it oneself in extreme distress. Alternatively, let it be arranged according to the difference between the ages (*yuga*): in other ages, having work done is the duty in times of distress, but in the Kali age, it is the primary duty, because it is presented as the principal practice.
Regarding that, Hārīta states the rule for the number of oxen for a single plough in the case of agriculture:

"A plough with eight oxen is for those who follow the Dharma; one with six oxen for those seeking a livelihood; one with four oxen for the cruel; and one with two oxen for those who have slain a Brahmin" (Hārīta Smṛti 5.13).
Among these, the last two options are to be rejected; as for the other two, they should be understood as the primary and the secondary alternatives respectively. || 2 ||
Regarding agriculture, he states which oxen are to be avoided:
one should not yoke an ox that is hungry, thirsty, or exhausted.
A Brahmin shall not cause a bull that is deficient in limb, diseased, or impotent to carry a load. Thus [it is said]. (3)
Hunger and other such states are to be understood through their respective signs. One with deficient limbs is one lacking feet. A eunuch is one devoid of virility. || 3 ||
What kind of ox, then, should be yoked to the plough? To this he says:
"One with firm limbs, free from disease, well-fed, lowing pleasantly, and devoid of impotence—one should make such an ox work for half a day; thereafter, one should perform a bath. (4)

"Sthirāṅgaḥ" means having firm limbs, being free from defects such as lameness in the feet and so forth. "Nīrujaḥ" means free from disease. "Tṛptaḥ" means not afflicted by hunger or thirst. "Sunardaḥ" means one who is not timid; that is to say, one who is bold and free from fatigue. The term "ṣaṇḍha" is a designation emphasizing the abstract state; it means one who is devoid of impotence and endowed with virility—that is, one who is capable. "Half of the day" refers to two *yāmas*. "Afterwards, he should perform the bath" means he should bathe the oxen. Thus says Hārīta: "Having bathed the oxen and adorned them, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas" (Hārśn 4.10). A specific rule regarding the driving [of the oxen] is shown in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan].
One should drive it away by means of the sound "dhūṃ" alone, or with a branch bearing leaves;
never, however, with a staff, nor with a stick, nor again with a noose.
One should not cause an animal to carry a load when it is exhausted by hunger, thirst, or fatigue, or when its senses are impaired;
rather, one should eat only after the animals have been well-satisfied, and drink water only after they have drunk.
The yoking of draft animals is prescribed for the first two watches of the day;
they should rest during the middle watch and may be used as desired during the final watch.
Where there is urgent business to be done, or where there is danger on the road, one may drive the draft animals swiftly;
in such a case, he is not tainted by sin.
O King, he who drives them otherwise certainly goes to the Raurava hell;
that lowest of men who, out of delusion, makes them shed blood.
"O son of Pāṇḍu, his sin would be equal to that of killing an embryo. Thus [it is said]. (4)
He states what is to be performed after the bathing of the bull:
[8] One should thus practice the recitation of mantras, the worship of the deities, the fire sacrifice, and the study of one's own Veda.
A twice-born man should feed one, two, three, or four *snātaka* Brahmins.

Just as one bathes an ox to remove the exhaustion it has incurred, so too, to remove the fault of harming living beings, one should perform one or another of the recitations (*japa*) and other rites according to one's ability. One should feed one, two, three, or four *snātaka* Brahmins according to one's means. The *snātakas* are the nine types of mendicants. Regarding this, Manu says: "One who seeks to marry for the sake of progeny, one who intends to sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions, one who seeks wealth for the sake of his teacher, one who seeks wealth for the sake of his parents, one who seeks wealth for the sake of Vedic study, and one who is afflicted by illness" (MDh 11.1).

A *sāntānika* is one who seeks wealth for the purpose of marriage for his lineage. A *sarvavedasa* is one who, having performed a sacrifice in which all one's possessions (*sarvasva*) are given as the sacrificial fee, has fallen into destitution and seeks wealth; this is the meaning. One who seeks [the welfare of] father and mother is one who desires to serve his father and mother. A seeker of sacred study (*svādhyāyārthin*) is one who seeks wealth for the maintenance of his own Vedic recitation and teaching. The compound *svādhyāyārthyupatāpī* is a *madhyamapadalopa* (elliptical) compound, meaning "one who is afflicted while being a seeker of sacred study. || 5 ||
He states the application of the grain produced by cultivation:
"[9] One should perform the five sacrifices and cause the initiation for a ritual to be carried out with grain grown on a field ploughed by oneself and acquired by one's own effort. (6)

With all the grains that have ripened on a field plowed by himself, as well as those grains acquired by himself on a field plowed by servants, he should perform the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) prescribed by the *Smṛtis* and the initiation for Vedic sacrifices (*kratudīkṣā*) such as the *agniṣṭoma*. The causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the word *kārayet* is used in its own sense (i.e., it does not imply having another do the action). Alternatively, he may perform the great sacrifices himself; or, having given grain to those desiring to sacrifice, he may have them perform the sacrificial initiation. This application is also shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "Having obtained a gain, one should worship the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins."
"Being satisfied, they undoubtedly pacify his defects. (KūP 1.2.25.7) || 6 ||
It prohibits the sale of sesame and other grains by a farmer who is possessed of such crops, out of greed for wealth:
"Sesame seeds, being liquids, are not to be sold; those that are to be sold are grains or things equal to them.
For a Brahmin, such a livelihood as the selling of grass, wood, and so forth [is permitted]. (7)

Flavors (*rasa*) refer to curd, honey, clarified butter, and so forth. If, for one who lacks other grains, neither livelihood nor merit can be accomplished without the sale of sesame seeds, then sesame seeds should be bartered for other grains; with this intention, it is stated that "grains equal to them may be sold. The meaning is that as many *prastha* measures of sesame seeds as are given, that same amount of other grain should be received, and nothing more. This was stated by Nārada: "In cases of incapacity, for the sake of medicine, and likewise for the purpose of sacrifice..."
"But if sesame seeds must necessarily be sold, they may be exchanged for an equal amount of grain," so says [Nārada] (NSm 4.66). Yājñavalkya also states:
"For the sake of dharma, sesame seeds may be sold by being exchanged for an equal amount of grain" (YDh 3.39).
The principle regarding sesame seeds should also be applied to liquids. For this very reason, Manu says:
"Liquids may be bartered for liquids, but salt must never be exchanged for liquids;
prepared food for unprepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these [liquids] for equal amounts [of other goods]. (MDh 10.94)

Āpastamba also says: "By food for food, men for men, juices for juices, fragrances for fragrances, and knowledge for knowledges" (ĀpDh 1.7.20.15). Regarding the exchange of juices, Vasiṣṭha states a specific rule: "[11] Juices may be exchanged for juices that are either superior or inferior" (VaDh 2.37). Regarding the exchange of food, Gautama states a specific rule: "But with cooked food, it may be exchanged for an equal or unequal amount" (GDh 7.3). Now, one might object: the sale of sesame seeds has been permitted by Manu.
"Having generated a desire for agriculture, a farmer himself may sell pure sesame seeds for the sake of dharma, provided they have not been kept for long. (MDh 10.90)

On this point, some say: "This refers to the intention of exchange. Others, however, believe: "The sale of sesame for the sake of necessary religious duties, such as the repayment of debts, is not prohibited. This latter position alone is correct, because it accords with the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "Or, at their own will, they may produce sesame by cultivation and sell them" (VaDh 2.31). If, however, the intention were exchange, an unavoidable redundancy would result with another scriptural statement; for Manu himself has already shown that rule in another passage: "Sesame may be exchanged for grain of equal value" (MDh 10.94). For example, as shown by Manu and Yama:

"Whatever else one does with sesame seeds other than giving them as food or as an ointment, having become a worm, he sinks into the excrement of dogs along with his ancestors. (MDh 10.91) This is not a fault, because it refers to matters other than obligatory duties (*avaśyaka-dharma*). This exchange of sesame seeds on an equal footing with grain, as well as the sale of grass and so forth—this is the livelihood for a Brahmin intended for the sake of subsistence. And thus says Nārada:
"But for a Brāhmaṇa, dry wood, grass, and the like may be sold. (NSm 4.64) || 7 ||
Now, in order to state the remedy for the incidental sin attached to agriculture, [the author] first shows that sin:
"If a Brāhmaṇa should practice agriculture, he would incur a great fault.
For because violence is unavoidable in agriculture, a fault attaches even to a farmer who is careful. On this point, the statement of Manu, "predominantly involving violence," has already been cited.
[13] He clarifies the gravity of the aforementioned fault: "Whatever sin a fisherman may incur in a year... (8).
"With an iron-tipped wooden [spear], Lāṅgalin [kills] that in a single day.
Thus, it is stated that because there is a diverse slaughter of living beings with an iron-tipped plow-head, the sin is greater than that of killing fish. || 8 ||
In accordance with the manner stated above, since the consequence of sin would apply even to a mere cultivator, [the author] specifies [the subject] in order to exclude him:
"The gambler, the fisherman, the hunter, and likewise the fowler. (9)
"The non-giver and the farmer alike—all these share an equal portion [of sin].

A *pāśaka* is one who captures deer and other animals by spreading a snare. A *vyādha* is one who lives by killing deer. A *śākunika* is a bird-killer. A *adātā* (non-giver) is one who does not give to those who have arrived at the threshing floor where the grain heap is located. For all of them, the transgression is equal. Therefore, the *pāśaka* and others are described here as examples; the meaning is that just as the sin of the *pāśaka* and others is great, so too is the sin of the non-giving farmer. (9)
Having shown the sin of the farmer for whose sake [the sin] was demonstrated, he now describes the method for avoiding that sin:
"Having cut down trees, having split the earth, and having killed worms and insects... (10).
"A farmer is liberated from all sins by means of the *khalayajña* (the sacrifice at the threshing floor).
[14] Whatever sins are produced by cutting, splitting, and killing, the gift of grain at the threshing floor is the expiation for them all. And so says Hārīta:
Having broken the earth, having cut down plants, and having killed insects and ants, farmers purify themselves by means of the *khalayajña*; of this there is no doubt.

"This post which has been set up in the middle is indeed called the *meḍhi* by farmers; therefore, one who has not performed the *atantra* rite should give there a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of grain. (Hārīta Smṛti 5.14–15) || 10 ||
He states the transgression incurred by failing to perform the *khalayajña*: "He who, having arrived at the threshing floor, does not give to the twice-born... (11).
"He is a thief, he is a sinner; one should designate him as a slayer of a Brahmin.

This is understood from the force of two statements: that this *khalayajña* (threshing-floor sacrifice) of the farmer is both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*). Its obligatoriness follows from the fact that there is sin (*pratyavāya*) in its non-performance, and its optionality follows from its capacity to remove sins such as cutting [grain]. The obligatoriness of the *khalayajña* is shown in the *Śaiva Purāṇa*:
"O Goddess, that farmer who should bring grain inside without having given [a portion], [is a sinner]."
O Queen, I shall describe the evil that comes to one who is overcome by craving.
For a thousand divine years, that evil-minded cultivator shall become a tree devoid of flowers and fruit in a desert region.
At the end of that [existence], having become human again, after the lapse of time, he is born sometimes poor, diseased, foolish, and of low family. Thus [it is said]. (11)
[15] He states the measure of the grain to be given:
having given a sixth part to the king, and a twenty-first part to the gods. || 12 ||
One who gives a thirtieth part (*triṃśaka*) to Brahmins is liberated from all sins.

A "sixth part" (*ṣaḍbhāga*) is one part out of six parts; a "twenty-first part" (*ekaviṃśaka*) is any one part out of twenty-one parts; and similarly, it should be understood that a "thirtieth part" (*triṃśa*) is any one part out of thirty parts. Just as [offerings] are given to the gods, they should also be given to the ancestors. This has been stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "One should give a twentieth part to the gods and to the ancestors."
"But by cultivating [land] for a thirtieth part of the Brahmins, one incurs no fault. (KūP 1.2.25.8) || 12 ||
Having described the agriculture along with its duties for the Brahmin, he now describes it for the other castes as well:
"A Kṣatriya also, having practiced agriculture, should worship the gods and the Brahmins. (13)

"A Vaiśya and a Śūdra should likewise perform agriculture, trade, and crafts" (16). Although agriculture was prescribed for the Vaiśya in the previous chapter, it is mentioned here again in order to prescribe the specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*). By the extension (*atideśa*) "he should act in that manner," the entire procedure prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa regarding agriculture becomes prescribed here as well. Just like agriculture, the phrase "trade and crafts" is used to show that in the Kali age, trade and crafts are common to all four social classes (*varṇa*). || 13 ||

Anticipating the objection that if agriculture and the like were permitted for a Śūdra as well, then since his livelihood would be established by those means alone, service to the twice-born should be abandoned in the Kali age, he says:
"Śūdras, deprived of service to the twice-born, engage in improper occupations. (14)

"They indeed become short-lived and undoubtedly go to hell. Thus it is said. Because agriculture and the like are causes for a distinguished livelihood through excessive gain, they are called *vikarman* (unlawful occupation). However, through service to the twice-born (*dvija*), one obtains only worn-out clothes and such; thus, there is no excessive gain. Therefore, if those who, out of a desire for excess, should abandon service to the twice-born while performing only agriculture and the like, then both their worldly and otherworldly welfare would perish. (14)
Having thus expounded the dharma that is the cause of livelihood common to the four castes, he concludes:
"This is the eternal dharma for all four castes. (15)
The term "eternal" (sanātana) is used to indicate that even in past Kali ages, activities such as agriculture were practiced by Brahmins and others.

[17] Although it would have been appropriate to state the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*) immediately after the duties of the castes (*varṇa-dharma*), as is done in other Smṛtis, they were nevertheless omitted by the Teacher because Vyāsa did not ask about them. We, however, shall describe them for the benefit of our listeners. Nor should it be thought that they were not described simply because they were not dealt with in the preceding chapter; for there was no occasion for them there. Here, however, there is an occasion, since they have come to mind through the word "stages of life" (*āśrama*) in the phrase "pertaining to the four castes and stages of life. And these stages of life are of four kinds. As it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—
these are the four distinct stages of life (āśramas) for Brahmins, in their proper order.
Thus [says] Manu as well.
"The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—these four distinct stages of life originate from the householder. (MDh 6.87)

The meaning is that they originate from the householder and are useful to the householder. Among these, one who has been consecrated by the *upanayana* ceremony is a *brahmacārī*, according to the wording of the mantra: “I have come for the sake of *brahmacarya*; lead me near. The meaning is: “With reference to *brahmacarya*, lead me, who have come, near [to you]. And because it is recited among the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*, the *upanayana* is a *brāhma* (Brahmanical) sacrament (*saṃskāra*). Regarding this, Hārīta says: “Indeed, the sacrament is of two kinds: *brāhma* and *daiva*. That which pertains to the Smṛti, beginning with *garbhādhāna*, is *brāhma*. The *pākayajñas*, the *haviyajñas*, and the *saumyas* are *daiva*. One consecrated by the *brāhma* sacrament attains equality and union (*sāyujya*) with the Ṛṣis; one consecrated by the subsequent *daiva* sacrament attains equality and union with the gods” (HārSm 11.1–5). The rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* have been enumerated by Gautama.

Conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the rite for preventing miscarriage (*anavalobhana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), and the initiation (*upanayana*); the four *vedavrata*s; the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) and union with a wife who shares the same religious duties (*sahadharmacāriṇīsaṃyoga*); the performance of the five sacrifices—those to the gods, the ancestors, humans, spirits, and Brahman—and the seven forms of domestic sacrifice (*pākayajña-saṃsthā*): the *aṣṭakā*, the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, the *śrāvaṇī*, the *āgrahāyaṇī*, the *caitrī*, and the *āśvayujī*; the seven forms of the *haviryajña-saṃsthā*: the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *āgrayaṇa*, the *cāturmāsya*, the *nirūḍhapaśubandha*, and the *sautrāmaṇī*; and the seven forms of the *somasaṃsthā*: the *agniṣṭoma*, the *atyagniṣṭoma*, the *ukthya*, the *ṣoḍaśī*, the *vājapeya*, the *atirātra*, and the *aptoryāma*. These constitute the forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*s).

Thus (GDh 8.13–20). Among these, the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) and ending with *cūḍā* (tonsure) are for the purpose of removing defects arising from the seed and the womb. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya, having defined the sacraments ending with the *cūḍā*, says: "In this way, the sin originating from the seed and the womb is pacified" (YDh 1.13). Therefore, they are described prior to the stage of the student (*brahmacarya-āśrama*). Among these, for the twice-born (*dvija*), the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* must be performed with mantras. Regarding that, Yājñavalkya says:
"The castes are the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra; however, the first three are the twice-born.
For them, the rites beginning with conception and ending at the cremation ground are indeed performed with mantras. (YDh 1.10).
He [the same author] states the specific times for the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*:

For a male child, the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) are performed; the *puṃsavana* (male-securing rite) is done before the fetus moves; the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) is in the sixth or eighth month; and these, along with the *jātakarman* (birth rite), are performed at birth.

"On the eleventh day [after birth] the naming ceremony is performed; in the fourth month, the rite of going forth; in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food; and the tonsure should be performed according to family custom. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.11–12).
The menstrual period (*ṛtu*) consists of sixteen days starting from the day of the appearance of menses. Regarding this, Manu says:
The natural menstrual period of women is said to consist of sixteen nights,
along with another four days that are censured by the virtuous.
Of these, the first four nights, as well as the censured eleventh, are to be avoided;
the remaining ten nights, occurring in pairs, are recommended.
"Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights; therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during her season on the even nights. (MDh 3.46–48) [20].
Thus, beginning from the appearance of the menses, four days are strictly forbidden. "On even nights" means on the same-numbered nights. "Should approach" means he should go to her.
Thus ends the rite of conception (garbhādhāna).

Now, the *puṃsavana* rite. Having thus performed the *garbhādhāna* during the fertile period, the *puṃsavana* should be performed before the movement of the fetus. That movement occurs either in the second or the third month. Regarding this, Baijavāpa says: “In the second or the third month, before the throbbing [of the fetus]. Pāraskara also states: “In the second or the third month; on that day, the moon should be conjoined with a male asterism” (PārGṛ 1.5.14.2–3). The male asterisms, such as Hastā and others, are well known in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*). The *anavalobhana* rite is to be understood from the *Āśvalāyanagṛhyapariśiṣṭa*.
Thus ends the Puṃsavana rite.

Now, the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*). Regarding the *sīmantonnayana*, times other than those stated by Yājñavalkya have also been shown by the sages. Among them, Laugākṣi says: “The parting of the hair should be performed in the third month of pregnancy. Āpastamba also says: “In the first pregnancy, in the fourth month. Baijavāpa also says: “Now, the parting of the hair [is performed] in the fourth, fifth, or even the sixth [month]. In the *Sāṅkhyāyana-gṛhya* it is also said: “In the seventh month of the first pregnancy, the parting of the hair. Śaṅkha also says: “The parting of the hair [should be performed] upon the movement of the fetus, or until the birth. Since no specific distinction is heard, it should be performed only once, not for every pregnancy. And so Hārīta says: “Twice-born women are consecrated by the *sīmanta* rite only once. Devala also [says the same].
"A woman who has been consecrated once is consecrated for all subsequent pregnancies.

However, according to the view that it is a rite for the fetus (*garbhasaṃskāra*), it must be repeated for each pregnancy. And so Viṣṇu states: "The *sīmantonnayana* rite is not intended as a consecration of the woman."
Some, for the sake of purifying the womb, apply [the mantra] to each individual womb.

The arrangement between these two views is according to what has been traditionally accepted. Regarding the birth of a woman for whom the *sīmanta* rite has not been performed, Satyavrata says: "If a woman should somehow give birth while the *sīmanta* has not been performed, she, having taken hold of her son, deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) again according to the rule."
Thus ends the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*);

now follows the birth-rite (*jātakarman*). Regarding the timing for that birth-rite, Yājñavalkya has shown it thus: "These two [rites] and the birth-rite [should be performed] within the month" (YDh 1.11). "Within the month" means when the child has been born. Viṣṇu also says:
"Then one should perform the birth-rite as prescribed when a son is born."
The word "in one's own *gṛhya* [text]" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. And that [rite] is to be performed immediately after the bath. Thus says Saṃvarta:
"When a son is born, a bath with one's clothes on is prescribed for the father.
Furthermore, the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) must be performed even before the cutting of the umbilical cord. Thus says Manu:
"The birth-rite (*jātakarma*) for a male child is ordained prior to the cutting of the umbilical cord;
and there is the ritual consumption of gold, honey, and clarified butter accompanied by mantras" (MDh 2.21).

"Cutting" (*vardhana*) here means severing. Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of entitlement to perform the rite due to the fear of ritual impurity (*āśauca*), because impurity does not exist before the cutting of the umbilical cord. Thus said Jaimini:
"As long as the stalk is not severed, one does not incur the impurity of birth (*sūtaka*);
once the stalk is severed, thereafter the impurity of birth is ordained.
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
"A Śrāddha must indeed be performed at the birth of a son when the umbilical cord has not yet been severed;
or else it should be performed by those of self-restraint once the period of impurity has ceased.
And that Śrāddha should be performed with gold as the material. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:

"In the absence of materials, in the absence of twice-born [Brahmins], during travel, upon the birth of a son, or when one's wife is in her menses, one should perform a Hema-śrāddha (gold śrāddha). Thus it is stated. In the Āditya Purāṇa, the prohibition of cooked food is shown.
"One should not give cooked food even to Brahmins at a birth-śrāddha;
for their purification comes from the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, and not otherwise.
On that day, a gift should be made according to one's capacity. This has been stated in the Ādi-purāṇa:
"When a son is born to the twice-born, both the gods and the ancestors come;
therefore, that day is always meritorious and worthy of worship.
On that occasion, one should give gold, land, a cow, a horse, and a chariot. Thus it is said.

Śaṅkha also states: “[24] One should give to all the agnatic kinsmen two-footed and four-footed animals, grain, gold, and so forth. And this must be performed even during a period of impurity (āśauca).
For it is said: “But when the birth of a son occurs while a period of impurity has arisen, there is immediate purification for the performer; he is purified by the preceding impurity.”
Thus ends the birth-rite (*jātakarman*);
now follows the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). Regarding this, Manu has shown other times as well than those stated by Yājñavalkya:
"One should cause his name to be given on the tenth or the twelfth [day]."
"On an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with good qualities" (MDh 2.30).
The causative suffix (*ṇic*) in "he should cause [the name] to be made" is used reflexively;
therefore, the father himself should give the name on the tenth day (ViPu 3.10.8).

Thus, according to the statement in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*. Alternatively, in the absence of the father or if he is unfit, another person may perform it. To this effect, Śaṅkha says: "The father, or another elder of the family, should establish the connection with the family deity and the lunar mansion. In the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*: "O King, some desire the naming on the tenth day;
others on the twelfth day, or at night, or when the month is complete."
"Likewise, other wise men say it should be on the eighteenth day.

Also, in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "The naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) takes place when ten nights have passed from birth, or after one year. In this matter, the arrangement follows one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. Manu shows the nature of the name according to the distinction of castes: "That of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with strength."
That of a Vaiśya is associated with wealth, while that of a Śūdra is contemptible.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in a word meaning "shelter" (śarman); that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with a word meaning "protection" (rakṣā);
that of a Vaiśya should be joined with a word meaning "prosperity" (puṣṭi); and that of a Śūdra should be joined with a word meaning "servant" (preṣya).
"For women, [the name] should be easy to pronounce, not harsh, clear in meaning, pleasing to the mind, auspicious, ending in a long vowel, and containing a word of benediction. (MDh 2.31–33)

The first members of the compound are auspicious terms (*maṅgalya*), and the latter members are terms such as *śarma* and so forth. Thus, names are formed in this manner: Śrīśarmā, Vikramapāla, Māṇikyaśreṣṭhin, Hīnadāsa, and others; for women, however, [names such as] Śrīdāsī and the like. "Easy to utter" means capable of being spoken. Regarding this, Baijavāpa states a specific rule: "The father gives the name—consisting of one syllable, two syllables, three syllables, four syllables, or an unlimited number; it begins with a sonant (*ghoṣavat*) and ends with a semivowel (*antastha*) and a long vowel or a visarga (*abhiniṣṭhāna*). [26] The meaning of this is as follows: those sonant letters which are the third and fourth of the consonant classes should be placed at the beginning; the semivowels (*antarastha* = *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*) should be placed in the middle; and at the end, there should be a "final breath" (*abhiniṣṭhāna*), which is the visarga. Thus, names such as Bhadrapāla and Jātavedas come into being. Śaṅkha and Likhita state the fruit of giving a name according to these rules: "When the name has been given in this way, that family becomes pure."
Thus concludes the naming ceremony; now follows the rite of first going forth. Regarding this, Manu says: "In the fourth month, the infant's first exit from the house should be performed" (MDh 2.34).
Regarding what must be performed therein, Yama says:
"Then, in the third month, the viewing of the sun must be performed;
in the fourth month, the viewing of the moon must be performed. Thus it is said.
Laukāxi also says: “[The rite of] seeing the sun occurs in the third fortnight. And in the Purāṇa as well:
“O Indra among kings, on the twelfth day the infant’s exit from the house should be performed;
likewise, it is agreed by others that it should be done in the fourth month.”
In this matter as well, the rule is determined according to one's own specific Śākhā.
Thus concludes the rite of going forth; now follows the rite of the first feeding of solid food. Regarding that, Yama says:

"Thereafter, the *annaprāśana* (the first feeding of solid food) should be performed according to the prescribed rule in the sixth month, or it should be performed in the eighth month, or at whatever auspicious time is desired by the family.

Śaṅkha also says: "The *annaprāśana* is in the [first] year, or in half a year, according to some. Laugākṣi says: "The *annaprāśana* is in the sixth month, or when the teeth have appeared. Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya states a specific detail:
In the presence of the deity, while he is seated on his nurse’s lap and adorned with ornaments, food should be given to him in a golden vessel.
"One should have him consume milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with honey, clarified butter, and gold;
once he has consumed it, the nurse should release the child from her lap. Thus [it is said]. Following the consumption, the examination of the future livelihood is shown by Mārkaṇḍeya:
[28] Then, having laid out all the various craft implements,
weapons, and garments in front of him, he should thereafter examine their characteristics.
"Whatever the child first touches, and likewise whatever vessel he touches himself,
by that alone shall the livelihood of that child be determined.
Thus ends the section on the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*).
Now, regarding the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*). On this matter, Yama states: "Then, when the year is complete, the tonsure rite is prescribed;
or it should be performed in the second or third year, according to the evidence of the revealed scriptures (*śruti*)."

Baijavāpa says: “The tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*) is performed in the third year. Śaṅkha also says: “The tonsure rite (*cūḍākarma*) is in the third year, or in the fifth. Laugākṣi also says: “The tonsure ceremony is performed when the greater part of the third year has passed. Śaunaka also says: “The *caula* is in the third year, or according to the family custom. Regarding this, Laugākṣi states the rule for the tonsure according to different sages (*ṛṣi*): “For the Vāsiṣṭhas, there is a single lock of hair (*kamuñjā*) on the right side; for the Atris and Kaśyapas, locks on both sides; the Bhṛgus are shaven; the Aṅgirases have five locks; others have a top-knot (*śikhin*) for the sake of adornment; or it may be according to family custom. *Kamuñjā* refers to a line of hair. In these matters, the arrangement is determined by one’s own *śākhā*. Here, the rites mentioned ending with the tonsure ceremony pertain to those who are not yet initiated (*anupanīta*); therefore, following that context, certain other duties of the uninitiated are now described. Regarding this, Gautama says: “Prior to initiation, one may act as he pleases, speak as he pleases, and eat as he pleases” (GDh 2.1). “Acting as he pleases” means moving according to his will. “Speaking as he pleases” means uttering vulgarities and the like. “Eating as he pleases” means consuming stale food and so forth. This is also stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.

"In matters of what is edible and inedible, as well as what may be drunk, what may be spoken and what may not be spoken, and likewise in falsehood—there shall be no fault at this time so long as he has not been initiated. (ViP 3.10.9).
And this consumption of forbidden food refers to cases other than those involving substances that cause a *mahāpātaka* (grave sin); for this very reason, another *smṛti* states:
"There may be mention of eating according to one's own will, provided it does not involve a great sin.

Thus, just as there is no restriction regarding what is fit or unfit to eat, likewise there is no requirement for performing acts such as ritual sipping (ācamana) and so forth. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says: "Indeed, no ritual duty whatsoever exists for him prior to the tying of the girdle (mauñjībandhana)."

"By his mode of life he is equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born in the Veda. (VaDh 2.6). Gautama also says: "He remains in a state of impurity with urine and excrement according to their occurrence; for him there exists no rule for ritual sipping (ācamana); he should not utter the Veda, except for the recitation of *svadhā* at the offering of funeral cakes. Thus ends the section on the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*).
Now, however, the practice of the syllables (akṣara-abhyāsa) must be performed. Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"When the fifth year has arrived, while Janārdana is not yet asleep, one should avoid the sixth lunar day, the first, and likewise the eighth."

One should cause the commencement of learning at a well-determined time, specifically on the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight when it is empty (the new moon), as well as on Saturdays and Tuesdays.
Having worshipped Hari, the goddess Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī,
as well as the authors of the sūtras of one's own branch of knowledge and that branch of knowledge itself in particular.
One should offer clarified butter into the fire while reciting the names of these very deities;
furthermore, the honoring of the best of the twice-born should be performed with sacrificial fees.
[31] The teacher, seated facing the east, should first instruct the pupil, who faces the west (the direction of Varuṇa), while being well-honored by the twice-born.
"From that time forward, one should avoid those days designated as unfit for study (anadhyāya),

namely the two eighth days of the lunar fortnight and the three days at the end of each fortnight. Thus ends the section on the sacraments beginning with conception and ending with the tonsure ceremony.
Now, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Regarding this, Manu says:
"One should perform the initiation of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
that of a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year from conception; and that of a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception."
The initiation of a Brahmin who desires spiritual luster should be performed in the fifth year;
that of a King seeking power in the sixth; and that of a Vaiśya seeking wealth in the eighth.
The Sāvitrī does not expire for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year,
nor for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second, nor for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.
Beyond this time, all three of these, having become unrefined according to their respective periods, are fallen from the Sāvitrī; they are Vratyas, despised by the Aryas.
"A Brāhmaṇa should never, even under any circumstances, enter into spiritual or matrimonial alliances with those who have not been purified according to the prescribed rules. (MDh 2.36–40)

Āpastamba also says: “[32] ‘In the seventh year, one desiring Vedic luster; in the eighth, one desiring long life; in the ninth, one desiring splendor; in the tenth, one desiring food; in the eleventh, one desiring sensory power; in the twelfth, one desiring cattle’” (ĀpDh 1.1.1.20). And this applies equally to all three social classes (*varṇa*). Regarding the restriction of time according to the specific class, he himself states: “One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring, a Rājanya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn” (ĀpDh 1.1.1.19). Manu describes the procedure for initiation according to the sequence of the classes.
"Brahmacārins shall wear, in their respective order, the skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat; as well as garments made of hemp, flax, and wool."

The skins of the black antelope (*kārṣṇa*) and others serve as upper garments (*uttarīya*). Thus says Śaṅkha: “The skins of the black antelope, the *ruru*, and the goat are the upper garments. Vasiṣṭha also states: “A black antelope skin is the upper garment for a Brāhmaṇa; a *raurava* [deer] skin for a Kṣatriya; and a cow-hide or a goat-skin for a Vaiśya” (VaDh 11.61–63). Likewise, Pāraskara says: “An *aiṇeya* [antelope] skin is the upper garment for a Brāhmaṇa; a *raurava* for a Kṣatriya; a goat- or cow-skin for a Vaiśya; or, for all, a cow-skin” (PārGṛ 2.5.17–20). Flaxen cloth (*śāṇa*) and others may also serve as upper garments. Regarding this, Āpastamba says: “As for clothing: flaxen, linen, and skins; some prescribe saffron-dyed cloth for a Brāhmaṇa, madder-dyed for a Kṣatriya, and turmeric-dyed for a Vaiśya” (ĀpDh 1.1.2.39–41, 3.1–2). Vasiṣṭha states: “A white, unwashed garment for a Brāhmaṇa; cotton, madder-dyed, or linen for a Kṣatriya; and turmeric-dyed or silk for a Vaiśya” (VaDh 11.64–66). Manu speaks of the girdle (*mekhalā*):
[34] "The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya should be a bowstring made of mūrvā fiber; and that of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads. (MDh 2.42). "Triple-stranded" means consisting of three strands. Yama also says:
According to the Dharma, the girdle of a Brahmin is made of muñja grass, that of a Kṣatriya is a bowstring made of mūrvā fiber,
and that of a Vaiśya is a cord of hemp.
"But in the absence of even these, a triple-stranded girdle should be made of kuśa grass, aśmantaka, or balvaja, or it should be triple-stranded with a single knot. Thus says Manu as well.
"In the absence of muñja grass, however, [the girdle] should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja fibers; it should have three strands and be tied with one, three, or five knots. (MDh 2.43).
Manu speaks of the staff:
"A Brāhmaṇa deserves staffs made of Bilva or Palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, of Vaṭa or Khadira; and a Vaiśya, of Pīlu or Udumbara—this is according to the Dharma. (MDh 2.45).
Yama states the secondary alternative as follows:
"But in the absence of all these, those fit for all sacrifices [may be used].
Manu has stated the measurement of the staff:
"The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made to the length reaching the hair-tuft (keśānta) according to its measure."
"The staff of a king should reach his forehead, but that of a Vaiśya should reach the tip of his nose" (MDh 2.46).

Gautama also says: "The measurements are [respectively] the crown of the head, the forehead, and the tip of the nose" (GDh 1.28). Manu states the characteristics of the staffs: "They should all be straight, without blemishes, and pleasing to the sight."

"Those which do not cause distress to men, which have their bark intact, and which are not damaged by fire. (MDh 2.47). Gautama also says: "Unhurt, with the top like a sacrificial post, and possessing their scales. (GDh 1.27). Regarding the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), Manu says: "The sacred thread of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward, and triple-stranded."
"Made of hemp thread for a king, and of woolen thread for a Vaiśya.

(MDh 2.44). Paiṭhīnasi also says: "The sacrificial thread (*upavīta*) of a Brāhmaṇa is made of cotton; that of a Kṣatriya is made of linen; that of a Vaiśya is made of wool. [36] In the absence of the aforementioned sacrificial threads, materials such as cow-hair should be taken according to availability. Regarding this, Devala says: "Cotton, linen, cow-hair, hemp, bark, grass, and so forth..."
"The twice-born should always wear the sacred thread (*upavīta*) when performing ritual acts.

Thus says Ṛṣyaśṛṅga: "Alternatively, one may use two garments for the purpose of the *yajñopavīta*; in their absence, one should use a triple-stranded cord. And that [cord] should be made of nine threads. Devala states this:
"One should make the *yajñopavīta* with a cord consisting of nine threads."

Kātyāyana states: "It should be made with three strands twisted upward and three strands twisted downward. (KSm 1.1.2) The author of the *Saṃgraha* provides the definition of that which is twisted upward:

"With the right hand raised upwards and the thread tripled, the thread wound by men is known in the scriptures as *ūrdhvavṛta* (wound upwards). The meaning is that what is wound with the right hand raised upwards is called *ūrdhvavṛta*. Devala states the procedure for the *yajñopavīta*:
Having gone out from the village and counted [the distance], he should take a cord three times that length measured across his ninety-six fingers, and wash it with the three *ābliṅgaka* verses.
In a temple, or in a cow-pen, by a river, or elsewhere in a clean place, one should fashion a nine-stranded cord with the Sāvitrī mantra; it should be triple-stranded.
[37] One should tie up a branch from any one of the sacrificial trees, such as the *bilva* or *aśvattha*, while it is still alive, saying: "Obeisance to the ancestors."
One should not look at the *vyāma* (the space between the outstretched arms), for that brings satisfaction to the ancestors;
one should strike the palms three times, for that brings satisfaction to the gods.
Having taken earth in his left hand, he should place it in this [vessel] while saying "bhūḥ";
or he may cast in a leaf, a flower, or even a fruit with the vyāhṛtis.

"Then, having consecrated it with the three verses beginning with 'bhūr agniś ca,' one should wear it after bowing down to Hari, Brahmā, and Īśvara. The mantra for the wearing is "yajñopavītam," and so forth. Kātyāyana states the rule regarding the knot:
"The sacred thread (*upavīta*) should be threefold, and it is prescribed that it have a single knot. Thus [it is said].
He himself states the measurement of the *yajñopavīta*:
"That which, when held at the spine and at the navel, reaches the waist..."
"That sacred thread (*upavīta*) should be worn neither too low nor too high. Thus [says the *Karmapradīpa* 1.1.3]. Devala also says: "It should never be worn above the breasts or below the navel."
Bhṛgu states the number of sacred threads:
"One sacred thread is prescribed for a student (baṭu), two for the other two [orders], and for ascetics (yatis) there should be only one; such is the certainty of the scripture."

And this is intended to be lifelong, since many authorities enjoin it for as long as one lives. Thus Devala says: "There are many [rules] for one who desires long life. This sacred thread (upavīta) must be worn at all times. Thus Bhṛgu says:
"One should always be wearing the sacred thread and always have one's topknot tied;
whatever one does without the topknot or without the sacred thread is as if not done at all."
A wise person who desires his own welfare should not remove from his body the sacred thread that remains there, purified by mantras.
"And by lifting it [the sacred thread] even once, the twice-born man must perform an expiation.
Regarding the sacred thread (*upavīta*), Devala states a specific rule:
"If the thread should have hair on it, one should then remove that hair."
One should sprinkle that [person] ten times with water consecrated by the Sāvitrī mantra.
"Or if it has been torn, or has gone down [into the water], one should discard it after using it.
Thus Manu states the ritual disposal (*pratipatti*) for the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and other items when they are torn or otherwise damaged:
"The girdle, the deerskin, the staff, the sacred thread, and the water-pot..."
"Having thrown the spoiled items into the water, let him take others according to the mantra" (MDh 2.64).
Now, after taking up the staff and other items, the worship of the Sun must be performed. Thus says Manu:
"Having taken up the desired staff and having worshipped the Sun..."
"Having circumambulated the fire clockwise, he should go about for alms according to the rule" (MDh 2.48).

The meaning is that, having received the initiation (*upanayana*) accompanied by the ritual procedures ending with the taking of the staff, and having worshipped the Sun—who is the essence of the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*) of the *Gāyatrī*—and having realized "I am He," he should attend upon the fire and go about for alms. The attendance upon the fire has been shown by Manu:
"Having brought fuel from afar, he should place it in the open air."
"Unwearied, one should offer [oblations] into the fire with them both in the evening and in the morning. (MDh 2.186).

The meaning is that one should place [the fuel] in the *vihāyas*, that is, in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and not on the ground. Regarding the specific rules for fetching the fuel-wood (*samidh*), Baijavāpa says: "Before sunset, having gone toward the northern direction, one should fetch fuel-wood from the forest without causing injury. [Wood] that is dry is for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); moist wood is for one desiring food; for one desiring both, both types [are used]. Kātyāyana states the definition of the fuel-wood: "The fuel-wood should never be made thicker than a thumb."
It was not stripped of its bark, nor infested with insects, nor torn apart.
The sacrificial ladle (viśālikā) should not be more than a span (prādeśa) nor less;
it should not have leaves attached, nor should it be excessively long, by one who is knowledgeable in the oblations.

"Split, stainless, short, crooked, very porous, thin, long, or thick—a fire-stick defective in these qualities destroys the success of the ritual. Thus it is said. The rule regarding the fire-stick is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*.
"The fuel sticks should be made of *pālāśa* wood; in its absence, those of *khādira*;
in its absence, *śamī*, *rohitaka*, or *aśvattha*; and in their absence, *arka* or *vetasa*.
Regarding the transgression incurred by failing to perform the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), Hārīta says:
"In former times, Death indeed seized a religious student while he was practicing violence;
Agni liberated him from that [clutches]. Therefore, one should attend upon him. (Hārīta Smṛti 2.27).
Yājñavalkya describes the manner of wandering for alms:

"One should go for alms among blameless Brāhmaṇas for the sake of one's own subsistence. The practice of begging for alms among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is characterized by the word *bhavat* at the beginning, middle, and end, respectively. (YDh 1.29–30)
The phrase "among the Brāhmaṇas" is an illustration representing one's own respective caste. For this very reason, Vyāsa states: "Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas should go for alms every day;
they should do so either only in the houses of their own caste or among all castes."
The practice of begging from all castes (*sārvavarṇikatva*) pertains to times of distress (*āpad*). For this very reason, it is shown in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"O joy of the Kurus, one may beg alms from the four castes when [food] is not obtained. Even in times of distress, one should not accept cooked food from a Śūdra. Regarding that, Aṅgiras says:
One should take raw grain from the last person in the line; if there is no such source, one may take enough for a single night.
Raw grain is purified in this cycle of existence; that which is righteous is firmly established among them.
"Therefore, Aṅgiras has declared that one may accept raw food even from a Śūdra.
In times of non-distress, one should practice begging for alms only among those of one's own caste who are themselves praiseworthy. Regarding this, Manu says:
"From those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifice, and who are praiseworthy in their own duties..."
“A student, being self-restrained, shall collect alms daily from the houses [of people]” (MDh 2.183).

Regarding the phrase “at the beginning, middle, and end”—this is the meaning: in the statement that initiates the practice of begging, the word *bhavat* should be employed according to the sequence of the social classes (*varṇa*) at the beginning, middle, and end. And so says Manu:
“An initiated man of the highest twice-born class shall go about for alms, preceded by the word *bhavat*.”
"A Kṣatriya [should beg] in the middle of the word *bhavat*, while a Vaiśya [should beg] with *bhavat* following. (MDh 2.49).
He states an exception regarding some of those mentioned:
"One should not beg from the family of one's guru, nor from the families of one's paternal or maternal relatives."
But if houses belonging to others are not available, one should abandon each preceding one in turn.
"Or, in the absence of those previously mentioned, he may wander through the entire village, restraining his speech and remaining pure, but he must avoid those who have been accused. (MDh 2.184–85).
As for that which...

"He should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt—whichever of these will not treat him with contempt" (MDh 2.50). This refers specifically to the alms-begging that is an ancillary part of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), because otherwise a fault is heard [to be incurred]. To this effect, Yama says:

"One should not collect alms anywhere in excess of what is required for food; by intentionally collecting more than that, one incurs the fault of theft. Furthermore, that alms-food must be eaten only after having first obtained the permission of one's teacher. On this point, Manu and Yama have both stated:

"Having collected that alms-food according to his needs without deceit, and having offered it to the guru, he should eat, facing east, pure and having sipped water. (MDh 2.51) In the absence of the guru, he should offer it to the guru’s wife or others. Regarding this, Gautama says: "Having offered it to the guru, he should eat when permitted; in the guru’s absence, to the guru’s wife, son, or fellow student" (GDh 2.35–36). He should eat the alms-food permitted by the guru after honoring it. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having performed the fire-ritual, he should eat with speech restrained, by the permission of his guru, preceded by the *āpośana* rite, honoring the food and not disparaging it. (YDh 1.31)

And Hārīta has shown what constitutes respectful treatment: “Alms that have been inspected, circumambulated by fire, gazed upon by the sun, offered to the guru, and permitted—these they call equal to nectar (*amṛta*). When a student (*brahmacārī*) eats this, he attains perfection in the Veda (*brahmasiddhi*)” (HārSm 3.6–7). Gautama also says: “In the evening and in the morning, one should eat food that has been honored, without criticizing it” (GDh 9.30). Manu states the prohibition against eating the food of a single person: “[44] A student should always subsist on alms; he should not be one who eats the food of a single person.”
The subsistence of one observing a vow by means of alms is declared to be equal to fasting.
"As one observing a vow at a rite dedicated to the gods, and like a seer at a rite for the ancestors, he may eat at his pleasure when invited; his vow is not thereby violated. (MDh 2.188–89).
He [Manu] himself states the sin incurred by failing to do so:
"Without having gone for alms and without having kindled the sacred fire, one who is not ill shall perform the vow of an *avakīrṇin* for seven nights. (MDh 2.187).
Yama states the rule for one who has been initiated (*upanīta*):

"One should carry a staff, a water-pot, a bundle of *darbha* grass, and likewise a girdle made of *muñja* grass; while living with the teacher, one should observe celibacy and subsist on food obtained by alms. Here, "veda" refers to a handful of *darbha* grass. "Living with the teacher" means in the teacher's house. Yama says:
"A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) shall always wear a girdle, a deerskin, a staff, a sacrificial thread, a loincloth,
and a waist-string," so says Manu.

"A twice-born man who has undergone the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) shall perform the tending of the sacred fire, the practice of begging for alms, sleeping on the ground, and doing what is beneficial to his teacher, until his formal return home (*samāvartana*). Thus [says Manu, MDh 2.108]. Sumantu also says:
[45] "Celibacy, austerity, begging for alms, performing fire-rites at the two twilights,
Vedic study, and service to the teacher— this is the conduct of a student.
Vyāsa states the manner of serving the teacher as follows:
In the teacher's house, he should go to bed last and rise first;
furthermore, whatever must be done by a disciple or even by a servant, [he should do that].
Having performed all that, he should stand at the side,
saying "It is done," acting as a servant who performs everything and is skilled in all tasks.
"One should not eat when [the preceptor] has not eaten, nor drink when he has not drunk; likewise, one should not sit when he is standing, nor sleep while he is not asleep. Thus says Viśvāmitra.
"One must always perform service toward their wives and sons, as well as toward elders who are observant of dharma, through prostrations and other such acts.
Regarding those who are to be avoided, Yājñavalkya says:

"One should avoid honey, meat, collyrium, leavings of food, fermented acids, women, injury to living beings, gazing at the sun, vulgar speech, slander, and so forth. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.33). Manu also says:
One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, women,
all fermented acids, and indeed the harming of living beings.
[46] Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes and holding an umbrella,
as well as desire, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments;
Gambling, gossip about people, slander, as well as falsehood,
gazing at and touching women, and injury to others.
"One should always sleep alone and never spill one's semen. Thus [says Manu].
Yama says: "One should avoid sitting on a bed, sleeping on a bed, and cleaning the teeth [with a twig]."
"One should sleep alone upon *kuśa* grass and, being pure, should not spill semen.
Thus [it is said] in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "One should certainly not look at a mirror, nor should one perform the cleaning of the teeth."
"One should employ the remains of the teacher's food for medicinal purposes, not out of desire" (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.14.20–21).

Āpastamba also says: "The remains of one’s father and of an elder brother may be eaten" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.1.4.11). However, the remains of the teacher’s son and others must not be eaten. Regarding this, Manu says:
[47] "Rubbing the limbs, bathing, and eating the remains [of these persons...]"
One should not perform the washing of the feet for the teacher’s son.
"Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs, and the dressing of the hair—these must not be performed for the wife of one's guru. (MDh 2.209, 211).
Yājñavalkya states the limit of the period of studenthood (*brahmacarya*):
"For each Veda, the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) shall be twelve years or five;
some say it lasts until the [text] has been mastered; and the *keśānta* ceremony is performed in the sixteenth year.
(YDh 1.36) The *keśānta* is the rite known as *godāna*, and that should be performed in the sixteenth year. Regarding this, Manu says:
"The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya, in the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, two years after that. (MDh 2.65). Yama says:
"He should dwell [as a student] for twelve years, or indeed twenty-four, or thirty-six years; he should observe the vow for each Veda.
This refers to the intention of acquiring the three Vedas. For this very reason, Manu says:
"One should practice the vow pertaining to the three Vedas under a guru for thirty-six years, or for half that time, or for a quarter, or even until they have been mastered" (MDh 3.1).

Thus, the student (*brahmacārin*) defined by these characteristics is of two kinds: the *upakurvāṇaka* and the *naiṣṭhika*. The duties of the *upakurvāṇaka* have been stated; now those of the *naiṣṭhika* are being described. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:

"A lifelong celibate student, however, shall dwell in the presence of his teacher; in his absence, in [the presence of] the teacher's son, his wife, or even in the sacred fire. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.49). Manu also says:
But if a permanent residence in the family of this teacher should please you, you should attend upon him with devotion until the liberation of the body.
But when the teacher has indeed passed away, one should behave toward the teacher’s son who possesses good qualities,
or toward the teacher’s wife, or toward a sapinda relative, just as toward the teacher himself.
"In the absence of these [persons], one who is capable of standing, sitting, and moving about, by performing service to the sacred fire, shall perfect his own body. (MDh 2.243–48).
And this refers to virtuous Brahmins, gurus, and the like; otherwise, there is fault. That has been stated by that very same author:
"A disciple desiring the highest state should not dwell for life with a non-Brāhmaṇa teacher, nor even with a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied the Vedas" (MDh 2.242). Vasiṣṭha also says:

A student (*brahmacārī*) shall serve his teacher until the liberation from the body [i.e., death]. When the teacher has died, he shall serve the sacred fire. He must restrain his speech, eat at the fourth, sixth, or eighth meal-time, and subsist on alms. He is dependent upon his teacher. He should wear matted hair, or have a single lock of hair matted. Following the teacher when he goes out, he should stand when the teacher sits, and sit when the teacher lies down. He should study only when summoned. Having announced everything he has obtained, he should eat with the teacher’s permission. He must avoid beds, sleeping on them, cleaning the teeth, washing the feet, applying collyrium, anointing the body, shoes, and umbrellas. Devoted to standing or sitting postures, he should approach water three times a day. (VaDh 7.4–17)
The meaning is that he should bathe three times a day. The service of the sacred fire (agniparicaryā) has been described by Hārīta, Śaṅkha-Likhita, and Yama.

Having fetched sacrificial fuel-sticks, one should attend upon the fire with acts such as sweeping, smearing, kindling, gathering [the ashes], inflaming, carrying fire around [the oblation], circumambulating, standing in worship (*upasthāna*), offering oblations (*homa*), chanting hymns (*stotra*), and prostrating. One should not step over the fire; one should not drag it with the feet; one should not blow on it with the mouth; nor should one hold water and fire simultaneously. One should not add fuel while still hungry from a recent meal, nor while impure from eating remnants. Day by day, one should inflame the fire with various specific oblations dedicated to Agni. When departing, one should do so after taking leave [of the fire]. Having returned, one should report [one's arrival] with a focused mind. At the end of the body’s dissolution, one attains union (*sāyujya*) with Brahman—thus [it is said]. (HārSm 3.5–14)
Regarding the fruit for one who acts in this manner, Yājñavalkya says:
"One who, having conquered the senses, brings about the dissolution of the body according to this rule,
attains the world of Brahman and is not born again in this world" (YDh 1.50).
Manu also says:
"That Brahmin who serves his guru until the completion of his body goes straight to the eternal abode of Brahmā" (MDh 2.244).
Now, an objection: if lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*) is accepted, then the householder stage (*gārhasthya*) would become devoid of scope.

This is not so, because the householder stage is intended for those possessed of passion (*rāgin*). Thus says Jābāli: "If one should desire only the household life, then he should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice for as long as he lives.

On this point, some—considering lifelong celibacy to be for those such as the hunchbacked and others—state that the householder stage is for those other than them. And in that regard, they cite a statement of Viṣṇu.

"For those who are hunchbacked, dwarfs, those born blind, eunuchs, the lame, the distressed, and the diseased, the practice of the vow shall undoubtedly last for as long as they live. Thus it is said.

That is not so; for if lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*) were restricted solely to [the service of] hunchbacks and the like, then the statement that it is optional for one who is capable would be contradicted. And Vasistha has demonstrated this optionality: "There are four stages of life (*āśrama*): the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas, one whose student-life remains unbroken may enter whichever of these he desires" (VaDh 7.1–3). It is also stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "O King, if one desires the householder stage, he should take a wife."
Or he may spend his time in celibacy (brahmacarya), preceded by a formal resolve.

"Or he may become a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa), or else a wandering mendicant (parivrāj) according to his desire. [52] Therefore, the state of the householder (gārhasthya) must be established as being intended solely for those possessed of passion (rāgin). Thus ends the section on the religious student (brahmacāri-prakaraṇa).

Now, in order to define the stage of the householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*), the ceremonial bath (*snāna*)—which is the prerequisite for that qualification—is first defined. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having given a gift to the teacher and with his permission, one should take the ceremonial bath;
having completed the Veda, or the vows, or indeed both. (YDh 1.51)
In this regard, the boon to be given has been shown by Manu:
"One who knows the Dharma should not provide anything to the teacher beforehand;
however, when he is about to bathe and has been commanded by the teacher, he should procure the teacher’s fee according to his ability."
"A field, gold, a cow, a horse, an umbrella, sandals, a seat, grain, garments, or vegetables—one should bring pleasure to the guru with these. (MDh 2.245–46)

And this gift is for the sake of pleasing the teacher, not as a price for the knowledge, because a price worthy of Vedic knowledge is impossible to find. Thus says the *Chandogya Śruti*: "Even if one were to give him this earth, surrounded by water and filled with wealth, it would still be less than that" (ChU 3.11.6). The *Tāpanīya Śruti* also states: "The earth, with its seven islands, is not sufficient as a sacrificial fee" (NṛUTā 5.2). The *Hārīta Smṛti* also says: "If a teacher should impart even a single syllable to a disciple..."
"There is no substance on earth which, by giving it away, one would become free from debt. (Hārīta Smṛti 2.21)

By the phrase “or [having completed] the Veda and the vows,” the threefold nature of the *snātaka* is shown. Among these, one is the one who has completed only the Veda; the second is the one who has completed only the vows; and the third is the one who has completed both. By the word “vows” (*vrata*) here, the vows well-known from the *Gṛhyasūtras*—namely, the initiation vow (*upanayana-vrata*), the Sāvitrī vow, and the Vedic vow (*veda-vrata*)—are intended. The threefold nature of the *snātaka* was stated by Hārīta: “There are three types of *snātakas*: the one who has bathed after learning (*vidyā-snātaka*), the one who has bathed after the vows (*vrata-snātaka*), and the one who has bathed after both learning and vows (*vidyā-vrata-snātaka*). In the expression “having brought the Veda to its end,” the comprehension of its meaning is also intended. For this very reason, it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:

[54] "Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or likewise the Vedas, or all four Vedas, and having understood their meaning, the best of the twice-born should then perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*). (KūP 1.2.15.1).
The procedure for the bath is well known from the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. The duties of a *snātaka* are shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*.
A pair of sacred threads, a water-pot with water,
an umbrella, a stainless turban, sandals and shoes, and two golden earrings; having had his hair and nails clipped, he should remain pure and hold the Veda.
He should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda and should wear garlands made of flowers from outside [the village].
He should always wear white garments, be fragrant, and be pleasant to behold;
he should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes when he has the means to do otherwise.
"He should not wear dyed, gaudy, or clothes worn by another, nor a patched garment. Thus ends the section on the *snātaka*.
Now, marriage. Regarding this, Manu says:

"Having bathed with the permission of his teacher and returned home according to the rule, a twice-born man should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks. Thus [says Manu]. Yājñavalkya also says:
[55] Having remained steadfast in his vow of celibacy, he should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks—
one who has belonged to no other man before, who is pleasing to him, who is not a sapinda relative, and who is younger than himself.

"One who is healthy, has brothers, and is not born of the same *ṛṣi* or *gotra*" (YDh 1.52–53). "Endowed with auspicious marks" means possessed of both external and internal characteristics. The external characteristics have been shown by Manu:
"One whose limbs are unimpaired, who has a pleasing name, and whose gait is like that of a swan or an elephant."
"One should marry a woman whose body hair, hair, and teeth grow in the natural direction, and who has soft limbs" (MDh 3.10).
He himself states those [women] to be avoided:
"One should not marry a girl with reddish-brown hair, nor one with extra limbs, nor one who is diseased."
Neither hairless, nor excessively hairy, nor talkative, nor tawny-eyed.

"One should not [marry] a girl whose name is that of a constellation, a tree, or a river; nor one named after a low caste or a mountain; nor one named after a bird, a snake, or a servant; nor one with a terrifying name. (MDh 3.8–9).
*Kapilā* is the color of red rice grains; *piṅgalā* is the color of fire. *Antyā* refers to one with a Mleccha name. This is also stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.

She should not have a beard or secondary sexual characteristics, nor should she have the appearance of a man; she should not have a gurgling voice, nor be emaciated, nor have a voice like that of a crow.
Likewise, a wise man should not marry one whose gaze is unfocused, nor one with round eyes;
nor one whose shanks are hairy, nor one whose ankles are prominent; nor should he marry one who has hollows on her cheeks when she laughs.
Her skin was not excessively parched, her nails were pale, and her eyes were reddish-brown.
A wise man should not marry a girl whose hands and feet are swollen;
nor should he marry one who is dwarfish, nor one who is excessively tall, nor one whose eyebrows meet.
"And a man [should not marry] one whose teeth have excessive gaps, nor one with a gaping mouth. Thus [it is said].
As for the internal characteristics, they are set forth in the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-sūtra*.

"The characteristics are difficult to discern. Having made eight lumps [of earth], he should consecrate the lumps with the mantra: "In the beginning, Truth was born first; upon Truth is Reality established. That which this maiden has come from—that let her attain here. Let that which is Reality be seen! Having thus empowered the lumps, he should say to the maiden, "Take one of these. If she takes one from a field that yields crops on both sides, he should know: "Her offspring will be rich in food. From a cow-pen: "She will be rich in cattle. From the soil of a sacrificial altar: "She will be endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*). From the water of a lake that never runs dry: "She will be prosperous in every respect. From a gambling ground: "She will be a gambler. From a crossroads: "She will be prone to wandering. From a barren wasteland: "She will be unfortunate. From a cemetery: "She will be a killer of her husband. (ĀśGṛ 1.5.4–6)

A *vipravrājinī* is one who goes forth excessively in various ways; the meaning is a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*). By the phrase "one who has had no other [husband before]," she is understood as one not previously taken by another man through either gift or enjoyment. By this, the *punarbhū* (a remarried widow) is excluded. For this very reason, Kāśyapa says:
"Seven kinds of *punarbhū* maidens are to be avoided as the lowest of their families:
those given in word, those given in thought, and those for whom the auspicious marriage-rites have been performed."
She who has been touched by water, she who has been taken by the hand,
she who has circumambulated the fire, and she who has given birth again [to another man].

"Thus these [women], spoken of by Kāśyapa, burn the family like fire. Baudhāyana says: "One given in word, one given in thought, one who has circumambulated the fire, one led to the seventh step, one who has been enjoyed, one who has conceived, and one who has given birth—these are the seven kinds of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman). Having taken her, one shall find neither offspring nor dharma. Nārada also says:
"A maiden whose virginity is intact, even though she has been defiled by the grasping of the hand..."
"The *punarbhū* is declared to be the first [type], regarding the act of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskārakarman*). (NSm 12.46).
Yājñavalkya also says: "The *akṣatā* and the *kṣatā* are both *punarbhūs*, having been consecrated again. (YDh 1.67).

A beloved wife—one who is desirable and brings delight to the mind and eyes of the husband. For this very reason, Āpastamba states: "In her upon whom the binding of the mind and eyes rests, there is prosperity" (ĀpDh 1.3.20).
