Regarding the term *asapiṇḍām*: she who has a common (*samāna*) single body (*piṇḍa*) is a *sapiṇḍā*; one who is not a *sapiṇḍā* is an *asapiṇḍā*, her [the bride]. And *sapiṇḍatā* extends up to the seventh person. In that regard, there is one giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), three partakers of the cake—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—and three partakers of the smearings (*lepa*)—the great-great-grandfather and so forth. Thus it is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa.

"The fourth and subsequent [ancestors] are partakers of the unguent; the father and subsequent [ancestors] are partakers of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*); the giver of the rice-balls is the seventh among them; such is *sāpiṇḍya*, extending over seven generations. Thus [it is stated in] MatPurāṇa 18.29. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—
these three men are to be known as those connected by the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
"Furthermore, the other paternal relatives on the mother's side are said to extend back from the great-grandfather;
these three, with the sacrificer as the seventh—this is the seven-generational relationship proclaimed by the sages. (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 31.3–5)

This is what is meant: the cause of *sāpiṇḍya* is the inclusion within a single funeral oblation (*ekapiṇḍakriyā*) of seven persons. Thus, Devadatta has *sāpiṇḍya* with his own six ancestors, beginning with the father; likewise, he has *sāpiṇḍya* with his six descendants, beginning with the son.
But if this were the case, there would be no *sāpiṇḍya* with brothers, paternal uncles, and so forth, because they are not included among those enumerated.

This is not so, because here what is intended is the unity of the ritual action (*kriyaikya*) due to the identity of the deity addressed (*uddeśyadevatā*). In an action performed by Devadatta, those who participate as deities—even if they are brothers or paternal uncles participating in an action performed by another—share *sāpiṇḍya* with him. Likewise, wives also share *sāpiṇḍya* with their husbands because they are co-performers (*sahakartṛka*) in the ritual action of offering the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). This is what is called "sāpiṇḍya based on the offering" (*nirvāpyasāpiṇḍya*).

Others, however, explain *sāpiṇḍya* differently. For instance: those who possess a common (*samāna*) or single (*eka*) *piṇḍa*—that is, a portion of the body—are *sapiṇḍas*. In this regard, a son shares *sāpiṇḍya* with his father because he possesses a direct connection to the bodily constituents of the father. Likewise, he shares it with the grandfather and others through the father, owing to the connection with the bodily constituents of their bodies. He shares it with the mother because of the direct connection to the bodily constituents of the mother’s body; and likewise with the maternal grandfather and others through the mother, owing to the connection with the bodily constituents of her body. Similarly, he shares it with paternal uncles, paternal aunts, and so forth, due to the connection with the bodily constituents of the grandfather’s body. Likewise, he shares it with maternal aunts, maternal uncles, and so forth, due to the connection with the body of the maternal grandfather. A husband shares it with his wife because they together originate a single body. In the same way, brothers and sisters share it with their respective spouses, as they together originate a single body with them. Thus, in each case, *sāpiṇḍya* is to be applied through the connection with the bodily constituents of a single body, whether directly or through a lineage.
The two kinds of *sāpiṇḍya* have been stated; she who does not possess it is an *asapiṇḍā*, and one should marry her.

But surely—if this were so, marriage would be impossible anywhere, because *sāpiṇḍya* could somehow be established everywhere, since the persistence of the Creator’s body is difficult to avoid, according to the Vedic revelation: "May I become many, may I procreate" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).

This is not a fault, because *sāpiṇḍya*, which applies without distinction, is restricted to seven or five generations; thus, beyond that, *sāpiṇḍya* ceases. Accordingly, Gautama states: “The cessation of the *piṇḍas* occurs at the seventh or the fifth [generation]” (GDh 14.13). Yājñavalkya also says: “Beyond the fifth on the mother’s side and the seventh on the father’s side” (YDh 1.53).
This should be construed by supplying the words: “*sāpiṇḍya* ceases” after the phrase “beyond the fifth generation on the maternal side and the seventh generation on the paternal side.”

"Consanguinity (*sapiṇḍatā*) ceases with the seventh person," according to the traditional teaching of Manu (MDh 5.60). This means as follows: on the paternal side, when counting from the *kūṭastha* (the common ancestor) through his sons and so forth, marriage beyond the seventh degree between the bridegroom and the bride is not defective. On the maternal side, when counting from the *kūṭastha* through her sons and so forth, if the mother of the bridegroom and the bride becomes the fifth, then because their consanguinity has ceased, their marriage is not subject to fault. As for the statement of the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
[61] "A householder, O King, should marry a maiden from beyond the fifth degree on the mother's side and the seventh degree on the father's side, according to the lawful rite. (ViPurāṇa 3.11.23).

In this context, the words "having passed beyond the seventh and the fifth" must be supplied; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement: "Beyond the fifth and the seventh" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.53).
Those whose marriage ceremony takes place in the fifth or even the seventh year— even if they are devoted to sacred rites— they have in every respect fallen to the state of Śūdras.

And because this contradicts the statement of Marīci: "Even though Paiṭhīnasi has stated two alternatives—'One should avoid [marrying] the fifth from the mother's side and the seventh from the father's side; or three from the mother's side and five from the father's side'—Śaṅkha says:
'If there are many born of one [man], with separate fields and separate wealth, they share the same *piṇḍa* but have separate periods of purification; however, the *piṇḍa* recurs among three.'"

The meaning is this: those who have one father but mothers of different castes are of non-identical caste due to the difference of their mothers; nevertheless, because of the unity of the father, they possess *sāpiṇḍya*. And that [relationship] ceases after three generations have passed.

Objection: If this were so, since sapinda-relationship would cease after three generations even on the paternal side, it would contradict the statement, "five on the father's side" (*pañca pitṛto vā*). Reply: In that case, the statement of Paiṭhīnasi, "three on the mother's side or five on the father's side," is intended as a prohibition against marrying within those limits only among those of the same caste (*sajātīya*), or it may be considered a secondary rule (*anukalpa*). Furthermore, in the verse "likewise from the mother and from the father" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.53), the word "father" (*pitṛ*) includes the progenitor (*bījī*) as well. Thus says Gautama: "Beyond the seventh from paternal kinsmen and from the progenitor; beyond the fifth from maternal kinsmen" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 4.3–5). For he who procreates a son through *niyoga* is the "progenitor. The kinsmen of the father and mother are defined in another Smṛti.
The sons of one's father’s paternal aunt, the sons of one's father’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's father’s maternal uncle are to be known as paternal kinsmen (pitṛbāndhava).

"The sons of one's mother's paternal aunt, the sons of one's mother's maternal aunt, and the sons of one's mother's maternal uncle are to be known as maternal relatives (*mātṛbāndhava*). Now, an objection is raised: the phrase "not a *sapiṇḍa*" need not be stated; for by the rule to be cited later, "one who is not born of the same *ṛṣi* and *gotra*," the prohibition of marriage with a *sapiṇḍa* woman is already established.
True; nevertheless, this is stated in order to declare that she who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother is alone recommended for the rite of marriage. And so says Manu:
"She who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother and not of the same *gotra* as the father is recommended for the twice-born in the matrimonial rite of sexual union" (MDh 3.5).

[63] Thus: she who is not a *sapiṇḍa* nor of the same *gotra* as the mother, and she who is not of the same *gotra* as the father—and by the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied she is also not a *sapiṇḍa*—she is recommended for the twice-born in the matter of marriage, which is accomplished through sexual union; this is the meaning, namely, that she is to be wedded. Now, one might object: the mention of the "mother" here is redundant. For by the very prohibition of *sapiṇḍya* and *gotra* identity with the father, the prohibition of *sapiṇḍya* and *gotra* identity with the mother is already established. This is because she possesses no separate *piṇḍa* or *gotra* of her own, since it is said: "She has entered into oneness with her husband in regard to his *piṇḍa*, his *gotra*, and his *sūtaka*."
A woman falls from her own lineage at the seventh step of the marriage ceremony.
Because of this statement.

It is not so; for in the Gāndharva and other forms of marriage, since there is no formal giving away of the girl (*kanyā-pradāna*), the father’s lineage (*pitṛ-gotra*) and *sapiṇḍya* relationship do not cease. And thus says the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"In marriages such as the Brāhma and others, whatever girl may have been wedded..."
Her funeral rites, including the offering of rice-balls and water, must be performed by her husband's family name.
"In Gāndharva and other forms of marriage, [the bride takes] the father's *gotra* according to the law. (GaPu 2.26.21–22).

By this, even the dispute regarding the marriage to a maternal uncle’s daughter is refuted. For instance: prohibitory statements concerning that [marriage] refer to those wedded through Gāndharva and other such forms, because in those cases there is no cessation of *sāpiṇḍya*. They do not refer to those wedded through Brāhma and other [approved] forms, because in those cases there is a cessation of *sāpiṇḍya*, as supported by Śruti, Smṛti, and the conduct of the virtuous. And those prohibitory statements are as follows. Regarding this, Śātātapa says:
"Having married the daughter of a maternal uncle, and likewise one who bears the mother's *gotra*..."

“And a twice-born man who marries a woman of the same *pravara* shall perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. Paiṭhīnasi also says: “[64] ‘The daughters of one’s father’s and mother’s sisters, as well as the sons of one’s maternal uncles, are by law sisters; it is known that one should avoid them [as marriage partners]. Sumantu also says: “All the wives of one’s father are mothers; their brothers are maternal uncles; their sisters are maternal aunts; their daughters are sisters; and their children are sister’s sons (*bhāgineya*). Otherwise, they cause the confusion of castes. Vyāsa says:
"The mother's sapindas must be avoided with effort by the twice-born.
Now, one might ask: "How can these statements, which apply without distinction, have a specific scope?
We reply: "By the force of specific statements. And so says Manu:
Having approached a daughter of one's father's sister, a daughter of one's own sister, a daughter of one's mother's sister,
or the daughter of one's mother's brother, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
"A wise man, however, should not take these three as wives. (Manu Dharma Śāstra 11.172–173)

The term *bhaginī* (sister) is qualified by the words *paitṛṣvaseyī* (daughter of the father’s sister) and so forth. The word *āptasya* (of a kinsman) is a qualification of the mother’s brother. In this context, the word *sutām* (daughter) is to be supplied; the meaning is "the daughter of the mother’s brother who is a close (*āpta*) *sapiṇḍa* and who was married through the *gāndharva* or other such forms of marriage. Regarding the term *paitṛṣvaseyīm*, here too the intended meaning is the father’s sister whose *sapiṇḍya* has not ceased and who was married through the *gāndharva* or other forms. This being the case, the qualification "sister" (*bhaginī*) becomes meaningful for her daughter. Since *sapiṇḍya* ceases in marriages such as the *brāhma* form, the term *bhaginī* would not apply there. This same logic should also be applied to the case of the mother’s sister’s daughter (*mātṛṣvasrīyā*). Therefore, by the force of Manu’s statement containing the terms "sister" and "kinsman," the general prohibition is restricted to specific cases.

Now, one might object: regarding the Brāhma and other forms of marriage, would it not follow that one may marry the daughter of one’s mother’s sister (*mātṛṣvasṛ-sutā*), just as one may marry the daughter of one’s maternal uncle (*mātula-sutā*)?

That is not so; for since such a practice is censured by the learned (*śiṣṭa-garhita*), a prohibitive Smṛti rule must be inferred for it. Yājñavalkya states that what is censured by the learned is not to be adopted:
"One should not practice even a dharma that leads away from heaven and is loathed by the world" (YDh 1.156).

Although the marriage of a maternal uncle’s daughter is censured by the cultured (śiṣṭa) of the North, nevertheless, because it is practiced by the cultured of the South, this custom of the Northerners is not itself condemned. Nor should it be suspected that the practice of the Southerners is rooted in passion (rāga), for they perform such marriages only after examining the injunctions and prohibitions. However, the marriage of a mother’s sister’s son is censured by the uncondemned practice of the cultured. In favor of the marriage of a maternal uncle’s daughter, there are the Śruti and other authorities; among these, the collection of mantras is as follows:
"Come, O Indra, by the paths invoked; enjoy this our sacrifice as your portion.
They have carried [the offering] satisfied, like a maiden to her maternal uncle; your portion is like the sacrificial fat of a father’s sister's son. (RV 7.4.3.22.6)

The meaning is this: O Indra, come to this sacrifice of ours by means of the paths praised [by us]; and having arrived, enjoy the portion being offered by us and others. They have offered—that is, they have relinquished—the *vapā* (omentum), prepared with clarified butter and other substances, intended for you. In this regard, there are two similes: just as the daughter of a maternal uncle (*mātula*)—that is, the sister’s daughter—is the "portion" (*bhāga*) of a nephew (*bhāgineya*), meaning she is fit to be wed by him; and just as the daughter of a paternal aunt (*paitṛṣvaseyī*) is the "portion" of a grandson, so too is this *vapā*, known as your portion. In the *Vājasaneyaka* as well: "Therefore, from one and the same person, both the eater and the eaten are born. 'Let us unite in the third generation,' 'let us unite in the fourth generation. From one and the same person, both the eater (*attṛ*)—the enjoyer—and the eaten (*adya*)—the object of enjoyment—are produced. These two do not intend to unite with each other directly; rather, starting from the common ancestor (*kūṭastha*), the meaning is: "let us unite—that is, let us marry—in the third or fourth generation."

Even though this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it is nonetheless authoritative with respect to its own meaning because there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge, because there is an absence of conflicting statements, and because it has been described as not referring to one's mother’s *sapinda* relations. Therefore, since it is restated by an uncontradicted explanatory passage, an injunction can be inferred, just as in the case of "holding [the firewood] above" (*uparidhāraṇa*). For instance, in the *Pretāgnihotra*, it is heard: "Holding the fuel-stick below, he should run after [the fire]; for he holds the sacrifice above for the gods. In that context, having enjoined the holding of the fuel-stick below the ancestral oblation (*havis*) accompanied by a mantra, there arises a doubt: is the statement in the remainder of that sentence—concerning the holding of the fuel-stick above the oblation in the rite for the gods—an explanatory passage, or is it an injunction? The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is an explanatory passage, because it attains syntactic unity with the injunction to hold [the stick] below by way of praising that very injunction. For it is appropriate to praise a well-known matter by restating it; however, holding [the stick] above is not established anywhere as a known fact. Therefore, since it cannot function as a praise, even if one accepts a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), it is construed as an injunction because it conveys a new, previously unknown matter (*apūrva-artha*).

Likewise, in cases such as "Let us unite with the son of the third generation," an injunction—"One should marry the daughter of one's maternal uncle"—is inferred on the grounds that it conveys a previously unknown meaning (*apūrvārthatva*). Therefore, this marriage is supported by the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). As for the Smṛtis, they have been shown to authorize the marriage with the maternal uncle’s daughter by means of setting aside the rule of *sāpiṇḍya* (sapinda relationship) among Brāhmaṇas. Furthermore, the unobjectionable practice of the Southerners (*dākṣiṇātya*) has been cited as authoritative custom (*śiṣṭācāra*).

Some, however, believe that even among the Asuras and others, marriage with the daughter of a maternal uncle is lawful by virtue of specific locality; they also cite scriptural statements to support this. Among them, Baudhāyana says:

In the south, there are five kinds of deviation: eating together with one who has not been initiated and with one's wife, eating food that has been kept overnight, and marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle or the daughter of a paternal aunt. Likewise, in the north, there are [five]: the sale of wool, the drinking of *sīdhu* liquor, transactions using double-faced coins, the profession of arms, and sea-voyaging. One who practices what belongs to the other region becomes blameworthy; the other likewise [becomes blameworthy] for practicing what belongs to the other. In each case, the authority of the local custom (*deśaprāmāṇya*) alone shall prevail. (BDh 1.1.2.1–6)

[68] Thus: a Southerner (*dākṣiṇātya*) is censured for entering into a relationship with a maternal uncle (*mātula*) in another region, the North; he is not so censured in his own country. Likewise, a Northerner (*udīcya*) is censured for drinking *sīdhu* wine and the like in another region, the South; he is not so censured in his own country. Why? Because of the authority of the country (*deśaprāmāṇyāt*). The meaning is that the authority of custom (*ācāra*) is dependent upon the country. And so Devala says: "In whatever country a certain custom is observed as right and well-established, it should be practiced in that very place, but not in another country, as is recorded in the tradition."
Bhṛgu says: "In whatever region, city, village, place of the three Vedas, or even town,
one should not subvert the dharma that has been ordained for that place."

Now, one might object: if the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) were a source of valid authority, then even the marriage of one’s own daughter would follow as a consequence, since Prajāpati acted in that manner. To this effect, the Śruti says: "Prajāpati indeed set his mind upon his own daughter.

This is not so, because of the maxim: "One should not imitate the conduct of the gods. For this very reason, Baudhāyana states: "But that which was enjoined by the gods, and that which was practiced by the sages..."
"That which is not to be performed by men, one should perform that action which has been so declared" (BDh 1.1.2.12).

Thus, according to the previously mentioned regulations regarding the Brāhma and other forms of marriage, as well as the regulations concerning different regions, the marriage with the daughter of a maternal uncle is established solely on the basis of scriptural injunctions such as "one who is not a sapinda," and so forth. In this regard, Manu states the specific limit for the deficiency in age:
"A man thirty years of age should marry a charming girl of twelve years."
"A man of twenty-four years [or] twenty-eight years should quickly marry a girl of eight years, lest he fall away from the Dharma. Thus [says Manu, MDh 9.94].
Bṛhaspati also says:
"A thirty-year-old man should take a ten-year-old bride who has not yet reached puberty."
"Or a man of twenty-one years may marry a girl of seven. Thus it is stated. Also in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"A man who is himself three times [the age] should marry a wife who is one-tenth his age. (ViPu 3.10.16)

"Healthy" means free from incurable diseases such as consumption (*rājayakṣman*) and the like. "Having a brother" means she who has either an elder or a younger brother; by this, the suspicion that she might be an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is excluded. For this very reason, Manu says:
"A wise man should not marry her whose brother does not exist or whose father is not known, for fear that she might be an appointed daughter according to the law" (MDh 3.11).

One should not marry a girl whose father’s intention—whether he intends to make her an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) or not—is unknown. However, where such a doubt does not exist, the intention is that one may even marry a girl who has no brother. From the statement, “or if the father is unknown,” it should be understood that a girl becomes an appointed daughter by the mere intention of the father alone, even without an agreement with the groom. Thus says Gautama: “According to some, she is an appointed daughter by mere intention; because of the doubt regarding that, one should not marry a girl who has no brother” (GDh 29.19–20). Manu also says:
"A sonless man may, by this rite, make a daughter an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), [stipulating]:

'Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be the one who performs the *svadhā* offering for me. (MDh 9.127). It is clearly understood that the making of an appointed daughter involves a formal agreement with the groom; and that agreement has been demonstrated by Vasiṣṭha.
“I shall give you this sisterless maiden, adorned with ornaments, so that the son who is born of her may be my son. (VaDh 17.17).

In some places, the reading is “sa nau putro bhavet” (“he shall be our son”). Furthermore, in the case of this appointed daughter (*putrikā*), there is no cessation of *sapiṇḍya* or *sagotra* status with her own father and others, as is the case in the *gāndharva* marriage and others. For this very reason, Laugākṣi says:
"A son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) should perform the offering of rice-balls and water for his mother according to the lineage of his maternal grandfather; thus said Prajāpati."

Thus, suspecting that the girl thus described might be his own daughter, one who desires a son should marry only a girl who has a brother. Regarding the phrase "not born of the same *ṛṣi* or *gotra*": *ārṣa* means "belonging to an *ṛṣi*," which refers to the *pravara*. A *gotra-pravarta* is a group of *muni*s that distinguishes a particular sage who is the founder of a lineage. For example: [71] for Bharadvāja, the founder of the *gotra*, the distinguishing [ancestors] are Aṅgiras and Bṛhaspati. For this very reason, they employ the formula: "I belong to the *gotra* of Bhāradvāja, with the *pravara* of Āṅgirasa-Bārhaspatya. Other examples may be cited in the same manner. A *gotra* is what is well-known through the succession of lineages. A bride who shares neither the same *pravara* nor the same *gotra* as the groom is eligible for marriage. In some cases, even when there is a difference in *gotra*, there is identity of *pravara*; for example, among the Yājñavalkya, Vādhūla, Mauna, and Mauka, although their *gotras* are distinct, their *pravara* is identical as Bhārgava-Vītahavya-Sāvetasa. Therefore, since a marriage might otherwise occur in such cases, the term "not born of the same *ṛṣi*" (*asamānārṣajām*) is stated to exclude them. In other instances, even when there is a difference in *pravara*, there is identity of *gotra*; for example, in the case of the *pravara* "Āṅgirasa-Ambarīṣa-Yauvanāśva" and "Māndhātṛ-Ambalīṣa-Yauvanāśva," although there is a difference in the *pravara* elements Āṅgirasa and Māndhātṛ, the *Yauvanāśva-gotra* is one and the same. Thus, to prevent marriage in such cases, the inclusion of the term "not of the same *gotra*" (*asamānagotragām*) is necessary. Furthermore, there are eight principal sages who are the founders of the *gotras*. These are the Seven Sages (*saptarṣi*s) with Agastya as the eighth. And so says Baudhāyana.
"Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, and Gautama—the offspring of the seven ṛṣis, with Agastya as the eighth, is called a *gotra*. Thus [it is said].
Also in another *smṛti*:
"Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Atri, and Gautama;
Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and Agastya—these sages are the founders of the *gotras*. Their offspring are considered to be the *gotras*. Thus it is said.
And the internal subdivisions of these *gotras* number in the thousands; their groups (*gaṇas*), however, are forty-nine. Thus says Baudhāyana:
"The *gotras* are in the thousands, millions, and billions;
there are forty-nine of them, [determined] by the vision of the sages in their ancestral lineages (*pravara*)."

The identity or non-identity of *pravara* and *gotra* is well known from the *Pravara-granthas* composed by Baudhāyana, Kātyāyana, Viśvāmitra, Garga, and others. Nor should it be suspected here that the combination of both *gotra* and *pravara* constitutes the ground for exclusion, because the fault is stated for each individually. Thus says Baudhāyana: "If one should unknowingly approach a woman of the same *gotra*, he should maintain her as he would his mother. Śātātapa also says: "But having married a woman of the same *gotra* or likewise the same *pravara*..."
"Having abandoned her, the purification is the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Thus says Āpastamba:
"Having married and approached a girl of the same *gotra* and *pravara*..."
"And having procreated a Caṇḍāla upon her, he falls from the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus, having examined the characteristics of the girl, her family must also be examined. For this very reason, Manu says:
"Even great prosperities consisting of cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain..."
In matters concerning marriage with a woman, one should avoid these ten families.

[73] “One who neglects his duties, one who has no male offspring, one devoid of Vedic study, one with hairy armpits or hemorrhoids, and families afflicted by consumption, chronic disease, epilepsy, leucoderma, or leprosy. (MDh 3.6–7) “One who neglects his duties” means one who is devoid of rites such as sacrifices and the like. “One who has no male offspring” means one where only women remain. “Devoid of Vedic study” means one who is excluded from recitation. Yama also says:
One should specify that these fourteen families are not to be intermarried with;
among Brāhmaṇas, one should avoid those who lack a lineage of Ṛṣis, as well as those who are not officiating priests.
One should avoid those who are excessively tall or excessively short,
those with abnormal complexions, those with missing limbs or extra limbs, and families afflicted by disease.
One should avoid those families afflicted with vitiligo, leprosy, and the like; one should always avoid the family of Kāmī as well as those families whose members have excessive body hair.

"And whatever family may be epileptic, and whatever family may be afflicted with jaundice. Thus, [a family] without a ṛṣi-lineage is one whose ancestral line is unknown. And this avoidance of families deficient in ritual acts and so forth is for the purpose of avoiding such offspring, according to the statement of Hārīta: "Offspring are born in accordance with the family" (HārSm 2.13). Also in the Purāṇa: "A son takes after his maternal uncle; a daughter takes after her paternal ancestors."
"As the mother is in character, so shall the son be.
Manu also says:
"He inherits the character of his father, or his mother, or indeed both."
In no way does one born of a base womb ever abandon their own nature.
[74] Thus, the family to be avoided has been described. As for the family to be accepted, Yājñavalkya says:

"From a great family of Vedic scholars renowned for ten generations" (YDh 1.54). The meaning is that one should marry a girl from such a great family—one renowned for five generations on the mother’s side and five on the father’s side—and which is prosperous with sons, cattle, and other assets. Manu also says:

"One who desires to lead his family to excellence should always form connections with the most excellent, and should avoid the lowest of the low. (MDh 4.244). Regarding those who are "excellent," he himself has stated:
They are purified by actions shown in the Śruti and Smṛti,
have remained unbroken in their celibate student life, and are endowed with noble lineage.
Their alliances are with great families, and they are established among the great themselves;
contented, intent on the welfare of the virtuous, they are holy men who look upon all with equanimity.
"Those free from greed, passion, hatred, resentment, pride, delusion, and the like;
those who are not prone to anger and are very serene—such persons should always be made one's kinsmen.
Regarding the lowest [class], he says the same:
Those who are thieves, slanderers, eunuchs, and those who follow the ways of nihilism; those living by improper occupations, as well as those of deformed appearance.
[75] Those who have harbored enmity against heroes, as well as royal offenders, those who constantly consume the property of Brahmins, misers, and those who have acted perversely;
"One should carefully avoid those families in which there are no offspring, where female offspring are born, or where women are killers of their husbands.

Regarding the giving of a daughter in marriage, Gautama has shown the restriction on the groom: "One should give [the girl] to one who is endowed with learning, good conduct, kinship, auspicious marks, and character" (GDh 4.5). Yama also says:

"Family, character, physical form, age, learning, wealth, and a protector—having examined these seven qualities, a daughter should be given [in marriage] by the wise; the rest need not be considered. Thus says Yājñavalkya.

"A bridegroom of the same caste who possesses these very qualities, who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), carefully examined for virility, young, wise, and beloved by the people [is recommended]. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.55). He is one endowed with these qualities mentioned in relation to the maiden. As for the means of examining virility, it has been shown by Nārada:
He whose semen floats in water, who is radiant, and whose urine is frothy—by these characteristics he would be a man;
by the opposite characteristics, however, he is a eunuch.
[76] In the treatise, sixteen types of impotent persons (ṣaṇḍha) have been observed by the wise;
the method for their treatment, both curable and incurable, has been stated in due order.
One who is naturally impotent, one who is castrated, and likewise one who is impotent for a period of time;
as well as those rendered so by a teacher’s curse, by disease, or by the wrath of fate.

The jealous man, the eunuch, he who emits semen through the wind, he whose sexual organ is in the mouth, the one who is rejected, the one with sterile seed, the modest man, and likewise the husband of another woman. (NSm 12.10–13)

A *nisargaṣaṇḍha* is one who is naturally devoid of sexual organs and testicles by his very nature. A *vadhri* is one whose testicles have been severed. A *pakṣaṣaṇḍha* is one who, while engaging with a woman for fifteen days, has the capacity for emission only once. The three types beginning with the *guruśāpaṣaṇḍha* (one rendered impotent by a teacher’s curse) are clear. An *īrṣyāṣaṇḍha* is one in whom virility is produced through jealousy. A *sevyaṣaṇḍha* is one whose power of virility arises through specific modes of service to a woman. A *vātaretāḥ* is one whose semen is destroyed by wind (*vāta*). A *mukhebhaga* is one whose power of virility exists only in the mouth, not in the vagina. An *ākṣiptaṣaṣaṇḍha* is one who has become impotent due to the suppression of semen. A *moghabīja* is one whose seed is incapable of conception. A *śālīna* is one whose virility is lost due to timidity or agitation. An *anyāpati* is one who possesses the male faculty toward other women besides his own wife. This must be understood after investigation. He himself states the reason for this:
"Women were created for the sake of offspring; women are the field and men are the seed-bearers.
The field should be given to one who possesses the seed; one without seed does not deserve the field.
(NSm 12.19) Thus, Kātyāyana states that other men who should be avoided are like eunuchs.

"A wise man should not give his daughter to those who live far away, to those lacking in learning, to those following the path of liberation (ascetics), to those who are brave, or to those who are destitute.
To whom, then, should she be given? To this, Manu says:
"To one who is distinguished, handsome, excellent, and suitable, one should give that maiden to him according to the prescribed rite, even if she has not reached [marriageable age]. (MDh 9.88).
The phrase "even if she has not reached [age]" means even a girl who has not yet attained the time for marriage. Marīci states the excellence [of this practice]:

"The selection of a bridegroom for a maiden, her gift in marriage, and likewise the binding of the girdle are auspicious after the fifth year from birth or from conception. Thus [says the tradition]. Baudhāyana also [states]:
"One should give a maiden who is still prepubescent (*nagnikā*) to a virtuous celibate;
or even to one lacking in virtues, but one should not withhold her once she has reached the age of menstruation. (BDh 4.1.11).
As for that which was stated by Yama:
A householder may indeed let a maiden remain [in his home] until death, even if she has reached puberty;
however, he must never give her to one who is devoid of good qualities. (MDh 9.89)

[78] Thus, this statement—that one should not give a daughter to one devoid of qualities—is intended to mean that such a gift is possible for one who possesses qualities; it does not, however, intend an absolute prohibition against giving to one devoid of qualities. Otherwise, the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) stated by Baudhāyana, "Or even to one devoid of qualities" (BDh 4.1.11), would be rendered purposeless. Furthermore, the statement "She may even remain [unmarried] during her menses" (MDh 9.89) does not have its own literal meaning as its primary intent according to the reasoning already stated, because it would contradict the rule, "One should not obstruct a woman in her menses" (BDh 4.1.11). For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha also says:
"The father should give away his daughter while she is still a maiden, out of fear of her reaching puberty;
for if she remains until she has reached her menses, the fault falls upon the father. Thus says Saṃvarta as well.
When the time of puberty has arrived, Soma enjoys the maiden;
at the time of menstruation, the Gandharvas; and when the breasts appear, Agni.
"Therefore, one should marry off a girl before she reaches puberty. (Saṃsm 1.65, 68).
By the word "girl" (*kanyā*), one who possesses an age not yet characterized by the signs of shame and so forth is intended. And thus says the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"As long as a girl does not [conceal] her limbs with shame in the presence of a man..."
"A girl remains such [only] as long as she covers her vulva and so forth. Thus says Saṃgrahakāra:
"As long as she does not take up a garment, as long as she plays with dust..."

"As long as one does not know [her] to have reached the age of menstruation, she remains a *kanyā* (virgin). Regarding the specific rewards for the giver according to the girl's particular age, Marīci says:
"By giving away a *gaurī*, one attains the surface of heaven; by giving away a *rohiṇī*, one attains Vaikuṇṭha."

"One who gives away a maiden [in marriage] goes to the world of Brahmā, but one who gives away a menstruating girl goes to Raurava. Thus has Saṃvarta shown that she is worthy of being designated by such terms as "Gaurī" and so forth:
"An eight-year-old girl shall be a Gaurī, while a nine-year-old is a Rohiṇī."
"A girl becomes ten years old; beyond that, she is *rajasvalā* (menstruating). Thus [says Saṃvarta 1.66]. Yama also says:
"She should be a *gaurī* at eight years; in the ninth year, she becomes a *nagnikā*."
"In the tenth year she is called a *kanyakā* (maiden), and in the twelfth she is known as a *vṛṣalī*.
Thus [it is said]. Nārada states the specific types of givers according to the distinction between the primary and secondary options:
"The father himself should give the maiden, or the brother with the father's permission."
The maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, a kinsman, and likewise a relative.
[80] But in the absence of all [other relatives], if the mother remains in her natural state,
then while she is not in that state, the uterine kinsmen shall give away the girl.
"But when there is no one at all [to give her away], the maiden may approach the king. Thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya also says:
"The father, the grandfather, the brother, a *sakulya* relative, and likewise the mother..."
In the absence of the preceding giver, each subsequent person who is in their natural state is the giver of the maiden.
"If he does not give her away, he incurs the sin of killing an embryo at every menstrual cycle.
However, in the absence of givers, a maiden may choose a husband for herself from among those who are fit. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.63–64).
"Fit" (*gamya*) means worthy of being approached, that is to say, one endowed with qualities such as being of the same caste (*sāvarṇya*). And so says Nārada:

“[A man] should perform the religious duties together with one who is of the same class (*savarṇa*) and of corresponding character, conduct, age, and learning; and from her he should procreate sons. (NSm 12.23). This should be construed by supplying the words “having obtained a husband of the same class. And this is to be understood as applying when the appearance of menses has not yet occurred. But once the menses have appeared, even if [the father and others] are present, she should wait for some time to observe the father’s command; having disregarded it, she may choose a husband of the same class herself. Thus says Baudhāyana:
[81] A woman who has reached puberty should wait for her father’s command for three years;
thereafter, in the fourth year, she may take a suitable husband.
"If a suitable [husband] is not available, she may resort even to one deficient in qualities. (BDh 4.1.14). Manu also says:
"A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years."
But after this time has passed, she may find a husband of equal status.
"If she obtains a husband of her own accord when not being given away, she incurs no sin whatsoever, nor does he whom she obtains. (MDh 9.90–91).
The meaning is that he whom she obtains as a husband also incurs no sin. As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu:

"A maiden, having waited for three menstrual periods (*ṛtu*), should indeed choose a husband for herself (*svayaṃvara*). This [rule] is to be understood as applying when a bridegroom endowed with good qualities is available.

Now, one might ask: how can the word "maiden" (*kanyā*) be applied to one who has reached puberty, since Yama has stated, "A ten-year-old shall be a maiden," and menstruation is not possible in the tenth year?

This is not a fault, because the word *kanyā*, like the words *gaurī* and others, has been technically defined (*paribhāṣita*) by Yama; and that definition is useful in contexts such as the description of ritual results. This has already been cited previously: "By giving a maiden [in marriage], one attains the world of Brahmā. However, the word *kanyā* as commonly used in the world denotes simply any woman who has not yet married. This being the case, many instances of the word *kanyā* in the scriptures are thus validated. Accordingly, it is employed for an elderly woman in the narrative of Aṣṭāvakra in the *Anuśāsana-parvan*.
[82] "My celibacy has been from my youth; I am indeed a maiden, there is no doubt about this" (MBh Āśvamedhika 20.22).
This [statement] was also addressed by Nārada to an elderly woman in the Śalyaparvan:
"O sinless one, how can there be worlds for you, who are an uninitiated maiden? (MBh Śalya 51.10).
Also in the Umāmaheśvara-saṃvāda:
"A girl who has bathed after her menses and is pure is designated as a *kanyā*."

Now, an objection: In the statement "of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtāyāḥ*)," it was said that for one who has not undergone marriage there is no higher world; this is untenable. For even among those women who do not marry but are exponents of the Veda (*brahmavādinī*), the attainment of the higher world is possible through initiation (*upanayana*), Vedic study, and so forth. It is for this very reason that Hārīta stated: "Women are of two kinds: Vedic exponents (*brahmavādinī*) and newly-wed brides (*sadyovadhū*). Among them, for the Vedic exponents, there is initiation, the kindling of the sacred fires, Vedic study, and the practice of begging for alms within their own homes. But for the newly-wed brides, when marriage is imminent, one should perform the marriage after somehow performing the mere rite of initiation" (HārSm 21.23).
Not so; for that [practice] pertains to another *kalpa*. And thus says Yama:
"In a former *kalpa*, the tying of the girdle of muñja grass was prescribed for virgins, as well as the teaching of the Vedas and the recitation of the Sāvitrī."
Neither her father, nor her paternal uncle, nor her brother, nor anyone else should teach her;
for a maiden, the practice of begging for alms is prescribed even within her own home.
"One should avoid the deerskin, rags, and the wearing of matted hair.

Thus [it is said]. By such statements as "A girl of eight years shall be Gaurī," the time for marriage has been declared. Now, the different types of marriage are described. Regarding this, Manu says:
"For all four castes, [these marriages] are beneficial or harmful both in this world and after death."
Learn now these eight forms of marriage for women in brief.
"The Brāhma, the Daiva, likewise the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, the Āsura, the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca as the eighth and lowest"—thus [it is said].
He himself states the definition of these in their respective order: (MDh 3.20–21).
Having clothed and honored her himself, and having invited a man of learning and virtuous conduct,
the giving away of the daughter is proclaimed as the Brāhma rite.
When a sacrifice has been properly extended and the officiating priest performs his duty,
the giving away of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared to be the divine (daiva) form of marriage.
Having taken one or two pairs of cattle from the bridegroom according to the law,
the giving away of the daughter according to the prescribed rule is called the Ārṣa rite.
Having addressed the words, "May you both perform dharma together," and having honored the gift of the maiden, this is recorded as the Prājāpatya rite.
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride according to one's own ability,
the giving away of the daughter at one's own will is called the Āsura dharma.
The mutual union of the maiden and the bridegroom through desire is to be known as the Gāndharva marriage; it is carnal and arises from passion.
Having killed, maimed, or broken [the groom], and having forcibly abducted a maiden from her home while she is crying out and weeping,
this is called the Rākṣasa rite.
"He who approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged—this is declared to be the eighth and most sinful of marriages, the Paiśāca. Thus [says Manu, MDh 3.27–34].
Nārada also says:
Of these, the first is the Brāhma, and the next is the Prājāpatya;
then the Ārṣa, the Daiva, the Gāndharva, and likewise the Āsura.
"The Rākṣasa follows immediately after that, and the Paiśāca is considered the eighth. Thus [it is said].
Manu declares the rule for marriage according to the sequence of the castes:
"Six [are] in the direct order for a Brāhmaṇa; four [are] inferior [forms] for a Kṣatriya."
"But one should know that for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra, those same [forms] are lawful and not Rākṣasa.

(MDh 3.23). Of these, the first six forms of marriage are lawful for the Brāhmaṇa; the four beginning with the Āsura are lawful for the Kṣatriyas; and those same ones, excluding the Rākṣasa, are also lawful for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra. Among these, beginning with the Brāhma, the author himself states which are the most praiseworthy:
"The wise know the first four of the Brāhmaṇa as praiseworthy."
"The Rākṣasa for a Kṣatriya, and the Āsura for Vaiśyas and Śūdras" (MDh 3.24).
Also, in another Smṛti:
"The first four are prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa; the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa [are also] recommended."
"Likewise for a king, an Asura [form] for a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra; but the Antya is censurable.
The meaning of "censurable" is that it is not recommended for anyone. Vatsa permits even the Paiśāca form for Brāhmaṇas and others when no other form of marriage is available:
"If a maiden cannot be won by any other means, she may be taken by a man [in the Paiśāca manner]."
"She is to be wedded even by stealth through a marriage performed in secret.
Manu states the fruit of the Brāhma and other forms of marriage:
"Ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first."
The son of a Brāhmaṇī woman, having performed good deeds, liberates his ancestors from sin.
A son born of a woman wedded according to the Daiva rite [sanctifies] seven generations of ancestors and seven of descendants;
a son born of a woman wedded according to the Ārṣa rite [sanctifies] three of each; and a son born of a woman wedded according to the Kāya rite [sanctifies] six of each.
In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma,
sons who possess spiritual luster and are esteemed by the learned are born in due order.
Endowed with beauty, strength, and virtue, wealthy and renowned,
possessing abundant enjoyments and being most righteous, they live for a hundred years.
"In the remaining [other] marriages, however, cruel and untruthful speakers are born; through an improper marriage, sons who hate the Veda and the Dharma are produced. (MDh 3.37–41).
Even among the four praiseworthy forms of marriage, each preceding one is more praiseworthy than the next. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:

Of these, four belong to the Brāhmaṇa; among them, each preceding one is superior. Each succeeding one among the latter [four] is more blameworthy. (BDh 1.11.20.10–11) Now, it may be objected: even the Ārṣa form is more blameworthy than the Āsura, because there is no difference in their both being obtained through purchase. For this very reason, Kaśyapa says:

"But a woman who has been purchased for a price is not called a wife; she is neither for rites to the gods nor for rites to the ancestors—Kaśyapa declared her to be a slave. (Kāśyapa Smṛti 49) Among the forms of marriage beginning with the Brāhma and ending with the Āsura, three—the Brāhma, Daiva, and Prājāpatya—are lawful because they lack the element of purchase. Two—the Ārṣa and Āsura—are unlawful because they involve being purchased. Furthermore, even between those two, the Āsura form, like the Paiśāca, must not be performed even in times of distress.

That is not so, because the statement "of five" is intended to introduce an alternative opinion (*matāntara*). Why is this? Because later on, [the author] himself restates that a pair of cattle (*gomithuna*) constitutes the bride-price (*śulka*) as an alternative opinion and then refutes it:
"Some say that in the *ārṣa* marriage a pair of cattle is the bride-price; that is indeed false.
Whether small or large, it is simply a sale. (MDh 3.53)

As for what some say—that the *ārṣa* rite consists in a pair of cattle as the bride-price (*śulka*)—that is entirely false; for it is impossible for that [rite] to constitute a bride-price, as it lacks the defining characteristics thereof. Indeed, the price used as a means of purchase may be small or great depending on place, time, and other factors; however, in the present case, the quantity is fixed. Since the *ārṣa* rite is accomplished by that very pair of cattle and not otherwise, it is therefore truly lawful (*dharmya*), because it is not purchased by means of a price. For this very reason, Devala says: "The first four marriages are lawful, being accompanied by the offering of water."
“Those who are free of bride-price and worthy of Brāhmaṇas rescue both families.

Nor should it be suspected that in marriages such as the Gāndharva and others, there is an absence of husbandhood and wifehood because of the lack of the ritual of taking the seven steps (*saptapadābhikramaṇa*) and so forth; for although those rituals may be absent prior to the formal acceptance [of the bride], they do exist subsequently. Thus Devala says: “In marriages such as the Gāndharva and others, however, the marriage rite [is performed] again.”
"And it should be performed by the three castes when capable, with fire as witness.
Also, in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"The Gāndharva, Āsura, Paiśāca, and Rākṣasa forms of marriage..."
"First there is the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) of them, and afterwards the fire-oblation (*homa*) is prescribed. Thus it is said.
However, in the absence of the fire-oblation, there is no status as a wife. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha and Baudhāyana state:
"If a maiden has been carried off by force and has not been consecrated with the sacred formulas (*mantras*)," [she is not a wife].
"She should be given to another according to the prescribed rule, just as the maiden was [given] before. (VaDh 17.73; BDh 4.1.15).

Therefore, since the ritual circumambulation of the seven steps (*saptapadābhikramaṇa*) is possible even in the Gāndharva and other forms of marriage, the status of wifehood (*bhāryātva*) exists in them as well. Regarding the marriages beginning with the Brāhma form, the gift that has been mentioned is to be made only once. And so says Yājñavalkya: "A maiden is given only once; he who carries her off [after she has been given] shall be subject to the punishment for theft. (YDh 1.65).
Manu also says:
"A share of inheritance falls [to one] once; a daughter is given once;
'I give' is said once—these three things happen but once among the virtuous."
And this refers to the case where the groom’s intention is not corrupt; as Nārada says:

[90] "If a man has given a maiden to a groom in accordance with the law and then does not give her to him, and the groom is not corrupt, he shall be punished by the king there like a thief. (NSm 12.32)

Is this a general rule? No, says Yājñavalkya: "Even if she has been given, one may take her back if a more excellent suitor arrives. (YDh 1.65) This refers to the intention of the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*). If another suitor who is more praiseworthy than the one to whom she was verbally betrothed is obtained, then she should be given to him, but not to the former suitor if he is defective. And so says Gautama: "Even after having promised her, one should not give her to one who is joined with unrighteousness" (GDh 4.5). The defects of the suitor have been stated by Kātyāyana.
One who is insane, fallen [from caste], afflicted with leprosy, likewise a eunuch, one born of the same lineage (sagotra),
one deprived of sight or hearing, and one corrupted by epilepsy;
"Likewise, these defects of a bride are proclaimed to be exactly like the defects of a groom.
As for the remarriage of one who has already been wedded, it has been shown by Yama and Śātātapa:
"If the groom should in any way be lacking in lineage and character..."
In that case, the mantras are not the cause, nor would there be any falsehood regarding the maiden.
"Having forcibly seized that maiden while her virginity remains intact, one may give her again to a virtuous man; thus said Śātātapa."

"One who takes away a girl from a family inferior in lineage and character does not incur guilt; in that case, neither the sacred mantras nor the falsehood regarding the girl constitute an offense. Thus says Kātyāyana as well.

But if he belongs to another caste, is an outcast, or even a eunuch; if he is engaged in improper occupations, is a member of the same lineage, a slave, or afflicted by a chronic disease; [then he is not eligible].
"Even if she has been wedded, she should be given to another, together with her veil and ornaments. So too says Manu:
"When he is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or likewise fallen [from his caste]..."

"In five calamities, another husband is ordained for women. (NSm 12.97) This remarriage pertains to other *yugas*. Thus says the *Ādityapurāṇa*: "Remarriage of a woman already wedded, the inheritance of the eldest share, and likewise the killing of a cow..."
"In the Kali age, one should not perform these five [acts]: [approaching] a brother's wife, [using] a water-pot...
Thus says Nārada: "But he who gives away a girl without disclosing her defects is to be punished by the king.
And: "He who gives away a defective girl without having declared her faults..."
"The king shall inflict upon him the punishment prescribed for the first degree of violence" (NSm 12.33).
Yājñavalkya also states:
"One who gives [a gift] without declaring its defect shall be punished with the highest fine" (YDh 1.66).
[92] Thus. The defects of a maiden, however, have been shown by Nārada:

"A maiden who is tall, loathsome, afflicted by disease, deformed, one who has had sexual intercourse, or one whose affection is seen to be directed toward another—these are proclaimed as the defects of a maiden. (NSm 12.36)
Manu states that not only is there punishment for one who gives a gift without disclosing its defects, but the bride herself must also be abandoned:
"Even after accepting her according to the prescribed rule, one may abandon a girl who is blameworthy,
diseased, severely defiled, or one who was presented through deception" (MDh 9.72).
Nārada also says:
"One should not defile an unblemished maiden, nor should one defile an unblemished groom;
if a defect exists, there is no fault in their mutual abandonment of one another. (NSm 12.31)
This should be understood as occurring prior to the seventh step; for it is precisely there that the status of wife arises. Therefore, Manu says:
"The mantras associated with the taking of the hand are the definitive mark of a wife;
their completion, however, should be recognized by the wise at the seventh step" (MDh 8.227).
Yama also says: "Neither by water nor by word alone is one desired as the husband of a maiden;
husbandhood arises from the sacrament of taking the hand at the seventh step."

[93] Thus, even if the husband dies before the sacrament of taking the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*), the maidenhood of the girl is not lost. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "If the groom should die first after she has been given by water and word, she has not yet been led away by the sacred mantras; she remains a maiden belonging to her father alone. (VaDh 17.72)
Regarding the specific rule for departing to another country after the betrothal, Kātyāyana says:
"But when a man who has been chosen should perish,
the girl, having passed three menstrual periods, may choose another groom."
Nārada also says: "But if a groom, having accepted a maiden, should depart for another country, after three menstrual seasons have passed, the maiden may choose another groom. (NSm 12.24)

Regarding what should be done if the groom dies after the bride-price (*śulka*) has been paid, Manu says: "If the giver of the bride-price dies after the bride-price for the maiden has been given, she should be given to his brother-in-law, provided the maiden consents. (MDh 9.97)

Regarding travel to another country, however, a specific rule has been stated by Kātyāyana: "If a man departs after having given the bride-price (*śulka*) as well as the woman’s property (*strīdhana*), she should be maintained for one year; thereafter, she should be given to another according to the prescribed rule."

Thus, it is stated that from the time of the giving of the word until before the seventh step is taken, if a fault is perceived or in the event of death and so forth, one may give the girl to another. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: "When she has been given to many, but remains unmarried, then the son born of her shall receive this daughter for the sake of all."
"Then, if she should come [to him], the former suitor shall take what was given for the bride.

This means that if she is unmarried, she belongs to the one to whom she was previously promised; however, if she has been married by another, he shall only recover the bride-price (*śulka*) he gave, not the girl herself. Regarding the statement, "One should marry a woman with auspicious marks" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.52), the girl to be married is of two kinds: of equal caste (*savarṇā*) and of unequal caste (*asavarṇā*). Of these two, the first is recommended. As Manu says: "For the twice-born, a wife of equal caste is recommended as the foremost jewel of a household."
"But for those who engage [in sexual intercourse] out of desire, these [following] shall be the inferior [penalties] in successive order. (MDh 3.12)

For a *snātaka* (one who has completed his Vedic studies), at his first marriage, regarding the duty of marriage (*dārakarma*) and religious rites such as the *agnihotra*, a woman of the same caste (*savarṇā*)—she whose caste (*varṇa*), whether Brāhmaṇa or otherwise, is equal to that of the groom—is recommended. For instance, a Brāhmaṇa’s wife should be a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriya’s a Kṣatriyā, and a Vaiśya’s a Vaiśyā. Having first married a woman of the same caste for the sake of dharma, if they subsequently desire pleasure (*riraṃsu*), then these women of lower castes (*avarāḥ*), namely the Kṣatriyā and others in their respective order, are recorded in tradition (*smṛta*) as their wives. Thus says Yājñavalkya: [The Sanskrit verse would follow here.]

[95] "Three wives in the order of the castes, likewise two, and one respectively, are the lawful wives for the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya; for one born as a Śūdra, she alone. Thus [says the law]. Manu also says:

"A Śūdra woman alone is the wife of a Śūdra; she and his own [woman] are prescribed for a Vaiśya; those two and her own [woman] may belong to a Kṣatriya; and all those [three] and his own [woman] belong to one of the first-born caste (Agra-janman). (MDh 3.13).
Nārada also says:
For a Brāhmaṇa, there are exactly three other wives in the direct order [of castes];
likewise, for a Śūdra, there are three other husbands in the inverse order.
"A Kṣatriya is declared to have two wives, while another [the Vaiśya] has one;
a Vaiśya woman is to be known as having two husbands, and the other [the Śūdra] has one husband who is a Kṣatriya. (NSm 12.5–6)

Vasiṣṭha and Pāraskara also state: “A Brāhmaṇa may have wives of three castes in the order of their sequence; a Rājanya, two; a Vaiśya, one. Or, according to some, all may have a Śūdra wife as well, though without the recitation of mantras” (VaDh 1.24–25; PārGṛ 1.4.8–11). Paithīnasi says: “[96] ‘In the absence of a [suitable] girl, he should observe the vow of a Snātaka. Or he may procreate a son through a Kṣatriya woman, or even through a Śūdra woman, so say some. Viṣṇu also states: ‘For a twice-born man, a Śūdra wife shall never serve the purpose of dharma.’”

"She is proclaimed for the sake of pleasure alone for that man who is blinded by passion" (ViDh 26.5). Thus, according to the opinion of these twice-born [authorities], the taking of a Śūdra woman in times of distress—even if the result is merely pleasure—is permitted due to the mildness of the fault. Now, according to the opinion of others, it is stated that for Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, the avoidance of a Śūdra woman is more appropriate, and not marriage with her. Regarding this, Manu says:
"For even when they are standing in distress, neither a Brāhmaṇa nor a Kṣatriya..."
In no instance whatsoever is a Śūdra woman prescribed as a wife.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of low birth,
quickly reduce their own families, along with their progeny, to the status of Śūdras.
According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste];
according to Śaunaka, by the birth of a son; and according to Bhṛgu, by having offspring from her.
By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by fathering a son upon her, he is indeed fallen from his Brāhmaṇahood.
"For one who has drunk the saliva of a *vṛṣalī*, who has been afflicted by her breath, and who has begotten a child upon her, no atonement is prescribed. Thus [it is stated in] MDh 3.14–19.
Also in the *Āśvamedhika* [Parvan]:
[97] The seed falling into the womb of a Śūdra woman made the cry of "Alas! Alas! from the twice-born man; it fell into pits of excrement, and he was filled with grief, crying out, "I have fallen!"

"This evil-souled one, deluded by passion, shall fall me down and quickly go to a downward state"—having thus cursed it, that [fruit] fell. Now, if it is argued: "Manu has indeed permitted the marriage of a Brāhmaṇa to a Śūdra woman in the verse, 'And those [wives] and his own [are for] the first-born' (MDh 3.13), yet he has prohibited it again in the same work with the words, 'Not [for] a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya' (MDh 3.14); therefore, there is a contradiction. [Response: This is not so. The former statement is a general permission, while the latter is a prohibition based on specific considerations such as the lack of progeny or the presence of obstacles. Furthermore, the prohibition is intended for cases where the Śūdra woman is of low character or is a widow; otherwise, the following would be the case: if a Brāhmaṇa were to marry a Śūdra woman who is of good family and endowed with auspicious marks, and she were to bear a son, then that son would be entitled to perform the *Śrāddha* and other rites. If, however, he marries a Śūdra woman who is of low birth, he would incur the sin of violating the law (*dharma-vyatikrama*). Thus, there is no contradiction. Moreover, the word "own" (*svā*) in the verse refers to a wife of equal caste (*savarṇā*), and the phrase "and those" (*tāś ca*) refers to wives of the three higher castes (*dvijāti*). Therefore, there is no inconsistency. As for the prohibition regarding the Śūdra, it applies specifically to the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya, whereas for the Vaiśya, the marriage to a Śūdra woman is permitted provided she is of good family and possesses auspicious marks. Consequently, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Furthermore, the prohibition is intended for those who have already married a wife of their own caste; for one who has not yet married, the marriage to a Śūdra woman is not forbidden. Thus, all is consistent. As stated: "One should not marry a Śūdra woman even if she is beautiful, nor should one give her away in marriage; for by doing so, both the giver and the taker fall into hell. And: "If a Brāhmaṇa, out of lust, should approach a Śūdra woman, he becomes a Vṛṣala within six months, and his offspring are excluded from the *Soma* sacrifice. Therefore, the prohibition is established. However, this does not apply to the Vaiśya, for whom the marriage to a Śūdra woman is permitted if she is of good family and possesses auspicious marks. It is not so, for the arrangement is justified by differences of opinion or by differences of age. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya has clarified the difference of opinion: "The taking of a Śūdra wife by the twice-born—this is not my view, because in that case he himself is born [as a Śūdra]" (YDh 1.56).
Also in the *Ānuśāsana-parvan*:
"The virtuous do not praise the birth of offspring from a Śūdra woman;
others say that even for the sake of pleasure, a Śūdra woman should not be taken. Thus it is said.
The systematic arrangement according to the divisions of the Yugas has been clarified in another Smṛti:
after enumerating such passages as "the marriage of twice-born men with girls of different castes," and so forth, [it continues: [98] ... [the text proceeds].
"For the Kula and Yuga [ages], the wise declare these duties to be abandoned"—thus [it is stated] in the concluding summary. Furthermore, the procedure for marriage has been set forth by Manu:
"The sacrament of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste (*savarṇā*)."
This rule is to be understood as applying to the rite of marriage with women of the same caste.
"A Kṣatriya woman should take hold of an arrow, a Vaiśya maiden a goad, but a Śūdra woman the hem of the garment when marrying one of a higher caste. (Manusmṛti 3.43–44)

Śaṅkha and Likhita also state: "A Kṣatriya woman takes hold of an arrow; a Vaiśya woman, a goad; a Śūdra woman, the hem of the garment; but a Brāhmaṇa should take the hand of a woman of his own caste. Paiṭhīnasi says: "He should take the hand of a Brāhmaṇa woman including the thumb; a Kṣatriya woman, an arrow; a Vaiśya woman, a goad; a Śūdra woman, the hem of her garment. The circumambulation is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa; for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, it is the circumambulation of the preceptor. Manu states the rule regarding approaching the wife after marriage: "He should always approach his own wife during her fertile period and remain devoted to his own wife."

"He should approach her for the sake of sexual pleasure, observing that vow except on forbidden days" (MDh 3.45). The period beginning from the appearance of the menses, consisting of sixteen days and nights, is indeed the *ṛtu*, capable of conceiving a child. During that *ṛtu*, one who desires offspring should always approach his wife; and that approaching should be only with his own wife. Even during the *ṛtu*, he should avoid the *parva* days. Even outside the *ṛtu*, if requested by that woman, he should approach her even without the aim of procreation. Yājñavalkya shows the *ṛtu* as it has been specified:
"The night of women consists of sixteen seasons; one should approach them during the even nights among those, remaining celibate on the sacred days (parvan) and avoiding the first four. (YDh 1.79)

During that season, having avoided the days of the lunar conjunctions (*parvan*) and the first four nights, one should approach his wife for the sake of a son on even-numbered nights beginning from the sixth night. One should not approach her on odd-numbered nights due to the fear of giving birth to a daughter, but not because it is forbidden. Furthermore, one should approach her only at night and not during the day, as it is prohibited. Thus says the *Atharva* Śruti: "Those who unite in sexual pleasure by day indeed spill their vital breath (*prāṇa*). That which is union in sexual pleasure by night is truly celibacy (*brahmacarya*)" (Praśna Upaniṣad 1.13). Śaṅkha and Likhita also state: "One should not engage in sexual intercourse by day during the season. Regarding the injunction "one should approach her during the season," two rules are to be understood: the first rule is that one must certainly approach her during the season and not avoid her; the second is that one should approach her only during the season and not outside of it. For this very reason, Devala says:
"If a man who is healthy does not approach his own wife when she has bathed after her menses,
he incurs the sin of killing an embryo by destroying the fetus that has been conceived. Thus says Baudhāyana as well.
He who does not approach his wife when she is in her season for three years undoubtedly incurs a guilt equal to that of killing an embryo.

"He who does not approach his wife during her season, and he who approaches her outside the season—they both incur equal sin, as does he who discharges seed into a place other than the womb. (BDh 4.1.17, 19)

By the phrase "except on festival days" (*parvavarjam*), prohibited lunar days (*tithi*) and asterisms (*nakṣatra*) are indicated. The prohibited festival days, however, are the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*). Regarding these, sexual intercourse with a woman is prohibited by Śruti: "One should not approach a woman on the new moon or the full moon; if one should approach her, he would become devoid of virility" (TS 2.5.6.4). Other prohibited lunar days include the eighth day (*aṣṭamī*) and so forth. Concerning this, Manu says:

"A twice-born *snātaka* who is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should always remain chaste on the new moon, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth, even during the fertile period (*ṛtu*)" (MDh 4.128).

[101] Thus. Regarding those lunar days (*tithi*) beginning with the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the phrase "by abandoning sexual union with women" must be supplied and applied. He himself states that even during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*), six days are to be avoided:
"Of these, the first four, the censured eleventh, and the thirteenth are excluded; the remaining ten nights are recommended. (MDh 3.47)
Yājñavalkya indicates the prohibited lunar mansions:
"Proceeding in this manner, one should avoid a woman who is emaciated, as well as the asterisms Maghā and Mūla" (YDh 1.80).

"Emaciated" means one who has become thin due to a light diet and so forth. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states the specific dietary requirements for the man and woman along with their underlying causes.
If the female seed is in excess, a female shall be born; if the male seed is in excess, a male shall be born.
Therefore, for the sake of increasing the seed, one should consume unctuous and aphrodisiac food.
"One should thus make her eat light food; in this way, one shall produce a son. Manu also says:
"A male is born when the male seed is in excess, and a female when the female seed is in excess."
"The same applies to a male; or for both male and female when [the semen or blood] is diminished or scanty, there is the opposite result" (MDh 3.49).

The word *apumān* is to be split [as *a-pumān*]. Furthermore, the *saṃkrānti* (the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign) is to be avoided because it falls within the five forbidden lunar days (*parvan*). This is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"The fourteenth day, the eighth, the new moon, and the full moon..."
These are the holy days (parvan), O Indra among kings, as well as the transit of the sun (ravi-saṃkrānti).
"O King, a man who indulges in oil, women, and meat on these specific festival days goes to the hell named Viṇmūtrabhojana (Feeding on Excrement and Urine). (ViPu 3.11.114–15).
Furthermore, the regions to be avoided are shown in that very same place:
Not in shrines, at crossroads, or in palaces; nor indeed in cremation grounds, groves, or waters, O Lord of the Earth.
"A wise man, oppressed by the urge to urinate or defecate, may go to engage in sexual intercourse. (ViP 3.11.118–19).
By the phrase "devoted to his own wife," it is intended to show that approaching the wives of others—even in thought—is prohibited. This too is shown in that very same place:
"One should not approach the wives of others even in thought under any circumstances."
For men, taking pleasure in another's wife brings fear in both worlds.
"Thinking thus, a wise man should approach his own wife when she is in her fertile season. (ViPu 3.11.121–23).
Other things to be avoided are also shown in that same place:
"One should not approach a woman who has not bathed, nor one who is ill, nor one who is menstruating."
Neither one who is undesirable, nor one who is angry, nor one who is ill-omened, nor one who is diseased.

[103] One should not [approach] a woman who has given her fee, nor one who desires another, nor one who is without desire, nor the wife of another; nor one emaciated by hunger, nor one who has overeaten; and one should do so only when one is oneself endowed with these same qualities.
“Having bathed, wearing garlands and perfumes, and being joyful, a man may engage in sexual intercourse. (ViP 3.11.111–13)

By the phrase "one who observes that vow" (*tadvrataḥ*), he recalls the Vedic boon (*vara*). And so says the Śruti: “He approached the women, saying, ‘Accept a third part of this Brahman-murder. They said, ‘Let us choose a boon: let us obtain offspring from our husbands during their season (*ṛtu*); let us have intercourse at will until we give birth. Therefore, women obtain offspring from their husbands during their season and have intercourse at will until they give birth; for they accepted a third part of the Brahman-murder as their chosen boon. She (the murder) became a woman with stained garments” (TS 2.5.1.5). The meaning is as follows: Indra, having incurred the sin of Brahman-murder due to the killing of his priest named Viśvarūpa, took it upon himself with his joined palms and carried it for a year. Fearing public reproach, he divided it into three parts. Having given the first portion to the Earth and the second to the trees by way of a boon, he approached the assembly of women to give the third portion. They requested a boon: “May we obtain offspring from approaching our husbands during their season; may we have intercourse at will until we give birth. Having obtained the boon, they accepted the third portion. That portion transformed into the form of menstrual blood (*rajas*). From that time forward, every month a woman becomes one with stained garments (*malavadvāsāḥ*). Yājñavalkya also says: [104] (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.20–21)
"Or he may act according to his desire, recollecting the boon granted to women;
yet he must remain devoted to his own wife, for it is traditionally taught that women are to be protected. (YDh 1.81). Bṛhaspati also says:
"A man should diligently approach his wife during the period favorable for conception, or at all times except on forbidden days; for that is indeed pleasing to women.

Regarding the phrase "approaching during the period favorable for conception," some explain it thus: "This rule applies only to one who has not yet fathered a son, but not to one who has already fathered a son. And they provide proof for this from the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"He should approach his wife during her fertile period until a son is born" (KūPurāṇa 1.2.15.11).

For the procreation of a son is for the purpose of discharging one's debts. And so says the Śruti: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts: through the life of a student (*brahmacarya*) to the *ṛṣis*, through sacrifice to the gods, and through offspring to the ancestors; he alone is free from debt who has a son, who is a sacrificer, and who has lived the life of a student" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.10.5). There is also a Vedic mantra: "In him he pays off the debt and attains immortality."
"If a father should see the face of his son born alive" (AitĀ 7.3.4).
This discharge of the debt is accomplished by the procreation of even a single son, since by that much alone the status of being a "son" is established. And so says Manu:
"By the mere birth of the eldest son, a man becomes a father of a son."
And because he is indeed free from debt to his ancestors, he therefore deserves everything.

"He upon whom one discharges one's debt, and through whom one attains infinity—he alone is the son born of dharma; others they know as born of desire" (MDh 9.106–107). Now, it may be objected that even the state of having many sons is heard of in some [scriptural] passages.
"O bounteous Indra, make her rich in sons and fortunate;
bestow ten sons upon her, and make her husband the eleventh. (RV 8.3.28.5) "Playing with their sons. (RV 8.3.28.2)
"He has given us wealth and sons," so it is said. (RV 8.3.28.1)

True; this is not an injunction (*vidhi*), but rather a praise of having many offspring. Therefore, this rule regarding approaching one’s wife during her fertile period (*ṛtugamana*) applies only to one who has not yet fathered a son. Others, however, do not accept this. For even though the state of being freed from debt (*anṛṇatva*) through the procreation of a son is accomplished by a single son alone, there nevertheless exists an injunction for having many sons. This is because it is recorded in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* (1.5.2): “‘I meditated upon this very one [the sun], therefore you are my only son,’ thus said Kauṣītaki to his son. ‘You should turn toward the rays; indeed, many shall be yours. The meaning of this is as follows: the sage named Kauṣītaki, while personally meditating upon the solar orb as a single object and performing the *udgītha* chant, obtained only one son as the fruit thereof and said to him: “I performed the chanting while contemplating this very sun as a single entity; therefore, out of that fault, you are my only son. And having only one son is not praiseworthy. Therefore, for the sake of having many sons, you should turn toward the many rays at the time of meditation.”
In the Mahābhārata as well:
"O Bhārata, you alone are our offspring in this great lineage."
Those who speak according to the Dharma say that a man with only one son is as if childless.
O Bhārata, there is both the eye and the son; [one may ask] whether they exist or not.
Upon the destruction of the eye comes the destruction of the body; upon the destruction of the son comes the destruction of the lineage.
[107] "O dear son, reflecting on the impermanence of mortals, I grieve; yet I desire the non-extinction of my lineage—may prosperity be yours! Thus [it is said].
Now, one might object: since the discharge of one's debt to the ancestors is accomplished by the eldest son alone, the procreation of other sons is useless.

That is not so, because [the status of being] free from debt (*anṛṇya*) pertains to all sons. For a father does not become free from debt merely by the birth of a son. Rather, freedom from debt is accomplished only when the son has been properly instructed and has performed the duties prescribed by the scriptures. For this very reason, the rule for instructing a son is recorded in the *Vājasaneyibrāhmaṇa*: “Therefore, they say that a son who has been instructed is beneficial to the world; therefore, they instruct him. Whatever he has done improperly or contrary to the scriptures, from all that his son delivers him. Therefore he is called ‘son’ (*putra*). By means of a son alone does one find firm footing in this world” (BĀU 1.5.17). The meaning of this is as follows: there is a rite known as *saṃpratipatti* (the handing over). When the time of the father’s death arrives, he should summon his son and transfer to him everything that is to be done—whether it be the study of the Vedas, the performance of sacrifices, or worldly affairs. This is the *saṃpratipatti*. Since only an instructed son is qualified for this *saṃpratipatti*, those learned in the scriptures say that a son who has been instructed is beneficial for the next world. For this reason, fathers should provide instruction to their sons.
