And that instructed son, by himself performing the scriptural duties correctly, delivers his father from whatever improper, crooked, or scripture-contrary acts his father may have committed. Thus, based on the etymology “he protects (*trāyate*) from the hell named *punnāman*,” he is called a ‘son. Furthermore, that father, having died himself, continues to perform actions according to the scriptures in this world through the very body of his son.

This being the case, among many, instruction according to the truth occurs for only one person due to the abundance of obstacles such as dullness of intellect; even among those who have been instructed, correct practice occurs for only one. Therefore, whether he be the eldest or the youngest, he alone who is such [as described] is the cause of freedom from debt. For this very reason it is stated in the Purāṇa:
"Many sons are to be desired, so that even if only one should go to Gayā. (ViDh 85.67)

“Place ten sons in her” (RV 8.3.28.5)—mantras such as this, being so, corroborate the injunction for having many sons. As for that which was cited by Manu, namely, “others are born of desire,” that refers to cases where one has not been instructed [to procreate]. Therefore, even one who already has a son should indeed approach his wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu*). Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of the fertile periods of many wives, Devala states the sequence: “When the times [of menstruation] coincide, he should approach them according to the order of caste, beginning with the Brāhmaṇa; or for the sake of protection, he may approach the childless wife first, or else according to the order of marriage.”

The *tīrtha* (the fertile period) is the menstrual season (*ṛtu*). When there are women of different castes, he should approach them according to the order of their castes; when they are of the same caste, he should approach them according to the order of their marriage. However, when one woman is childless while the others have sons, he should approach the childless one first. Regarding the restriction on the time for approaching even during the fertile season due to differences in caste, Devala says:
"For a Brāhmaṇī woman, the duration of the fertile season mentioned in the Veda shall be twelve days;
for the remaining [castes], ten, eight, and six days are prescribed respectively."

The number of days, beginning from the fifth day up to the twelfth and so forth, is to be understood. However, going on the fourth day is optional (*vaikalpika*), because it is both prescribed and prohibited. Thus Hārīta prescribes: "On the fourth day, after she has bathed, or during even-numbered nights, the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) should take place" (HārSm 2.9). Vyāsa prohibits it: "She should not be approached on the fourth day; if she is approached, she gives birth to one of short lifespan."

This is an alternative based on a settled distinction, like the offerings of the *uditahoma* and *anuditahoma*. When menstrual flow has ceased, there is a rule on the fourth day; when it continues, there is a prohibition. Thus says Manu:
"When her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who is menstruating becomes pure by means of a bath" (MDh 5.66).

"Virtuous" (*sādhvī*) means fit for performing prescribed rites such as *garbhādhāna* (conception-rite) and so forth. Regarding intercourse on specific days, specific results are declared in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*.
If she goes on the fourth day, she gives birth to one of short lifespan,
devoid of learning, fallen from his vows, degraded, or an adulterer.
And she gives birth to a son who is submerged in an ocean of poverty;
therefore, one seeking a daughter should again go according to the prescribed rite on the fifth lunar day.
On the sixth day, a highly fortunate woman approached may become the mother of a virtuous son;
and on the seventh day, one seeking a daughter should approach her, and she shall give birth to one.
On the eighth day, she gives birth to a son endowed with all prosperity.
On the ninth day, it will be for the sake of a girl; likewise, on the tenth, for a wise man;
and on the eleventh, it gives birth to a woman, just as before.
On the twelfth day, he saw one who knew the truth of Dharma and who promoted the Śrauta and Smārta rites;
on the thirteenth day, a dull-witted woman who caused the intermixture of castes.
Therefore, a woman gives birth [to a child]; one should not approach her with every effort.
If one should approach her on the fourteenth day, she will become the mother of a virtuous son.
"And on the fifteenth day [one attains] the state of righteousness, and on the sixteenth day, one reaches the further shore of knowledge" (LiPu 1.89.109–18).
Vyāsa states an exception to the fault that has been declared regarding not approaching one's wife during her fertile period:
"When afflicted by disease, when held in captivity, when traveling abroad, or on the sacred festival days (*parvan*)."
Even for women during their fertile period, the sin of destroying an embryo is thus released.

"By avoiding one who is old, barren, destitute, whose children have died, who has not yet reached puberty, a maiden, or one who has many sons, one is released from fear. *Bhrūṇahatyā* means the killing of an embryo. According to the stated method, every woman—whether she is free from defects such as old age and so forth, in whom approaching during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*) is mandatory, or in whom it is not mandatory due to being old and so forth—is to be properly protected. And thus says Manu:
These women should be honored and adorned by their fathers, brothers, husbands, and kinsmen who desire abundant prosperity.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, all ritual actions there become fruitless.
Where female relatives grieve, that family quickly perishes;
but where they do not grieve, that family indeed prospers forever.
Those households which female relatives curse when they have not been honored perish on all sides, as if struck by a magical spell.
Therefore, those who desire prosperity should always worship these [goddesses] with ornaments, clothing, and food, both at regular ceremonies and during festivals.

"In that family where the husband is content with his wife and likewise the wife with her husband, there is certainly perpetual prosperity. (MDh 3.55–60). Furthermore, this status of being worthy of honor (*pūjyatva*) is to be understood as applying to women other than those who have not been wedded (*avṛttā*). As for one who has not been wedded, however, she is to receive food only sufficient for the maintenance of life. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"One should cause the unfaithful wife to dwell deprived of her authority, soiled, subsisting on mere alms, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground" (YDh 1.70).
Just as a virtuous wife who has been superseded (*adhivinā*) must be maintained, so too must she who has been superseded; thus he himself says:

"Even one who is unfaithful must be maintained; otherwise, there would be a great sin. (YDh 1.74) *Adhivedana* means the taking of another wife. He (the author) also states the grounds for supersession:
"A woman who drinks liquor, one who is diseased, one who is deceitful, one who is barren, one who destroys wealth, or one who speaks unpleasantly..."
"And likewise, she who gives birth only to daughters, or she who hates her husband, may be superseded.

(YDh 1.73) "Surāpī" means a drinker of intoxicants (*madya*). However, in the case of drinking *surā*, it is not merely supersession; rather, there is actual abandonment, because it is stated as a ground for abandonment in the rule, "likewise in the case of a great sin" (YDh 1.72), and because of the statement: "Half of his body falls [with the sin] if his wife drinks *surā*" (VaDh 21.15).
And because of this statement, Manu likewise says:
"A woman who drinks liquor, is of bad conduct, or is antagonistic; or one who is diseased, harmful, or always wasteful of wealth—she may indeed be superseded. (MDh 9.80)
"Afflicted" means one who is chronically ill. Also, in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"One should abandon for the sake of protecting one's dharma a wife who creates obstacles to dharma, who is unchaste, excessively wrathful, and likewise one who speaks unpleasantly."
One may abandon her and take another in marriage, but one must not abandon the enjoyment [of the wife].
The specific times for taking a second wife have been shown by Manu: "A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year, but one whose children have died in the tenth."
"In the eleventh year, she gives birth to a daughter and is moreover a speaker of unpleasant words" (MDh 9.81).
He himself states the specific rule regarding one who is diseased:
"But she who may be diseased, yet is well-disposed and endowed with good character..."
"She may be superseded with her permission, but she must never be treated with contempt" (MDh 8.82).

Supersession (*adhivedana*) is of two kinds: for the sake of dharma and for the sake of pleasure. In the case of dharma—such as the procreation of a son—the aforementioned grounds, such as being a drinker of intoxicants and so forth, are required. However, for the sake of pleasure, those [grounds] need not be considered; rather, the previously married wife must be satisfied. Thus, it is said in another *smṛti*:
"He who, having passed over one wife for the sake of pleasure, desires to obtain another..."
"One who is capable, having gratified the previously married wife with wealth, may marry another.
If she herself does not satisfy him, then the king shall cause wealth to be given for her gratification. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"One who obeys his commands, is skillful, bears heroic sons, and speaks kindly..."

"Abandoning her, he shall be made to pay a third part [of his property]; if he is without wealth, he must provide maintenance for the woman. (YDh 1.76) [115] Thus, for one who possesses wealth, there is the giving of a third part; for one without wealth, there is nourishment by means of food, clothing, and so forth. Regarding a woman who departs in another manner because she is dissatisfied with the aforementioned property, Manu says:
"But that woman who, having been superseded, departs from the house in anger..."
"She must be restrained immediately, or abandoned in the presence of the family" (MDh 9.83).

"Abandonment" means sending her away to the family of her own father. Regarding what was stated [in MDh 3.55], "They should be honored and adorned," Manu declares the order of honoring for one who has many wives:
"If twice-born men marry women who are both their own [caste] and lower..."
Among them, seniority and honor in the household shall be according to the order of their castes.

"A woman of the same caste alone, and never one of a different caste, should perform the service of her husband’s body and his daily religious duties for all [the wives]. (MDh 9.85–86). Yājñavalkya determines who among many wives is the partner in dharma (*sahadharmacāriṇī*).
If there is another wife of the same caste, one should not have religious duties performed by her;
among wives of the same caste, according to the rule of dharma, none other than the eldest may perform them. (YDh 1.88)

[116] Thus: "One should practice dharma only with a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*), not with one of a different caste. However, the meaning is obtained by implication that, in the absence of a wife of the same caste, one may practice dharma even with another. Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, practicing dharma with a *śūdra* woman would follow as a consequence; for that is prohibited by the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "A dark-complexioned woman is for pleasure alone, not for dharma" (VaDh 18.18). But when there are several wives of the same caste, the middle or youngest wife must not be employed in the performance of dharma without the eldest. Rather, the younger wives are to be employed by the eldest. And so says Baudhāyana: "One should cause each one to lead the sacrificial horse (*sānnāhya*); each one should look upon the *gārhapatya* fire; each one should gaze at the clarified butter (*ājya*)," and so forth. Kātyāyana [says the same].

"The installation of the sacred fires by the twice-born cannot be accomplished even without a single wife; one should know that which is performed [by only one] to be as if unperformed, since all [wives] must hold on together. (KSm 1.8.5).
Because all [wives] must hold on together, therefore, even what is done by one alone is indeed as if undone.

Some here explain the statement, "Without the eldest, not the others" (YDh 1.88), otherwise: that the eldest alone is the companion in dharma, and not the others. And they cite a statement of Viṣṇu on this point: "In sacrifices such as the Agnihotra, a second wife shall not perform them together;
otherwise, it is fruitless for him, even with hundreds of well-performed rites."

This explanation is not to be respected because it contradicts the statements of Baudhāyana and Kātyāyana. However, the statement of Viṣṇu refers to the case of a second wife who is of a different caste (*asavarṇa*), or it refers to the case of one who was married while the sacred fires were still present. Since she also possesses the status of an agent during the re-establishment of the fires (*punar-ādhāna*) when the fires have been lost, she has a joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*) in the Agnihotra and other rites. Regarding this very point, Kātyāyana states the specific rule: "A man with many wives should have the service of the Agnihotra and other rites performed by a wife of the same caste; and if there are many such wives, he should have it done by the eldest, provided she is not censurable."
Or rather, among these women, one should employ here that woman who has borne heroic sons, who carries out orders, who is skillful, sweet-spoken, and pure.

"Or they may perform the work according to their seniority, in accordance with their own capacity, either by dividing it among themselves or by doing it together; and they should act according to their knowledge, following the scriptures. (KSm 2.19.3–5)

If the eldest wife is not censurable, then one should have her perform it; if she is censurable, then one should have the youngest wife who has borne a hero-son (*vīrasū*) perform it. If there are many such wives who have borne hero-sons, one should appoint among them the one endowed with qualities such as obedience to commands. If a single woman is unable to perform it every day, then they should perform it according to the sequence of days in order of seniority. If even on a single day a single woman is unable to perform the whole task, then all of them should divide that work according to their knowledge and perform it. As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana himself:
The first wife shall be the lawful consort, while the second increases pleasure;
the fruit of this is seen in this very world, not something that pertains to the unseen realm.

Thus, this is identical in meaning to the statement of Viṣṇu. In this manner, marriage with specific qualifications has been described. Now, in connection with marriages between those of the same and different castes (*savarṇa* and *asavarṇa*), the distinctions among the various classes (*jāti*)—which have arisen in the mind regarding those born in the direct (*anuloma*) and inverse (*pratiloma*) orders—are described for the purpose of establishing the conventional designations useful in social practice. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"From those of the same caste, born of women of the same caste, indeed arise those of the same lineage (*sajātayaḥ*);
through blameless marriages, sons are born who increase the progeny. (YDh 1.90) "Those of the same lineage" means those belonging to the same caste as the mother and father. Manu also says:

"Among all castes, those born in the direct order (*ānulomya*) from wives who are equal [in caste] and whose virginity is intact should be known as belonging to that very caste. (MDh 10.5) One born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇa mother becomes a Brāhmaṇa by birth; the same applies to the Kṣatriyas and others. Devala also says:
"One born to a Brāhmaṇī from a Brāhmaṇa becomes a consecrated Brāhmaṇa;

in this same way, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are to be known when born from their own [wives] of their own caste. Thus Manu speaks of those born in the direct order (anuloma) from women of a different caste.

[119] "Regarding women born of endless lineages, sons procreated by twice-born men are said to be similar [to their fathers], yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers" (MDh 10.6). A son born from a wedded Kṣatriya woman by a Brāhmaṇa is similar to a Brāhmaṇa, but not a primary Brāhmaṇa, because of his connection to a mother of a lower caste; the same applies elsewhere as well. These, known as *anuloma* (born in the natural order), are of six types according to the distinctions of castes such as the *Mūrdhāvasikta*. And these have been shown by Yājñavalkya:
For from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother is born a Mūrdhāvasikta; from a Vaiśya woman, an Ambaṣṭha; and from a Śūdra woman, a Niṣāda or a Pāraśava is born.

"From a Kṣatriya [father], a Vaiśya and a Śūdra woman give birth to two sons, known as the Māhiṣya and the Ugra; from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra woman, a Karaṇa is born. This is the rule prescribed for women who have been wedded.
(YDh 1.91–92). Among these, three are born from a Brāhmaṇa, two from a Kṣatriya, and one from a Vaiśya. This was stated by Manu:
"For the Brāhmaṇa, [sons] from the three castes; for the Kṣatriya, from two castes;
for the Vaiśya, from one caste—these six are declared to be *apasadās* (outcasts). (MDh 10.10).
They are called *apasadās* because they lack the primary paternal caste.

Now, an objection: are not the ranks such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* distinct castes (*jātyantara*), since those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) belong to the caste of their mother? To this, Viṣṇu says: [120] “Sons born of women of the same varṇa are of the same varṇa; those born of women in the direct order are of the same varṇa as their mothers; those born of women in the inverse order are despised by the noble. Śaṅkha also says: “One born of a Kṣatriya woman by a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Kṣatriya indeed; one born of a Vaiśya woman by a Kṣatriya becomes a Vaiśya indeed; one born of a Śūdra woman by a Vaiśya becomes a Śūdra indeed.”

This is not a fault, because these two statements are intended to establish the acquisition of the dharma pertaining to the mother’s caste; otherwise, there would result the absurdity of the excellence of the seed being rendered useless. Just as the deficiency of the field prevents the attainment of a superior caste, why should the excellence of the seed likewise not prevent [the child] from being of an inferior caste? Therefore, [these castes] such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others are indeed distinct castes.
But surely, Devala has described the *anuloma* castes differently: "From a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya woman is born one named Savarṇa... [and so forth].

"And one born from a Kṣatriya on a Vaiśya woman is known as an Ambaṣṭha. This is not a fault, because the two designations "Mūrdhāvasikta" and "Savarṇa" apply optionally to the very same caste. The same applies to the Ambaṣṭhas and others. Nor should it be suspected that there is no precedent for such optional variation in designation in a single case; for Manu, Devala, and Yājñavalkya have cited the optional variation between the designations "Niṣāda" and "Pāraśava" in a single instance. Furthermore, those born in the reverse order (pratiloma) have been shown by Manu: "From a Kṣatriya on the daughter of a Brāhmaṇa, a Sūta is born by birth."
From a Vaiśya [father] are born the Māgadha and the Vaideha; from a Kṣatriya [father] are born the Rājanya and the Ambaṣṭha; and from a Brāhmaṇa [father] is born the Āyogava.
From a Śūdra, on women of the Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa castes, are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men— through the intermixture of the castes.
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
these three base-born (apasada) sons are born from a Śūdra in the reverse order of castes.

"The Māgadha and Vaideha [are born] from a Vaiśya; however, the Sūta alone is born from a Kṣatriya. (MDh 10.11–17). Devala also says: "From a Śūdra [are born] the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—these are those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*)."
In a Vaiśya woman, a Kṣatriya woman, and a Brāhmaṇa woman, respectively.
"Likewise, the Māgadha and the Vaidehaka are born from a Vaiśya;
and the Sūta is born from a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇī woman, both by birth and by occupation.
Thus [says] Yājñavalkya as well.
From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise, from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehika;
and from a Śūdra, a Caṇḍāla is born, who is excluded from all religious duties.

"A Kṣatriya woman from Māgadha, and a Vaiśya woman from a Śūdra, likewise gives birth to a Kṣattṛ; a Vaiśya woman indeed gives birth to an Āyogava son from a Śūdra. (YDh 1.93–94). Furthermore, there are many kinds of specific castes, such as the Śvapāka, Pulkasa, Kukkuṭa, and others, produced through the mutual intermixture of those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) and those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*). These, along with their respective occupations, are detailed in the *Purāṇasāra*. Regarding these specific castes, Devala distinguishes between their superior and inferior status.

"Among them, those born of the same caste (savarṇaja) are the best; after them follow those born in the natural order (anulomaja); those born in the intermediate classes (antarāla) are outside the [proper] castes (bahirvarṇa), and those born in the inverse order (pratilomaja) are outcastes (patita). Thus, those produced from unions between different castes are the "intermediate" (antarāla). They are of two kinds: those born in the natural order and those born in the inverse order. Among these, although those born in the natural order are inferior to those born of the same caste, they are not excluded from the caste system because they share the same caste as their mother. However, those born in the inverse order are outcastes and base because they are outside the caste system. Yājñavalkya also says:
"But those born in the inverse and direct orders are to be known as non-existent and existent [respectively]. (YDh 1.95).

In some cases, even one of a lower caste may attain a higher caste; regarding this, the same author says: "An elevation of caste is to be known [as occurring] in the seventh or even the fifth generation. (YDh 1.95).

In a calculation starting from the original (kūṭastha) couple consisting of a man and a woman, caste is elevated in the fifth, sixth, or seventh generation according to the natural order (anuloma). For example: a Brahmin man and a Śūdra woman constitute the original couple. From them is born a Vaiśya woman; she too is married by a Brahmin, and their union is the second couple. In this way, when each daughter born from that lineage is married by a Brahmin, there is a succession of third and subsequent couples. In that seventh couple, the offspring born becomes endowed with Brāhmaṇahood. Similarly, a Vaiśya woman and a Brahmin man constitute the original couple. From them is born an Ambaṣṭha woman; her union with a Brahmin is the second couple. In this manner, when the daughter born from that union is married by a Brahmin, the offspring born from the sixth couple attains Brāhmaṇahood. Likewise, a Kṣatriya woman and a Brahmin man constitute the original couple. From them is born a Mūrdhāvasiktā woman; her union with a Brahmin is the second couple. In that lineage, the offspring born from the fifth couple attains Brāhmaṇahood. This is what is meant: the options "in the fifth, sixth, or seventh" are fixed alternatives. Depending on whether the offspring is one degree, two degrees, or three degrees removed from the original couple, the fifth and subsequent generations are to be understood accordingly. Thus, because a Śūdra woman and a Vaiśya woman, or a Vaiśya woman and a Kṣatriya woman, are separated by one degree, caste is elevated in the fifth generation; however, for a Śūdra woman and a Kṣatriya woman, it is elevated in the sixth. In some cases, even the highest caste may attain the status of a lower caste. As he himself says: [123] ... [The text continues with further examples and rules regarding mixed castes. ... Thus ends the section on the determination of caste through successive unions.
"In the reversal of actions, there is equality; and as before, there is the distinction between lower and higher. (YDh 1.96)

Regarding the duties prescribed for the four castes, beginning with the Brahmins—namely, officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), protecting [the earth], animal husbandry (*paśupālana*), and service to the twice-born (*dvija-śuśrūṣā*)—if, in times of distress (*āpad*), there occurs a transgression or reversal of these duties, and if, even when that distress has ceased, one does not abandon that inferior mode of livelihood (*adhamavṛtti*), and likewise his sons, grandsons, and descendants do not abandon it, then the offspring born in the fifth, sixth, or seventh generation from such a union attains a status equal to the caste appropriate to that livelihood. For example: if a Brāhmaṇa living by the livelihood of a Śūdra begets a son, and that son likewise lives by the same means, then through such a succession, the status of a Śūdra accrues to the one born in the seventh generation. Similarly, a Kṣatriya living by the livelihood of a Śūdra begets a Śūdra in the sixth generation; a Vaiśya, however, begets one in the fifth generation—so it should be understood. The phrase "as before" (*pūrvavat*) means "starting from that point. The term *adharottara* is an expression emphasizing the state of being; just as in the confusion of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), acting in the reverse order (*prātilomya*) is inferior and the natural order (*ānulomya*) is superior, so too is it in the confusion of livelihoods (*vṛttisaṃkara*). For instance, for a Kṣatriya, even in times of distress, subsisting on the Brāhmaṇical livelihood of officiating at sacrifices and so forth is inferior, because Vasiṣṭha prohibits it, stating: "But never [should he adopt] a higher [livelihood]" (VaDh 2.23). Conversely, subsisting on the Vaiśya livelihood of animal husbandry and so forth is superior, because Vasiṣṭha also prescribes: "Those unable to live by their own duty (*svadharma*) should adopt the next lower or even a more inferior livelihood" (VaDh 2.22). Furthermore, there is another interpretation of the phrase "as before" and "inferior/superior" (*adharottara*). For confusion (*saṃkara*) is indeed manifold: there is confusion of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), confusion of mixed castes (*saṃkīrṇasaṃkara*), and confusion of castes and mixed castes (*varṇasaṃkīrṇasaṃkara*). For example: the marriage between a man of a superior caste and a woman of an inferior caste is *varṇasaṃkara*. The marriage between the offspring of those two—the *Māhiṣya* and the *Karaṇa*—is *saṃkīrṇasaṃkara*. The marriage between those of mixed castes is *varṇasaṃkīrṇasaṃkara*. Among these, the offspring born of *varṇasaṃkara* through the natural order are shown by the rule: "From a Brāhmaṇa [comes] the *Mūrdhāvasikta*" and so forth. Those born of *varṇasaṃkara* through the reverse order are shown by the rule: "From a Kṣatriya [comes] a *Sūta* in a Brāhmaṇī" and so forth.
From a Mahiṣya and a Karaṇī, a Rathakāra is born. (YDh 1.95)

[125] Thus have been shown those born from the mixture of mixtures (*saṃkīrṇasaṃkaraja*). Now, by the phrase "the lower and the higher" (*adharottaram*), those born from the mixture of the mixed castes (*varṇasaṃkīrṇasaṃkaraja*) are demonstrated. The "lower" (*adhara*) refers to those born in the reverse order (*pratiloma*); the "higher" (*uttara*) refers to those born in the natural order (*anuloma*). For example: those produced by the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes—the lower castes—upon a Mūrdhāvasikta woman who is a mixed caste and of the highest rank, are "lower. Those produced by the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes—the higher castes—upon a Niṣāda woman who is a mixed caste and of the lowest rank, are "higher. Both the lower and the higher constitute "the lower and the higher" (*adharottaram*). By the word "as before" (*pūrvavat*), the meaning of the statement "but they should be known as non-existent and existent" (YDh 1.95) is extended. Just as those born from the mixture of castes and those born from the mixture of mixtures were previously explained—those born in the reverse order being non-existent and those born in the natural order being existent—so too should it be understood that among those born from the mixture of the mixed castes, those born in the natural order are existent, while those born in the reverse order are non-existent. Regarding the threefold classification mentioned, there are sixty types of "semblances of castes" (*varṇābhāsa*) arising based on the mixture of castes or the mixture of mixed castes. The "semblances of classes" (*jātyābhāsa*) arising based on the mixture of mixtures are infinite. As it is said in another Smṛti:

"By means of the reverse and direct order [of castes], and by those born from them according to caste, sixty other [mixed castes] are produced; however, the offspring of those are infinite. Thus it is said.

Twelve [castes] are produced by the castes through both inverse (*prātilomya*) and natural (*anuloma*) order. Six are born from the natural order: the Sūta, Vaideha, Caṇḍāla, Māgadha, Kṣattṛ, and Āyogava; these six are born from the inverse order. Thus, forty-eight [castes] are produced by those twelve born from the castes through their connection with the castes. In this way, sixty other "semblances of castes" (*varṇābhāsa*) arise, characterized by that same number. For example: the Mūrdhāvasikta, Ambaṣṭha, Niṣāda, Māhiṣya, Ugra, and Karaṇa—these six are born from the natural order. Thus, there are twelve. Among them, three are produced by the Mūrdhāvasikta in the natural order from Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra women, and one in the inverse order from a Brāhmaṇī woman. Two are produced by the Ambaṣṭha in the natural order and two in the inverse order. One is produced by the Niṣāda in the natural order and three in the inverse order. Two are produced by the Māhiṣya in the natural order and two in the inverse order. One is produced by the Ugra in the natural order and three in the inverse order. One is produced by the Karaṇa in the natural order and three in the inverse order—thus, twenty-four are produced from the first group of six. Likewise, for each of the six castes beginning with the Sūtra, there is one [offspring] from each of the four castes—thus they too are twenty-four. Combined, they total sixty. From the offspring produced by those sixty in number, the number of semblances becomes infinite. Thus concludes this incidental discussion on the distinctions of castes.
Thus concludes the determination of the distinctions of caste.

The sacraments (*saṃskāras*) beginning with the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) that occur subsequent to marriage, and ending with the *soma* rites, have already been described in the section on daily duties (*āhnika*) and the section on the six duties (*ṣaṭkarma*); therefore, they are not stated again here. Now, the remaining duties of the householder (*gṛhasthadharma*) are determined. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the rule for the *upākarma* ceremony:
"The commencement of the study of the chapters [of the Veda] shall take place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Śravaṇā."
Or, in the absence of the aforementioned medicinal herbs, [it may be performed] on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa. (YDh 1.142)

The Vedas are called *adhyāyas* because they are studied (*adhīyante*). Their *upākarma* is the commencement [of their study]. This should be performed on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, or on another lunar day in that month conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa, or on a day conjoined with the asterism Hasta, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa. However, when medicinal herbs do not appear in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should perform it in the month of Bhādrapada on the aforementioned lunar days. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says: "Now, therefore, the commencement of Vedic study is on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or of Prauṣṭhapada" (VaDh 12.9). Manu also says:

"Having performed the *upākarma* according to the rule on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedic hymns for four and a half months. (MDh 4.95).

Those of whom the fifth is half are "those [lasting] four and a half months"; the meaning is four months and a half. However, when there is an obstacle such as the setting of Venus (*śukrāstamaya*) on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, then it should be performed on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha. This has been stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:

"O best of the twice-born, the commencement of Vedic study (*vedopākaraṇa*) is prescribed for the full moon of the month of Śrāvaṇa, or the full moon of Āṣāḍha, or the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada. (KūPurāṇa 1.2.14.62). Baudhāyana also says: "Having commenced [the study] on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Āṣāḍha, one should conclude it on the full moon of Taiṣya or Māgha. (BDh 1.5.12.16). In all three of these months, the full moon, the *Śravaṇa* asterism, and the *Hasta* asterism are established according to the division of Vedic schools (*śākhā*). Regarding this, Gobhila says:
"On the full-moon day of Śrāvaṇa, the Taittirīyakas should perform it;
the Bahvṛcas, however, on the day of the Śravaṇa asterism, and the Sāmavedins on the day of the Hasta asterism.
Thus says Gārgya as well.

"On the *parvan* occurring at sunrise, the followers of the Taittirīya school should perform [the sacrifice]; the followers of the Ṛgveda should perform it on the day of Śravaṇā, provided it is free from planetary conjunctions (*graha*) or transits (*saṃkrānti*). Here, the term "occurring at sunrise" (*audayika*) is connected to all [the times] beginning with the *parvan*. He states the specific rule regarding the *parvan* occurring at sunrise:

"But if the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa occurs after the *saṅgava* period, then the one coinciding with sunrise (*audayikī*) is to be accepted; otherwise, the one at sunrise would not be [the one to be taken].
Thus, Vyāsa has demonstrated through both positive and negative concomitance that the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa must coincide with sunrise.
But by merely hearing [the Veda] under the conjunction of Uttarāṣāḍhā,
the year-long interruption of study perishes at that very moment.

[129] "Whatever rite of Śrāvaṇa is to be performed when conjoined with Dhaniṣṭhā, that rite known as Upākaraṇa should be understood as fruitful. Thus, one should not perform the rite prescribed for Śrāvaṇa when conjoined with Uttarāṣāḍhā; if one were to do so, it would perish—this is how the passage is to be construed. Regarding what was stated, namely "avoiding planetary transits," Gārgya states a specific exception therein:
If a solar transit (saṃkrānti) or an eclipse occurs before midnight, one should not perform the Upākarma rite; if it occurs after midnight, it does not cause any fault.
"If an eclipse or a solar transit occurs prior to midnight,
one should not perform the *upākarma* on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, even if the asterism Śravaṇa is present.
As for the statement— "The *upākarma* must not be performed in the month of Karkaṭa"— so it is said in another Smṛti:

"When the commencement of the Vedas (upākaraṇa) is due, if the sun is situated in Cancer, the Upākarma should not be performed; it should be performed when [the sun] is joined with Leo. This refers to other regions. And so says Bṛhaspati:
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, the rite should be performed when the sun is in Leo;
however, when the sun is situated in Cancer, one should perform the Upākarma on the southern bank.
[130] Thus it is said.

But surely—the *upākaraṇa* (commencement ceremony) is a duty of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), because from the injunction "having performed the *upākaraṇa*, one should study," it is understood to be an auxiliary to the study for the purpose of memorization (*grahaṇādhyayana*). And that study for memorization belongs only to the religious student, since it is understood to precede the ritual bath (*snāna*) by the rule "having studied the Veda, one should bathe."

This is not a fault, because even for a householder, there is the possibility of eligibility for the study of the *graha* texts. For this very reason, Śaunaka says, following the word "one should study": "One who has returned [from studentship] [should study] according to the rule of a student; others [i.e., those who have not returned] according to the prescribed method; likewise even one who is joined with a wife. The meaning of this is: with whatever specific observances a student studies, with those same observances one who has returned [from studentship] should also study. But others than the one who has returned—namely, the students—should study according to the rule, in the manner prescribed by their own injunctions. Likewise, even a householder joined with a wife should study endowed with the observances of a student. Nor should it be suspected that the eligibility of the one who has returned and the householder for the study of the *graha* texts contradicts the statement, "Having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*)," because that statement refers specifically to the *vidyā-snātaka* (the graduate who has completed his studies). For this very reason, [it is so].

[131] “Having brought either the Veda or the vows, or indeed both, to completion” (YDh 1.51)—thus the presentation of two alternative views has been shown. If it is accepted that the *upākaraṇa* (commencement of study) is a duty of the householder, then its inclusion in the section on the duties of householders in the *Manu-smṛti* and *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* is also supported. The procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the *upākaraṇa* has been shown by Kārṣṇājini:
“At the *upākarma* and the *utsarga*, having assembled at the proper time...”
"Having fashioned the sages out of *darbha* grass, one should then worship and offer libations to them. Baudhāyana also says:
"Furthermore, having fashioned the seven sages beginning with Gautama out of *dharma* [wood]."
"Having performed worship according to one's ability, one should offer libations while uplifting one's lineage.
Thus ends the section on the *upākarma*; now follows the *utsarjana*. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:

"On the Rohiṇī asterism in the month of Pauṣa, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā day, one should perform the formal dismissal of the Vedic scriptures (chandasām utsarga) outside [the village] at the edge of water according to the rule. (YDh 1.143). Manu also says:

"A twice-born man should perform the *utsarjana* (concluding rite) of the Vedas outside [the village] under the asterism Puṣya, or when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived in the forenoon" (MDh 4.96).

This alternative is fixed according to the rule: when the *upākarma* (commencement rite) occurs on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, then the *utsarjana* takes place in the forenoon on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Puṣya; if the *upākarma* occurs on the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada, then it takes place in the month of Māgha. Manu further prescribes the resumption of study for that which was concluded at a specific time prior to the *upākaraṇa*.
"From this point forward, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic meters (*chandāṃsi*) during the bright fortnights;
one should recite the Vedāṅgas and the secret doctrines (*rahasya*) during the dark fortnights. (MDh 4.98).
Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"A twice-born man should study the *chandasyas* (Vedic hymns) from this point forward during the bright fortnights, and the *vedāṅgas* and *purāṇas* during the dark fortnights" (KūPurāṇa 1.2.14.65).

If, out of fear of future obstacles, he thinks that he must study immediately, then he should suspend [the formal study] before the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) for a year, according to the Vedic injunction: "Whatever portion of his own Veda he studies for a year. Kātyāyana praises both the commencement and the suspension [of study].
By that annual *upākarma* ceremony, performed according to rule by the twice-born along with the *utsarga*, there occurs a renewal of the Vedic hymns (*chandas*).
Whatever rite is performed by the twice-born with Vedic meters that have not lost their potency,
even if they are doing so while playing, it always brings about success for them.
Other duties as well are shown in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*.
One should not dwell in a village surrounded by unrighteous people, nor in one where diseases are exceedingly prevalent;
one should not live in a kingdom ruled by Śūdras, nor in one overrun by heretics.
A twice-born man should not dwell anywhere else except in that auspicious region situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains to the east and west, and between the two oceans.
Or where the black antelope roams constantly by its very nature,
or where there are famous, holy rivers— there a twice-born man should dwell.

A wise man should not speak with another's wife, nor should he officiate at a sacrifice for one unworthy to offer sacrifice; nor should he ever circumambulate a temple in a counter-clockwise direction.
One should not fan oneself with a garment, and one should avoid crowds;
one should not travel alone on a road, nor together with unrighteous people.
"One should not revile yogins, perfected ones, those observing vows, or likewise ascetics. Thus [it is said]. Manu also says:
"Of the deities, the guru, the king, as well as the *snātaka* and the teacher..."
One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of a leper or of one who has been initiated for a sacrifice.
One who desires prosperity should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they appear weak.
One should seek prosperity until death; one should not consider it difficult to attain.
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant;
nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal dharma.
One should not travel too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor when it is high noon;
one should not travel with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with low-caste people (vṛṣala).
One should not look down upon those who have missing limbs, those with extra limbs, those lacking in learning, those advanced in age, those deficient in beauty or wealth, or those of low birth.
"One should not serve an enemy, nor the companion of an enemy, nor an unrighteous person, nor a thief, nor the wife of another. Thus [says Manu, MDh 4.130–41]. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
One should avoid idle chatter, falsehood, and harsh speech;
and one should avoid false scriptures, false debate, and the company of the wicked, my son.
One should not learn the language of the Mlecchas, nor look at one's own excrement;
one should not stand upon excrement, urine, hair, ashes, or potsherds.
"A twice-born man should avoid chaff, charcoal, bones, fragments, ropes, clothes, and the like, as well as the dust from a broom; he should not drink water that is unfit for drinking.
Thus Manu has stated the Dharma in brief in a general sense.
By that path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by that way, he does not come to harm.
[135] "Whatever action he performs that brings satisfaction to his inner self, that he should perform with diligence; but he should avoid the opposite. (MDh 4.161–78).
Thus have the duties of the stages of life for the student and the householder been described.
Now, the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) is described.

Now, some do not accept any stage of life (*āśrama*) other than the householder’s state; they cite the *Gautama-smṛti* in this regard: “The teachers [maintain] that there is only one stage of life, because the householder’s state is directly enjoined in scripture” (GDh 3.36). These teachers hold that the householder’s state alone is a stage of life and that no other exists. They state the reason as follows: because the householder’s state is enjoined in the direct Vedic texts (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), whereas for the others, such an injunction is absent. For instance, the followers of the *Bahvṛca* (Ṛgveda), beginning with “I praise Agni” (*agnim īḷe*, RV 1.1.1.1), prescribe throughout the entire Veda—consisting of both Mantra and Brāhmaṇa—that only the duties of the *Hotṛ* priest are to be performed. The followers of the Yajurveda, by means of passages such as “For food, thee” (*iṣe tvā*, TS 1.1.1.1), prescribe the duties of the *Adhvaryu*. The chanters of the Sāmaveda likewise, through passages such as “O Agni, come hither” (*agna āyāhi*, SV 1.1.1.1), prescribe the duties of the *Udgātṛ*. And the *Hotṛ* and other priests are exclusively householders. Thus, since the duties of the householder are declared within the directly studied Vedas, the injunction for that stage of life is inferred; however, we do not see anything similar that could serve as the basis for inferring an injunction for the other stages of life. For this very reason, the scriptural text, “One performs the *Agnihotra* as long as one lives,” assigns the entirety of a person’s lifespan solely to the duties of the householder. Another scriptural passage states: “This *Agnihotra* is indeed a sacrificial session (*sattra*) that lasts until old age; for one is released from it either by old age or by death. Nor should it be doubted how the stage of the student (*brahmacarya*) can be accepted under these circumstances. This is because the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) is relegated to a mere fringe of the argument, while the temporary student (*upakurvāṇaka*) is a mere observer of vows and thus lacks the status of a formal stage of life. If such is the case for the student and the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), who are considered performers of ritual action (*karmin*), then what need is there to mention the ascetic (*yati*), who has renounced all ritual action? Therefore, the householder’s state is the only stage of life—this is the position of the teachers.

To this it is replied: Indeed, there is a direct Vedic injunction for all four stages of life (*āśrama*). Thus the Jābālas declare: "Having completed the stage of the student (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller (*vanī*); having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce" (JābUp 4). However, the Teachers (*Ācāryas*), intending those possessed of passion and considering them ineligible for the three stages beginning with the lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*) among those who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), described only the state of the householder. As for the claim that the entire Veda prescribes only the duties of the householder, that is incorrect, because even for the forest-dweller, provided he is accompanied by his wife, the *agnihotra* and other rites exist. Furthermore, the duties of the lifelong celibate are recited by the Chandogas: "The student lives in the teacher’s family; the third [type of student] dwells in the teacher’s family until the very end of his life" (ChU 2.23.2). The duties of the temporary student (*upakurvāṇaka*) are well known in all the branches (*śākhā*) within the sections on initiation (*upanayana*), and the duties of the ascetic (*yati*) are found in the Upanishadic portions. Therefore, since scriptural texts such as "as long as life lasts" refer to those who possess desire, the other stages of life cannot be denied. Moreover, the four stages of life have been established in the *Brahma-sūtra* (Uttara-mīmāṃsā).
Therefore, the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), which follows in due order, is now introduced. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya prescribes it thus:

"Having entrusted his wife to his sons, or accompanied by her, he should go to the forest as a forest-dweller, observing celibacy, maintaining the sacred fires, and keeping the domestic fire. (YDh 3.45)

A forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) who desires to do so should go to the forest after entrusting his wife to his sons for their protection—since she is no longer required for his own practice of celibate discipline (*brahmacarya*)—on account of her being one who must be guarded. When she too, being self-restrained, desires to serve her husband, then he should go to the forest with her. In that case, he should go together with the two fires, the *vaitānika* and the *gṛhya*. However, in the case of entrusting her to his sons, he should renounce the world after having internalized the fires within himself (*ātmani samāropya*). Regarding this, Chāgaleya says: "A Brahmin without a wife, having internalized [the fires], should renounce the world from his home. Having gone to the forest, such a person should establish the sacred fire according to the method taught in the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra*. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says: "A forest-dweller shall have matted hair, wear rags and skins, and shall not stand upon land ploughed by a plow. He shall gather unploughed roots and fruits. He shall remain chaste (*ūrdhvaretas*), sleep on the ground, give gifts but never accept them. After five months, having established the *śrāmaṇaka* fire, he shall be a maintainer of the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). Dwelling at the foot of a tree, after six months he shall be without fire and without a fixed dwelling. He shall give to the gods, sages, ancestors, and men; he shall go to eternal heaven" (VaDh 9.1–13). The *śrāmaṇaka* refers to the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra*, which sets forth the duties of ascetics. By specifying "unploughed roots" as food, it indicates the abandonment of village food. For this very reason, Manu says: [Manu 6.15–20] "He shall live in a hermitage, subsisting on roots and fruits, or on grains obtained without cultivation, or on what has been naturally provided. He may eat vegetables, flowers, and roots in their proper season, or he may eat at every fourth mealtime. Or he may always subsist on water or air, or on what has fallen [of its own accord]. He shall offer oblations to the gods and ancestors according to the rule, and perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice and hospitality toward guests. He shall wear matted hair, carry a staff, wear an antelope skin, and be pure. He shall bathe three times a day, be self-controlled, and dwell in the forest until the end of his life. [Manu 6.21–24] "Or, having entrusted his wife to his sons, he may depart alone, having internalized the fires within himself. He shall enter the water at dawn, midday, and sunset, and subsist on water, air, and [fallen] leaves. He shall practice austerities in the forest, remaining chaste. He shall not step upon ploughed land, nor shall he eat anything grown in a village. He shall wear rags, skins, or grass garments, and let his beard, nails, and hair grow long. He shall honor the gods, ancestors, guests, and dependents, and he shall give to others, but never receive from them. [Manu 6.25–28] "He shall give to the gods, ancestors, sages, humans, and insects, and thus he shall attain the infinite world of heaven. He shall live on fallen fruits and roots, or on what has been spontaneously provided, or on unhusked grain obtained without cultivation. He shall eat at every fourth, sixth, or eighth mealtime, or even less frequently. He shall be content with whatever comes to him, whether it be bitter, pungent, astringent, sour, or sweet. He shall eat only what is fit for an ascetic, and he shall avoid all that is forbidden. He shall be patient, self-controlled, and ever devoted to the welfare of all beings. [Manu 6.29–32] "He shall dwell at the foot of a tree, in a temple, in an empty house, in a mountain cave, or in a place where animals congregate. He shall not be attached to any one place, and he shall wander through villages and cities. He shall not travel more than one *yojana* in a single day, except during the rainy season. He shall not stay in a village for more than one night, nor in a city for more than five nights. He shall always be intent on the welfare of all creatures, and he shall be free from anger, greed, and delusion. [Manu 6.33–36] "He shall constantly practice yoga, study the Vedas, and perform austerities. He shall be indifferent to praise and blame, and he shall look upon gold and a clod of earth as equal. He shall be impartial toward friends and enemies, and he shall not seek to harm anyone. He shall be a friend to all beings, and he shall be free from envy and pride. Thus disciplined, he shall conquer the senses and attain the supreme state. [Manu 6.37–40] "Whether he lives in a village or in the forest, he shall always maintain the sacred fires according to the rule. He shall offer sacrifices and give gifts, and he shall never neglect the ancestral rites. He shall be firm in his vows, and he shall not abandon the path of righteousness. He shall be constant in his devotion to the gods and ancestors, and he shall be ever vigilant in his duties. Thus, by following this way of life, he shall attain the highest goal. [Manu 6.41–44] "Having lived thus in the forest, he may eventually renounce all possessions and enter the fourth stage of life (*saṃnyāsa*). He shall give up the sacred fires and the ritual implements, and he shall wander without a fixed abode. He shall wear a single garment or be naked, and he shall beg for alms from the houses of those who are not known to him. He shall not be attached to any object, and he shall be free from desire and fear. He shall contemplate the Self, and he shall attain liberation. [Manu 6.45–48] "He shall not speak of his own virtues, nor shall he disparage others. He shall be silent regarding worldly matters, and he shall be intent on the welfare of all. He shall not seek to acquire wealth, and he shall not be concerned with the future. He shall be content with whatever comes to him, and he shall be free from attachment. Thus, by practicing this discipline, he shall attain the eternal state. [Manu 6.49–52] "He shall not be proud of his learning, nor shall he be arrogant because of his austerities. He shall be humble before the wise, and he shall be gentle toward the ignorant. He shall be patient with the wicked, and he shall be compassionate toward the suffering. He shall be a refuge for the distressed, and he shall be a teacher of the truth. Thus, by following this path, he shall reach the end of suffering. [Manu 6.53–56] "He shall not be attached to the pleasures of the senses, nor shall he be distracted by worldly concerns. He shall be focused on the Self, and he shall be free from the bonds of karma. He shall be indifferent to heat and cold, and he shall be unmoved by praise or blame. He shall be like a stone in water, and he shall be like the wind in space. He shall be like the sky, and he shall be like the earth. Thus, by attaining equanimity, he shall reach the state of Brahman. [Manu 6.57–60] "He shall not be concerned with the past, nor shall he be anxious about the future. He shall live in the present, and he shall be free from all mental agitation. He shall be like a child, and he shall be like a madman. He shall be like a fool, and he shall be like a sage. He shall be like a cloud, and he shall be like a mountain. Thus, by transcending all dualities, he shall attain the supreme peace. [Manu 6.61–64] "He shall not be attached to the body, nor shall he be attached to the mind. He shall be detached from the senses, and he shall be detached from the objects of the senses. He shall be detached from the world, and he shall be detached from the self. He shall be detached from everything, and he shall be free from all attachments. Thus, by becoming detached, he shall attain the state of liberation. [Manu 6.65–68] "He shall not be concerned with the rituals of the Vedas, nor shall he be concerned with the rituals of the world. He shall be beyond both, and he shall be established in the Self. He shall be beyond the reach of speech, and he shall be beyond the reach of thought. He shall be beyond the reach of the mind, and he shall be beyond the reach of the senses. He shall be beyond the reach of all things
"Having abandoned village food and all personal belongings, and having entrusted his wife to his sons, he should go to the forest, either alone or together with her. Thus [it is said].
Yama states the occasion for a householder’s entry into the forest:
Having lived the second part of his life at home, the twice-born man,
as a householder, should dwell in the forest during the third part of his life.

"Having produced sons according to the law of nature, having performed sacrifices according to his ability, and having seen the offspring of his offspring, a Brāhmaṇa should enter the forest. In this passage, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended as an illustration for all three social classes (*traivarṇika*), following the introductory statement: "But having lived in the house, the twice-born... Manu also says:
"But when a householder sees his own wrinkles and grey hair, and indeed the offspring of his offspring, then he should resort to the forest. (MDh 6.2)

Śaṅkha and Likhita also state: “[140] Having procreated sons, performed their sacraments, taught them the Veda, provided for their livelihood, united them with wives, and entrusted the family responsibilities to a virtuous son, one who has manifested the signs of departure should proceed through the specific modes of life. Having followed the mode of life of the *yāyāvara* [wandering ascetics] in due order, he should resort to the forest during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight. This is to be understood as referring to the position that the stages of life (*āśrama*) are to be practiced cumulatively. However, according to the position that they are not cumulative, even one who has not fulfilled the householder stage is qualified for the forest-dweller stage (*vānaprastha*). To this effect says Vasiṣṭha: “There are four stages of life: the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant. Having studied the Veda—one, two, or all three—without violating the vow of celibacy, he may enter whichever among them he desires” (VaDh 7.1–3). Āpastamba also, having begun by stating, “The four stages of life are the householder’s, the teacher’s household, the silent sage’s, and the forest-dweller’s,” concludes with, “He may undertake whatever he desires” (ĀpDh 2.9.21.1). Yājñavalkya states what must be done by one established in the forest:

"Self-possessed and wearing matted hair and body hair, he should constantly satisfy the sacred fires, the ancestors, the gods, guests, and his dependents with food not produced by the plow. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.46).
"Not produced by the plow" refers to vegetables, roots, wild rice (*nīvāra*), and the like. And so Manu says:
[141] "With various kinds of pure food fit for sages, and with vegetables, roots, and fruits—with these very things one should perform the great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule. (MDh 6.5)

Nor should it be argued: "How can there be an offering to the fires for forest-dwellers (*vanastha*) who are without fire, such as celibate students (*brahmacārin*) and widowers (*vidhura*)," because the fire prescribed in the *Vaikhānasa-śāstra* exists for them. Nor should one suspect that if a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is made from wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like grown without plowing, the Vedic injunction "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*) would be contradicted; for rice that grows without plowing is indeed possible. Therefore, one should perform the Vedic ritual (*vaitānika-karma*) with rice and other grains that ripen without cultivation. And so says Manu: "And one should offer the Vedic fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*) according to the rule."
Without omitting the new moon sacrifice, and especially the full moon sacrifice.
One should perform the Ṛkṣeṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsyas,
as well as the Turāyaṇa and the Dakṣāyaṇa, in their proper sequence.

"With pure, seasonal foods fit for sages, gathered by himself, he should offer the *puroḍāśa* and the *caru* according to the prescribed rule. (MDh 6.9–11). "Pure" means fit for sacrifice; "foods fit for sages" means grains that ripen without cultivation. Yājñavalkya states the quantity of the materials to be collected:
"One should accumulate wealth for a day, a month, six months, or likewise for a year; once it has been accumulated, one should relinquish it in the month of Āśvayuja. (YDh 3.47)

One should accumulate as much wealth as is sufficient for the task to be accomplished in a single day; this same principle should be applied to the cases of a month, a year, or a fortnight. In that regard, if anything remains accumulated, one should discard it all in the month of Āśvayuja. As Viṣṇu says: "There may be accumulation for a month or accumulation for a year. One who has accumulated for a year should discard that previous accumulation in Āśvayuja. Having discarded the former, one should then accumulate anew. Manu also says:
"In the month of Āśvayuja, one should discard the forest-dweller’s food previously accumulated."
And likewise, worn-out garments, as well as vegetables, roots, and fruits.
"He may be one who washes [his food] immediately, or one who stores for a month,
or one who accumulates for six months, or even one who accumulates for a year" (MDh 6.15–18).
Regarding that, the same author states those things which are to be avoided:
One should avoid honey and meat, as well as mushrooms growing from the earth,
bhūstṛṇa grass, śigruka, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree.

[143] “One should not eat what has been ploughed by a plow, even if it has been abandoned by someone; nor, even when distressed, should one eat the flowers and fruits of village-grown trees. (MDh 6.14, 16).
*Kavakāni* refers to mushrooms (*chatrākāṇi*). Yājñavalkya states the rule for ascetic discipline (*taponiyama*):
Self-controlled, bathing at the three sessions of the day, abstaining from accepting gifts,
devoted to sacred study, habitually generous, and intent on the welfare of all sentient beings.
Using his teeth as a mortar, eating only what ripens naturally in due time, or using a stone for grinding,
he should perform the rites and activities prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti with fruits and oils.
One should pass the time with Cāndrāyaṇa fasts or always subsist on Kṛcchra penances;
one may eat only when a fortnight has passed, or when a month has passed, or even when a day has passed.

Being pure, he should sleep on the ground at night; during the day, he should pass the time by standing on tiptoe, or by alternating between standing, sitting, and walking, or likewise by the practice of yoga.

"In summer he should stand amidst five fires; during the rains he should sleep on the bare ground; and in winter he should wear wet clothes, or else perform penance according to his ability. (YDh 3.48–52)

The teeth themselves are the mortar; one who possesses this as his means for dehusking is a *dantolūkhalika*. The meaning is that he is independent of external implements such as a mortar and so forth. [144] "Ripe by time" refers to fruits such as the jujube (*badara*), *iṅguda*, and breadfruit (*panasa*). One who grinds with a stone—that is, threshes—is an *aśmakuṭṭaka*. "Oils produced from the fruits of particularly pure trees" refers to oils born from the fruits of trees such as the *likuca* and *madhuka*. "Activities" refers to eating, anointing the body, and so on. Viṣṇu also says: "He may eat flowers; he may eat fruits; he may eat roots; he may eat vegetables; he may eat leaves; or he may eat barley-food once at the end of each fortnight" (ViDh 95.7–12). It is also stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
One may stand on one leg, or always drink the rays of the sun;
or one may inhale the smoke of five fires, or inhale heat, or drink the soma.
One should drink milk during the bright fortnight and cow dung during the dark fortnight;
or one may subsist on withered leaves, or always conduct oneself according to the *kṛcchra* penances.
A student of the *Atharvaśiras*, devoted to the study of the Vedānta,
should constantly practice the restraints (*yamas*) and the observances (*niyamas*) with unwearied diligence.
Having conquered the senses and subdued anger, reflecting upon the knowledge of reality,
he should always remain a celibate student and should not resort to a wife.
But he who, having gone to the forest with his wife, should engage in sexual intercourse out of desire, his vow would be broken; that twice-born man must perform an expiation.
One should eat food at night after having gathered it by day according to one's ability;
or one may observe the fourth-meal rule, or even the eighth-meal rule.
Or he should observe the Cāndrāyaṇa rules during both the bright and dark fortnights;
in each fortnight, he should eat boiled barley gruel only once.
"Or he may always subsist solely on flowers, roots, and fruits—those that are natural and have fallen of their own accord—remaining established in the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas. Thus [it is said].
Yājñavalkya speaks regarding one who is incapable of performing the service of the sacred fires:
Or, having internalized the sacred fires within himself, dwelling among trees and restricting his food,
he should beg for alms solely for the sake of sustenance at the dwellings of forest-dwellers.
"Or, having brought morsels from a village, he should eat eight of them while restraining his speech. Thus [it is said]. Manu also says:
"Having formally deposited the Vedic sacrificial fires within himself according to the rule..."
He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, a sage subsisting on roots and fruits.
Exerting no effort for the sake of pleasures, he was a celibate student sleeping on the ground,
among other householders, twice-born men, and forest-dwellers.
[146] Living in the forest, he should bring food from the village and eat eight mouthfuls,
having received it either in a leaf-cup, in his hand, or in a potsherd.

"A Brahmin living in the forest should practice these and other initiations. Having cast off his body by means of one or another of these practices of the great seers, the Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahman. (MDh 6.25–32)
Now, an objection might be raised: would this not contradict the injunction regarding the rule of eight morsels, namely the statement, "The forest-dwellers [take] sixteen" (ĀpDh 2.4.9.13)?

That is not so, because the arrangement is justified by the distinction between those who are capable and those who are incapable. With reference to one who is unable to perform all the practices, Yājñavalkya says:
"Subsisting on air, he should go toward the northeast until his body is completely worn away" (YDh 3.55).
In the Kūrma Purāṇa as well: "Abiding by the rule for the attainment of Brahman, he should undertake the Great Departure, or fasting, or entering the fire, or some other [method]."
But he who correctly takes refuge in this auspicious stage of life, which destroys the multitude of inauspicious things,
goes to the supreme, divine state that removes all suffering, wherein the stability of this entire world resides.
the stage of the forest-dweller has been described in this manner.
Now the fourth stage of life is described. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Having thus spent the third part of his life in the forests, he should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life" (MDh 6.33).

Yājñavalkya also says: "Having performed from the forest or from the house the sacrifice to Prajāpati, for which the sacrificial fee consists of all one's possessions, and at its conclusion having internalized those fires within himself..."

"Having studied the Vedas, performed recitations, fathered a son, given food, maintained the sacred fires, and offered sacrifices according to his ability, one should then set one's mind on liberation; not otherwise. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.56–57).

With the intention of prescribing the integration of all four stages of life (*āśrama*), it is stated that "one should set one's mind on liberation from the forest [stage]. With the intention of prescribing the integration of only three stages of life, the alternative view is presented as "or from the householder stage."

Now, one might object: "In this case as well, let it be intended that there is simply a conjunction of all four stages, since it is possible to practice the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) immediately after the stage of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). Do not say so; for the ascent through the four stages of life, beginning with studentship (*brahmacarya*), is fixed by rule. Thus, the Jābālas record the ascent of the stages: "Having completed studentship, one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce" (JābUp 4). However, such a descent is nowhere recorded in scripture. On the contrary, Dakṣa prohibits descent.
There may be movement in the natural order of the three [castes], but not in the reverse order;
there is no one more wicked than he who proceeds by way of the reverse order.
"He who, having entered the householder stage of life, becomes a celibate student again, neither a renunciant nor a forest-dweller—he is excluded from all stages of life. (DaSm 1.9–13)

If a householder should somehow descend from his stage and become a *brahmacārin* again, he would then be excluded from all stages of life (*āśrama*) because he has fallen after having ascended. Consequently, he cannot be designated by words that denote the stages of life, such as "forest-dweller" (*vanastha*) and so forth. This absence of descending is described in the third chapter of the *Uttara-mīmāṃsā*. Regarding the phrase "from the forest or from the home," one should also understand "or from the student stage" (*brahmacaryād vā*). When detachment arises even in childhood due to the ripening of merit performed in previous births, then one who has not yet married may renounce directly from the student stage. Thus says the *Jābāla-śruti*: "Or otherwise, one may renounce directly from the student stage, or from the home, or from the forest" (*JābUp* 4). Having previously presented the combination of the four stages of life for Jābāla when he was not yet detached—dividing his lifespan according to the stages—the alternative beginning with "or otherwise" is presented with reference to one who is detached. "Otherwise" means when detachment occurs while still in childhood. The renunciation of one who has not married is shown in the *Nṛsiṃha-purāṇa*.
"He whose tongue, genitals, stomach, and head are well-guarded—such a Brahmin, remaining celibate and unmarried, should renounce. Thus [it is said].
Aṅgiras also says:
Having seen that cyclic existence itself is devoid of essence, and desiring to see the essential,
he renounces the world without having performed marriage, relying upon supreme dispassion.
"One should go forth with the practice of celibacy; one may go forth even from the home;
or the wise man, whether afflicted or suffering, may go forth from the forest.
Here, "suffering" means being oppressed by disease, thieves, tigers, and so forth; "afflicted" means desiring to die. Regarding this, the *Mahābhārata* states:
When a terrible crisis has arisen— a crisis involving thieves, tigers, and the like—
the sage Aṅgiras declared that renunciation is for one who is terrified by fear.
In the case of those who are ill, there is neither formal procedure nor ritual action for renunciation;
having merely uttered the command, one should proclaim the renunciation in that instance.
[150] Thus it is said.
But surely—if one were to undertake renunciation immediately after the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*), the words of Manu would be contradicted:
"Having discharged the three debts, one should apply the mind to liberation."
But one who pursues liberation without having discharged [these debts] goes downward.
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma,
and having performed sacrifices to the best of one's ability, one should direct the mind toward liberation.
"Without having studied the Vedas from his teacher, without having procreated sons, and without having performed sacrifices, one who desires liberation goes downward. (MDh 6.35–37)

The three debts are shown by the Śruti: "Indeed, a Brāhmaṇa, being born, is born with three debts: to the sages through studentship (*brahmacarya*), to the gods through sacrifice (*yajña*), and to the ancestors through progeny (*prajā*). He indeed is debt-free who has a son, who is a sacrificer, or who is a student" (BDh 2.9.26.7). When even the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇamārga*), which leads to heaven, is not possible without the discharge of these debts, what then can be said of the path to liberation (*mokṣamārga*)? For this very reason, the Vedic mantra says: "May we be debt-free in this world, debt-free in the next, and debt-free in the third world."
May we pass through all the paths—those leading to the gods and those leading to the fathers—free from debt.

[151] Thus it is said. Furthermore, the Brāhmaṇa states: "He wanders through all the worlds free from debt. This is not so; for these statements refer to those who are not yet dispassionate. For this very reason, the Jābāla Śruti prohibits delay in the time for renunciation for one who is dispassionate: "On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce" (JābUp 4).

Now, an objection is raised: according to the method stated, it would follow that only those who have duly performed the duties in the stages of life (āśramas), such as studentship and the rest, may "renounce from their respective stage"—and this being the case, renunciation (saṃnyāsa) would not be possible for those outside the stages of life, such as the *snātaka* or the widower, nor for certain members of the stages of life who, due to some obstacle, fail to perform the prescribed duties even though they possess dispassion (*vairāgya*).

Not so; for they are enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) itself: "Now, whether he be one who observes vows or not, whether he be a graduate (*snātaka*) or not, whether his sacred fires have been extinguished or he is without fires—if on the very day he becomes detached, on that very day he should go forth" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4). Yama also says:
"In the absence of taking a wife again, one whose wife has died may go forth;
or one dwelling in the forest, having shaken off his sins, may resort to the supreme path."

In the third chapter, it was deliberated that those situated in the intermediate stages—such as *snātakas* and *vidhurakas*—possess eligibility for the stage of liberation (*mokṣāśrama*), because the purification of the mind can be achieved through practices such as recitation (*japa*), fasting (*upavāsa*), and pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*), even while remaining independent of the formal stages of life (*āśrama*). Furthermore, for one who feels remorse despite a lapse in duty, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is possible as a means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Accordingly, another *smṛti* states:
"The faults born of one's lineage and those arising from one's actions—all these renunciation burns away, just as fire in a crucible purifies gold."
Manu also says:

"That which is to be purified is cleansed by earth and water; a river is purified by its current; a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born is purified by renunciation. (MDh 5.108)

On this point, some maintain that the qualification for renunciation belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone, and not to the Kṣatriya or the Vaiśya; they cite both Śruti and Smṛti as evidence. In this regard, the Vājasaneyaka-Brāhmaṇa states: "Having known this very Self, Brāhmaṇas, rising above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, then lead the life of a mendicant" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1). Manu, moreover, employs the word "Brāhmaṇa" in both the opening and the conclusion [of his discussion]: "Having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa may depart from his home into the life of a wandering ascetic" (Manusmṛti 6.38).
Thus is the introduction;
[153] "This fourfold dharma of the Brāhmaṇa has been declared to you" (MDh 6.97)—thus is the conclusion. Nārada also says:
Or even from the first stage of life, a Brahmin who is disenchanted with the ocean of existence and seeks liberation should renounce all attachments and go forth as a wandering mendicant.
Thus [says] Yājñavalkya the Yogin:
"Four stages of life are prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa as enjoined by the Śruti;
three are declared for the Kṣatriya; and two, indeed, for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra. (YogY 1.28)
Thus it is said. Also in the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"These four stages of life (āśrama) are proclaimed for the Brāhmaṇa:
the householder's stage, the student's stage, and the forest-dweller's stage—these are the three stages of life."
The same conduct that has been prescribed for the twice-born is indeed declared for the Kṣatriya as well;
however, for the Vaiśya, there are only two stages of life: studentship and the householder stage.
"O night-stalker, the householder's stage alone is appropriate for a Śūdra. (Vāyu Purāṇa 14.16–18).
Now, one might object: "But there is no stage of life at all for a Śūdra;
O dear one, there are four stages of life, and among them, a Śūdra does not qualify."

Because of this prohibition, how can his acceptance of the householder’s stage (*gārhasthya*) be justified? It is replied: it is marriage accompanied by mantras that is prohibited, not marriage without mantras. Otherwise, the statements cited in the section on marriage concerning the Śūdra, as well as the statements regarding the Śūdra’s entitlement to the duties of a householder—such as the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and so forth—would be contradicted. Therefore, the householder’s life exists for the Śūdra. However, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), according to the manner already stated, belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone. For this very reason, in another Smṛti, the wearing of the ochre robe, staff, and other insignia is forbidden for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya.
This dharma, which is the wearing of the marks of Viṣṇu, is for those born from the mouth;
it is not ordained as a dharma for those born from the arms or those born from the thighs.

Thus [it is said]. Others, however, maintain that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is intended for those belonging to the three twice-born castes (*traivarṇika*), because the four stages of life (*āśrama*), whether as a combined whole or by option, are prescribed in many *smṛtis* for any twice-born person who has studied the Vedas. For this very reason, the word "twice-born" (*dvija*) is employed by Yājñavalkya in the section on renunciation:
