"Having restrained the collection of senses and having abandoned passion and hatred..."
"Having removed the fear of living beings, the twice-born becomes immortal" (YDh 3.61).
However, another Smṛti text ordains renunciation for the three castes by specifically naming them:
"Having discharged the three debts, free from the sense of 'mine' and free from egoism..."
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, one may go forth from the home.
Thus it is said. In the *Kūrma Purāṇa* as well, the term "twice-born" (*dvija*) is employed:

"Having established the sacred fires within himself, the twice-born should become a renunciant (*pravrajita*), devoted to the practice of yoga, tranquil, and intent upon the knowledge of Brahman. (*KūPu* 1.2.28.2)

Thus, those previously cited statements are intended to prohibit the wearing of saffron robes and carrying of staffs by Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. Accordingly, the statement "of those born from the mouth" was cited. Baudhāyana also says:
"This is the duty of Brāhmaṇas, namely the bearing of the marks of Viṣṇu;
it is not so for Rājanyas and Vaiśyas"—such is the word of the sage Dattātreya.

Thus it is said: one who desires to become a wandering mendicant (parivrāj) should perform the Prājāpatya sacrifice, giving away all his possessions as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Regarding this, Manu says:

"Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's wealth is given as the fee, and having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa may depart from his home to wander forth. (MDh 6.38)

Thus it is said. Or else, one should perform an *iṣṭi* sacrifice to Agni. Regarding this, it is stated in the Śruti: “Now, some indeed perform an *iṣṭi* to Prajāpati; but one should not do so. One should perform only that to Agni. For Agni is breath; by means of this [sacrifice], he makes [himself] breath” (JābUp 4). Also in the Kūrma Purāṇa: “Having performed an *iṣṭi* either to Prajāpati or to Agni, and having internally purified his passions (*kaṣāya*), he should take recourse to the stage of life of a Brahman (*brahmāśrama*)” (KūPu 1.2.28.4).

[156] Thus it is said. Among these, the *prājāpatyeṣṭi* pertains to one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), because of the mention of a plurality of fires in the phrase "having consigned the fires" (*agnīn samāropya*). The *āgneyī*, however, pertains to one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), because in the supplementary portion of that passage it says, "he should smell the fire," which refers to a single fire. And that sacrifice is to be performed preceded by the *śrāddha* and other rites. Accordingly, the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa* states:

"Thus, while remaining in the forest hermitage, having burnt away his sins through austerity, the twice-born man should enter the fourth stage of life after renouncing according to the prescribed rule."
One should diligently offer gifts to the ancestors, to the gods, and to one's own forefathers; likewise, having performed the śrāddha for the sages, for human beings, and for oneself.

"Having performed either the Vaiśvānara-iṣṭi or the Prājāpatya-iṣṭi, and having established the fire within himself according to the mantras, he should then go forth again as a wandering mendicant. (NṛPu 60.2–4).
Furthermore, there are eight types of Śrāddhas, beginning with the Daiva; thus Baudhāyana says:

"One should perform the eight types of *śrāddha* offerings: those for the gods (*daiva*), the sages (*ārṣa*), the celestial beings (*divya*), the ancestors (*pitrya*), the mothers (*mātṛka*), humans (*mānuṣa*), the elements (*bhautika*), and finally for the Self (*ātman*). Thus it is said.
The fitness for the aforementioned *śrāddhas* and other rites must be accomplished through *kṛcchra* penances. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:

"Having performed four *kṛcchra* penances for the sake of purification, if he is not yet in a stage of life (*anāśramin*), or if he is already in one (*āśramin*), he should perform the *taptakṛcchra*; by that, he shall attain fitness.
Thus Baudhāyana states the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) pertaining to the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) which occurs after the *śrāddha* and precedes the subsequent rites.
Having performed all the *śrāddha* rites for the ancestors and others individually on the *aṣṭaka* days,
and having had his hair and other [body hair] shaved, he should purify these maternal deities (*mātṛkā*).
Three staffs made of bamboo, as thick as a finger, reaching up to the head,
and having eleven, nine, two, three, four, seven, or eight joints.
The bamboo splints should be without blemishes, smooth, with joints of equal length,
wrapped with a rope made of black cow-hair, and four finger-breadths in width.
Or such a staff may be made of a single piece of wood, devoid of cow-hair,
or it may be made of threads of kuśa grass, cotton, or even linen.
The cord, knotted with auspicious knots and fashioned in the shape of a lotus,
should have six or five strands and extend for the distance of two fist-lengths.
With disheveled hair, white and indistinct, measuring twelve finger-breadths on both sides;
or else double or triple that, or eight finger-breadths all around.
Or, a water-purifier is known to be made of fine cotton fibers, one span in length, free from holes,
and not handled by outcasts such as Caṇḍālas.
If he has taken up a water-pot along with its carrying-sling, consecrated with mantras—
whether it be made of wood, bamboo, clay, or gourd.
The vessel should be made of stone, copper, or even of leaves and the like;
the auspicious seat should be made of wood, either square or circular.
A garment to cover the private parts, a patched cloak to ward off the cold,
and sandals for the sake of cleanliness— these are declared to be the ten [requisites].
An umbrella, a purifier, a water-strainer, a tripod, as well as a deerskin,
lotuses, a rosary, a clay digging-stick, and a small dagger.
The meditation belt and the outer garment—these constitute the twenty-one [articles].
Of these, five or more are essential; ten or all of them may be used as well.
Having taken these, he then comes to a temple, a fire-chamber,
the outskirts of a village, the boundary of a village, or any other pure and pleasing place.
Having consumed clarified butter, milk, and curd— or indeed water, which is threefold—
while reciting "Oṃ Bhūḥ" and so forth, one should thereafter fast for the night.
By this very rule, a twice-born man may become a mendicant in times of distress;
then, before the setting of the sun, he should distribute the sacred fires.
Having consecrated the clarified butter over the Gārhapatya fire,
he should offer it into the Āhavanīya fire with a full sruva-spoon while reciting the syllable Om.
This shall be the Brahmānvādhāna after the Agnihotra has been offered;
having then spread darbha grass to the north of the Gārhapatya fire.
Then, having set out the vessels, he should sit in the very place of the Brahman priest upon strewn darbha grass,
or rather upon those covered with an antelope skin.
One should remain awake during this night until the Brāhma-muhūrta;
having attained this state, even one who has died enjoys infinity.

"Having performed the Agnihotra at its proper time, one should then perform the morning [Agnihotra] and subsequently offer either the Vaiśvānara-iṣṭi or the Prājāpatya-iṣṭi. After consuming the clarified butter and other substances, but before the carrying forth of the fire (agnivaharaṇa), one should perform the entry of the Sāvitrī. This is stated in the Baudhāyana-dharma:
Oṃ bhūḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *tatsavitur vareṇyam*. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *bhargo devasya dhīmahi*.
Oṃ suvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*.

"Thus, either verse by half-stanza or with the whole [verse]" (BDh 2.10.14). Having completed the *iṣṭi* sacrifice and having internalized the fires within himself, he should utter the *praiṣa*. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"Having internalized the fires within himself and standing in the middle of the altar, [he worships] Hari."
Having meditated thus in his heart and being authorized by the Guru, he should utter the command.
[160] Thus it is said. Then, having uttered the command (*praiṣa*), one should perform the granting of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*). This is stated in the *Kapilamata*:
"Having duly uttered the command three times in a whisper and twice aloud, [one should say]:
'Fearlessness to all beings from me, svāhā! and [pour] water upon the ground."
"Desiring to lead [the fire], he should then go outside, taking the staff, the sling, and so forth.
Regarding the mantras for the staff and other items, Baudhāyana says:
"With the mantra beginning 'sakhā me' (my friend), one should take the staff offered by the Guru."
Having recited "yena devāḥ pavitreṇa," [he places] the water-strainer.
With the verse beginning "That which is on the further shore of this darkness, the radiant," he should [offer] a small net;
likewise, with the *vyāhṛtis*, a vessel; and then, with the *ṛc* beginning "The loincloth."
Taking that auspicious sacred thread with the mantra "The youth well-attired," he should go forth and abandon his own village and kinsmen.
"Free from desire for anything else, having gone forth, he should always conduct himself according to his own vows.

And this [practice] of the water-strainer (*jalapavitra*) and so forth pertains to the first two among the four types of mendicants (*bhikṣu*). Regarding the fourfold classification of mendicants, Hārīta says:
"Mendicants are said to be of four kinds, those who bear the common marks..."
The distinct knowledge of each of them, including their differences in function and so forth, has been heard [from the scriptures].
"The Kuṭīcaka, the Bahūdaka, and the Haṃsa as the third;
the fourth is the Paramahaṃsa: whichever comes later is the superior. Thus [says] Pitāmaha.
[161] O monks, four types of ascetics are proclaimed from the mouth of Brahmā:
the *kuṭīcaka*, the *bahūdaka*, and the *haṃsa* as the third.
"The fourth is the *parahaṃsa*; thus they are proclaimed through these different designations.
In this regard, the specific qualification [for each] is shown in the Purāṇa:
"Detachment is said to be of two kinds: intense (*tīvra*) and extremely intense (*tīvratarā*)."
But when his intense [desire] has indeed subsided, the yogi Kuṭīcaka should deposit [the breath].
"One capable [of practice] is in Bahūdaka; in Tīvra-yāya, one is called a Haṃsa;
one desiring liberation is in Parama-haṃsa, which is the direct means for attaining realized knowledge. (NṛPu 60–13)

Regarding that, Prajāpati describes the specific mode of life for the *kuṭīcaka*: “The one called *kuṭīcaka*, residing in his own home, pure and unsullied, eating alms among those who maintain the sacred fires, having abandoned desire, anger, greed, and delusion, and being free from egoism, effects his own spiritual benefit. Vṛddha-Parāśara also says: “Those called *kuṭīcakas*, having had a cottage built by their sons and others, and having abandoned desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, take up renunciation according to rule; wearing the triple staff, the water-purifier, and ochre-colored garments, they are devoted to bathing, purification, sipping water, recitation, study, celibacy, and meditation; at the time of begging, consuming only as much food as is necessary for subsistence from their sons and others, and dwelling constantly in that cottage, they liberate themselves. This is also stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
But the *kuṭīcaka*, having renounced, should always take alms and eat either in his own home or in the house of his own kinsmen.
"He should have a topknot, wear the sacred thread, carry a triple staff, and possess a water-pot.
Since the *kuṭīcaka* mode is intended for those who lack full capacity, residence in a house and so forth is appropriate for him. This was stated by Baudhāyana:
"The *kuṭīcakas*, having renounced the world, [should remain] constantly in their own respective homes."
"Having received alms from their kinsmen, they eat due to the exhaustion of their [other] means.
Skanda describes the specific mode of life for the Bahūdaka:
"But the Bahūdaka, having renounced, is devoid of kinsmen, sons, and so forth."
One should go for alms at seven houses and renounce eating food from a single source.
A triple staff bound with a cow-hair rope,
a raised sling, a water vessel, a strainer, a digging tool, and a small knife.
"One should maintain the topknot (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and perform the worship of the deity.

Thus says Vṛddha-Parāśara: "In this regard, those known as Bahūdakas carry three staffs, a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a lotus, a purifier (*pavitra*), and an alms-bowl, and wear ochre-colored garments; they are those who understand the meaning of Vedānta, and by practicing the life of begging for alms in the houses of Brahmins of virtuous conduct, they liberate themselves. Pitāmaha also says: "He should be known as a Bahūdaka when he is free from all attachments."
He should not beg from his circle of kinsmen, nor should he dwell in his own land.
Immovable and become like a pillar, always intent upon liberation,
he should not form an attachment in his mind toward a hut, water, or clothing.

"A renunciant should not indeed harbor attachment toward his dwelling, seat, food, bedding, or his triple staff, nor toward his own measure of [other] staffs and such. Thus is the "Swan-like Conduct" (*haṃsavṛtti*) shown in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
The swan [should provide] a water-pot, a carrying-net, and likewise an alms-bowl;
a patched garment, a loincloth, a covering, a body-wrap, and an outer cloth.
"One should always respectfully carry a single staff made of bamboo;
one should perform meditation and worship [the deity] without making any distinction among the deities. Thus [says the text]. Viṣṇu also [states]:

"The sacred thread, the staff, the garment, and the means for warding off insects—this much is declared to be the possession [of a renunciant]; there is no other possession for a *haṃsa*. Thus says the Grandfather (Brahmā). Furthermore:
The third is to be known as the *haṃsa*, the monk who is intent upon liberation;
he should bathe daily at the three sessions of the day and always remain with wet clothes on.
"One should subsist by means of the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance, according to the instruction on the duties of an ascetic;
one should always dwell at the root of a tree, or in a cave, or on the bank of a river.
Thus [says] Baudhāyana as well.
Carrying water-pots, shoulder-bags, staffs, and bowls, these swan-like ascetics stay for only one night at a village pilgrimage site, and for five nights in a city.
"Those who fast for three six-night periods, those who fast for a fortnight or a month,
and those whose bodies are emaciated by vows such as the *kṛcchra* and *sāntapana* [are Paramahaṃsas]. Thus is the conduct of the Paramahaṃsa shown in the Skanda Purāṇa.
He should take a garment for covering his private parts, a patched cloth to ward off the cold,
a rosary of beads, and a flawless staff made of bamboo.
The Parahamsa should practice eating from a single source, like honey collected by bees;
the Parahamsa [should also discard] the triple staff and the rope made of cow-hair.
"One should permanently abandon the topknot (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) from one's daily rites.

Regarding this, some—incapable of tolerating the abandonment of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*), the *gāyatrī*, the topknot, and the sacred thread due to the dullness of their faith—hate the state of the Paramahaṃsa as it has been described. They cite certain scriptural passages to support their view; among them, Hārīta says:
"Indeed, even these four stages of life (*āśrama*) are devoid of the twilight prayers."
"They fall from their status as Brahmins even if they possess fierce asceticism" (Hārīta Smṛti 14.18). Baudhāyana also says:
"Those who do not attend the morning [service] before it has arrived, nor the evening [service] after it has passed..."
"How can those Brahmins who do not perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) be considered Brahmins? (BDh 2.4.15). Also in another Smṛti:
"Those Brahmins who never perform the twilight devotions in the evening and in the morning..."
"A righteous king may, if he so desires, employ them in the tasks of Śūdras. Thus [says the law]. Manu also says:
"Those who have fallen away from the Sāvitrī become Vratyas, despised by the Āryas. (MDh 2.39)
Atri also says:
"The sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is the means to liberation for all twice-born (*dvija*).
Those men who abandon it out of delusion go to hell. (AtrSm 3)
Also in the Padma Purāṇa:
"How can he be a twice-born man if he has abandoned the topknot and the sacred thread?"

It is not so; for these statements are also consistent with referring to those other than the *paramahaṃsa*. But how can one possibly harbor hatred toward the state of the *paramahaṃsa*, which is perceived in many direct scriptural texts (*pratyakṣa-śruti*)? Thus says the Jābāla Śruti: "In that regard, those known as *paramahaṃsas*—namely Saṃvartaka, Āruṇi, Śvetaketu, Durvāsas, Ṛbhu, Nidāgha, Jaḍabharata, Dattātreya, Raivataka, and others—bear unmanifest signs, follow unmanifest conduct, and though not insane, behave like the insane" (JābUp 6). Furthermore, their abandonment of the topknot (*śikhā*) and so forth, as well as their duties such as self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*), are heard of in that very same text: [166]

Having cast away the staff, the water-pot, the sling, the alms-bowl, the water-strainer, the top-knot, and the sacred thread—saying "Bhūḥ Svāhā"—into the waters, he should seek the Self. Wearing his natural form, free from the pairs of opposites, without possessions, perfectly established on the path of the Brahman-Tattva, pure in mind, and for the sake of sustaining life, he should practice begging at the prescribed times as one who is liberated. Remaining equal in gain and loss, using his hands as a bowl, he dwells without a fixed home in empty houses, temples, straw huts, anthills, at the roots of trees, in potteries, near sacrificial fires, on riverbanks, in mountain caves, ravines, or on open ground. Effortless, free from the sense of "mine," devoted to pure meditation, and grounded in the inner self, intent on uprooting inauspicious karma, he who abandons the body through renunciation is called a Paramahaṃsa. Thus. (Jābāla Upaniṣad 6)

And in that very same scripture, in the form of a dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya, the abandonment of the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) is addressed as follows: "I ask you, Yājñavalkya: how can one be a Brahmin without the sacrificial thread? He, Yājñavalkya, replied: "This very Self (*ātman*) is his sacrificial thread" (JābUp 5). Furthermore, the state of the Paramahaṃsa is elaborated upon in the Āruṇi-śruti:
Āruṇi went to the world of Prajāpati. Having gone there, he said: "O Blessed One, by what means are all actions completely [abandoned]?"

"Release them," he said. Prajāpati spoke to him: "One should release one's sons, enemies, kinsmen, and so forth; the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), the sacrifice (*yāga*), the sacred cord (*sūtra*), and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*); as well as the *bhūrloka*, *bhuvarloka*, and *svarloka*; the *atala*, *vitala*, *sutala*, *talātala*, *mahātala*, *rasātala*, and *pātāla*; and the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). One should accept only a staff, a covering garment, and a loincloth (*kaupīna*); everything else should be released. Whether one is a student (*brahmacārī*), a householder (*gṛhastha*), or a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), one should internalize the worldly fires (*laukikāgni*) into the fire of the stomach. One should release the sacrificial thread into the earth or into water. A *kuṭīcaka* ascetic who was a student should release his family; he should release his alms-bowl; he should release his staff and the worldly fires—so he said. From this point forward, one should act without mantras; one should release the upward movement [of the breath]; one should perform the ritual bath at the three junctions of the day (*trisandhya*). One should practice the union (*saṃdhi*) within the self through meditative absorption (*samādhi*). One should recite the *Āraṇyaka* from all the Vedas; one should recite the *Upaniṣad*. (ĀrUp 1)"

Thus it is said. Also in the *Maitrāyaṇa-śruti*: "With the mantra 'Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt,' one should hold three bamboo staffs in the right hand, or one. If there is only one, then having shaved the hair including the top-knot (*śikhā*) and having discarded the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*)," so it says. Also in the *Pippalāda-śākhā*:
"Having shaved the hair including the top-knot, the wise man should discard the external thread;
he should maintain [the realization] that the imperishable Supreme Brahman is the thread."
They say that a *sūtra* is so called because it provides instruction; the *sūtra* is indeed the supreme state.
He by whom that *sūtra* is known is a true Brahmin who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
The yogi who knows yoga and perceives reality should wear that thread by which all this is strung together, like clusters of jewels on a string.
The wise man, established in the supreme yoga, should discard the external thread;
he who possesses true consciousness should wear this thread, which is the very nature of Brahman.
By wearing this sūtra, one shall neither be defiled by food remnants nor impure;
for those who possess the sūtra within, they wear the sacrificial thread of knowledge.
[169] They indeed are the knowers of the Sūtras in this world, and they are the ones who wear the sacrificial thread;
they have knowledge as their crest-lock, they are established in knowledge, and knowledge is their sacrificial thread.
For them, knowledge alone is the supreme purifier;
knowledge is said to be their crest, just as the flame of fire is its crest—there is nothing else for one whose crest consists of knowledge.
That wise man is called "one with a crest" (śikhin), and not others who merely wear hair;
rather, it refers to those Brāhmaṇas and others who are authorized to perform Vedic rites.
This sutra is to be maintained by these [vows], for it is indeed remembered as a constituent part of ritual action;
he whose topknot consists of knowledge and whose sacred thread is likewise composed of that [knowledge]—[he is a true ascetic].
Those who know Brahman understand that his entire status as a Brāhmaṇa consists of this supreme sacred thread, which is the ultimate refuge.
"The learned man should wear the sacred thread; he is the sacrifice, and he is the knower of the sacrifice. Thus it is said. Also, in the *Vyāsa-smṛti*:
"Those of supreme intelligence declare that the sacred thread is an integral part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*)."
Because, according to the principle of what precedes, such a thing is not seen in the world prior [to its arising].
As long as one performs actions, for that long alone does it persist;
therefore, its abandonment is carried out together with those actions.
[170] Just as one would discard the *juhū* and other sacrificial ladles upon the destruction of the *agnihotra*,
and just as one discards the girdle and other such items out of a desire for the householder stage of life;

"Just as the wife discards the marriage-thread at the conclusion of an *iṣṭi* sacrifice, and as one discards the cups at the end of a Soma sacrifice, even so do the yogins desire the casting off of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Thus it is said.

Viśvāmitra also says: "Furthermore, some hold that the mark of a wandering mendicant is complete liberation from everything; having abandoned both truth and falsehood, pleasure and pain, these Vedas, and this world as well as the next, one should seek the Self, renouncing the topknot, the sacred thread, the water-pot, and the skull-bowl. Baudhāyana also says: "From this point forward, having discarded the sacred thread, the mantra, the garment, the staffs, the sling, the water-strainer, the water-pot, and the bowl, he takes up a single staff, saying: 'O friend, protect me! It is also stated in another Smṛti.
"But when that eternal Supreme Brahman has been realized, then, having taken up the single staff, one should discard the sacred thread and the topknot. Thus it is said.

On this point, some say: the injunctions regarding the abandonment of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) refer to the ancient sacrificial thread. Thus states the *Smṛti*: “Having clipped his nails, and having discarded his old garment, his sacrificial thread, and his water-pot, and having taken new ones, he should enter the village. If the sacrificial thread were merely an ancillary part of the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), then one would fall from Brahminhood itself. Therefore, even for the *paramahaṃsa*, there exists a sacrificial thread.

That is incorrect, because the aforementioned Smṛti refers to those such as the Bahūdaka, and because of the Śruti: “The Paramahaṃsa wanders about without a sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) nor clothing” (ParUp 2), and from another Śruti: “One who is without a sacrificial thread, being devoted to purity, may at will take up a single bamboo staff” (ĀśUp 4). Nor is it the case that rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and so forth are impossible without an external sacrificial thread, for this is established through a question and answer in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa: “What is his sacrificial thread? What is his crest-lock (*śikhā*)? How is his ritual rinsing? is the question; “This very thing is his sacrificial thread, which is meditation on the Self; knowledge is his crest-lock,” etc., is the answer. Furthermore, it is stated in the Pippalāda Śruti that Brahminhood is fully realized only for one who possesses the sacrificial thread and crest-lock consisting of knowledge.

However, some maintain that even for the *paramahaṃsa* there should be three staffs (*tridaṇḍa*), and they cite scriptural authorities for this. In that regard, Dakṣa, while describing the characteristics of all the stages of life (*āśrama*) in sequence, states the characteristic of the ascetic (*yati*) as "the ascetic indeed [is characterized] by the triple-staff" (*DaSm* 1.14). Having thus stated the characteristic of the ascetic, he prohibits the status of an ascetic for one devoid of the triple-staff: "He who does not possess these characteristics is neither one who requires penance nor a member of an order" (*DaSm* 1.15). Furthermore, Hārīta, Dattātreya, and Pitāmaha, after introducing the four types beginning with the *kuṭīcaka*, prescribe the triple-staff for all of them.
"And those twice-born ones are not distinguished by their outward signs (liṅga) due to the difference in their modes of life (vṛtti);
rather, their sign consists of a bamboo staff with three sections and a purifying ring (pavitra).
Thus says Atri as well.
"Some have their hair tied in a topknot, while others are shaven-headed mendicants;
mendicants are said to be of four kinds, and all of them indeed carry three staffs" (Atri Smṛti 1.13).
However, the statements regarding the single staff apply to cases where the triple staff is unavailable. Thus says Medhātithi.
"As long as the three staffs are not present, one should wander about with only one. Hārīta also says:
"If, through negligence, the water-strainer or the triple staff is lost..."
But he should carry a single staff made of bamboo, or one from the Palāśa or Bilva tree.
"Having taken them, he should wander about until a triple-staff (*tridaṇḍaka*) is obtained" (HārSm 11.14).

To this it is replied: To negate the single staff for the *paramahaṃsa* would result in contradiction with many scriptures (*āgama*). Indeed, the *śruti* and *smṛti* passages cited establish the single staff for the *paramahaṃsa*. This being the case, the statement by Medhātithi and Hārīta that the single staff is a secondary option (*anukalpa*) must refer to those such as the *bahūdaka*; for the *paramahaṃsa*, however, the single staff is not a secondary option. For Vyāsa says:
"The abandonment of the triple staff and the bearing of the single staff is seen in a single statement; therefore, this [latter] is primary.

As for the statement, "And all indeed are bearers of the triple staff," that refers to the staff of speech and so forth, and not with the intention of [referring to] the three physical rods. And thus says Manu:
The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of body— he in whose intellect these are established is called a "triple-staffed" ascetic (tridaṇḍin).
"Having cast aside this triple staff toward all beings, and having restrained desire and anger, a human being then attains perfection. (Manu Smṛti 12.10–11). Dakṣa also says:
"The staff of speech, the staff of mind, and likewise the staff of action—
he for whom these three staffs are restrained is called a *tridaṇḍin*.
He [the author] himself has also stated the nature of these three staffs:
The restraint of speech is said to be silence; the restraint of action is lack of exertion;
but for the restraint of the mind, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is prescribed.
[174] Thus it is said. Furthermore, as stated by Pitāmaha:
"The Supreme Paramahaṃsa is called the Fourth (turya); so the Śruti declares.
Endowed with restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), he is the bearer of the triple staff (tridaṇḍin) and has Viṣṇu as his form."
Thus, that too is intended to refer to the "staff of speech" and so forth, according to the manner already stated. Furthermore:
"Their staff, however, is made of bamboo, triple-tipped, and accompanied by a pavitra."

Thus is the mention of the three staffs (*tridaṇḍa*); that too is appropriate as referring specifically to the *bahūdaka*. For he who, while being a *bahūdaka*, practices the "swan-like" conduct (*haṃsa-vṛtti*) such as staying for only one night in a village, becomes a *haṃsa* by virtue of his conduct. And if he resorts to the conduct of a *paramahaṃsa*, such as listening to the Vedānta and so forth, then he becomes a *paramahaṃsa* by virtue of his conduct. For those [classes] beginning with the *haṃsa*, the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) alone is the outward mark (*liṅga*). With this very intention [it is said]:
"And those twice-born ones, though distinguished by differences in conduct, are not at all distinguished by their outward marks."

Thus it has been stated. Otherwise, the cited scriptural passages enjoining a single staff for both the *haṃsa* and the *paramahaṃsa*, who are the primary [categories], would be rendered meaningless. Therefore, there is only one staff for the *paramahaṃsa*.

Now, an objection: in the *Paramahaṃsopaniṣad*, even the single staff (*ekadaṇḍa*) is heard of only as secondary: “One may accept a loincloth, a staff, and a covering for the sake of the maintenance of one’s own body and for the benefit of the world; yet that is not the primary [path]. If it is asked, ‘Who is the primary?’—this is the primary: the Paramahaṃsa wanders without a staff, without a sling, and without a covering” (ParUp 1).
"Certainly. For a learned Paramahaṃsa, there is no utility whatsoever for an external staff. For this very reason, it is stated in the subsequent passage that knowledge alone is his staff:
'He by whom the staff of knowledge is held is called a single-staffed one' (ParUp 3)."

The carrying of a staff (*yaṣṭidhāraṇa*), however, pertains to the *paramahaṃsa* who is still desirous of knowledge (*vividiṣu*). Nor should one suspect that there is a lack of authority for the twofold division of the *paramahaṃsa* state based on the distinction between the knower (*vidvat*) and the seeker (*vividiṣu*), because such a distinction is found in the *Vājasaneyibrāhmaṇa*. “Having known this very Self, the Brāhmaṇas rise above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and then lead the life of a mendicant” (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.5.1). This is the authority for the renunciation of the knower (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*). “In this very way, having known [the Self], one becomes a sage (*muni*). Desiring this world alone, those who have gone forth (*pravrājinaḥ*) go forth” (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.22). In this passage, both the renunciation of the knower and the renunciation of the seeker are clearly understood. “The whole of this, saying ‘bhūḥ svāhā,’ having abandoned in the waters, one should seek the Self” (*Jābāla Upaniṣad* 6). In this statement of Jābāla, the *paramahaṃsa* state of the seeker (*vividiṣu*), consisting of the abandonment of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and so forth, is enjoined. And the Śruti, after censuring austerities such as the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*), sacrifice, and charity, prescribes the *paramahaṃsa* state with the words: “Renunciation (*nyāsa*) is Brahman; for Brahman is supreme, and the supreme is Brahman. These other austerities are indeed inferior; renunciation alone excels them” (*Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad* 21.2). Then, it demonstrates the eligibility of that seeker-paramahaṃsa for the knowledge of the Self with the words: “With ‘Om,’ one should unite with this Self” (*Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad* 24.2). Therefore, since the twofold division exists, the prohibition of the staff and other emblems refers specifically to the *vidvat-paramahaṃsa*, who is devoid of all ritual action. The Blessed One has declared the state of the knower to be free from anything to be performed.
"But for that man who finds delight only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self,
and who is content in the Self alone— for him there exists no duty" (Bhagavad Gītā 3.17).
Dakṣa also says:
"It should never be studied, spoken, or heard;
one who is proficient in all these [prohibitions] becomes an ascetic (*yati*), and not otherwise. Thus [it is said].
Also in another *Smṛti*:

"For the yogin who is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished his purpose, there is nothing whatsoever left to be done; if there were anything left to be done, he would not be all-knowing. Thus it is said. Also in the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa*: "Knowing this, indeed, the seers of the Kavaṣeya lineage said: 'For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we perform sacrifices? However, for one who merely desires to know (*vividiṣu*), since duties such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) still exist, the observance of rules such as carrying a staff is appropriate as being an aid to those [duties].
But surely, the prohibition of the staff is also traditionally taught even for one devoid of knowledge:
"He who holds a wooden staff, eats all things, and is devoid of knowledge—he goes to the terrible hells known as Mahāraurava" (Parāśara Up. 3).

This is not a fault, because the prohibition refers specifically to one who carries a single staff solely for the sake of livelihood, without possessing either knowledge (*vidyā*) or the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). For this very reason, it is qualified by the term "eating all things" (*sarvāśī*). It is likewise stated in the *Smṛti*:
"Many men live by resorting to the single staff;
due to their abandonment of [prescribed] action, they fall into the terrible Raurava hell."

And falling into hell is certain, because even though external punishment exists, there is an absence of internal punishments that would turn one away from sin. That these [external marks] do not turn one away from sin is shown in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"Those bamboo staffs which are prescribed are merely reminders of the [ascetic] mark (*liṅga*);
they should indeed be worn for the manifestation of that mark, but they are not causes of dharma."
"Those born of the body, which always liberate men from sin, should indeed be maintained by the wise who have conquered their senses and anger, and who perceive the truth.
This is the syntactical connection: those three staffs born of the body are to be maintained for the sake of liberation from sin.

Now, it may be objected: an option between the single-staff and the triple-staff is recorded in certain Smṛtis. Regarding this, Viṣṇu and Baudhāyana state: "The sage may be either a single-staffer or a triple-staffer. Vyāsa says:

"Having undertaken the vow of either the triple staff (tridaṇḍa) or the single staff (ekadaṇḍa), the knower of reality should constantly wander the earth and remain stationary during the rainy season.

Thus [says the scripture]. Śaunaka also says: "Then, wearing ochre robes, [the seeker] takes up the triple staff or the single staff with the mantra, 'O friend, protect me. This is the word of the Blessed One in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan].

"Whether he carries a single staff or a triple staff, whether he has a topknot or is shaven, even if his only essential possession is the saffron robe—a renunciant is worthy of honor, O Yudhiṣṭhira. (MBh Āśvamedhika 105.8–9). Certainly; the distinction between those two should be understood according to the manner stated. In that regard, the triple staff belongs to the *kuṭīcaka* and *bahūdaka*; the single staff belongs to the *haṃsa* and *paramahaṃsa*. This being so, the scriptural citations adduced in their respective places become consistent.
Thus, the fourfold renunciation has been described; now its duties are described. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:
"Having risen at the time of dawn and performed purification according to the rule,"
Having cleansed his teeth and sipped water according to the rule, except on the [forbidden] lunar days.
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rule, standing or even sitting,
he should place the water-purifier or the rosary in both hands.
Likewise, when the purifier made of cow-hair— which destroys evil deeds—
is present, one should perform the twilight worship according to the rules at sunrise and recite the threefold prayer.
"Having performed the worship with the [verses] beginning with *mitrasya carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ* and others that purify,
and having offered libations as before, one should then recite [the mantra] properly with a concentrated mind.
Thus [says] Manu as well.
One should always wander alone, without companions, for the sake of spiritual perfection; seeing that perfection belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons nor is abandoned. (MDh 6.42)

[180] Thus: when one wanders alone without a companion, because there is an absence of obstacles such as passion and hatred, he determines the accomplishment characterized by gnosis (*jñāna*) and does not abandon that accomplishment. He proceeds toward that accomplishment without hindrance; having proceeded, he does not fall away from that accomplishment, but rather reaches its further shore. However, when he wanders accompanied by a second or third person, then, due to the possibility of passion and hatred arising, he falls away from the aforementioned accomplishment. For this very reason, the skillful one says: "A single mendicant is as described; two are considered a couple."
Three villages are declared to be a *grāma*; beyond that, it becomes like a city (*nagara*).
A city must not be built, nor a village, nor likewise a pair [of attendants];
by undertaking these three things, an ascetic falls away from his own duty.
"For between them, there will undoubtedly arise talk of kings and talk of monks, as well as affection, backbiting, and envy, due to their close proximity. (DaŚm 7.35–37)

But when, due to the absence of the perfection of hearing and so forth, one is personally incapable of achieving self-knowledge, then one should wander together with a second person who is capable in that regard. As the Śruti says: "During the rainy season, a mendicant should remain in one place for eight months; he may wander alone or in pairs" (ĀrU 3). The sense is that he should wander, or two of them should wander. Śaunaka also says: "He should wander alone and act for the benefit of all beings. Yājñavalkya states this as well:
"Beneficial to all beings, peaceful, carrying the triple staff and the water-pot..."
"Delighting in solitude, having renounced the world, he should resort to a village for the sake of alms.

(YDh 3.58) "Practicing what is beneficial" (*hitācaraṇa*) means merely the non-performance of injury; it does not, however, imply engagement in acts of service, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "One should neither undertake injury nor bestow favor" (GDh 3.24). For this very reason, Atri stated the [five] principles beginning with non-violence:
"Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession."
Purity of being, devotion to Hari, contentment, cleanliness, and straightforwardness.
Faith in the existence of the Supreme, contact with Brahman, study of the Vedas, equanimity of vision, absence of arrogance, freedom from dejection, serenity, steadiness, and gentleness.
Affection for one's own kin, service to the guru, faith, patience, self-restraint,
tranquility, equanimity, fortitude, sweetness, endurance, and likewise compassion.
"Modesty, austerity, knowledge, realization, yoga, moderation in eating, fortitude, wandering for alms, recitation of mantras, the twilight devotions, and the renunciation of the fruits of action—
this is proclaimed as the specific duty (svadharma) of ascetics who have restrained their minds. Thus it is said.

Even after having undertaken renunciation in the presence of a guru, one should dwell there until the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman. Thus it is stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*: "For one who has described the three stages of life and attained the supreme stage, then, at the end of a year, having obtained unsurpassed knowledge..."
Having obtained permission from his guru, he should indeed wander this earth,
free from attachment, having conquered anger, moderate in diet, and with his senses subdued.
"Having closed the doors with the intellect, one should become single-minded through meditation. Thus [it is said in the Liṅga Purāṇa, 1.90.15].
Also in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Appointed by the Guru, he should dwell there for a year, remaining disciplined."
One should always be vigilant regarding the observances (niyamas) and likewise ever heedful regarding the restraints (yamas).

"And having finally attained the unsurpassed yoga of knowledge, the ascetic should wander the earth without contradicting dharma. (Liṅga Purāṇa 1.89.5–6). The phrase "for a year" is an elliptical expression; he should reside [with the teacher] as long as it takes for knowledge to arise, because dwelling in the presence of the guru is for the sake of attaining knowledge. Kaṇva states a specific rule regarding wandering the earth:
"One should dwell for one night in a village and five nights in a town;
except during the rainy season, one should dwell for four months during the rains.
Thus it is said in the Matsya Purāṇa as well.
For eight months, there should be wandering for ascetics of self-restrained mind;
furthermore, they should dwell in one place for the four months of the rainy season.
"No body shall exist there; this has been seen in the ancient scripture. Thus [it is said].
Medhātithi states the purpose for residing during the Cāturmāsya:
"For the sake of protecting living beings that move upon the surface of the earth..."
And from the month of Āṣāḍha until the month of Kārttika, the ascetic [should observe] these four months.
"Purified, one should dwell at the edge of a village that is rich in righteousness and abundant in water.
Having thus summarized other dharmas as well—both those to be avoided and those to be adopted—he says the same:
"Endowed with supreme faith, having the Supreme Self as one's ultimate goal..."
Those who know the ten and six [principles] are liberated from the gross and subtle bodies.
He should accept these six items: a triple staff, a water-pot, a water-strainer, an alms-bowl, a seat, and a garment consisting of a loincloth.
Immovable things, moving things, seeds, fire, poison, and weapons—
these six a renunciant should not take up, treating them like urine or excrement.
One should avoid the doctrine of elixirs, astrology, buying and selling,
and various crafts, just as one avoids the wives of others.
Alms-gathering, recitation, bathing, meditation, purification, and worship of the gods—
these six must be performed in every way, like the punishment of a king.
One should never look at six things: a performance by actors and the like, gambling, a woman, a friend, food to be chewed, and food to be swallowed, nor a woman in her courses.
A renunciant should never dwell for any length of time in these six places: in a military camp, in a threshing floor, in a caravan, in a city, in a village, or in a house inhabited by women.
A renunciant should never, even in thought, contemplate these six— passion, hatred, pride, deceit, hypocrisy, and delusion— toward others or oneself.
A couch, white garments, talk of women, indulgence in sensual pleasures,
sleeping during the day, and traveling— these are the six causes of downfall for ascetics.
One should contemplate conjunction and disjunction, as well as the means of disjunction,
and the essential natures of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and primordial matter (pradhāna).
An [excessive] seat, the loss of the alms-bowl, hoarding, gathering of disciples,
sleeping during the day, and idle chatter— these six are the bonds for an ascetic.
A place where one stays for more than one day in a village and more than five days in a town,
other than during the rainy season retreat, is designated as an "āsana" (a fixed seat).
If not even one of the aforementioned alms-bowls is maintained by a mendicant who subsists on alms,
that is called the "loss of the bowl."
The acquisition of a second item, such as a triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) already in one's possession,
for the purpose of enjoyment at a later time, is proclaimed to be "accumulation" (*saṃcaya*).
[185] Accepting disciples for the sake of service, gain, or honor, or for the sake of fame,
and not out of compassion— that is attachment, not the gathering of disciples.
Knowledge is called day because of its luminosity; ignorance is called night.
Negligence in the practice of knowledge is called sleeping during the day.
Except for discourse on the inner self, on the practice of mendicancy, or on the praise of the gods,
a question intended merely for favor is called idle chatter.
One who is tongueless, a eunuch, a cripple, blind, deaf,
and foolish— a monk liberated by these six qualities has no doubt.
He who, even while eating, is not attached, thinking "this is delicious" or "this is not," and speaks what is beneficial, true, and measured— he is called one who is tongueless.
He who, upon seeing a woman whether she be newly born, sixteen years of age, or even a hundred years old, remains free from any change of emotion, is a eunuch.
He who does not travel more than a *yojana* for the sake of alms or for the evacuation of excrement and urine is, in every respect, truly a cripple.
Whether standing or walking, he whose vision does not reach far,
having abandoned fear for the duration of the four ages, is called a blind wandering mendicant.
He who, having heard speech that is beneficial or pleasing to the mind, yet does not listen as if it were speech bringing grief, is proclaimed to be deaf.
"One who, despite the presence of sense objects and being capable with unimpaired faculties, always behaves as if asleep—he is called a deluded monk. Thus [it is said].
Manu describes the rule for wandering for alms:
One should go for alms at a single time and not become attached to abundance;
for a mendicant who is overly intent on alms becomes attached even to sense-objects.
When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal,
and when the removal of the dishes has taken place— then the ascetic should always go for alms.

“He should not be despondent in the absence of gain, nor should he rejoice in its presence. He should possess only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, having emerged from attachment to material objects. (MDh 6.55–57). “Material objects” (*mātrā*) are so called because they are measured; he is one who has emerged from attachment to them. The meaning is that, when striving [for liberation], neither joy nor despondency should be felt. Yama also says:
Having bathed, being pure, in a clean place, having performed his silent prayers with a concentrated mind,
and free from passion and hatred, he should enter the village seeking alms.
A renunciant may collect alms from even a family of barbarians, provided they are honey-like (sweet);
however, he should not eat food from a single source, even if he were equal to Bṛhaspati.
[187] He should always consume pure food, remaining silent and pure at the time of sunset;
wearing a single garment, with a purified soul, walking slowly, and looking ahead only the distance of a yoke.
"One should eat whatever is obtained, avoiding the consecration with clarified butter;
this alms-food, known as *mādhūkara*, destroys all sins.
Thus [says] Baudhāyana as well.

When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, and when the people have finished their meal— at that time, toward the latter part of the day, he should go forth for alms.
Having put on one garment above the knees and below the navel,
and a second as an inner garment, he should carry an alms-bowl and a staff, remaining restrained in speech.
Taking the bowl in his left hand and the triple staff in his right hand,
he should worship the Sun while meditating on the unity of the Self.
Having recited the *virajas* mantra, having performed a circumambulation from left to right with the *ākṛṣṇena* verse,
and having recited again the verse beginning with *ye te panthānaḥ*, [he should proceed].
Having meditated upon him— the person named Viṣṇu who dwells within the sun and within the heart— as "I am that god Nārāyaṇa," and having bowed down to him;
Having even removed his sandals for the sake of purifying his alms-bowl and other implements,
he should then proceed slowly to the village, looking only a yoke’s length ahead.
Meditating on Hari with a mind fixed upon Him, he should recite this:
"May Viṣṇu, the Vaikuṇṭha, be present for me in the intermediate directions, below, above, and in every cardinal and intermediate point."
May Rāma protect me from all sides, as well as the archer Keśava and the wielder of the discus;
having approached the house for alms, one should first urge [the host] with the words "Bhavat" (Sir).
Then, remaining silent with his face turned downwards, he should stand for as long as it takes to milk a cow;
having seen the alms held in the hand of the giver, purified by his gaze.
Then, having fixed the triple staff against his right side with his arm,
he should tear off the armor with his right hand.
"Having placed the bowl in the left hand, one should hold it with the right;
free from longing, one should beg for food sufficient for the journey of life.
Thus [it is said]. Uśanas states that there are five kinds of begging:

Alms are traditionally taught to be of five kinds: that gathered like honey from many sources, that which is not specially prepared for the mendicant, that which was set aside beforehand, that which is obtained without asking, and that which is received at the appropriate time.
Houses free from mental attachment, numbering three, seven, or five;
that which is brought like honey is known as *mādhūkaraka*.
The venerable sage Uśanas declared that whatever is requested by those endowed with devotion prior to the rite of awakening from sleep is termed "previously offered" (prākpraṇīta).
Manu has declared that almsfood which has been invited before the effort to wander for alms begins is indeed "unasked for" (ayācita) and should be eaten.
And that which was prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of alms during the period of attendance— known as "temporary"— that should be eaten by one desiring liberation.
"Whatever food is brought by devotees to the monastery is considered 'obtained' (upapanna); thus say the sages who desire liberation.
Thus Yama praises alms-food.
He who wanders among all social classes for alms and consumes them as such should not eat anything else; "alms consist of water"—this is the established rule.
He who drinks three drops of water from the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,
yet lives by the right method as a mendicant eating almsfood, is superior to the one previously mentioned.
One who drinks barley-gruel with cow's urine, which has the color of molten gold,
for twelve years— that would not be equal to begging for alms.
Those who subsist on vegetables, those who subsist on milk, and others who subsist on barley-gruel—
all these, even if they live entirely on alms, do not equal a sixteenth part of him.
"Alms are not the food of another's cooking, nor is alms-taking an act of acceptance;
alms are equal to the drinking of Soma. Therefore, one should subsist on alms.
In this context, the phrase "among all castes" refers to times of distress (*āpad*). For this very reason, Baudhāyana says:
One should take food from the pure classes of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
however, if the former is unavailable, one may accept it from each subsequent class.
"But when all [sources] are unavailable, one who knows the truth should preserve his life by subsisting on two kinds of alms even from a Śūdra, while fasting.
Furthermore, he should not employ portents such as the falling of meteors, nor the unfavorable positions of planets, nor any other pretext in order to obtain alms. As Manu says:
"Neither by means of portents and omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor by instructions and discourses, should he ever seek alms. (MDh 6.50).
Atri states what food is to be avoided:
An ascetic should always eat food that is wholesome and moderate, which is easily digested;
he should avoid that food by which the bodily constituents (dhātus) are provoked.
A mendicant should avoid food prepared by a menstruating woman, food served to twice-born men that has been prompted by a Śūdra,
or food placed upon a living creature or a crow.

"One should avoid such alms-food as that which was previously prepared for the sake of the ancestors, or for the sake of the gods and others, as well as that which causes harm to others. With reference precisely to the possibility of causing harm to others, Manu said:
"One should not approach another house that is crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, or dogs, or with other mendicants" (MDh 6.51). Regarding this,
Baudhāyana states that one should avoid the house of a person who, though capable of giving alms, does not give them out of atheism (*nāstikya*).
"Should they ever fail to give alms for five or seven days in a house where people, out of folly, reject [the mendicant] like an outcaste (caṇḍāla), one should avoid that house.
He himself states the prohibition regarding the avoidance of irreproachable houses:
"If an ascetic should avoid a virtuous Brahmin who has not fallen from his status, he gives away that man's merit and takes upon himself his demerit.
Furthermore, the alms of one who, being poor, offers alms while fasting himself out of devotion, are not to be accepted. This is stated in another Smṛti:
If one offers alms even after having caused pain to oneself, that alms is to be known as defiled; an ascetic should not accept such an offering.

[191] Thus it is said. Regarding one who is too lazy to wander among many houses for the sake of alms, Baudhāyana says: "If a monk, out of greed, desires to fill his bowl from a single house, the giver attains heaven, while the eater consumes sin."
Manu distinguishes the mendicant’s bowl:
"His bowls should be non-metallic and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, as in the case of the *camasa* cups during a sacrifice."
"A gourd, a wooden bowl, one made of clay, or likewise one of split bamboo—
these, Manu Svāyambhuva declared, are the vessels for an ascetic" (MDh 6.53–54). Yama also says:
"Golden vessels and those made of black iron—these are unfit vessels for ascetics; a mendicant should avoid them. Thus says Baudhāyana as well.
One should eat from leaves gathered by oneself or those that have fallen naturally;
however, one must not eat from the leaves of the vaṭa, aśvattha, or karañja trees.

Whether it be from the *kumbhī* and *tinduka*, or likewise from the *kovidāra* and *arka* trees, one who eats from bell-metal is a consumer of impurity; even in times of distress, one must not eat from bell-metal.
“[The vessel] may be made of gold, silver, copper, tin, or lead.

He [Yājñavalkya] states the rule for eating as follows: “Having returned from the practice of begging... having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he should offer [the food] before the sun while reciting *ud u tyam*, *citram*, ... *brahmajajñānam*, ... and *ud vayaṃ tamasaḥ pari*; having muttered these, he should eat” (BDh 2.10.18.7–12). Also, in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
“Then, having returned, the self-controlled one should set down that vessel and perform the ritual sipping of water.”
Having rinsed [the mouth] with four finger-breadths of water, one should consume a mouthful while remaining concentrated.
One should offer food prepared with all its various condiments in separate vessels;
having sprinkled the food with water, one should present it to the deities beginning with the Sun and to the elemental spirits.
The ascetic, restrained in speech, should eat from a leaf-cup or a vessel;
having eaten, the ascetic should always wash the vessel with the accompaniment of mantras.
His vessel shall not be defiled, like the chalices in sacrifices;
then, having sipped water and restrained his vital breath, he should worship the Sun.
The wise man should spend the remainder of the day with specific recitation and meditation;
having performed the twilight rites, he should then pass the night in a temple or similar sacred place.
Having meditated upon the stainless Self within the abode of the heart-lotus,
the ascetic— devoted to dharma, tranquil, equanimous toward all beings, and self-controlled— [attains liberation].
“He attains the supreme state, reaching which he does not return. Thus [it is said] in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa* (60.13–20). Also in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
“Having shown the food to the sun, one should eat facing the east, without haste.”
Having offered the five oblations of breath, he should then consume eight morsels with a concentrated mind.
Having sipped water for purification, one should meditate upon the god Brahmā, the Supreme Lord,
during the early night, the late night, and likewise at midnight.

"One should always meditate upon the Lord, especially during the twilights and throughout the day. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.22.7–10). Now, there are other duties of the ascetic as well. Regarding this, Atri says:
"Henceforth I shall proclaim the conduct that is prescribed for the ascetic."
Rising to greet them and honoring them like teachers with pleasant conversation.

"One should indeed offer salutation according to the prescribed rule to ascetics who are advanced in their vows and who follow their own dharma, regarding them as the very form of Viṣṇu. Thus [says the text]. Manu also says:
With his hair, nails, and beard clipped, carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot,
he should wander constantly with self-restraint, never causing pain to any living beings.
[194] A skull, the roots of trees, tattered rags, solitude,
and equanimity toward all things— these are the characteristics of one who is liberated.
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life;
one should simply await the time, just as a servant awaits his master's command.
One should set down one's foot purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is pure.
One should endure harsh words and never, under any circumstances, show contempt;
nor, relying upon this single body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone.
One should not respond with anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates.
Delighting in the inner self, seated, free from partiality and free from worldly desire,
one who seeks happiness should wander here with the self alone as his companion.
For the sake of protecting living beings, during the night, the day, and at the two twilights,
and even when his body is failing, he should walk upon the earth after carefully scanning the ground.
By consuming little food and by staying and sitting in solitude,
one should withdraw the senses when they are being carried away by sense-objects.
"By the restraint of the senses, by the destruction of passion and hatred, and by non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality. (MDh 6.44–68) [195].
Thus says Dakṣa as well:

"One should not study, nor speak, nor listen in any way whatsoever; one who has perfected himself through all these becomes an ascetic (*yati*), and no other. Thus [says the *Dharmasamhitā* 7.33]. Bṛhaspati also says:
A self-controlled ascetic should not consume anything other than medicine or a tooth-stick,
except at the time of a meal.
An ascetic should never take any provisions for his journey except in times of distress;
in times of distress, he may accept cooked food, but only as much as can be consumed in a single day.
"A renunciant (yati) should not always dwell at sacred bathing places (tīrtha), nor should he be intent on fasting;
he should not be habitually devoted to Vedic study, nor should he be intent on giving expositions. Thus it is said.

The prohibition "one should not study" refers to the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*); otherwise, the scriptural injunction "one should repeat the Upaniṣad" (*Āśvalāyana Upaniṣad* 2) would be contradicted. The prohibition "one should not listen" refers to matters other than the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmamīmāṃsā*), because that inquiry is enjoined by the rule: "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon. Furthermore, the prohibition against bathing at sacred fords, fasting, study, and exposition is appropriate, since the order of renunciation (*kaivalyāśrama*) is characterized primarily by the duty of cessation (*nivṛttidharma*). For he himself has said:
He into whom words have entered like stones cast into a well and do not return to the speaker— such a person should dwell in the hermitage of liberation (kaivalya).
He into whom desires enter, having been withdrawn from their objects, and who no longer pursues those objects— he should dwell in the stage of absolute liberation (kaivalyāśrama).
He in whom anger, having arisen fully, becomes fruitless and subsides like a sword struck against the sky, shall dwell in the hermitage of absolute liberation.

He in whom there is patience, tranquility, purity, truthfulness, contentment, straightforwardness, freedom from possessions, and lack of hypocrisy— he shall dwell in the stage of liberation (kaivalyāśrama).
He who does not engage in idle chatter, who is not intent on winning over the world,
and who is not occupied with other branches of knowledge— he shall dwell in the stage of absolute liberation (kaivalya-āśrama).
One should not remember past enjoyments, nor likewise those yet to come;
one should not rejoice in those already obtained—he shall dwell in the stage of absolute liberation.
"He who remains like one blind, mute, lame, deaf, or impotent,
and who always moves about [in this manner], he shall dwell in the stage of absolute liberation (kaivalyāśrama).
Thus Dakṣa praises the ascetic (yati) endowed with the aforementioned qualities.
Whatever accumulated sin a householder has committed until the end of life,
an ascetic who has stayed for even a single night will consume it all by his presence.
"Upon seeing a twice-born man renouncing the world, the Sun moves from his station, thinking:
'He shall pierce my orb and proceed to the supreme state. (DaSm 7.45–46).
Thus, the duties of the ascetic have been described.

Each of the four stages of life (āśrama), beginning with studentship (brahmacarya) and ending with renunciation (saṃnyāsa), which have been mentioned, has four internal subdivisions. As it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—these are declared to be the four stages of life;
each one of these is of four kinds."
And regarding that, the *Kātyāyana-smṛti* has explained its fourfold nature:

The four stages of life (*āśrama*)—the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*)—consist of sixteen subdivisions. Among them, students are of four kinds: the *Gāyatra*, the *Brāhma*, the *Prājāpatya*, and the *Bṛhan*. One who, from the time of initiation (*upanayana*) onwards, eats food free of pungent spices and salt for three nights and studies the *Gāyatrī* verse is a *Gāyatra*. One who practices Vedic celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for forty-eight years—twelve years for each Veda, or until he has mastered a Veda—is a *Brāhma*. One who is devoted to his own wife, approaches her only during her fertile period, and always avoids the wives of others is a *Prājāpatya*. Alternatively, one who dwells in the teacher’s house for twenty-four years is a *Brāhma*, and one who dwells there for forty-eight years is a *Prājāpatya*. One who does not abandon the teacher until death is a *Naiṣṭhika*, known as the *Bṛhan*. [197] [=ĀśrUp 1]

Householders, too, are of four kinds: those who subsist by agriculture and trade (*vārtākavṛtti*), those who live in settled households (*śālīnavṛtti*), those who wander from place to place (*yāyāvara*), and those who practice the severe asceticism of renunciation (*ghorasaṃnyāsika*). Among them, those who subsist by agriculture and trade employ unobjectionable means such as farming, cattle-rearing, and commerce; performing sacrifices with rites lasting a hundred years, they seek the Self. Those who live in settled households perform sacrifices but do not officiate for others; they study but do not teach, and they give gifts but do not accept them; performing sacrifices with rites lasting a hundred years, they seek the Self. Those who wander from place to place perform sacrifices and officiate for others, study and teach, and give gifts and accept them; performing sacrifices with rites lasting a hundred years, they seek the Self. Those who practice the severe asceticism of renunciation perform their duties with water that has been boiled and purified; subsisting daily on food gathered through the *uñcha* method of gleaning, they perform sacrifices with rites lasting a hundred years and seek the Self. [ĀśrUp 2]

Forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) are also of four kinds: the *vaikhānasa*, the *audumbara*, the *vālakhilya*, and the *phenapa*. Among them, the *vaikhānasas*—having performed the service of the sacred fires with uncultivated plants and forest trees grown outside the village—fulfill the rites of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and seek the Self. The *audumbaras*, having risen at dawn, perform the service of the sacred fires and fulfill the rites of the five great sacrifices with *udumbara*, jujube (*badara*), wild rice (*nīvāra*), and *śyāmāka* grains gathered from whichever direction they look; thus they seek the Self. The *vālakhilyas*, wearing matted hair and clothed in rags, skins, or bark, discard their flowers and fruits on the full moon day of Kārttika; for the remaining eight months, they provide for their livelihood, perform the service of the sacred fires, fulfill the rites of the five great sacrifices, and seek the Self. The *phenapas*, acting like madmen, eating withered leaves and fruits, dwelling anywhere at all, perform the service of the sacred fires, fulfill the rites of the five great sacrifices, and seek the Self. (ĀśrUp 3)

Wanderers (*parivrājaka*) are also of four kinds: the *kuṭīcaka*, the *bahūdaka*, the *haṃsa*, and the *paramahaṃsa*. [200] The *kuṭīcakas* practice the life of begging for alms in the houses of their own sons and seek liberation for themselves. The *bahūdakas* carry the triple staff, water pot, sling, lotus-strainer, water-purifier, sandals, seat, topknot, sacred thread, loincloth, and ochre-colored robes; they practice the life of begging for alms in families of Brahmins of virtuous conduct and seek liberation for themselves. The *haṃsas* carry a single staff, are devoid of a topknot, wear the sacred thread, and hold a sling and water pot in their hands; they stay for one night in a village and five nights in a city or at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), practicing penances such as the one-night fast, the two-night fast, the *kṛcchra*, and the *cāndrāyaṇa*, and seek liberation for themselves. The *paramahaṃsas* do not carry a staff; they are shaven-headed, clothed in rags and a loincloth, with unmanifested signs and unmanifested conduct; though not insane, they behave like the insane, having abandoned the triple staff, water pot, sling, lotus-strainer, water-purifier, sandals, seat, topknot, and sacred thread. [201] They dwell in empty houses or temples; for them there is neither dharma nor adharma, neither truth nor falsehood. Enduring all things and equal toward all, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same, they practice the life of begging for alms among the four castes as they happen upon them and liberate themselves. (ĀśrUp 4) Thus it is said.
Kātyāyana also says:
"For those dwelling in the forest, the dharma is tranquility and self-restraint;
for householders, it is charity alone; and for students, it is service."

And it is appropriate for wandering mendicants (*parivrājakas*) to seek their own liberation, because the life of renunciation culminates in the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). With this very intention, its etymological definition is shown in another *Smṛti*:

"He is called a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) because of thorough awakening, because of thorough discernment, because of thorough complete vision, and because of the attainment of the complete fruit."
"He constantly wanders about, or he wanders further still;
having abandoned even another birth, he is called a wandering mendicant (parivrājaka).

Thus, at the beginning of this chapter, in the root text, by the word "āśrama" in the phrase "pertaining to the four castes and the stages of life," the duties of the four stages of life present in the mind are fully encompassed.

In the second chapter, however, the means of livelihood such as agriculture and so forth were clearly explained; furthermore, the most weighty duties pertaining to all the stages of life (āśramas) and the specific characteristics of those stages have now been somewhat elucidated.
Thus did the all-pervading Lord Mādhava, whose intellect is exalted, declare that very thing.

Thus ends the second chapter of the *Mādhavīyā*, a commentary on the *Parāśara-smṛti*, composed by the minister Mādhava, who was the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the Great Emperor, Supreme Lord, promoter of the Vedic path, and patron of the state. || 1 ||
Now begins the third chapter.

In the first and second chapters, the four social orders (*cāturvarṇya*) and stages of life (*āśrama*) were directly expounded, and the duties (*dharma*) pertaining to those stages were indicated. Regarding those duties, only one who is pure (*śuddha*) is entitled to perform them, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*) which states, "Rites must be performed by one who is pure. Although such purity is natural to a person, it is nevertheless obstructed for a certain period by a certain adventitious defect called impurity (*āśauca*), which is a specific state (*atiśaya*) residing in the person. That impurity is to be removed by bathing and other means once its duration has elapsed. Therefore, desiring to expound that [purity] in the third chapter, [the author] first declares the purity established by the removal of the obstruction:

Therefore, I shall explain purification in the case of birth as well as death. Since impurity, which obstructs one’s eligibility for religious duties (*dharma-adhikāra*), arises upon birth and death, I shall explain purification by means of teaching the methods that remove it. And that birth and death bring about impurity has been shown by Manu: "When a child who has teethed, or one who has not yet teethed, or one for whom the *caula* ceremony has been performed, dies..."
"All kinsmen are impure, and it is likewise declared in the case of birth-impurity" (MDh 5.58).
He now demonstrates the purification promised for each caste in its proper order: "Brāhmaṇas become pure after three days in the event of a death or birth-impurity. (1)
A Kṣatriya is purified in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in one month, according to the word of Parāśara. (2)

Now, an objection: the statement that "Brāhmaṇas are purified in three days" contradicts many Smṛtis. For instance, Dakṣa says: "A Brāhmaṇa is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month. (DaSm 6.7)
Devala also says:
"For Brāhmaṇas it is ten days; for Kṣatriyas, fifteen;
for Vaiśyas, twenty nights; and for Śūdras, exactly one month."

Vasiṣṭha also states: “A Brāhmaṇa is purified in ten nights; a Kṣatriya in fifteen nights; a Vaiśya in twenty nights; a Śūdra is purified in a month” (VaDh 4.27–30). This is not a fault, because the three-day period of impurity (*tryahāśauca*) applies specifically to those who offer water (*samānodaka*). Furthermore, Manu says: “But for those who offer water, [impurity lasts] three days” (MDh 5.64). The statements of Dakṣa and others that establish a ten-day period of impurity refer to *sapiṇḍa* relatives, as it is ordained: “Impurity due to death (*śāva-āśauca*) lasts ten days among *sapiṇḍas*” (MDh 5.59).
Thus it is stated in the *Manusmṛti*. Also in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"The wise declare that the period of impurity for those belonging to the same *pinda* [lineage] lasts ten days. (*KūPu* 1.2.23.1). Bṛhaspati also says:
Within ten days, the sapinda relatives become pure after a death or a birth;
the sakulyas become pure in three nights, and those born of the same lineage (gotrajas) become pure by bathing.
[206] Thus it is said.

But surely—this statement, “A Kṣatriya [is purified] in twelve days,” is also contradicted by many Smṛtis. In that regard, Vasiṣṭha and Devala have stated that the period of impurity for a Kṣatriya is fifteen days; that very passage has been cited. Śātātapa, however, says eleven days: “A Rājanya [Kṣatriya] after eleven days, and likewise a Vaiśya after twelve.”
"A Śūdra is purified in twenty nights from birth or death impurity. Thus says Vṛddha-Parāśara:
"A Kṣatriya, however, who is devoted to his own duties, becomes pure in ten days."

"In the same way, a Vaiśya shall attain purity in twelve days. To this it is replied: the contradiction is to be resolved by the relative degree of learning and austerity (*vidyā-tapas*). To the extent that learning and austerity increase, to that same extent the period of impurity (*āśauca*) is contracted. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states that even for a Śūdra who conducts himself according to the law, the period of impurity is halved:
"For a Kṣatriya, twelve days; for a Vaiśya, fifteen indeed."
"For a Śūdra it is thirty days, and half of that for one who conducts himself according to the law" (YDh 3.22).
Devala also, intending this very point, stated the gradations of impurity for the Brahmins and others:
"For those who have studied the Vedas, the impurity is held to last four days."
For a Brahmin who maintains the Vedic fires, a period of impurity lasting three days is prescribed.
[207] For one who has heard and reflected upon these two, purification is prescribed after one day;
for one who is engaged in ritual action along with these, there is no doubt that he becomes pure immediately.
For a king endowed with these [qualities], the fines are twelve, eleven, and ten;
for a Vaiśya, they are fifteen, twelve, and eleven respectively.

"But for a Śūdra who serves [the deceased], impurity is prescribed for half a month. As for that period of three, five, and so on days mentioned by that same author for Kṣatriyas and others, that refers to those devoid of learning and austerity; however, the impurity for ordinary members of the castes has been fully proclaimed [as follows].
This is because of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). Dakṣa also, having set forth ten positions, states the regulation based on the excellence or deficiency of qualities:
"Immediate purification, as well as one day, three days, four days, six, ten, twelve days, a fortnight, and likewise a month."
Likewise, there is another [period] ending at death, as well as the ten fortnights during the period of birth;
I shall explain them all in their proper sequence without omission.

If one understands the Veda together with its limbs, along with the ritual manuals and secret doctrines, both in letter and in spirit, and is engaged in the performance of rites, there is no impurity due to birth.

Immediate purification is prescribed for kings, officiating priests, and those initiated for sacrifice; likewise for children, when abroad in another country, and for those observing vows or engaged in sacrificial sessions.
A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and possesses the Vedas is purified in one day;
if he is deficient in these, or even more deficient, he is purified in three or four days respectively.
Likewise, for the lowest of the low, a period of six days is proclaimed;
and those periods of ten days and so forth that have been mentioned for the social classes are to be applied in their respective order.

"Furthermore, for a twice-born man who eats without having bathed, without having offered oblations, and without having given gifts—for such a Brahmin, there is always impurity (*sūtaka*). (DaŚm 6.2–9).
In this context, the reduction of impurity mentioned in the passage beginning with "four [days] for those who have studied the Vedas" refers to other *yugas*.
Having enumerated such things as "the reduction of sin depends upon one's conduct and Vedic study," [the text continues]:
"In the Kali age, however, the wise declare these duties to be abandoned."
Because it is stated thus in another Smṛti:
"When a death among sapindas occurs, for a Brahmin the period is indeed ten days; one who performs other rites in the Kali age is a sinner through delusion. (Hārīta Smṛti 18.32)

And because of this statement by Hārīta, the contradiction with other texts regarding the Vaiśya—as in the case of the Kṣatriya—must be resolved according to the method already stated. This being so, it remains established that for a Brāhmaṇa, the impurity lasts three nights among *samānodaka* relations and ten nights among *sapiṇḍa* relations; whereas for Kṣatriyas and others, the periods of twelve days and so forth as declared in the root-texts remain in force.
