Although, following the statements regarding fifteen days and twenty nights for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, the rule of twelve and fifteen days appears to be intended for cases where the deceased possesses special qualities (*guṇavat*), and Devala cited it precisely as referring to such qualified individuals; nevertheless, due to the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) and the support of many Smṛtis, the primary rule for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas is indeed that declared in the root-texts. For this very reason, Manu, Kūrma, and Dakṣa [state as follows].
"A Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days,
a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month" (MDh 5.83). Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"A Brāhmaṇa shall remain for ten days, abstaining from giving gifts, performing fire-oblations, and other such rites;
a Kṣatriya for twelve days, and a Vaiśya for half a month;
but a Śūdra shall remain for a full month, abstaining from his own specific duties. Thus it is said.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"A Kṣatriya is purified after twelve days in the event of birth or death;
a Vaiśya after fifteen days; a Śūdra is purified after a month."

Viṣṇu also states: "For a Brāhmaṇa, there is impurity for ten days upon the birth or death of his sapindas; twelve days for a Kṣatriya; fifteen days for a Vaiśya; and one month for a Śūdra" (ViDh 22.1–4). As for the statements regarding fifteen days or twenty nights, they should be explained as being intended for censure—much like the rule on lifelong impurity—or as pertaining to other ages. By the phrase "just as the words of Parāśara," he indicates that this is his own view while suggesting that there exist other opinions concerning the contraction or expansion of impurity; these have been established by us. || 2 ||

Since the aforementioned impurity (āśauca) acts as an obstacle to eligibility for ritual acts, it would follow that even the performance of worship such as the *saṃdhyā* is suspended; therefore, he states an exception:
"But in the case of the worship of the Brahmins, purification of the limbs occurs.

Worship (*upāsana*) refers to the performance of the *saṃdhyā-vandana*, the *agnihotra*, and so forth. When that [worship] is occasioned, there is temporary purification of the body at that time. Thus says Gobhila:
"Regarding the *agnihotra* and other oblations, purity is declared to be temporary;

for one who is impure, he must not perform the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*), as he remains [impure] once again. Thus says Pulastya: "Purity lasts only for as long as it takes to complete the *agnihotra*, but not beyond that."
One should perform the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*), the sacrificial oblation (*caru*), and the fire sacrifice (*homa*) throughout one’s entire life;
even during a period of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*), one must not abandon them, for by abandoning them, a twice-born man goes to a lower state.
"During both birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka), one should not abandon the twilight rites (saṃdhyākarma).

A twice-born man should mentally recite the mantras, except for the breath-control (prāṇāyāma). This statement implies that vocal recitation is intended for the offering of the joined palms (añjaliprakṣepa); thus Paiṭhīnasi says: "During birth-impurity, having offered the joined palms with the Sāvitrī mantra, having performed circumambulation, and meditating upon the Sun, one should pay obeisance. Since mental recitation is established even for the mantras of sprinkling (mārjana) and so forth, the specific rule regarding the joined palms intends vocal recitation. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"For ten days in both cases, the food of the family is not eaten;
giving, receiving, burnt offerings, and Vedic study are suspended" (MDh 5.62).
This refers to the Vaiśvadeva and other rites prescribed by the Smṛti. To this effect, Jātūkarṇya says:
"And one should not perform the ritual of the five sacrifices at the times of death or birth.
As for that which was stated by Jābāla: "The twilight prayers, the five great sacrifices, the daily rites, and the duties prescribed by the Smṛti..."
One should certainly omit it during that interval; however, its performance takes place at the end of the period of impurity.

Thus, that refers to the intention regarding the *vācika-saṃdhyā* (verbal twilight devotion). The avoidance of *smārta* rituals pertains to cases where one is the performer oneself; however, one may certainly have them performed by another. Bṛhaspati says:

"In the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), or when unable to eat at a *śrāddha*, or due to causes such as being away on a journey, one should cause [the rites] to be offered, but never let them be omitted."
Jātūkarṇya also says:
"When birth-impurity (sūtaka) has arisen, how should the Smārta rite be performed?
One should have the Piṇḍayajña, the Caru, and the Homa performed by one who does not belong to the same gotra."

In the original statement, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for Kṣatriyas and others as well. Impurity is of two kinds: characterized by disqualification from religious rites (karmānadhikāra) and characterized by untouchability (aspṛśyatva). Of these, by the phrase "purity of the limbs" (aṅgaśuddhi), the cessation of one type is stated; by the word "and" (ca), the other is also included. Just as there is a twofold impurity during the period of death, so too does it apply to birth; regarding the attainment of that [impurity], he states the distinction: "But in the case of the birth of Brāhmaṇas, touching the body is prescribed. (3)

Regarding birth, the touching of the limbs of *sapiṇḍa* relatives may take place at any time; it is not restricted to that specific moment as it is in the case of death. For this very reason, Aṅgiras states:
"In the case of birth, touching is not forbidden, with the exception of the woman who has given birth;
however, in the case of touching the woman who has given birth, bathing alone is prescribed."
Also in the *Kūrma-purāṇa*:
"During the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), however, there is no fault whatsoever in the physical contact of *sapiṇḍa* relatives. Thus [it is said]. Paiṭhīnasi also [states]:
"During [the period of] birth, all sapindas other than the mother and father are pure; however, there is impurity (sūtaka) for the mother and father.
The impurity belongs to the mother alone; having performed ablution, the father becomes pure.

Thus, at the time of birth, all sapindas other than the mother and father are touchable, whereas the mother and father do not possess touchability. Even in that case, the father becomes touchable by means of bathing. The ten-day period of untouchability belongs to the mother alone. And so says Vasiṣṭha:
"No impurity exists for a man if he does not undergo contact;
in that case, it is the *rajas* (menstrual flow) that should be known as impure, and that is not found in a man" (VaDh 4.23). Saṃvarta also says:
"When a son is born, bathing with one's clothes on is prescribed for the father;
the mother becomes pure after ten days, but the father may touch her after bathing. (Saṃskāra-smṛti 1.43) || 3 ||

Purification after death has been shown according to the order of the castes; now he shows purification after birth as well, according to the order of the castes: "Upon birth, a Brāhmaṇa is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month" (4).

*Jātau* means "in birth. The rest is clear. And this purification pertains to eligibility for ritual acts (*karmādhikāra*), because the immediately preceding statement has already described the purification regarding physical contact (*sparśa*). On the day of birth, however, there is no impurity regarding matters such as giving gifts (*dāna*) and so forth. For this very reason, Manu says:
"When a son is born, on that day one may freely accept gifts:
gold, grain, cows, clothing, sesame seeds, molasses, and clarified butter."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “Upon the birth of a son, before the umbilical cord has been severed, there is no fault in accepting gifts of molasses, sesame, gold, garments, upper cloths, cows, and grain; some say this applies only to that very day. [214] Thus says Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya: “On the day of a son’s birth, Brāhmaṇas should accept gifts of gold, land, cows, horses, goats, clothing, beds, seats, and so forth.”
"In that regard, one may accept all things, but one must not eat cooked food;
if a twice-born man eats it out of delusion, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Thus says Baudhāyana as well.
"On that day, the giving of molasses, oil, gold, cattle, grain, and garments, as well as their acceptance by Brahmins, should be performed;
others have declared that these [gifts] are to be accepted prior to the cutting of the umbilical cord. Thus it is said.

As for those deities known as the *janmadā*, who preside over the birth-chamber (*sūtikāgṛha*), there is no impurity regarding their worship on the first, sixth, tenth, and other such days. Thus says Vyāsa:
"The deities named *janmadā* reside in the birth-chamber;
for the purpose of sacrificing to them, purity is prescribed at birth."
"On the first day, the sixth, and always on the tenth— on these three days, one should never observe *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) upon the birth of a son.
Thus says Mārkaṇḍeya.
Likewise, the sixth night must be protected with special care;
one should perform a vigil at night and likewise offer an oblation to the birth-giving goddesses.
"Men with weapons in hand and women with dance and song should keep a vigil at night on the tenth day and during the period of birth-impurity.
As for that which was stated by Aṅgiras:
"Impurity is not declared for those who maintain the sacred fires during birth, even though they are *sapiṇḍas*.

This [statement] must be understood as referring either to the previously mentioned *agnihotra* and other rites, or to the offerings (*bali*) for those who have given birth mentioned immediately above. Otherwise, the statement "a Brahmin [becomes pure] in ten days after birth" would be rendered meaningless. || 4 ||
He states an exception in certain cases regarding the previously mentioned impurity for the deceased and the impurity for a birth:
"A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and the Vedas is purified in one day; one who possesses only the Vedas is purified in three days; but one who lacks both is purified in ten days. (5)

Here, by the word *agni*, the *āhavanīya* and other sacrificial fires are intended; and by them, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites accomplished by those fires are indicated. "Deprived of two" (*dvihīna*) means deprived of two: the sacred fires and the Vedas. This contraction of impurity (*āśauca*) is to be understood as applying to one who has a large number of *sapiṇḍa* relatives, whose livelihood is restricted, and who is devoted to Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), specifically regarding the acceptance of gifts and similar acts; however, it does not apply to all ritual activities. Thus says Gautama: "For the sake of preventing the cessation of Vedic study for a Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 14.21). The meaning is this: if full impurity were accepted for a Brāhmaṇa, his Vedic study would cease; let that not happen. The mention of "non-cessation of Vedic study" is also intended to indicate the acceptance of gifts. Otherwise, if full impurity were accepted for those with restricted livelihoods such as the "one-day-provisioner" (*aśvastanika*), their very survival would be impossible. Such being the case, the rule of one day applies to the *aśvastanika*, the rule of three days applies to the "three-day-provisioner" (*tryāhika*), and ten days apply to one whose livelihood is unrestricted—this is the settled distinction. In the manner thus described:

"Immediate purification, as well as one day, three days, four days, six, ten, twelve days, a fortnight, and likewise a month"—these options mentioned by Dakṣa are to be applied according to the circumstances. The author of the *Saṃgraha* states that the reduction of impurity follows the reduction of one's livelihood: *sadyaḥśaucaṃ tathaikāhaṃ tryahaś caturahas tathā |* *ṣaḍdaśadvādaśāhaṃ ca pakṣo māsas tathaiva ca ||* (DaSm 6.2) Thus, the alternatives declared by Dakṣa are to be established [according to the specific case]. The author of the *Saṃgraha* declares that the contraction of impurity results from the contraction of one's means of subsistence.
"An excellent twice-born man living by means of gleaned grains or begged food shall be purified immediately.

Now, one might object: why is this restriction regarding impurity not accepted as applying to all ritual acts, based on the distinction between the learned and the unlearned, given the force of the qualification "he who is endowed with the sacred fires and the Vedas"?
That is not so.
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among the sapinda relatives. (MDh 5.59)

This is because the rule for ten days of impurity (*daśāhāśauca*) is prescribed without distinction. Nor should one suspect that the ten-day impurity, which applies generally, is set aside in the case of learned men (*vidvat*), for such a setting aside must be based on an underlying inconsistency (*anupapatti*). Only so much should be set aside as is necessary to resolve that inconsistency. In this context, the inconsistency lies solely in the matters of Vedic study and receiving gifts; since the prescription of one day of impurity (*ekāhāśauca*) achieves its purpose by setting aside the ten-day impurity only in those specific cases, there is no setting aside of the ten-day impurity in all circumstances. Furthermore, the requirement of being "endowed with the sacred fires and the Vedas" (*agnivedasamanvitatva*) is intended as a praise for the rule of one-day impurity for one who does not store provisions for the morrow (*aśvastanika*), and is not a qualifying attribute for the person entitled to the rule of one-day impurity. As for that which...

"In both cases, for ten days, the food of the family is not eaten; giving, receiving, burnt offerings, and Vedic study are suspended" (MDh 5.62). Thus, the prohibition of receiving gifts and so forth made by Manu refers to those whose livelihood is unrestricted. Alternatively, this [rule] should be understood as intended to provide a counter-exception to what was previously stated. 5.

If the contraction or non-contraction of one's conduct (*vṛtti*) alone were the cause for the contraction or non-contraction of impurity (*āśauca*), then it might be feared that a person of uncontracted conduct who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) would remain impure until death. Anticipating this objection, the author shows the limit of impurity:

"A Brahmin who has fallen away from birth-rites and sacraments, and who neglects the twilight prayers (*sandhyopāsana*), being a mere nominal Brahmin, shall remain in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for ten days. (6)

One who has fallen away from the duties of birth, being devoid of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), and who is bereft of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*)—that is, one who does not perform the daily and occasional obligatory rites such as the *saṃdhyopāsana*—is for that very reason a "Brahmin in name only" (*nāmadhārakavipra*). For him too, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts exactly ten days. Vyāsa describes the nature of a Brahmin in name only: "One born from the seed of a Brahmin, yet devoid of the purificatory rite of mantras (*mantrasaṃskāra*), and subsisting merely by caste—that one shall be a Brahmin in name only."

"One who is endowed with the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* as well as the *upanayana*, yet neither knows the ritual acts nor has studied [the Veda], he would be a mere bearer of the name. (VyāSm 4.42–43).
Now, it is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* that for a Brahmin who is a mere bearer of the name and devoid of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), there is impurity lasting until death.
"For one who is devoid of ritual action, for a fool, for one who is gravely ill, and for one who acts according to their own whims, they say that impurity lasts until death. Thus [it is stated].
Dakṣa also says:
[The wealth] of one who is diseased, miserly, perpetually burdened by debt,
devoid of religious rites, foolish, and especially one who is dominated by his wife.
For one whose mind is attached to vices, who is perpetually dependent on others,
and who is devoid of faith and renunciation, his impurity (sūtaka) shall last until the end of his ashes.
"There shall never be a time when there is no birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), for as long as one lives there is indeed birth-impurity.

(DaSm 6.9–11) [219] If it is asked, "How then can there be impurity lasting ten days (*daśāhāśauca*)?", it is replied: because these statements are *arthavādas* intended as censure, they do not have the purpose of enjoining impurity for the duration of one's life. Otherwise...
Otherwise, this statement— "A Brahmin who merely bears the name [of his lineage] shall be impure for ten days" (Parāśarasmṛti 3.6)— would be contradicted.

Having thus described the period of impurity for all four castes, [the author] now states the impurity pertaining to birth and death when those born of a higher caste from women of a lower caste are involved:
"Those who share a single funeral cake (piṇḍa) are heirs, even if they have separate wives and dwellings;
upon their birth or their death, that same impurity (sūtaka) shall apply to them. (7)

Those for whom there is a single *piṇḍa*—that is, a body of the highest caste (*uttamavarṇa*) as their progenitor—and who have separate wives and households—that is, those whose places of birth (*niketana*) are women of lower castes—are the heirs (*dāyādāḥ*), namely the sons. When birth or death occurs among them that pertains to the highest caste, the resulting impurity (*sūtaka*) shall be the ritual defilement (*āśauca*) pertaining to the highest caste. And so says Manu: "In all cases, they should respectfully observe the impurity of the higher castes;
however, regarding their own [lower] births, they should observe their own impurity according to the rules prescribed for those castes" (MDh 5.87).

The meaning is this: all those of lower castes, in relation to the birth or death of those of higher castes, shall observe the impurity for ten nights and so forth as prescribed by the rules for the higher castes. However, in the case of births or deaths among their own kind, they shall observe their own specific impurity. This is also stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: “When a Brāhmaṇa has passed away, the purification for Śūdras, Vaiśyas, and Kṣatriyas shall be accomplished in ten nights; thus spoke the Lotus-born One. (KūP 1.2.23.45)
Devala also says:
"Among all castes, those who are heirs and kinsmen of a Brahmin—
for them, a ten-day period of impurity is prescribed when there is an impurity affecting a Brahmin."
And this impurity pertains to those who are undivided. Thus Āpastamba says:

"If death or birth occurs among the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, their impurity is that pertaining to the paternal estate; however, for those who are divided, it is not that pertaining to the paternal estate."

"Apaitṛka" means that which is not derived from the father, but rather from the mother. Regarding the birth and other events involving a person of a lower caste, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) for one of a higher caste is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:

"The impurity for a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, and a Brāhmaṇa [upon the birth of a Śūdra] shall be six nights, three nights, or one night respectively; and indeed, there is no impurity at all for a Śūdra. (KūPu 1.2.23.42)

Viṣṇu also states: "For a Brāhmaṇa, in the case of sapinda relations who are Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, the periods are six nights, three nights, and one night respectively; for a Kṣatriya, among Vaiśyas and Śūdras, they are six nights and three nights; and for a Vaiśya, among Śūdras, it is six nights" (ViDh 22.22–24). Bṛhaspati, however, describes the period of impurity in another manner: "A Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after ten days following a birth or a death among those of his own caste; but among those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, he is purified in seven, five, and three nights respectively. [221]
In this regard, there is an option between the six-night and seven-night courses, or they are determined by [the patient's] oiliness and other factors.

Regarding the impurity (*āśauca*) concerning those of a different caste (*bhinnajātīya*) that has been mentioned, since it might be assumed—just as in the case of those of the same caste—that it extends for seven generations, [the author] states its limit:

"That *sūtaka* [impurity] pertains to the lineage (*gotra*) up to the fourth generation. That *sūtaka*, which refers to the impurity mentioned in relation to offspring of a different caste, lasts for as long as three generations; however, it ceases with the fourth generation, because at that point the *sāpiṇḍya* relationship terminates.
Sapiṇḍa-relationship ceases with the seventh person among those of the same caste,
but among those of different castes, it ceases with the fourth.
Thus, from the statement of Vṛddha-Parāśara; and Śātātapa also says:

"If many born of one [father] have separate wives and separate property, they share a single *piṇḍa* but have separate periods of impurity (*śauca*); however, the *piṇḍa* recurs among three [generations]."
In order to state the gradations of impurity (*āśaucatāratamya*) among those of the same class (*sajātīya*), beginning with the fifth, he describes the cessation of *sāpiṇḍya*:
“He reaches the severance of the inheritance (*dāya*) at the fifth, or one born in his own lineage.

(8) By the word *dāya*, the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) is indicated. From that, he reaches the severance. “Born in his own lineage” means the fifth; by the word “or,” it includes the sixth or the seventh. In that case, *sāpiṇḍya* ceases—so it is said. That was stated by Gautama: “The cessation of the funeral cake occurs at the fifth or the seventh” (GDh 14.7). By the word “or,” it is understood to be at the sixth as well. (8)
He now states the purpose for which that cessation of sapinda-relationship was declared:
"In the fourth generation, there shall be ten nights; in the fifth male generation, six nights;
in the sixth, purification occurs after four days; but in the seventh, after three days. (9)

In the paternal line, counting from the *kūṭastha* (the common ancestor), there is ten days of impurity (*āśauca*) on the fourth degree; six nights on the fifth; four nights on the sixth; and three nights on the seventh. Now, an objection may be raised: since *sāpiṇḍya* extends only up to the seventh person, and since a rule of ten-day impurity is prescribed without distinction for all *sapiṇḍas*, this prescription for the reduction of impurity is untenable. That *sāpiṇḍya* extends up to the seventh person is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"The fourth and subsequent ancestors are the partakers of the *lepa* (smearings); the father and subsequent ancestors are the partakers of the *piṇḍas* (funeral cakes)."
"The giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) is the seventh among them; their *sāpiṇḍya* extends for seven generations. Thus [says the Matsya Purāṇa, 18.29]. Manu also says:
"But the state of being a *sapiṇḍa* ceases at the seventh person."
"But the status of being a *samānodaka* [relative] exists when the birth and name are not known" (MDh 5.60).

This is true; nevertheless, since the cessation of *sapiṇḍatva* is recorded in the Smṛtis as occurring optionally at the fifth or seventh generation, it is appropriate that the rule for the contraction of impurity (*āśauca*) be applied optionally in accordance with that. And the statement of Gautama has been cited: "The cessation of the *piṇḍas* occurs at the fifth or the seventh" (GDh 14.7). Paiṭhīnasi also says: "Having passed three on the mother's side, and five on the father's side."

[Objection: But if this is so, then for those beginning with the fifth generation, by virtue of being *samānodaka* (distant sapindas), the three-day period of impurity prescribed by the rule, "But for those who offer water [the impurity lasts] for three days," would apply; therefore, the prescription of six nights and so forth is untenable. [Reply:

True—though the three-day impurity would indeed apply to those beginning with the fifth, it is nevertheless set aside by a specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhāna*). For it is logical that a general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*) should be understood as referring to cases other than those falling within the scope of a specific rule (*viśeṣaśāstra*). || 9 ||

He states an exception in certain cases to the aforementioned impurity for deceased persons: "In the case of death by leaping from a precipice or by fire, likewise upon death in a foreign land, and when a child has died or one has renounced the world (saṃnyasta), immediate purification is ordained. (10)

Bhṛgu is a precipice. Agni is well known. Death by Bhṛgu or Agni—meaning death through such means other than by accident—is an indication for all types of "bad deaths" (durmaraṇa), as required by the rules of expiation (prāyaścitta). When death occurs due to these causes, there is immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) for all the sapiṇḍas related to the deceased, and not the ten-day period of impurity (daśāhāśauca). Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"In the case of those killed by kings, cows, or Brahmins, and of suicides, purification is immediate. (YDh 3.21)

A "king" is a consecrated Kṣatriya. The word "cow" (go) is indicative of all animals possessing horns, fangs, and so forth. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to include the Caṇḍāla and others. For those who are relatives—specifically *sapiṇḍas*—of persons killed by these [kings and others], as well as for those who commit suicide, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts "immediately," meaning as long as the corpse is visible, and not for a duration such as ten days; this is the meaning. Furthermore, there is no offering of water or other rites for those who have died an untimely or violent death (*durmṛta*). Thus says Yama: "From a Caṇḍāla, from water, from a serpent, from a Brāhmaṇa, and even from lightning..."
And for those of evil deeds, death comes at the hands of fanged beasts and wild animals.
Whatever water and offerings of food are given to the departed spirits, none of that remains; it perishes in mid-air.

"There shall be no impurity, no water libation, no tears, nor funeral rites such as cremation for those slain by the *brahmadaṇḍa*; one should not even carry their bier. Here, *brahmadaṇḍa* refers to a Brahmin’s curse or a malevolent incantation (*abhicāra*). By the word *kaṭa*, the mat or similar object used for carrying a corpse is denoted. Āpastamba also says:
If one should cause his own death by means of fire, water, or other such methods,
for him no period of impurity is prescribed, nor is the performance of water-libation rites required.

[225] Thus [it is said]. And this refers to the case of intentional death. For this very reason, Gautama states: “For those killed by cows or Brahmins; for those [killed] due to the king’s wrath; in battle; and for those who desire [death] through fasting, starvation, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling [from a precipice]” (GDh 14.6–9). *Prāya* means setting out on the Great Journey (*mahāprasthāna*). *Anāśaka* means fasting. *Prapatana* means falling from a cliff (*bhṛgupatana*). The meaning is that for the sapinda of those killed intentionally by these means, the impurity (*āśauca*) lasts until the sight [of the corpse]. And from this, the following is implied: this prohibition regarding the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth applies only to one who is killed while engaging in a conflict with snakes, Caṇḍālas, or the like. Likewise, this prohibition of impurity and so forth applies to the death of one who goes forward to seize wicked fanged beasts and the like. Likewise, in the case of death while acting in opposition to a king. Likewise, even in the case of crossing a river by means of one's arms. Thus it should be understood in all cases. For this very reason, the *Brahmapurāṇa* says:
He who plays with horned animals, fanged beasts, clawed creatures, serpents, poison, fire, or great waters— things that should be avoided from afar— and then dies [thereby], [is reborn as a ghost].
[226] Those who act against the wishes of the Nāgas, or are burned by lightning,
as well as those who have been arrested somewhere by the king on account of the crime of theft;
And those who, out of anger, abducted the wives of others were slain by their husbands;
likewise, those who engaged in conflict with those of unequal status, with those of mixed caste, and with Caṇḍālas and the like.
Having done so, they were killed by them; likewise, out of anger, they resorted to executioners and the like, or to fasting, poison, fire, weapons, hanging, or water.
Those lowest of men who cause mountains, trees, or precipices to collapse,
as well as those who commit the great sins (mahāpātaka), are proclaimed to be outcasts (patita).

"For those who have fallen [from their caste], there shall be no cremation, no funeral rites, no collection of bones, nor the shedding of tears, nor the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), nor should any *śrāddha* or similar ceremonies ever be performed. Now, an objection: "This prohibition of cremation for those killed by *caṇḍālas* and the like refers only to those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). If it were applicable to those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), it would entail the violation of the scriptural injunction regarding the disposal of the fires and sacrificial vessels, as stated: 'One should cremate the maintainer of the sacred fires with his fires and his sacrificial vessels.'"

Not so; for another Smṛti prescribes a different method of disposal for the fires and sacrificial vessels belonging to one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) when killed by a Caṇḍāla or others:
"One should cast the Vaitāna fires into water and the Āvasathya fire at a crossroads; but if the sacrificer dies an untimely death (vṛthā), one should burn the vessels in the fire."
"For those who have abandoned their own bodies and likewise for those who have fallen from their caste, there are no funeral rites;
yet even for them, it is beneficial to place them in the waters of the Gaṅgā.

Therefore, there is a prohibition against cremation and other rites for all who have died an unnatural death, without distinction. This prohibition regarding impurity (*āśauca*), *śrāddha*, and so forth, lasts for one year. However, when the year is complete, one must certainly perform all the post-mortem rites (*aurdhvadaihika*) after performing the Nārāyaṇabali, in order to establish the deceased's fitness for receiving the *śrāddha* and other offerings. This has been stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:

"And for those killed by cows or Brahmins, as well as for those who have fallen [from their caste], all funeral rites (aurdhvadaihika) must be performed after one year has passed. Thus it is said. Furthermore, Vyāsa has stated that the Nārāyaṇabali brings about purification from the state of being a ghost (preta-śuddhi).
"Whatever is offered dedicated to Nārāyaṇa or Śiva, that act shall be the means of purification for him; it cannot be otherwise.

However, in the case of one killed by a snake, there is this specific rule: having performed the worship of the serpent on the fifth lunar day (pañcamī) for the duration of a year, and after the year has passed, having performed the Nārāyaṇa-bali sacrifice, one should give a golden serpent and a living cow. This is stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.

"Having fashioned a Naga from gold and likewise a cow, and having given them to a Brahmin according to the prescribed rite, one shall attain freedom from debt to one's father. Thus it is said. However, in the case of death due to negligence, impurity (āśauca) certainly remains; and so says Aṅgiras:
"If anyone dies through negligence by means of fire, water, or the like, for him the period of impurity must be observed and the water-libation rite (udakakriyā) must be performed.
Thus it is stated; and also in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
Then, due to negligence or out of fearlessness, impelled unexpectedly by fate,
one may encounter horned animals, fanged beasts, clawed predators, serpents, poisons, lightning, water, or fire.

[228] "If he has been killed by Caṇḍālas or thieves anywhere, his cremation and other rites must be performed, because he has not fallen from his caste. Regarding death by leaping from a precipice or by fire according to the prescribed rule, however, there is a distinction. And so says Śātātapa:
An aged man who has ceased ritual purification, for whom medical treatment has been abandoned,
and who kills himself by means of leaping from a precipice, fire, fasting, or other such methods— [is not to be mourned].
"In that case, there is impurity for three nights; on the second day, the collection of bones takes place;

on the third day, having offered water, one should perform the *śrāddha* on the fourth. Furthermore, there is a rule regarding [suicide by] falling from a precipice (*bhṛgu*) and so forth. Likewise, the *Ādityapurāṇa* states:
If a man is afflicted by great diseases that are difficult to cure,
he may enter a blazing fire or likewise practice fasting unto death.
One might go to a bottomless mass of water, or even to a fall from a precipice,
or tread the great path, or with devotion ascend the mountain of snow.
Or if one casts off the body upon a branch of the banyan tree at Prayāga, one shall attain the highest worlds; such a person is never considered a suicide.
He who dies in Vārāṇasī after having rejected medical treatment,
remaining amidst wood and stone while situated in the midst of the waters of the Jahnavī;

"Facing toward the Unmanifest (Avimukta), Hara, having gone to the root of his ear, utters the *praṇava*, the Savior (*tāraka*); it is never otherwise, anywhere, at any time. Thus says the *Brahmagarbha*.
"He who, being afflicted by a grave illness, is unable to perform [the rites], does not incur sin in the hereafter by undertaking a great journey by fire or water.

Regarding the phrase "one who has died in another country," the meaning is that there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) when a person who is not a *sapiṇḍa* has died in another country. Manu says this:

"When [the deceased] is a child, or when he is staying in another country, or when he has entered a separate *piṇḍa* [lineage], one becomes pure immediately after plunging into water with one's clothes on. (MDh 5.78). Alternatively, the *sapiṇḍa* is distinguished by being "staying in another country. The definition of "another country" was stated by Vṛddha-Manu:
"Where there is a great river or a mountain acting as a barrier,
and where speech is divided, that is called a different country. Thus it was said by Bṛhaspati as well.
"Some say the other country (deśāntara) is sixty yojanas in length;
some say forty, and others likewise thirty.
Regarding the definition of a yojana, it has been stated in another Smṛti:
Eight horizontal barley grains, or three vertical rice grains, are said to be the measure of one finger-breadth (aṅgula);
twelve finger-breadths constitute a span (vitasti).
"Two *vitastis* make one *aratni*; from that, a *kiṣku*; from that, a *dhanus*;

two thousand *dhanus* make a *krośa*; and four *krośas* make a *yojana*. Here, "the child" refers to one for whom the name has not yet been performed. The meaning is that when such a child dies, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) for its *sapiṇḍa* relatives on account of the death. And so says Śaṅkha: "Before the naming ceremony, there is immediate purification. Kātyāyana also says:
"But if one passes away before the ten-day period has elapsed, purification shall occur immediately; there is no [impurity for] the deceased, nor any water-rite.
This refers to cases other than those involving the mother, father, or uterine brother. And so Vyāghra says:

"When an infant dies, immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) is prescribed for the sapindas; likewise for the husband and wife, and for uterine brothers, it is by ten days alone. When a child is born and then dies, or dies at birth, there is immediate purification for the sapindas. If the infant dies on the day of birth, the mother and others attain purity after ten days alone; however, if death occurs on another day, purification comes after the remaining days [of the ten-day period]. And so says Vyāghra:

"Śātātapa has declared: 'When the *niṣkramaṇa* (first outing) of an infant who was born after an internal burning [of the mother] takes place, purification for the parents occurs through the [period of] *sūtaka* alone.

Another Smṛti also states: 'The impurity due to death that pertains to the father and others for one who has died within ten days is [removed] by the days of *sūtaka*'; the word 'passes away' is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. However, the impurity caused by birth remains in its entirety. And so says Hārīta: 'Whether a child dies after being born, or is born dead, the period for the *sapiṇḍas* is ten days. Bṛhan-Manu also [says the same]."

"If a child dies within ten days, its kinsmen shall not observe impurity for the dead (śāvāśauca), but shall instead observe the impurity pertaining to birth (sūtyāśauca). And this should be understood as applying after the cutting of the umbilical cord; so too says Jaimini.
"As long as the umbilical cord is not severed, so long does one not incur *sūtaka* (birth-impurity);
once the cord is severed, thereafter *sūtaka* is prescribed.
Thus said Bṛhan-Manu prior to the cutting of the navel.
"If born alive, but then dies, it is indeed *sūtaka* (birth-impurity);
the *sūtaka* for the mother lasts for the full period, while for the father and others it lasts for three nights.
As for the statement of Bṛhat-Pracetas:
If a child dies within a single muhūrta after being born,
the mother undergoes purification after ten days, while the agnates (gotriṇaḥ) are purified immediately.

Thus, that [text] is intended to establish immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for the purpose of the *agnihotra* sacrifice. And so says Śaṅkha: “For the sake of performing the *agnihotra* and other rites, by bathing and touching water, there is purity for that duration. When a renunciant (*saṃnyasta*) has died, there is immediate purification for his *sapiṇḍa* relatives. And likewise, the Vāmana Purāṇa states: “In the case of a child, one who has gone forth (*pravrajita*), or one who has died in another land, as well as in the case of death by lightning strike—immediate purification is declared. (VāPu 14.99–100)
Another Smṛti text also states:
"For one who has desisted from all attachments and is devoted to the practice of meditation, no cremation should be performed, nor any impurity observed, nor any water-libation rite. (10)

Having previously stated that there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for the *sapiṇḍas* upon hearing of the death of one who was not a *sapiṇḍa* residing in another country, [the author] now prescribes immediate purification even for the *sapiṇḍas* upon hearing of the death of a *sapiṇḍa* residing in another country after more than a year has passed:

"If it is heard that someone belonging to the same lineage (*sagotra*) has died in another country—[whether the news arrives after] three nights, a day and night, or immediately—one becomes pure by bathing. (11)

A *sagotra* is one who belongs to the same *piṇḍa* lineage (*sapiṇḍa*). When the death of such a person is heard of after he has gone to another country, for his *sapiṇḍas*, there is no impurity for three nights or even a single day and night; rather, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). Beyond ten days but before three fortnights (*tripakṣa*), the impurity lasts for three nights; before six months, it lasts for a "bird-day" (*pakṣiṇī*); and before a year, it lasts for one day—this is the meaning. And so Devala says: "Until three fortnights, it shall be three nights; until six months, a *pakṣiṇī*; beyond that, until a year, one day; after a year, one is purified by bathing. Viṣṇu also says: "Before three fortnights, it is three nights; until six months, a day and night; and before a year, a single day—even in the case of those who have died in a foreign land. Here, by the word "day," two days are meant, according to another statement: "Until six months, a *pakṣiṇī*. Yājñavalkya also [says]:

"When [the relative] has gone abroad, purification shall consist of the remainder of the period; when [the year] is complete, one becomes pure after offering water. (YDh 3.21) The meaning is as follows: if a *sapiṇḍa* who has gone abroad and resides in another country dies while one is in the midst of a period of impurity (*āśauca*), purification occurs by the mere remainder of that period. If the full year has elapsed before hearing of his death, one becomes pure by bathing and offering water. Thus says Manu: "But when a year has passed, one becomes pure simply by touching water. (MDh 5.76)

As for that which was stated by Gautama: “And having heard [of a death] after the tenth day, [the impurity lasts for] two days with an intervening night” (GDh 14.11), that should be understood as occurring after three fortnights but before six months, because of the traditional teaching of Devala: “After six months, it is two days with an intervening night. Furthermore, as for the statement of Vasiṣṭha: “If one hears of someone who died while residing in another country after ten days have passed, [the impurity lasts for] one night” (VaDh 4.36); and as for the prose statement of Viṣṇu: “[234] But when the period of impurity has elapsed, at the end of a year it is by one night; beyond that, by bathing” (VaDh 22.40–41), that should be understood as occurring after six months but before a year, because of the traditional teaching: “Beyond that, up to a year, it is one day. Even as for the statement of Śaṅkha: “But when ten nights have passed, one shall be impure for three nights” (ŚaṅSm 15.12), that is to be seen as applying before three fortnights, because of the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: “Before three fortnights, it is three nights. In this regard, the rule of immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*) mentioned in the root text refers specifically to kinsmen (*jñāti*). However, regarding fathers and others, there is a distinction. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
"If both parents should die, even if the son is far away,
from the moment he hears of it, he shall be subject to impurity for ten days. Thus says Dakṣa as well.
"But upon the death of a great guru, even if a year has passed, the funeral rites must be performed according to the rule by one wearing wet clothes.

The meaning is that even after a year has elapsed, the impurity, the offering of water, and so forth must be performed; purification does not occur merely through bathing. A specific rule regarding the wife of a father who is distinct from one's mother has been shown by Dakṣa:

[235] "When the wife of one's father has passed away, the best of the twice-born shall remain impure for three nights even after a year has elapsed, with the exception of his own mother. And this rule regarding impurity that has lapsed refers to the death of one who has been initiated (*upanīta*). Thus says Vyāghrapāt:
"For all [initiations], it is the same when the age has passed;
however, once the initiation has been performed, it is unequal, as that very [initiation] is born of excessive time."

The meaning is this: regarding the age consisting of six months and so forth, whatever impurity (*āśauca*) is prescribed by such statements as "until the eruption of teeth, [impurity is] immediate" (*sadyaḥ*), that is equal and without distinction for all [classes], beginning with the Brāhmaṇas. When the ten-day period and so forth have elapsed, whatever three-night impurity and the like there is, that is common to all. However, when one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) dies, the impurity for the Brāhmaṇas and others is unequal, being ten, twelve, fifteen, or thirty days respectively. But the "impurity arising after the time limit" (*atikālaja*) applies only to the death of one who has been initiated, not to the death of one who has not been initiated. Regarding birth, however, there is no impurity arising after the time limit. As Devala says:
"There is no impurity even when the days of birth-impurity have passed. So too says Manu:
"Having heard of the death of a relative or the birth of a son after the ten-day period has elapsed..."
"A man becomes pure by bathing with his clothes on. (MDh 5.77).

Here, because of the mention of the "son," it means that even after the ten-day period has passed, the father’s purification occurs through bathing; however, for the *sapiṇḍas*, there is no impurity once the period has elapsed. But if death occurs within the ten days, purification is achieved by the remaining days. And so says Śaṅkha:
"Having heard of a relative who has gone to another country, whether of their well-being or likewise of their death..."
"He shall remain impure for exactly as long as remains of the ten-night period. (Śaṅkha-smṛti 15.11)

For one who has died in another country is of two kinds: one for whom the funeral rites have been performed (*kṛtasaṃskāra*) and one for whom they have not (*akṛtasaṃskāra*). Regarding the former, upon hearing of his death, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) is established by two statements as being either before or after one year. However, regarding the hearing of the death of one for whom the rites have not been performed, the specific timing for the undertaking of impurity, the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*), and so forth, is now distinguished. One for whom the rites have not been performed is also of two types, based on the distinction between knowing or not knowing the day of death. For him whose day of death is known, the annual *śrāddha* and other rites must be performed on that very day. As for the undertaking of impurity, the offering of rice balls, and the libation of water, these should be performed at a time when favorable constellations and other factors are considered, because the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) proceeds in such a manner. (11)
But for one whose day is not known, this is said:
"If a Brahmin who has gone to another country meets his death due to exhaustion caused by time, and the lunar day is not known... (12)
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the new moon day, and on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight,
one should perform the offering of water, the presentation of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), and the ancestral rite (śrāddha).

When a Brahmin who has gone to another country for some reason, such as a pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*), meets with the destruction of his body anywhere due to the great exhaustion resulting from wandering through many lands for a long time, his date of death is consequently unknown, and news of his passing is only heard at some indefinite point. In that case, both the undertaking of the period of impurity (*āśauca*)—including the commencement of offerings of sesame water and funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*)—and the annual *śrāddha* ceremony must be performed on any one of the three lunar days beginning with the eighth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*), according to one’s preference; and the annual *śrāddha* itself must be performed on that very same lunar day.

Although the acceptance of impurity (*āśauca*) is not explicitly mentioned in this statement, it is nevertheless understood that its inclusion here is intended; for, since the preceding and following statements concern the subject of impurity, they constitute a single context, and because the offering of water, sesame, land, and funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) would be impossible without the acceptance of impurity. Furthermore, by the presentation of numerous duties such as the offering of water, the inclusion of the entire section on the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) is intended here. That section has been summarized [above] and will be explained in detail by us further below. (12–13)

Previously, it was stated that upon the death of a child who has not yet been named, the sapindas attain immediate purification. Now, he prohibits the impurity associated with the funeral rites even for the death of a child who has been named but whose teeth have not yet emerged:
"Those children whose teeth have not emerged and those who have just issued from the womb—for them there is no cremation with fire, no period of impurity, and no water libations. (14)

The meaning is that for those children who have died without teeth having grown—that is, before the teeth have emerged—and for those who have died after names were given, as well as those who have fallen stillborn immediately upon emerging from the womb, their *sapiṇḍas* must not perform the cremation or other such rites. Thus says the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"But in the case of women, a fetus that has fallen, or one born alive and then dead, or one that dies before the teeth have grown, or likewise one that has passed six months [in the womb];"
"Having adorned [the corpse] with garments and other ornaments, it should be abandoned like a piece of wood;
having slowly dug into the earth, immediate purification is prescribed. Thus it is said.

A fetus of women that has miscarried, one who dies at the very moment of birth, one who dies before six months, and one who dies after six months but without having cut teeth—such a person should be buried in the ground like a log of wood. The meaning is that other *sapiṇḍas*, excluding the mother and others, need not perform the period of impurity (*āśauca*) and so forth. Viṣṇu also states: "When a child who has not yet cut teeth dies, [the purification] is immediate; there is no cremation with fire nor the offering of water" (ViDh 22.27–28). || 14 ||

Having previously described the period of impurity for the sapindas and other relatives in the event of a miscarriage, [the author] now states that there is a period of impurity for the mother on account of that same cause:
"If the fetus of a woman should perish or be lost by miscarriage, the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) lasts as many days as the number of months the fetus had been situated [in the womb]. (15)

If there should be a miscarriage or a birth of the fetus, then for as many months as the fetus remained in the womb, for that same number of days there is *sūtaka*—meaning the impurity of childbirth—for the mother; such is the meaning. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"In the case of a miscarriage, nights equal in number to the months are the cause of purification" (YDh 3.20).

Regarding the phrase "nights equal in number to the months," this should be understood to apply from the fourth month up to the seventh. Prior to that, however, the periods of three nights and so forth apply according to one's caste. Thus says Marīci:

In the case of a miscarriage, the period is according to the month of pregnancy; however, for a recent miscarriage, it is three days for a Brahmin, four nights for a Kshatriya, and five days for a Vaishya.

"But for a Śūdra, this purification is proclaimed to take eight days. Thus it is said. Regarding a miscarriage occurring within three months, for a Brāhmaṇa of the highest caste, the period is three days. Gautama also states: "In the case of a miscarriage, the night [of impurity] is equal in number to the months of gestation; or else, it is three days" (GDh 14.10–11). Here, there is an alternative arrangement between the nights equal to the months of gestation and the three-day period: until the third month, it is three days, and beyond that, the nights are equal in number to the months of gestation. This is also stated in the Ādipurāṇa: "If a miscarriage should occur within six months..."

"Then, purification for them is desired after days equal to the months [of pregnancy]. And this impurity caused by miscarriage applies to the mother alone; however, that caused by birth applies to the father and others as well. Thus says Marīci: "In the case of miscarriage, there shall be three nights of impurity for the mother, with the exclusion of the impurity for the *sapiṇḍas*."

"In the case of a miscarriage, [the impurity lasts] for as many days as the months [of pregnancy]; for the sapinda relatives, it is three days. Vasiṣṭha also says: "When a child under two years of age has died, or in the case of a miscarriage, the sapindas shall observe impurity for three nights" (VaDh. 4.34). Regarding a miscarriage, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha states a specific rule for the father: "In the case of a miscarriage, the nights [of impurity] for women are equal to the number of months; for the man, there is merely bathing. || 15 ||
Now, one might ask: since there is no difference between miscarriage (*srāva*) and abortion (*pāta*) in that neither has reached the time of delivery, what is the distinction between these two?

To this he says: "Up to the fourth month it would be a miscarriage (*srāva*); in the fifth and sixth months, an abortion (*pāta*). Beyond that, it would be a birth (*prasūti*), and for ten days there shall be impurity (*sūtaka*). (16)

Within the fourth month, the destruction of the embryo is called a miscarriage (*srāva*). In the fifth and sixth months, the destruction of the embryo is called a fall (*pāta*). In those cases, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) prescribed according to the number of months shall apply to the mother. Beyond this, from the seventh month onwards, the emergence of the embryo is called birth (*prasava*). In that case, the meaning is that the ten-day period of impurity caused by birth shall apply to the mother. As for what is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "Below nine months, how can there be purification upon birth?
Whether he [the child] dies or lives, purification occurs by days according to the number of months."

This is its meaning: when a birth occurs before nine months—that is, starting from the seventh month—the impurity (*āśauca*) caused by that event is prescribed for all *sapiṇḍas* other than the woman who has given birth (*sūtikā*) for a number of days equal to the number of months. If this were intended to apply specifically to the *sūtikā*, it would result in a contradiction with the rule regarding the ten-day period.

But, one might object, if that were so, it would contradict the statement: "A Brahmin [is purified] in ten days upon a birth," which prescribes a ten-day impurity for all *sapiṇḍas* caused by a birth.

That is not so, because that [text] is applicable to the case of birth in the ninth or tenth month; or else, even if the subject matter is the same, let there be a settled rule by way of option (vikalpa). || 15 ||
It indicates the period of impurity when there is the cremation of a child:

"When one who has teethed, one who has not yet teethed, or one for whom the *cūḍā* ceremony has been performed, passes away, one shall remain impure for three nights upon their cremation. (16) Thus it is said.

"One whose teeth have grown" (*dantajāta*) refers to one who has developed teeth. "Subsequently born" (*anujāta*) means born after that, which is to say, one whose teeth have not yet emerged. "One for whom the rite called *cūḍā* has been performed" (*kṛtacūḍa*) refers to one who has undergone the tonsure ceremony. The meaning is this: when there is cremation (*agnisaṃskāra*) for those who have teeth but have not had the *cūḍā* performed, as well as for those subsequently born (who have no teeth) and for one for whom the *cūḍā* was performed in the third year, their *sapiṇḍa* relatives shall remain impure for three nights. Regarding that, in the case of cremating one who has teeth but has not had the *cūḍā* performed, Aṅgiras has stated that the impurity lasts for three nights: "Even if he has not had the *cūḍā* performed, if he has teeth and has passed away..."
"Even after cremating him in this manner, one should observe impurity for three days.
Also, in the Purāṇa:
"But where a deceased person who has not yet passed two years is cremated..."

"However, for the relatives, there is impurity for three nights. As for the statement of Viṣṇu, "But if [the child] has teethed but the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has not been performed, [impurity lasts] for one day and night" (ViDh 22.29), that should be understood to apply to the case of burial. Regarding the cremation of one who has teethed but whose tonsure has been performed, a three-night impurity is prescribed in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Even if he has not yet teethed, if he has passed away after the tonsure was performed..."
"Nevertheless, one should cremate him and observe impurity for three days.
As for that which was stated by Yama: "In the case of a son whose teeth have not yet emerged, or a child, or likewise in the case of a miscarriage..."
For all sapindas, however, the period of impurity lasts for one day and night.
Thus, that refers to the case of one whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has not been performed.
But if it is asked: "How can there be the state of having performed the tonsure for one who has not yet grown teeth, since that [ceremony] is prescribed for the third year?"—it is not so.

"According to the law, the *cūḍākarma* for all twice-born classes must be performed in the first or third year, as enjoined by the *Śruti*" (MDh 2.35). Since Manu has thus recorded this as an option, the mention of "the rite of consecration with fire" (*agnisaṃskaraṇa*) is also stated as an alternative specifically for those whose teeth have just appeared and for those born later [in the womb]. It does not apply to one whose *cūḍā* was performed at three years of age, because in that case the fire-consecration is mandatory. In other cases, the option regarding the fire-consecration has been shown by Manu.
"The ritual of water-libation should not be performed by relatives for one who has not reached three years of age;
however, it may be performed for one who has teethed, or once the naming ceremony has been completed" (MDh 5.70).
Here, the term "ritual of water-libation" is intended as an indicative mark for the funerary rite involving fire. 16.
He shows the specific impurity according to the particular stage of age: "Until the eruption of teeth, it is immediate; until the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), it is declared to last one night;
until the initiation into Vedic study (vratādeśa), it lasts three nights; beyond that, ten nights" (17).

For a child who has died before the eruption of teeth, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for the *sapiṇḍa* relatives. After the eruption of teeth but before the performance of the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*), for those who have passed away, the impurity for the relatives lasts for a night and a day (*naiśikī*), meaning an entire day and night. The "instruction in the vow" (*vratādeśa*) refers to the initiation (*upanayana*). For one who has died prior to the tonsure but after that [eruption of teeth], the impurity for the relatives lasts three nights; beyond that, it is ten nights—this is the meaning. And so says the author of the *Saṃgraha*: "In order, from naming, to the eruption of teeth, to the tonsure, and below the initiation..."
"Immediate purification, one day, three days, or for others who maintain the sacred fires and perform water-libations. Śaṅkha also states:
"In the case of a son whose teeth have not yet emerged, immediate purification is ordained."
Likewise, purification from death occurs after one day and night in the case of a child who has not yet had the tonsure ceremony performed.
"Likewise, in the case of one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*), the relatives become pure after three days. (Śaṅkha-smṛti 15.4–5).

As for the statement of Kāśyapa: "For children whose teeth have not yet emerged, purification occurs after three nights" (Kāśyapa-smṛti 6.8), that refers specifically to the mother and father. For this very reason, Manu says:
"A man, having emitted semen, becomes pure by touching water."
"Due to the connection through the seed, one should observe impurity for three days" (MDh 5.63).
The "connection through the seed" refers to the relationship between the progenitor and the procreated. As for another Smṛti text:
"Prior to the naming ceremony, [impurity lasts] immediately; for one day, until the eruption of teeth."

Thus, this should be understood regarding cremation. However, in the case of burial, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śuddhi*), because of the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: “When a child who has not yet cut its teeth dies, purification is immediate; there is neither the rite of cremation nor the water-libation” (ViDh 22.27–28). As for the statement of Vasiṣṭha: “When one dies before reaching two years of age, or in the case of a miscarriage, the impurity for the *sapiṇḍas* lasts three nights” (ViDh 4.34), that should be understood to apply to a child who has cut its teeth when the rite of cremation is performed. Consequently, the settled rule (*vyavasthā*) is as follows: prior to the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), immediate purification is fixed. After that and prior to the eruption of teeth, if the rite of cremation is performed, the impurity lasts one day; otherwise, there is immediate purification. Even for such a child who has not cut its teeth, if the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*) has been performed, the impurity lasts three nights. After the eruption of teeth but before the tonsure, if there is burial, it lasts one day; but if there is cremation, it lasts three days. After the tonsure but prior to the initiation (*upanayana*), it lasts three days. After initiation, for Brāhmaṇas and others, it lasts ten days and so forth. This settled rule is to be understood in the case of the death of a male offspring. Regarding a female offspring, however, a distinction has been shown by the elder Manu:

"Immediate purification is prescribed when a girl is immature; however, for unmarried girls, purification lasts one day, and likewise three days for those who have been given away in marriage. Here, "immature" means one whose *cūḍā* ceremony has not been performed.
For a girl who has not yet undergone the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*), immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed;

this is according to the traditional teaching of Āpastamba. Regarding unmarried girls, if they have not been betrothed by word, purification lasts one day and night; if they have been betrothed by word, it lasts three days. And so says Marīci: "In the case of the tonsure ceremony, there is immediate purification; prior to the betrothal by word, it is one day; for those who have been betrothed, prior to the marriage, it is three days. Also in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "If a girl dies from birth until the end of the tonsure ceremony..."
In that case, there shall always be immediate purification for all social classes.
Therefore, until the point of the giving of the bride in marriage, it is indeed for only one day;
beyond that, when [the impurity] has increased, the settled rule is three nights.
When the formal betrothal has been performed there, it should be understood that for three days the status belongs to both [the father and the groom];
thereafter, for those who have been given away, it belongs to the husband alone.
"The impurity regarding death and birth shall be as prescribed for one's own caste. Thus [says Manu]. Pulastya also says:
"In the case of an unmarried girl, purification is immediate; in the case of a married woman, one becomes pure after a day."
If she has been given away, it lasts for three nights; if she has been formally bestowed, it lasts for a pakṣiṇī period.

[246] Thus: "When she has been given," meaning when the gift has been commenced but not yet verbally bestowed; that is to say, if she dies after the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*), the impurity lasts for three nights. Manu also says:
"But for female relatives who have not undergone the sacramental rites, the kinsmen become pure after three days;
however, those of the same lineage (*sanābhi*) become pure according to the very rule already stated" (MDh 5.72).

Relatives (*bāndhava*) are those who are *sapiṇḍas* through the husband; kinsmen (*sanābhayaḥ*) are those who are *sapiṇḍas* through the father. According to the prescribed rule, this is for three nights. For this very reason, Marīci states: "A woman who has been given away [in marriage] but not yet formally bestowed [with water], and who is thus considered uninitiated (*asaṃskṛtā*), for her it is ordained that both [the husband and the paternal kinsmen] observe impurity for three nights."

Regarding both sides of the paternal lineage: the rule of immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) prescribed for one whose tonsure (*cūḍā*) has not been performed, and the rule of one-day purification (*ekāha*) prescribed for one whose tonsure has been performed, apply to cases other than those involving the mother and father. As it is said:

"In the case of women—whether married or unmarried, whether consecrated by marriage rites or not—the period of impurity for the mother and father shall be three nights; for others, it shall be according to the rule."

This is because Śaṅkha and Kārṣṇājini specifically record: “In the case of girls who have not yet cut their teeth, there is one night for the parents. Since the prescription of three nights applies to those who have cut their teeth, whereas the prescription of one day applies to those who have not, it should be understood that the three nights for the parents refers to the death of a girl who has undergone the sacramental rites (*saṃskṛtā*) while in her father’s house. Thus says Viṣṇu: “There is no impurity on the paternal side regarding women who have been consecrated with sacraments. However, in the event of their birth or death, the rule is one night for the circle of kinsmen and three nights for the parents” (ViDh 22.31–34). This is also stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.

"A woman who has been given away in marriage shall become pure after one day, whether she gives birth or dies while still in her father's house; her kinsmen [become pure] after three days. Thus it is said. For women who have been consecrated [by marriage], there is a period of impurity lasting three nights upon the death of both parents. And so says Vṛddha-Manu:
"But what shall be the case for women who have been married when their parents pass away?
Purity comes after three nights alone," so said the venerable Yama.

This means that upon the passing of the parents—both mother and father—the purification for daughters who have been consecrated by the sacrament of marriage occurs after three nights. For an unmarried daughter's son and a sister's son, the impurity lasts for a "two-night" period (pakṣiṇī); for those who are married, it is three nights. And thus says Vṛddha-Manu:

"When a daughter's son or a sister's son has died, [the impurity] lasts for a *pakṣiṇī* night; but when he has been consecrated [by initiation], it shall be three nights—thus the law is settled. This means that if a daughter's son or a sister's son who is uninitiated (*anupanīta*) dies, the maternal grandfather and others must observe the impurity for a *pakṣiṇī* night—that is, a night flanked by the two days of the future and the present. However, if he dies after being initiated (*upanīta*), the meaning is that the maternal grandfather and others shall observe three nights of impurity. Likewise, upon the death of the maternal grandfather and others, the daughter's son and others observe three nights of impurity. And so says Bṛhaspati:

"One shall be impure for three days upon the death of a maternal grandfather, a teacher (*ācārya*), or a *śrotriya*. Here, the "teacher" is one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* relative but is the performer of the initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites. A *śrotriya*, however, is one who has studied a single branch (*śākhā*) of the Veda and is endowed with qualities such as friendship or being a neighbor. Upon the death of these—the maternal grandfather and the others—it is for three nights. Viṣṇu also states: "When a teacher or a maternal grandfather has passed away, [one is purified] after three nights" (ViDh 22.42). Manu also says: "But upon the death of a *śrotriya* who is well-qualified, one shall be impure for three nights" (MDh 5.81).
This three-night period of impurity is to be understood as applying to cases such as cremation performed by others;
however, when a disciple performs the funeral rites for his deceased teacher, he becomes pure after ten nights, together with those who carry the corpse. (MDh 5.65)

Thus, because Manu has recorded this specific rule regarding cremation and other rites performed by oneself, there is a three-night period of impurity (*āśauca*) for the death of a maternal aunt and others. To that effect, Pracetas says:
"Upon the death of a maternal aunt, a maternal uncle, a mother-in-law, a father-in-law, a teacher, or an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), one is purified after three nights."

The *guru* is the preceptor (*ācārya*). The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is one who has come down through a family lineage; the person for whom he sacrifices (*yājya*) is likewise of that same kind. As for the statement of Yājñavalkya:
"And among the pupil, the resident student, the learned one (*anūcāna*), the maternal uncle, and the *śrotriya*... (YDh 3.24).

Thus, regarding the statement of Viṣṇu: “Upon the death of the teacher’s wife, son, sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), maternal uncle, father-in-law, mother-in-law, brother-in-law, fellow student, or pupil, purification occurs after one night” (ViDh 22.44), in this context the term *guru* refers to the sub-teacher. A *antevāsī* is a pupil initiated by another; however, for a pupil initiated by oneself, Baudhāyana prescribes a three-night period—“For a pupil, a fellow-student (*satīrthya*), or a co-resident celibate (*sabrahmacārin*), [purification is] three nights, a day and night, or one day” (BDh 1.5.11.30). The maternal uncle is one who provides no assistance or resides in a foreign land. A *śrotriya* is one who has not been formally initiated. The mother-in-law and father-in-law are also those who provide no assistance or reside in a foreign land. A fellow student is one who studied for a short time in the same teacher’s household. For these cases, the rule is one night. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"Regarding a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, and a kinsman, [there is impurity] for a *pakṣiṇī* night" (MDh 5.81).

This is its meaning: in the case of a maternal uncle who provides little assistance, a pupil who has studied the Veda with its auxiliary limbs under another teacher, an officiating priest who performs the priestly duties from the consecration (*ādhāna*) onwards as long as life lasts, and kinsmen who are relatives of the mother or father—among these, there is impurity for a *pakṣiṇī* night. For non-aurasa sons and others, there is three-night impurity. Thus says Viṣṇu:
"In the case of non-aurasa sons, whether they are born or die..."
"When wives who have had other husbands before have given birth or have died" (ViDh 22.43).
The phrase "for three nights" is understood to carry over. Hārīta also says:
"In the case of wives who have had other husbands before, and in the case of adopted sons..."
"There shall be a three-night period for a maternal grandfather, but one day for those who are *sapiṇḍas*. Śaṅkha also says:
"In the case of non-aurasa sons, and in the case of wives who have gone to another [man]..."
"And for women who have had previous husbands, purification is held to occur after three nights" (Śaṅkha Smṛti 15.13).

"Non-aurasa sons" refers to those born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) and others; "women who have had previous husbands" refers to remarried women (*punarbhū*); and "those who have gone to another" refers to unchaste women (*svairiṇī*). The meaning is that this three-night period of impurity applies specifically to that status of being a wife or being a son which exists in relation to these non-*aurasa* sons and others. As for the rule prescribing a single day: "In the case of non-*aurasa* sons, and wives who have gone to another... (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.25).
Thus, that [rule] refers to cases where [the relatives] are not present. Even when they are present, for the paternal *sapiṇḍas*, it is only one day. And so says Marīci:
"But for the *sapiṇḍas* it is one day, whereas for the father it is indeed three nights.
As for that which was stated by Prajāpati:

In the case of wives who have not returned home, and in the case of the sons of another's wife, those of the same lineage become pure by bathing; however, their father becomes pure after three nights alone.

Thus, regarding the statement that "purity comes from bathing alone," that refers to the case of *samānodaka* (distant sapinda) relations or to the case of being absent (*asaṃnidhi*). When one of two fathers has died, for the other son born of the same mother, there is impurity (*āśauca*) for three nights. And so says Marīci:
"Two brothers born of one mother but by two fathers belong to different gotras;
in that case, there is one day of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), but for them both, there is three nights of death-impurity (*mṛtaka*)."

Upon the death of one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* relative, but is a blood relation (*yonisaṃbandhin*), there is impurity for a *pakṣiṇī* period. Gautama states this: “A *pakṣiṇī* [period of impurity applies] in the case of a non-*sapiṇḍa* blood relation and a fellow student” (GDh 14.12). This is the meaning: a non-*sapiṇḍa* who has died in one’s own house; blood relations such as the daughter of a maternal uncle (*mātṛṣvasrīya*) or the daughter of a paternal uncle (*pitṛṣvasrīya*) and so forth; and a fellow student who has studied the entire Veda together in the teacher’s household. By the use of the word “and” (*ca*), the wife of the teacher and others are also included. In their case, the person related to them should observe the *pakṣiṇī* period. And likewise, Vṛddha-Manu says:
In the case of a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a friend, a preceptor, or the wives of a preceptor, there is impurity for a "pakṣiṇī" night; likewise if one's maternal grandmother has died.

"And one should spend the night as a *pakṣiṇī* [with fasting on the day of the event and the following day] for the two parents-in-law, for a sister, for a maternal aunt, for a maternal uncle, and likewise for a paternal aunt.

As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: "If someone who is not a *sapiṇḍa* dies in one's own house, [one shall fast] for one night" (ViDh 22.46), that should be understood to apply to the death occurring in a secondary residence. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Aṅgiras:
[252] "If anyone who is not a *sapiṇḍa* should happen to die in someone's house, his impurity (*aśauca*) should be known to last for three nights; there is no doubt about this.
This refers to the case of a *śrotriya* who is not a *sapiṇḍa*. As for that which was stated by Bṛhan-Manu:
When a sister has passed away, or when a brother has also passed away;
when a friend, a son-in-law, or a daughter’s son has died; or when a sister’s son [has died].

"Regarding a sister-in-law (*śyālaka*) and her son, one becomes pure immediately by bathing. In this context, the mention of immediate purification (*sadyaḥśuddhi*) for a sister and others refers to cases where they have died in another country; however, for a son-in-law and a brother-in-law, purification occurs immediately only if they were present [at the time of death]. Regarding death occurring on the day of residence, the impurity lasts for that day; if it occurs at night, it lasts for the night only. Thus said Yājñavalkya:
"When a resident king has died, that day is the cause of purification" (YDh 3.25).

The place where one resides is called one's "home country" (*svadeśa*). When the king of that country has died, for those residing in that land, the cause of purification is the duration of the day on which he died; if it was at night, then the duration of the night. For this very reason, Manu says: "When a king has died, for one who resides within his territory, purification lasts as long as the light [of the sun or stars]. (MDh 5.82)

The impurity (*āśauca*) that occurs together with the solar light, the stellar light, or both, is called *sajyotis*. This means: if it occurs during the day, it lasts as long as the sun is visible; if at night, as long as the stars are visible. When a corpse remains within a village, the impurity of that village lasts for that duration. As Vṛddhamanu says:
"As long as the corpse of anyone remains in the middle of a village, the impurity of that village persists; once it has been removed, purity is restored. (253)
Impurity lasts as long as the light [of the sun or moon] even in the case of the lord of a village and others. Regarding this, the same author says:
"When the lord of a village, the head of a family, a learned *śrotriya*, an ascetic, or a pupil has met his death, purification occurs upon the appearance of the stars."
The head of a family is the leader of a community; a learned scholar may reside in another country. || 17 ||
He states an exception to the aforementioned impurity for the *agnihotrī* and the student (*brahmacārin*):
"For those in whose house the student dwells and the sacrificial fire is offered, and who do not engage in [impure] contact, there shall be no birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). (18) Thus.

The *brahmacārī* is of two kinds: the *upakurvāṇaka* and the *naiṣṭhika*. For those in whose household the sacrificial fire (*hutāśana*) burns and the *agnihotra* is performed, there is no impurity (*āśauca*) at the time of performing the *agnihotra*, provided they do not come into contact with those who are in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtakibhiḥ*). As it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:

"For *naiṣṭhika*s, forest-dwellers (*vanastha*s), ascetics (*yati*s), and *brahmacārī*s, no impurity has been proclaimed by the virtuous, even when a relative has fallen from his caste or died. (KūPu 1.2.23.71)
Devala also says:
"For lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika), forest-dwellers, ascetics, and students,
no impurity is declared in the case of birth (sūtaka) or likewise in the case of death (śāva)."
Bṛhaspati also says:

"Where Vedic study is performed and both daily fire-offerings (homa) are made at both times—morning and evening—the Vaiśvadeva rite is likewise maintained; for them, there shall be no impurity due to birth (sūtaka). || 18 ||
He establishes, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that contact brings about impurity characterized by untouchability and disqualification from ritual acts:
"A Brahmin is defiled by contact during birth as well as death;
but for one who has withdrawn from such contact, there is neither the state of a corpse nor the state of birth-impurity" (19).
This is clear in meaning. || 19 ||
Furthermore:
artisans, craftsmen, physicians, male and female slaves, barbers, kings, and those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas) are declared to be immediately pure. || 20 ||
