A twice-born man who observes his vows, who is purified by the Sattra sacrifice, and who has maintained the sacred fires—there is no period of impurity for him due to a king, provided the monarch so desires. [255] 21.
"A Brahmin who is invited for a funeral rite or a gift, even if he is distressed, becomes pure at that very moment; this was seen by the sages according to the proper time. (22) Thus it is said.

Artisans (*śilpin*) are painters and the like; craftsmen (*kāruka*) are cooks and so forth; physicians (*vaidya*) are medical practitioners; and *śrotriyas* are those who have recently completed their ritual ablutions (*sadyaḥprakṣālaka*). One who observes vows (*savrata*) is one who abides by rules such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*. A *sattrayājī* is one authorized for long sacrificial sessions (*sattra*) such as the *gavām ayana*. These are immediately pure (*sadyaḥśauca*) in the performance of their respective duties. In the case of a king, a person related to the king who is worthy of honor, and a domestic priest (*purohita*)—for whom [the king] desires the absence of impurity (*āśauca*) for the sake of accomplishing rites such as secret mantras or exorcisms that cannot be achieved by others—there is no birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for them either in the performance of those specific tasks. By the word "death" (*nidhana*), the battle that serves as its means is indicated. In that context, one who is intent on giving food and other gifts, one who has already commenced the work, one who is afflicted having fallen into calamity, and a Brahmin invited to a *śrāddha* or similar rite, become pure at that very moment; this is what was perceived by the seers (*ṛṣis*). The phrase "according to time" means that they do not become pure through the usual period of twelve nights or the like. And so it is stated in the *Ādi-purāṇa*:
Whatever work artisans, such as painters and others, are fully capable of accomplishing, no one else knows that work; therefore, they are pure in their own respective crafts.
Whatever task must be performed by a cook among men in this world, no one else knows it; therefore, that cook is pure.
Whatever a physician does cannot be accomplished by another;
therefore, a physician is always pure in his touch.
Whatever even the female and male servants do, even in play, no one else is capable of doing that; therefore, they are always pure.
How could an action that a king performs even in a dream belong to another?
This being so, the king remains pure even upon contact with death or birth impurity.

“Whatever work belongs to royal servants—such as riding elephants and horses—that [work] does not belong to anyone else; therefore, they are declared to be pure. Viṣṇu also states: “Regarding impurity: there is no impurity for kings in their royal duties; none for those observing a vow while on the vow; none for those performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*) during the session; none for artisans in their artisanal work; and none for those carrying out the king’s orders when acting by his will. Pracetas also says:
"Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, as well as male and female slaves,
kings, and royal servants are declared to be immediately pure. Thus says Vṛddha-Parāśara as well.
There is no birth-impurity for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those engaged in sacrificial sessions,
nor for all those who have been initiated, nor for whomever the king desires.
"There is no impurity regarding death or birth for those engaged in asceticism or the giving of gifts.
There is also another Smṛti text:
"Even for one who constantly gives food, there is no impurity during Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such penances."
When the performance of the Kṛcchra-homa and other such rites has begun, or when the feeding of Brāhmaṇas and others is underway;
"Even for one who has undertaken a vow, it shall not be [permitted] for anyone else when the Brahmins have been invited and the Śrāddha rite has commenced.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa* as well.
For a Brahmin who has been invited and is devoted to his private Vedic study,
there is never any impurity (aśauca) as long as the ancestors remain within his body.
"Likewise for those engaged in penance, and for givers and knowers of Brahman.
Manu also says:
"There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those performing sacrificial sessions (*sattra*)."
For they, being ever one with Brahman, occupy the station of Indra.
"Purity is prescribed immediately for a king in his high office; the reason for this is his seat [of authority] there, for the sake of protecting the subjects. (MDh 5.93–94). Yājñavalkya also says:

For officiating priests and those initiated for sacrifice while performing the sacrificial rite, as well as for those engaged in a sacrificial session (*sattra*), those observing vows, celibate students, donors, and knowers of Brahman;

"In the case of giving a gift, a marriage, a sacrifice, battle, a national calamity, or even in times of dire distress, purity of the assembly (*sadaḥ-śauca*) is prescribed. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.28–29). Hārīta also says:
"A kṣatriya standing in battle, a vaiśya standing in the midst of cows,
a brāhmaṇa who is a perpetual student (sattrin), and one who is always pure as a religious student (brahmacārī). Thus says Paiṭhīnasi as well.
"In marriages, sacrifices, times of distress, journeys, and rites at sacred fords (tīrtha), there is no impurity (sūtaka) in those cases; one should likewise perform rites such as sacrifices.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa* as well.
"Furthermore, it shall not be [performed] during the consecration of a deity, in rites such as the *gaṇayāga*,
in the *śrāddha* and other ancestral sacrifices (*pitṛyajña*), or at the giving away of a daughter in marriage. Thus says Aṅgiras as well.
"In birth and death, impurity does not exist in three cases:
during a sacrifice, at the time of a wedding, and likewise during a rite to the gods.

In this context, the immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) prescribed for weddings and the like refers specifically to the subject matter of the wedding and other such rites that have already commenced. However, in matters other than their specific duties, kings and others certainly remain subject to impurity. Thus it is stated in the *Brāhma Purāṇa*:
But by which [rite] the loss of the kingdom would occur within one's own territory in the absence of the king,
when he is about to depart for battle after having performed the propitiatory rite for departure?

Or likewise, for the rites of pacification for the subjects through mantras and other offerings, for the auspicious rites of cattle and so forth for Vaiśyas, and even during times of distress for farmers; [in these cases, one should perform the recitation].
"Impurity shall not exist in this world; it is found everywhere else. (20–22)
Furthermore:
"But a householder, during the act of procreation, should not cause confusion [of castes], if he is able to avoid it."

"Within ten days the mother is purified, but the father is pure by bathing. (23) This means: regarding "birth," that is, delivery; "the householder" refers to the *gṛhastha*; if the father does not come into contact with the woman who has given birth (*sūtikā*), then he becomes pure through bathing. But the mother becomes pure after ten days—this is the meaning. (23)

[Objection: "In that case, would it not follow that even the impurity characterized by the father's disqualification from performing rituals would not exist? To this he says: "The impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca) applies to all; however, the impurity due to birth (sūtaka) applies to the mother and father. The impurity due to birth belongs to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by touching water. (24)

Just as the impurity (*āśauca*) characterized by the disqualification from performing rites is complete for *sapiṇḍas*, so it is for the father as well. However, the impurity characterized by untouchability (*aspṛśyatva*) applies to both parents. Even therein, untouchability lasts for ten days for the mother alone; for the father, however, it lasts only until he has bathed—this is the meaning. And thus says Paiṭhīnasi:

"Upon a birth, the *sapiṇḍas* are pure, but there is birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for the parents. The birth-impurity belongs to the mother alone; having performed ablutions (*upaspṛśya*), the father becomes pure."

The meaning is this: at birth, all *sapiṇḍas* other than the mother and father are touchable; however, the mother and father do not possess touchability. Even among them, the father becomes touchable by means of bathing. But the state of untouchability for ten days belongs to the mother alone. And so says Vasiṣṭha:

"No impurity exists for the man, provided he does not come into contact [with the woman]; and here, the menstrual flow is to be known as the impure substance, and that does not exist in the man. (VaDh 4.23)
Saṃvarta also says:
"When a son is born, the father's bath with his clothes is prescribed;
the mother becomes pure after ten days, but the father may touch her after bathing. (Saṃsm 143)
Bṛhaspati also says:
"In the case of birth-impurity (jātāśauca), however, the birth-impurity (sūtaka) belongs to all [relatives], but the impurity belongs to the mother alone.
The father should perform a bath, but the kinsmen do not need to bathe with their clothes on."

Gautama also states: "Upon touching the birth-impurity of the parents, however, the father becomes pure" (GDh 14.23). In the Ādi-purāṇa as well: "But having seen the face of the newborn, the father who has become subject to birth-impurity (sūtakin) becomes pure at that very moment by performing a bath with his clothes on. || 24 ||
He states that by engaging in contact with a woman who has recently given birth, there is a period of ten days of impurity caused by that; as it is said:
"If a twice-born man, even if he is a Brahmin learned in the six Vedāṅgas, engages in contact when his wife has given birth, he shall indeed become subject to the impurity of birth (sūtaka). (25)

If a husband should have contact with his wife while she is in the state of *sūtikā* (having recently given birth), then even for a Brahmin who is engaged in the practice of *vidyā-karma*, there would arise *sūtaka* characterized by untouchability; how much more so for anyone else? This is the meaning. And thus Sumantu says: "The *sūtaka* belongs to the mother alone, and to him who touches her, but not to others. The meaning is that for the father who touches the woman in the state of *sūtikā*, there arises *sūtaka* characterized by untouchability, but not for others. || 25 ||

[Objection: But surely, why should the husband's untouchability—which has birth as its cause—not persist even after he has bathed? To this, [the author] says: "The defect arises from contact; indeed, there is no other defect in a twice-born man.
Therefore, a wise man should avoid contact with every effort" (26). Thus.

After bathing, only the defect arising from contact with the husband—which causes untouchability—occurs; there is no defect caused by birth. Therefore, the meaning is that a learned man should avoid contact, such as sharing a bed, a seat, or food. And so says Bṛhaspati: "Whether he be a sapinda relative or even a stranger, whoever performs lying down or eating together with them becomes pure after ten days."

Viṣṇu says: "If one should eat food even once from those who are in a state of impurity due to birth or death among Brāhmaṇas and others, his own impurity lasts for as long as theirs" (ViDh 22.8). Atri also says: "Defilement arises from contact regarding the death or birth of another;
by avoiding that [contact], immediate purification is ordained even for the father."
Purity for the performer has been stated regarding sacrifices and other rites already commenced. Now, he states that there is also purity even for materials intended [for such rites]:
"But during marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, if a death or birth-impurity occurs in the interim, material previously resolved upon does not become defiled when it is being given. (27) Thus.

In this context, the mention of "marriage" (*vivāha*) is intended as an illustration for all previously commenced purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as the tonsure (*caula*) and initiation (*upanayana*). "Festival" (*utsava*) refers to a festival for a deity; by this, the consecration of a deity (*devapratiṣṭhā*) and similar rites are indicated. "Sacrifice" (*yajña*) refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rituals. If, while these have begun, there should occur a death or a birth (*mṛtasūtake*) in the interim—that is, in the middle—then the substance previously intended for the deity or for being given to Brahmins does not become defiled; this is the meaning. And so says Kratu: "A substance previously intended, when being given, does not become defiled."
Regarding cooked food, however, a distinction is shown in another Smṛti:
"In the midst of weddings, festivals, sacrifices, and the like, if a death or birth-impurity occurs, cooked food should be provided by others; it shall not touch either the givers or the eaters."

Prepared food should be given by those who are not in a state of birth-impurity (*asūtakī*); the meaning is that one in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtakī*) must not touch either the givers or the eaters. As for another Smṛti text: "Objects that have become impure due to their connection with an owner are purified solely by the purification of the owner, even when sprinkled with water."

Thus, that [rule] refers to substances that have not been specifically set aside for a purpose. However, there are certain substances which are always pure even when not set aside. And so says Marīci: "In the case of salt, honey, and meat; in flowers, roots, and fruits;
in vegetables, wood, and grass; in water, curd, clarified butter, and milk."

"In the case of oil, medicinal herbs, and skins—whether cooked or uncooked—one may take them oneself; likewise, in the case of all commodities for sale, there is no impurity due to death or birth. (27)
This [verse] prevents the repetition of the occasional rite for every individual occasion when multiple causes of impurity coincide:
"But if death or birth occurs again within the ten-day period,
the Brahmin shall remain impure only so long as that [second period] has not yet reached its tenth day" (28).

When, within the period of ten days of impurity, there occurs a birth or death that constitutes an occasion for an impurity equal to or less than that [initial one], then the previously commenced impurity shall remain until the end of the ten days—that is, as long as the ten days have not elapsed; the Brāhmaṇa remains impure only for that duration, and does not become subject to a further ten-day impurity caused by the death or other event arising in the interim. Thus says Manu: "If another death or birth should occur within the ten days, the Brāhmaṇa shall remain impure only so long as that [original] period has not yet reached its ten days" (MDh 5.79).
Yājñavalkya also says:
"In the interval between birth and death, one is purified by the remaining days. (YDh 3.20)

Viṣṇu also states: [264] “If another birth-impurity should occur during the midst of a birth-impurity, then purification occurs upon the cessation of the previous impurity; likewise if a death among kinsmen occurs during the midst of a death-impurity. By the use of the word *api* (“also”), the meaning is that even in the case of a birth, purification occurs by the duration of the death-impurity itself. When a death falls within the ten-day impurity caused by a birth, then a ten-day period must be observed starting from the time of the death. And so says Aṅgiras: “If a death should occur during a birth-impurity, or if a birth should occur during a death-impurity...”
"In that case, one should perform purification with respect to the death-impurity (mṛtaka), not the birth-impurity (sūtaka). Thus it is said in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"When birth-impurity occurs while death-impurity has already arisen..."
"Birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but death-impurity is not purified by birth-impurity. Thus it is said. Also in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"The purification that occurs when there is a conjunction of death and birth is now described."
"One born is purified by the death [of the deceased], but the dead is not purified by the birth [of the child].
Thus, when a long-term period of impurity occurs during the midst of a short-term period of impurity, purification does not occur through the former. This has been stated by Uśanas:
"But if a long-term period of impurity should occur in the midst of a short-term period of impurity..."

"Purity does not come from the former [period]; one becomes pure by the time of one's own [period]. Thus it was said by Yama as well: "One should conclude a period of impurity that involves an increase in sin according to the latter [period]."

[265] "If, after a three-night period has commenced, one should enter a ten-day period, the impurity shall recur; having completed that [later period], one becomes pure. The meaning is this: if an increasing period of impurity should arise in the interim—due to the persistence of a longer duration in comparison to the period of the first-occurring impurity—then one should conclude it by its own subsequent time alone. Śaṅkha also says:

"When there is a concurrence of two periods of impurity of equal duration, one should complete [the rite] with the first; when they are unequal, one should do so with the second, according to the word of Dharmarāja. (Śaṅkha-smṛti 15.10).
"Unequal" means a period of impurity of longer duration. Hārīta also says:
"When a death occurs within the period of impurity caused by another death, one is purified by the preceding impurity;
however, a light [impurity] is purified by a heavy one, but a heavy one is never purified by a light one. Thus it is stated. Also in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"But when there is a simultaneity of sins, purification should be understood as being by the more serious one.

(KūP 1.2.23.24) Regarding the relative gravity or lightness of two [sins] of the same kind, it depends on the duration of time; for those of different kinds, it depends on their essential nature alone. As stated by that very same author:
"In the case of a conjunction of death and birth, death is the more serious. (KūP 1.2.23.6)

In some cases, when a heavy period of impurity occurs during a lighter period of impurity depending on the time elapsed, there is a removal [of the former] by the duration of the prior impurity. Regarding this, Devala says:
"When there is an increase in the duration of impurity, purification is ordained for each subsequent [period];
however, if that [increase] begins from the fifth day onward, in this case, the prior [period] alone remains."

[266] Thus: when there is an increase in impurity (*āghavṛddhi*)—that is, a period of impurity lasting for a long duration—due to a birth or other event occurring during the midst of an ongoing impurity, then the impurity is prescribed starting from the subsequent birth or event that has occurred. If, however, the previously commenced impurity should continue even beyond the fifth day, then purification is specifically ordained by the former alone; that is, by the very duration of the prior impurity, the purification of even a ten-day impurity is established. This is what is meant: although the intervening impurity may last for a long time, if the previously commenced impurity should be more than half as long as the duration of the subsequent impurity, then purification of the latter occurs by the very duration of the previously commenced impurity. For example, if a ten-day impurity should occur in the midst of a six-day impurity caused by a miscarriage, then the cessation of the ten-day impurity occurs by the remainder of the six-day impurity alone. In this same way, it should be understood elsewhere as well that the cessation of an impurity of longer duration occurs by the remainder of an impurity that is more than half as long.

Regarding the purification by the remainder of an impurity that has fallen in between, a specific rule was stated by Gautama: “If it occurs during the remainder of the night, purification is by two nights; if at dawn, by three nights” (GDh 14.7–8). By the word *rātri* (night), a full day and night (*ahorātra*) is indicated. When another impurity should occur while an existing impurity still has its night remaining, then purification occurs after two nights following the end of the previous impurity’s duration. At dawn—that is, in the final watch of that night before sunrise—if there is a concurrence of impurities, purification is by three nights. It is not, however, by the remainder of the previous impurity’s time. Likewise, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “Now, if someone should die or be born in the interval, one is purified by the very days remaining; if it is at the end of the day, by two nights; if at dawn, by three nights. So too, Śātātapa says:
"If one-third of the night remains, purification occurs after two days; if one watch of the night remains, one becomes pure after three days. Thus it is said.

Baudhāyana also states: "Now, if there is a concurrence of two ten-day periods of impurity, [the rule applies] from the first day of the first ten-day period until the ninth day" (BDh 1.5.11.18). The meaning of this is that until the completion of the ninth day, the subsequent impurity is not extinguished by the remainder of the preceding period of impurity. By the word "ninth," the penultimate day is indicated. Consequently, it should be understood that even for Kṣatriyas and others, when their final day of impurity coincides with another, there is a two-night period, and on the morning [of the tenth], a three-night period follows. Devala also says:
If another death occurs before ten days have passed, it is dealt with according to the previous rule;
however, if one should die on the tenth day, that person becomes pure after two days.
"But at dawn, after three nights; this is the rule for periods of ten nights.

Here, in the phrase "prior to the tenth day," the word *daśāha* (ten days) is indicative of the final day. Furthermore, the phrase "in periods of ten nights" is also indicative of twelve nights and so forth. An exception to the rule that "when two equal periods of impurity coincide, purification occurs through the remainder of the first" has been shown by Śaṅkha: "If the father dies while one is still in a state of impurity due to the mother having died previously..."

"By the remainder of the father's [period], there shall be purification; however, for the mother, one should observe a *pakṣiṇī* [period]. (Śaṅkha Smṛti 15.14) If the mother dies first, and the father should die during the period of impurity caused by that [mother's death], then purification does not occur through the remainder of the previous period of impurity. Rather, purification occurs only by the duration of the father's period of impurity. Likewise, if the father has died previously, and the mother should pass away during the period of impurity caused by that [father's death], purification does not occur through the remainder of the father's period of impurity. Instead, the meaning is that after completing the father's period of impurity, one should observe a *pakṣiṇī*. || 28 ||
He states an exception to the aforementioned impurity lasting ten days and so forth, even in other circumstances:
"For those who perish for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, or likewise in the capture of prisoners, and for those who perish in battles, the impurity lasts for one night. (29) Thus.

The meaning is that for those who are killed while facing the enemy in battles for the sake of protecting a Brāhmaṇa’s life, or when taken captive as prisoners, or when cattle are seized—those who are killed for the purpose of liberating them—their *sapiṇḍas* have impurity (*āśauca*) for only one night, and not for ten nights or other periods. As for that which was stated by Manu under the recurring phrase "immediate purity" (*sadyaḥśauca*): "And [there is immediate purity] for those killed in a riot or in battle, by lightning or by the king, for the sake of cows or Brāhmaṇas, and for whomsoever the king desires. (MDh 5.95)
Thus, that refers to the case of non-proximity. || 29 ||

In nine verses, as a supplement to the rule regarding one-day impurity (*ekāha-āśauca*) for those whose sapinda-relations have been killed in battle, [the author] praises one slain in combat. Therein, first, by means of the illustration of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), he shows that [the warrior] pierces the solar orb, thereby implying his attainment of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*):
"Two persons in this world pierce the solar orb:
the wandering mendicant disciplined in yoga, and he who is slain facing the enemy in battle. (30)

A wandering mendicant who, through the practice of yoga, worships the Lord and proceeds to the world of Brahmā by way of the path beginning with light, pierces in succession the spheres of Vāyu, Āditya, and Candra along the way. Having emerged from those apertures—which become increasingly superior one after another—and having traversed the worlds of lightning and so forth in order, he reaches the world of Brahmā. Furthermore, this emergence through the apertures is heard in the *Vājasaneyibrāhmaṇa*.

He comes to the wind; for him, it parts there as the hole of a chariot wheel, and by that he ascends upwards. He comes to the sun; for him, it parts there as the hole of a *lambara* drum, and by that he ascends upwards. He comes to the moon; for him, it parts there as the hole of a kettle-drum, and by that he ascends upwards. Thus (BĀU 5.10.1). 30.

In this regard—since it is inappropriate for one who has been slain in battle to attain the same destination as a wandering mendicant who has practiced yoga for a long time with great effort—it might be suspected that [the warrior’s merit] is inferior due to the brevity of his exertion. Anticipating this, the word "abhimukha" (facing the enemy) is used to indicate that even though the duration was short, his effort was equal [to the ascetic's] because of his extraordinary fortitude. He clarifies this very point thus:
"Wherever a hero is slain while surrounded by enemies, he attains imperishable worlds, provided he does not speak words of cowardice. (31)

In the world, even seeing a single person bearing a weapon gives rise to a great fear for one's life. But at the time of battle, all the enemies belonging to the opposing army—bearing weapons and intent on killing—surround him. At that moment, there is no limit to the fear that arises. For a hero who, having endured such fear, advances toward the adversary, his fortitude is even greater than that of a yogi. Indeed, no fear for one’s life is ever conceivable for a yogi regarding the observances (yama) and restraints (niyama) and so forth. Therefore, just as the entirety of enjoyments that would have been experienced over many years while awake are seen in a dream lasting only a moment, why should a courageous man in battle not attain a state equal to long-term yoga? To show that what is intended here is equality through an excellence of fortitude, it is said: "if he does not speak like a eunuch. If he does not speak words indicative of fear—that is, if he does not utter anything suggesting impotence or cowardice—then, by virtue of his equality with a yogi, he attains the specific sub-varieties of the imperishable world of Brahmā, such as *sālokya* (residing in the same world) and others. || 31 ||
In the illustration of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), the piercing of the solar orb is considered possible:
"Upon seeing a Brahmin who has renounced the world, the sun moves from its place, thinking:
'He will pierce my orb and proceed to the supreme station. (32) Thus it is said.

Although the solar orb consists of an insentient mass of rays, so that even when it is divided there is no sensation whatsoever on the part of the sun, nevertheless, for one who previously existed in an extremely low state, the attainment of a high position now becomes a cause of mental affliction. For this very reason it is said: "Having pierced through, he shall go to the supreme station. With this very point in mind, Vyāsa said:
"O son of Kuntī, the world of the gods is indeed crowded with those who perform ritual acts;
and this is not desired by the gods: that mortals should dwell above them."
[271] Thus, by the presentation of the movement of the sun as accomplished merely by the sight of the mendicant seeker of liberation, the aforementioned fruit for the yogin is confirmed. || 32 ||

It is stated in the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*) that one who is slain while facing the enemy [attains the fruit]; and that state of being slain is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) of an excellence of fortitude (*dhairya*). For even when one's own death does not occur, because the aforementioned fruit exists for the steadfast person who is intent on protecting others, he says:
"But he who, when the armies have broken and are fleeing in every direction, goes forth as their protector, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice" (33).}

In this context, the sacrifice is the Aśvamedha, because its fruit is the attainment of the world of Brahman. And that the Aśvamedha has that as its fruit is clearly understood from the question and answer in the Bhujyu Brāhmaṇa of the Vājasaneyi Śākhā: "Where do those who have sacrificed with the Aśvamedha go? (BĀU 3.3.2), and so forth. || 33 ||

It has been stated that for one who engages in action for the sake of protection, the fruit of the sacrifice is attained by the mere act of engagement itself. He now says that for one who has engaged in such action, even if his limbs are severed, there is a superior fruit despite the absence of being killed:
"Whose limb is wounded by arrows, mallets, or clubs—that hero celestial maidens carry off and delight. (34)
The body is the physical frame; it is afflicted by being cut and wounded through the severing of limbs such as the hands and feet. || 34 ||
[272] He shows that the fruit obtained from being killed while engaged in protecting others is even more excellent than that from having one's limbs severed:
"Thousands of celestial maidens [attend] a hero slain in battle."
They run about in haste, crying out, "He is my husband! He is mine! (35)
Thus [ends the section]. || 35 ||

Although both the performance of a multitude of sacrifices and dying in battle are equal means for attaining the same kind of fruit, nevertheless, because dying in battle is accomplished in an extremely short time and is free from the possibility of impairment, it is the superior means; thus he says:
"Just as the Brahmins seeking heaven go there by means of multitudes of sacrifices and by austerity, so too do they go here."
"For in an instant, heroes indeed depart from that place, casting away their lives through a noble battle. (36) Thus it is said.

By the word "vipra," those who are free from desire are intended; thus, the alternative "or those desiring heaven" is appropriate. Here, in those worlds of merit, whichever specific world they go to and in whatever manner—such as being attended by celestial maidens and so forth—the heroes slain in battle go to that very same specific world in that very same manner. By the use of the word "in an instant," it is indicated that the brevity of time is the excellence in these cases. || 36 ||

[273] Now, one might object: "Even if the duration of time is short, because the fear of death is difficult to overcome, the previously mentioned fortitude for battle is hard to attain. Anticipating this objection, the author intends to show that such fortitude is easily attained by a man possessed of discernment, and thus demonstrates that discernment: "By victory, prosperity is obtained; even by dying, the limbs of celestial nymphs are won."

"What concern is there for death in battle when this body perishes in an instant? (37). Here, the past participle *jita* is used in the active sense (*kartari niṣṭhā*). Since victory brings the attainment of fortune (*lakṣmī*), and death brings the attainment of celestial nymphs (*surāṅganā*), if one does not consider these two gains out of greed for the life of the body, then that person is left with nothing but the mere loss of what was gained. For the body does not live long at all; because it is subject to the lifespan obtained through karma, its nature is such that it perishes in a moment. (37)
"If even the drinking of blood, though absolutely forbidden, results in unsurpassed merit in that case, what wonder is there in attaining the world of the virtuous? Thus he says:
"But he whose blood flows from the region of the forehead and enters his mouth in battle..."
"That is indeed equal to the drinking of Soma, and it is seen to have been performed according to rule in the sacrifice of battle" (38).

In this regard, it is stated that "it was seen according to rule" because striking in the presence of the enemy is described as a characteristic of a hero in the treatises on ethics (*nītiśāstra*) and similar works that expound upon the sacrifice of battle.

Thus, by means of these nine verses, the praise of dying in battle has been established as a glorification of the rules regarding impurity (*āśauca*). Since one slain in combat is of an exceedingly meritorious nature, it follows that upon his death there is an absence of the additional period of impurity, just as in the case of the death of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). Alternatively, these nine verses should be extracted from the present context and placed among the duties of kings (*rājadharma*), because fighting is the duty of a Kṣatriya. This is just as the collection of observances for a menstruating woman, though heard in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), is extracted from that context and described as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) rather than for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*). (38)
For the sake of dharma, he prescribes immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for the carrying of the corpse of a destitute Brāhmaṇa and similar acts, following a commendation:
"Those twice-born who carry a deceased Brāhmaṇa who is without a protector obtain the fruit of a sacrifice at every step, in due order. (39)
"For those of virtuous deeds, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any sin;
for them, immediate purification is ordained simply by immersion in water. (40) Thus it is said.

Those twice-born who, for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), carry, touch, or cremate a *brāhmaṇa* who is helpless, devoid of kinsmen, and not a *sapiṇḍa*, obtain in succession the fruits of sacrifice at every step.
Likewise, they do not even have impurity (*aśubha*) and so forth; the meaning is that for them, immediate purification is ordained simply by bathing. And so says Vṛddhaparāśara:
"In the rite of touching a corpse, a Brāhmaṇa is not at all defiled;
both the carrier and the giver of the fire become pure immediately after bathing."

As for that which was stated by Hārīta: "Those who have touched a corpse shall not enter a village until the appearance of the stars; if it occurs at night, [until the appearance] of the sun"; and that which was stated by Devala: "If one performs the carrying [of the body] during the day, after the setting of the sun, the Brahmin, having bathed, may enter his home; if at night, [after the rising] of the sun."
Thus, this should be understood as referring to the performance of tasks that ought not to be done out of affection and the like. || 39–40 ||
It is said that not only [the recitation of] the *nāman* must be performed, but *prāṇāyāma* (breath control) must also be practiced:

"Having carried and having cremated a deceased person who is of a different lineage (*asagotra*) and not a relative (*abandhu*), even if he be the best of the twice-born (*dvijottama*), one becomes pure through *prāṇāyāma*" (41).

The meaning is that for those who carry or cremate the corpse of a deceased Brāhmaṇa who is of a different lineage (*asagotra*), not a *sapinda* relative (*asapiṇḍa*), and devoid of kinsmen (*abandhu*), purification occurs through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). It is not merely bathing and breath control; contact with fire must also be performed. This was stated by Aṅgiras:
"Whoever, being a non-*sapinda*, should somehow carry out a deceased person, having bathed with his clothes on and touched fire, he becomes pure on that very day."
There is impurity for one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* when performing the removal of a corpse with oil and other such means. Thus says Manu:
"A Brahmin, having carried out the body of a deceased twice-born person who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, like a kinsman, becomes pure after three nights; and likewise for the maternal relatives and kinsmen."
"If one eats their food, however, one is purified in ten days; but if one does not eat their food and does not dwell in that house, one is purified in a single day. (MDh 5.101–02)

However, for one who has carried out the removal of a corpse and dwells in that house but does not eat its food, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts three nights. For one who dwells in that house and eats its food, it lasts ten nights. Furthermore, for one who, having carried out the removal of a corpse, abandons both residence in that house and its food, the meaning is that the impurity lasts one day. This refers to cases involving those of the same caste (*savarṇa*). But when carrying out the corpse of a different caste (*asavarṇa*), the impurity appropriate to that specific caste must be observed. Regarding this, Gautama says: "If another caste touches a person of a higher caste, or a higher caste touches one of a lower caste, the impurity prescribed for that corpse shall apply" (GDh 14.16). Here, "touching" (*upasparśana*) means "carrying out" (*nirharaṇa*). The meaning is that for a Brāhmaṇa who carries out the corpse of a Śūdra, the impurity lasts one month; for a Śūdra who carries out the corpse of a Brāhmaṇa, the impurity lasts ten days. Moreover, for one who carries out the corpse of a different caste out of greed for wealth, the impurity becomes double. Thus says Vyāghra:

If a person of lower status carries the corpse of one of higher status, or if one of higher status carries that of a lower status, the period of impurity shall be the same as for the deceased; however, if this is done for the sake of livelihood, it shall be double.

[277] Thus it is said. Regarding the carrying out of the cremation of a deceased person of a different caste (*asavarṇa*), the aforementioned period of impurity (*āśauca*) applies. In that case, the meaning is that if one undertakes this for wages, the period of impurity becomes double. As for what is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "If a man, having carried a person of a different caste for a fee, should burn him, his period of impurity shall always be equal to that of the deceased's own class."

Thus, this should be understood as applying in times of distress (*āpad*). Out of greed for wealth, when carrying the corpse of one of the same caste (*savarṇa*) and so forth, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) prescribed for one's own class must be observed. And so it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "If one, with a mind overcome by greed, carries away a deceased person, a twice-born man (*dvija*) is purified after ten days, and a king after twelve days."

"A Vaiśya is purified in half a month, but a Śūdra in a full month. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.23.49–50). However, for one who is a *sapiṇḍa* relative and carries out the removal of the corpse, there is no additional period of impurity (*āśauca*), because the removal of the corpse is prescribed as a duty. Thus says Devala:
"The removal of the corpse and so forth is indeed prescribed for *sapiṇḍa* relatives."

"Whosoever performs these [rites] for them, no excess [of impurity] exists for him. Here, "excess" (ādhikya) means an increase in the period of impurity (āśauca). Regarding the carrying out of the corpse of a *samānodaka* relative, the period is ten days. On this point, that same author says:
"He who carries or burns the corpse of a *samānodaka* relative..."

"Regarding that, the sages who know the Dharma understand the period of impurity to be ten days. Furthermore, for a religious student (*brahmacārin*) who carries out the transport of a corpse, there is a violation of his vow. As Devala says:
"A religious student shall not perform actions such as carrying a corpse."
"If one should perform [it], he must undergo the *kṛcchra* penance and also the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*).
However, there is no fault in carrying the corpse of a father or other such relatives. Thus say Manu and Devala:
"The teacher, one's own sub-teacher, the father, the mother, and the guru..."
"But having carried out [the corpse], the one observing the vow is not deprived of his vow by that act" (MDh 5.91).

Vasiṣṭha also says: "For a student, the cessation of the vow occurs through the performance of funeral rites for a corpse, except in the case of his mother, father, or guru" (VaDh 23.7–8). Yājñavalkya also states:
"Even after carrying out [the corpse] of his teacher, father, or sub-teacher, the one observing the vow remains a vow-keeper."

"One should not eat food from a cart, nor should one dwell with those who are impure. (YDh 3.15) The meaning is that if a *vratī*—one observing a vow, such as a student (*brahmacārī*)—performs the cremation and other rites for Brahmins and others, and then avoids dwelling with those who are under ritual impurity (*āśaucin*) and their food, he is not deprived of his observance of the vow. This is also stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Whether it be a teacher (*ācārya*), a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), a preceptor (*guru*), or likewise a father..."
Or having himself burned his mother, he, remaining under a vow, partakes of food there.
Having done so, one indeed falls; therefore, one should not eat the food of the *preta*s.
One should take food elsewhere and should not dwell together with them.
"Having become impure for one day, he becomes pure on the second day. Thus, one should not employ a Śūdra for tasks such as carrying the corpse of a Brāhmaṇa. Regarding this, Manu says:
"While his own kinsmen are present, one should not have a dead Brāhmaṇa carried by a Śūdra."
"For that oblation would not lead to heaven if it were defiled by the touch of a Śūdra" (MDh 5.104).

Here, the phrase "while his own [kinsmen] are present" is not intended to be restrictive, because of the mention of the fault of not leading to heaven. Viṣṇu also says: "One should not have a deceased twice-born man carried out by a Śūdra, nor a Śūdra by a twice-born man" (ViDh 19.1–2). Yama also says:
"A Śūdra should certainly not carry a deceased sacrificer."
"He for whom a Śūdra brings the fire, grass, wood, and sacrificial offerings,
indeed remains forever in the state of a ghost, and he too is tainted by unrighteousness.
Thus, Manu has shown the restriction regarding the directions when carrying out the funeral procession of a Brāhmaṇa or others.
"One should carry out a deceased Śūdra through the southern city gate;
however, for the twice-born, one should do so through the western, northern, or eastern gates as appropriate" (MDh 5.92).
Hārīta also states: "They should not carry the corpse facing toward the village" (HārSm 19.13). || 41 ||
He states the impurity resulting from following [a corpse]:

"Having followed a deceased person out of one's own will—whether he be a relative or even a stranger—one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. (42) Thus.

A *jñāti* is a relative other than a *sapiṇḍa*, because following a *sapiṇḍa* is already prescribed. Having followed out of desire a deceased person who is not a *jñāti* or not a relative—meaning one of equal or superior caste—one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Thus says Yājñavalkya: "Having followed [the corpse], one becomes pure by bathing in water, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter" (YDh 3.26). Likewise in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"He who follows out of desire a twice-born man who has become a *preta* becomes pure by bathing with his clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. (KūP 1.2.23.53).
And regarding this, a specific detail has been stated by Kāvaṣeya:

"Having followed the corpse with the mind, having bathed and touched the fire, and having consumed clarified butter (ghṛta), one becomes purified by bathing again and performing breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma). Nor should it be said that because the consumption of ghee is prescribed for the purpose of eating, it implies the cessation of eating; for it is prescribed as a penance (prāyaścitta). Since the plural number in "by breath-control exercises" (prāṇāyāmair) results in the number three according to the Kapiñjala-nyāya, the meaning is: "one is purified by three breath-control exercises. || 42 ||
He now states the impurity resulting from following one of a lower caste:
"If a Brāhmaṇa, through ignorance, follows a deceased Kṣatriya, he remains impure for one day and is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). (43)
If a Brāhmaṇa follows a corpse of a Vaiśya out of ignorance, he shall observe impurity for two nights and perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). [282] 44.
If a Brāhmaṇa, weak in knowledge, follows a Śūdra who has become a *preta* while being carried away, he shall remain impure for three nights. (45)

"When three nights have then passed, having gone to a river that flows to the ocean and performed one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), he becomes pure by consuming clarified butter. Thus it is said.

A Brāhmaṇa who, out of ignorance or folly, follows a deceased Kṣatriya becomes pure after performing impurity for one day and purifying himself with *pañcagavya*. Having followed the corpse of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after two nights of impurity followed by six *prāṇāyāmas*. Having followed the corpse of a Śūdra, he completes three nights of impurity, bathes in a great river, performs one hundred *prāṇāyāmas*, and becomes pure by consuming clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). By examining the beginning and the conclusion [of this passage], it should be inferred that in the case of following the corpses of Kṣatriyas and others as well, bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter are to be applied accordingly. This being the case, it should be inferred that for a Kṣatriya, following the corpse of a Vaiśya entails one day of impurity, while following the corpse of a Śūdra entails two days; and for a Vaiśya, following the corpse of a Śūdra entails one day of impurity. Thus it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Purification for a Kṣatriya occurs in one day, while for a Vaiśya it should be in two days;
for a Śūdra, three days are prescribed, followed by one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.13.54) [283] Thus ends verses 43–46.
Regarding the prohibition against twice-born men following the corpse of a Śūdra, [the text] states when they may follow them:
"When the Śūdras have been sent back and have reached the edge of the water, then the twice-born may follow them; this is the eternal law (dharma). (47) Thus it is said.

By the word *udaka*, the water-rite (*udakakriyā*) is meant. Having completed its end—that is, having finished it and brought the period of impurity (*āśauca*) to a conclusion—when they have stood [ready], then they are to be followed or pursued by the twice-born (*dvija*). In this way, it should be inferred that the following of a sick Kṣatriya or Vaiśya by a Brāhmaṇa, and likewise the following of a sick Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya, occurs only after the period of impurity has passed. However, if one recognizes a sick person while in the midst of the period of impurity, there is indeed impurity; in that regard, concerning the recognition of a sick person upon the death of a Brāhmaṇa, Pāraskara states: "Before the collection of the bones, one should perform a bath after weeping."
"Within ten days for a Brāhmaṇa, sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed thereafter. Thus it is said.

Within ten days of the death of a Brāhmaṇa, before the collection of the bones, a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya and others should perform a bath after having assumed the appearance of one who is ill; thereafter, they should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Regarding the assumption of the appearance of one who is ill upon the death of a Kṣatriya, for Kṣatriyas and others, and regarding the assumption of the appearance of one who is ill upon the death of a Vaiśya, for both Vaiśyas and Śūdras, there is a bath with one's clothes on (*sacaila*) prior to the collection of the bones; thereafter, it is merely a bath. All of this has been declared in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
[284] As long as the bones of a deceased Brāhmaṇa have not been collected, whoever who is not a kinsman weeps there along with the kinsmen, [he incurs that same fate].
From bathing, his purification occurs; thereafter, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed.
For others, however, bathing with salt is required as long as the collection of bones has not been performed.
"But for those born as Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, there is only a bath when [the impurity] has been completed.

Thus, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa [mourning] for a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya who died while ill, the impurity lasts for one day with a bath including the clothes until the collection of the bones; after that, it is merely a bath including the clothes. And so says the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"If a Brāhmaṇa cries out during the collection of the bones of a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya..."
Then, having bathed with his clothes on, he becomes pure on the second day.
"But when an accumulation has been made, O Brahmin, one becomes pure through bathing alone. Thus [it is said].

Although no specific rule is heard regarding a Kṣatriya [impurity] when a Vaiśya dies, is sick, or is of indeterminate gender, it is understood by logical principle that the same impurity applies here as that which was intended for a Brāhmaṇa upon the death, sickness, or indeterminate gender of a Kṣatriya immediately following him. When a Śūdra dies, is sick, or is of indeterminate gender, the Brāhmaṇa’s impurity lasts three nights until the collection of the bones; for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, it lasts two nights; and beyond that, for the twice-born, it is only one night. For a Śūdra who is sick or of indeterminate gender, but not subject to touch, the impurity for the twice-born lasts one night until the collection of the bones; beyond that, the impurity lasts as long as the light (until dawn). Thus says Pāraskara:
If a Brahmin should shed tears before the collection of the bones [of a deceased person],
having gone to the house of a dead Śūdra, he becomes pure after three nights.
[285] After the collection of the bones, for up to one month, the twice-born are purified by a single day and night and by the washing of their clothes.

"For those of the same caste, purification occurs in a single day; for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, in two days; but for a Śūdra who follows [the corpse] without touching it, he is purified by a night. Thus [it is said].

Here, the shedding of tears is intended merely to indicate the manifestation of affliction (*āturavyañjana*). For a *śūdra* of the same lineage (*sajāti*), if one follows him in a procession without touching him prior to the collection of the bones, purification occurs through a day—meaning a full day and night—at the manifestation of affliction; beyond that point, it is by night alone. If this occurs at night, purification is by the night; if during the day, it is by the day. This period of impurity (*āśauca*) for those who are not *sapiṇḍas* is caused by the carrying out of the corpse, following it in procession, and the manifestation of affliction. However, for *sapiṇḍas*, there is no such impurity because these acts are prescribed for them. Thus says Hārīta: "For the carrying out of the deceased and so forth is indeed prescribed for a *sapiṇḍa*."

"There would be fault for one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* if they perform the funeral rites for one who is not their kin, except in the case of a helpless person. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "removal of the corpse and so forth," burning, the offering of water, and other such acts are intended. Furthermore, the procedure for following [the corpse] and other rituals has been shown by Yājñavalkya:
"Having followed [the corpse] as far as the cremation ground, the other [relative], surrounded by kinsmen..."

If he has maintained the sacred fires, he should be cremated with the worldly fire by those reciting the *Yama-sūkta* and the Gāthās, in accordance with the ritual procedure for one who has maintained the fires, as prescribed. (YDh 3.1–2)

[286] Thus: For one other than a child less than two years old who has died, the *sapiṇḍa* relatives should follow him as far as the cremation ground. He should then be cremated with the common fire (*laukikāgni*) by those reciting the *Yamasūkta* consisting of sixteen verses beginning with "pareyuvāṃsam," as well as the verses addressed to Yama. If he is one who has undergone initiation (*upeta* or *upanīta*), then he should be cremated in a manner that is meaningful—that is, according to the procedure for the consecration of one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). The intention here is this: among the rites prescribed for one who maintains the sacred fires, such as the purification of the ground and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), those whose performance serves a purpose—meaning they have a functional role as a means (*dvāra*) toward the final result—are not to be performed. However, those whose purpose has been lost, such as the use of specific sacrificial vessels, are to be performed. This is just as in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* seeds, where although threshing and sprinkling are extended to them by rule, the threshing and so forth are not performed because their functional role is absent, while the sprinkling and so forth are performed. In this context, the mention of the "common fire" applies when there is no fire produced from friction sticks (*jātāraṇi*). When such a fire exists, however, the fire churned from those sticks is to be taken, and not the common fire; for the latter is understood to serve only for purposes accomplished by ordinary fire. Furthermore, the common fire to be taken must be distinct from the fire of a *caṇḍāla* and others, as those are prohibited. And so says Devala:

"The fire of a Caṇḍāla, the fire of impurity, the fire of a woman who has recently given birth, the fire of an outcaste, and the fire of a funeral pyre—these are never fit for the acceptance of the learned.

However, one who maintains the sacred fires (āhitāgni) should be cremated with the Śrauta fire; one who does not maintain them (anāhitāgni) with the Gṛhya fire; and any other with the common (laukika) fire. Thus says Vṛddhayājñavalkya:
One who has maintained the sacred fires should be cremated according to rule with the three fires;
one who has not maintained them with a single [funeral] fire; and other people with a common worldly fire.
[287] Thus, with a single domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*), the cremation is to be performed immediately after the ritual bathing and other rites. And so says Kātyāyana:
"Having bathed the weak one and having clothed him in clean garments, one should place him on the ground strewn with *barhis* grass, with his head toward the south."
Having anointed him with ghee and bathed him while he is clothed and wearing the sacred thread,
one should adorn him, whose entire body is sprinkled with sandalwood paste, with flowers.
Having cast pieces of gold into his seven openings and having placed a cloth over his mouth, his sons and other relatives should carry him out.
Taking food in an unbaked clay vessel and following behind the deceased preceded by the fire,
he should go alone and leave half of it on the ground at the halfway point of the journey.

"Having reached half of the cremation ground, sitting facing south, and bending the left knee, he should slowly [offer the food] with sesame seeds, as in the rite of offering the *piṇḍas*. (KSm 3.21.3–7).

The meaning is that one should cast the food brought as far as the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) according to the procedure for offering the *piṇḍas*. After the cremation, the kinsmen, without looking back at the funeral pyre, go to the water's edge, bathe, and offer water once or thrice. And so says Kātyāyana:

Then, having gone to water without looking back, all those who have touched the corpse shall bathe with their clothes on, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and offer water for him on dry ground.
At the end of the word for the lineage name, one should immediately say "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi*).
Having placed *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing south, one offers [the water] separately, once, along with sesame seeds.

[288] Thus says Paiṭhīnasi as well: “Meditating upon the deceased in his mind, facing south, he should pour out three handfuls of water. And this should be performed on the odd-numbered lunar days, because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: “The water-rite is performed on the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth days” (GDh 14.19). However, with a view toward the specific benefit for the deceased, the offering of water should be repeated for as many days as the period of impurity lasts. Accordingly, Pracetas states: “Day by day, one should offer full handfuls of water for the sake of the deceased.”
"The increase [of the water-offering] should be made until the final *piṇḍa* is completed.
This means that as long as the tenth *piṇḍa* is not finished, the increase of the *añjali* (handful) must be performed. Another specific detail regarding this has been stated by that same author:
"Then, having gone to the riverbank and performed purification according to the rules..."
One should first thoroughly clean one's garment, and thereafter perform the ritual bath.
Then, having bathed with his clothes on, being pure and with a restrained mind,
he should take that stone and offer ten handfuls of water to the Brahmin.
One should give twelve to a Kṣatriya; fifteen are prescribed for a Vaiśya;
thirty are to be given to a Śūdra; thereafter, one may enter the house.
"Then one should perform the bath again and have the purification of the house carried out. Thus it is said.
In some cases, even by those who are not kinsmen, the offering of water must be performed. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"In this same manner, the water-rite for deceased maternal grandfathers and teachers [is to be performed]."
"Water for the sake of desire [is offered] for a female friend, a daughter-in-law, a sister's son, a father-in-law, and a sacrificial priest. (YDh 3.4)

A *prattā* is a daughter or sister who has been given away in marriage. A *svasrīya* is a nephew. In this context, the offering of water for the deceased maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and others must be performed regularly, just as for one’s own *sapiṇḍas*. However, for friends and the like, it is performed out of desire and not as a mandatory duty, since there is no sin incurred by its non-performance. Following the offering of water, the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) must also be performed. Thus says Viṣṇu: “Having offered water to the deceased, they should offer one rice ball upon *kuśa* grass” (ViDh 19.7). The offering of rice balls and water should be performed for as long as the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts. To that effect, he [Viṣṇu] himself says: “For as long as the impurity lasts, they should offer water and one rice ball to the deceased” (ViDh 19.13). The rule regarding the number of rice balls according to the order of the social classes (*varṇa*) has been stated by Pāraskara.
"Ten rice-balls (piṇḍas) are prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, twelve for a Kṣatriya;

fifteen are declared for a Vaiśya, and thirty are proclaimed for a Śūdra. Thus, when a reduction in the period of impurity occurs, the rule "for as long as the impurity lasts" from the words of Viṣṇu might lead to a corresponding reduction in the number of rice-balls; regarding this, Śātātapa states:
"And even when there is a reduction in the period of impurity (āśauca), one should nevertheless offer exactly ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Thus, Pāraskara has shown the method for offering the ten piṇḍas in the case of a three-night period of impurity:
"On the first day, three piṇḍas should be offered by those who are composed in mind."
"On the second day, one should offer four [oblations] as well as the collection of the bones;
on the third day, however, one should offer three and likewise wash the garments and other items. Thus it is said.

The offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is not to be performed by everyone, but rather by the son alone; in his absence, by a *sapiṇḍa* who is present; and in his absence, by a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother, and so forth. Thus says Gautama: “In the absence of a son, the *sapiṇḍas*, the *sapiṇḍas* of the mother, and the disciples should offer it; in their absence, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*)” (GDh 15.25–26). Even among sons, the eldest alone should offer the rice-ball. And so says Marīci: “When all have given their consent, that which is performed by the eldest alone [is valid].”
"Or rather, by means of undivided property, it would be as if performed by all [the heirs] together.

However, when another person performs the offering of the *piṇḍas* due to the absence of the sons or other reasons, then even if a son is present within the ten-day period, that same [other person] shall offer the *piṇḍas* for the full ten days. This is stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"Whether he be of a different lineage (*asagotra*) or of the same lineage (*sagotra*), whether a woman or a man..."

"Whoever performs [the rites] on the first day shall complete them over ten days. Just as there is a restriction regarding the performer for the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) for ten days, so too is there a restriction regarding the materials. To that effect, Śunaḥpuccha said: "One should offer [the oblation] with *śāli* rice, or with barley meal (*saktu*), or even with vegetables."
Whatever substance [is used] on the first day, that same shall be used for the ten-day period.

[291] Thus. But when the new moon (*darśa*) occurs within the ten-day period of impurity, then one should conclude the subsequent ritual procedure (*tantra*)—consisting of the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) and water—at that very new moon. Regarding this, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says:
"If the new moon should occur during the period of impurity for members of any caste, they should perform the completion of the funeral rites (*pretatantra*); so said Gautama. Thus.
Also in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"But if one who has entered upon the ritual procedure for impurity encounters the new moon (darśa),
he should complete the water-libations and the funeral cakes, and then perform only the ritual bath."
Paiṭhīnasi also says:
"The offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and the water-rite must be performed on the very first moon [of the month];
however, one who performs them on the second moon incurs the impurity of a death again."
Regarding the case of parents, however, a specific rule has been stated by Gālava:
"If the new moon (darśa) should occur during the period of impurity for the parents,
the subsequent ritual procedure shall conclude after three days have passed."

If, however, during the period of impurity for the parents, a new moon (darśa) occurs after the three nights have passed, one should conclude the subsequent ritual procedure at that very new moon; it is not [permissible] to conclude it upon the occurrence of a new moon within the first ten days. As for what was stated by Ślokagautama:
"But if a new moon occurs within the ten-day period, one should complete everything there;
however, until the end of the impurity for the parents, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and handfuls of water."

Thus, this should be understood as applicable when the new moon (*darśa*) occurs within three nights; for Gālava has specified that it applies "after three days. Following the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water, the relatives should offer consolation to the deceased. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"Once they have offered the water, emerged from the water, and are seated upon soft grass, the relatives should address those who have bathed with ancient historical narratives. (YDh 3.7)
Indeed, this very point has been demonstrated by that same [author] in the *Itihāsa*:
"He who seeks a core in human existence— which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree— is utterly deluded, for it is like a bubble on the water."
If this body, which was composed of five elements, has returned to its fivefold state,
what cause for lamentation is there in that, since it arose from one's own past actions?
"The earth, the vehicle, the ocean, and the deities shall go to destruction;
how indeed will the mortal world, which resembles foam, not pass away? Thus [says Yājñavalkya]. Kātyāyana also says:
When they have thus properly performed the water libations, are all seated upon the grass, have bathed, and have sipped water again, those followers should say:
"Do not grieve over anything impermanent that is subject to the nature of living beings; practice dharma with diligence, for it is that which will accompany you. Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, the fault in grieving has been shown by Yājñavalkya:
"Since the deceased, being powerless, must consume the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should therefore not weep; rather, the funeral rites should be performed according to one's ability.
(YDh 3.11) Thus, Yājñavalkya has stated what is to be done immediately after the consolation of the dying person.
Having reflected thus, they should go home preceded by children;
having bitten neem leaves, they should remain restrained at the door of their house.

"Having sipped water and touched fire and other [elements], water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds, they should enter [the house] after anointing themselves and placing their feet slowly upon a stone. (YDh 3.12–13).

Regarding this, another specific detail has been shown by Śaṅkha: "Having touched dūrvā grass shoots, fire, and a bull, and having offered a funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) for the deceased at the door of the house, they should subsequently enter. The rules concerning impurity (*āśauca*) have been shown by Manu.

"They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, they should immerse themselves for three days, they should not eat meat, and they should sleep separately on the ground. Thus [says Manu, MDh 5.73].
Mārkaṇḍeya also [states]:
They should eat food that has been purchased or obtained, remaining well-composed;
they should not eat meat, nor should they approach a woman. Thus it is said.

Gautama also states: “All shall sit together, sleeping on the ground and remaining celibate; they shall not eat meat until the *pradāna*. On the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth days, there is the water-rite (*udakakarma*). On the ninth day, there is the discarding of clothes. But on the last day, for those who are of the lowest class. (GDh 14.27–31). *Pradāna* refers to the *mahā-ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha. The discarding of clothes, however, means handing them over to a washerman for washing. The "last" is the tenth day. In that context, the meaning is the discarding of those clothes that are to be completely abandoned by the lowest class. On the first day, water and milk intended for the deceased should be placed in two vessels, such as a swing-basket (*śikya*) or similar, suspended in the air. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Water and milk should be placed in an earthen vessel and left in the open air for one day. (YDh 3.17).
The collection of the bones should be performed on any one of the first, third, seventh, or ninth days. Regarding this, Saṃvarta says:
"On the first day, or the third, or likewise the seventh or the ninth..."
"The collection of the bones should be performed on that day by the members of his lineage together.

(Saṃsm 139–40) [295]. Regarding the collection of the bones on the fourth day, Viṣṇu says: "On the fourth day they should perform the collection of the bones; their casting into the waters of the Gaṅgā [should follow]. (ViDh 19.10–11). Regarding the collection of the bones, Yama has stated the prohibition of certain lunar days, weekdays, and asterisms: "One should avoid the weekdays of Mars, the Sun, and Saturn, as well as the pairs of lunar days."
One should avoid a single-footed asterism, and one should perform the collection of bones under a two-footed asterism.
"Especially on the birth asterism of the donor, or on an asterism consisting of three quarters. Thus says Vṛddha-Manu:
"In the five asterisms beginning with Vasu (Dhaniṣṭhā), and in the three [asterisms] of one's own birth..."
And especially during the second and third quarters of the lunar mansions, and particularly on the Nandā day.
Indeed, in the second [month], there are Ajacaraṇa and the others, as well as the two Āṣāḍhās;
and in Puṣya, the Nakṣatra Hasta, and the two Phalgunīs.

One should avoid [performing rites] on Sundays, Tuesdays, and Saturdays; during the odd lunar days and at the twilights; on the fourteenth and thirteenth lunar days; and when the moon is in the eighth house (Naidhana).
"The collection of bones should be performed; it would cause the destruction of the family.
[296] Thus it is said. The sowing [of seeds] should be performed on the tenth day. Regarding that, Devala says:
"When the tenth day has arrived, the bath should take place outside the village."
"In that regard, the clothes, hair, beard, and nails are to be discarded.
However, in another *smṛti*, it is stated that prior to the eleventh day, the shaving should be performed without restriction:
"The rite of shaving with a razor must be diligently performed on the second day."

"On the third, the fifth, or even the seventh [day], until the offering is completed"—this refers to the *ekādaśāhika-śrāddha* (the funeral rite on the eleventh day). Here, from the expression "until the offering is completed" (*āpradānataḥ*), it is understood that there is no fixed rule. Baudhāyana also states:
"He who previously had his hair not shorn should have his hair shorn on this occasion."
On the second day, the third day, or even on the fifth or seventh day.
"Another opinion is that [the gift] should be given for as long as the faith lasts.

Furthermore, there is the shaving of the hair of the sons and the younger brothers. Thus says Āpastamba: "And there is the shaving of those who follow" (ĀpDh 1.3.10.6). "Those who follow" (*anubhāvinaḥ*) refers to those who come after, namely the sons and the younger brothers. Alternatively, the term *anubhāvinaḥ* refers specifically to the sons, as in the case of [the rule]:
"At the Gaṅgā, at Bhāsa-kṣetra, upon the death of the mother, father, or teacher..."
Shaving of the head is prescribed at the time of the fire-consecration (ādhāna) and during the Soma sacrifice, as well as on the seven [occasions].

[297] In this context, because of the specific mention of "the death of mother and father," everyone who is thus restricted should complete the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water at the end of their own period of impurity (*āśauca*). However, one should perform that *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha on the eleventh day. And so says Marīci:
"At the end of the impurity, the proper offering of rice-balls is then completed;
thereafter the śrāddha should be offered—this is the rule for all castes."

On the eleventh day after the period of impurity has ended, a Brāhmaṇa should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha. The meaning is that this rule—"one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* on the eleventh day"—is the same for all castes, including Kṣatriyas and others.

Now, one might object: why should the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* not apply to all castes immediately after the conclusion of the period of impurity (*āśauca*), given that Kṣatriyas and others who observe longer periods of impurity would lack purity on the eleventh day? For it is ordained that "a rite must be performed by one who is pure," thus establishing purity as an essential constituent (*aṅga*) of the ritual; furthermore, Viṣṇu, having introduced the subject generally with "now, upon the cessation of impurity" (*ViDh* 21.1), has prescribed the *ekoddiṣṭa*. [To this we reply: One who is impure may nevertheless perform the first *śrāddha* on the eleventh day.
There is a temporary purity for the performer at that moment, but he remains impure thereafter.

If it is argued that this is not so because of the statement of Śaṅkha—namely, that since the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is prescribed on the eleventh day even during a period of impurity (*āśauca*), one should not act thus—we say no. For there exists another possible scope: if the father should die while the mother has already passed away and one is still within the period of her impurity, then one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha for the mother on the eleventh day, even though one is impure.
As for the verse: "The śrāddha which is performed on the eleventh day is declared to be common to all;
however, the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for the four castes is distinct for each."

Such is the statement of Paiṭhīnasi; its meaning is this: the Śrāddha prescribed for the day immediately following the period of impurity (āśauca) is common to all four castes, and not for the Brāhmaṇa alone. If it is asked, "How then is the term 'eleventh day' (ekādaśāha) justified?"—it is not so, because that term is justified through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) as referring to the day immediately following the period of impurity.

To this it is replied: The *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha, characterized by the time of the eleventh day, is prescribed for all four social classes (*varṇas*). According to the maxim, “In an injunction, the primary meaning of a word is not to be set aside,” it is untenable to assume that the term “eleventh day” indicates, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the day immediately following the period of impurity (*āśauca*). Furthermore, since it is improper to resort to a figurative sense when the primary sense is possible, the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha must be performed on the eleventh day itself even by Kṣatriyas and the other classes. If it is argued: “But it has been stated that because Kṣatriyas and others lack purity on the eleventh day, they have no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform the śrāddha”—we say no. This is because of the scriptural statement, “The performer’s purity pertains to that specific moment,” and thus such momentary purity does exist. As for the claim that the intent of Śaṅkha’s statement—that one may perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* on the eleventh day even while impure if another period of impurity occurs during an existing one—refers to a specific case, that is incorrect. For the same objection applies there as well: namely, that there is still an absence of purity. Moreover, it is impossible to restrict a general rule of Śaṅkha to a specific case without a compelling reason. And as for the argument that Viṣṇu, having begun generally with the words “Now, upon the cessation of impurity,” prescribes the *ekoddiṣṭa*, therefore the *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed by everyone only after the period of impurity has ended—that too is incorrect. Viṣṇu’s statement is properly understood as referring specifically to Brāhmaṇas who observe a ten-day period of impurity. Therefore, it is rightly said that the *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed on the eleventh day itself even by Kṣatriyas and the rest.
Now, the determination of the *śrāddha* to be performed for those who have been gathered [as ancestors] is explained in detail.
A *śrāddha* is the renunciation of material goods with faith, intended for the deceased (*preta*). This has been stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"That which is performed in the proper place, at the proper time, toward a worthy recipient, with faith, and according to the prescribed rule..."
"Śrāddha is defined as that which is given to Brahmins for the sake of the ancestors. Thus it is said.

And that [śrāddha] is of two kinds, distinguished as *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa*. That which is performed with reference to three generations of ancestors is *pārvaṇa*; that which is performed with reference to a single person is *ekoddiṣṭa*. Thus, although there are these two types, the śrāddha is further divided into three according to the distinctions of obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*). Among these, that which is enjoined upon the condition of being alive is obligatory, such as that enjoined for the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). That which has an indefinite cause is occasional, such as [that performed] during eclipses and the like. That which has desire as its condition is optional, such as [that performed] on specific lunar days, asterisms, and so forth. As for the twelvefold classification stated by Viśvāmitra:

The daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), the optional (kāmya), the ancestral rite for prosperity (vṛddhi-śrāddha), the rite of offering the rice-ball (sapiṇḍana), the monthly rite (pārvaṇa), and the eighth, performed in a cow-pen for the sake of purification— these are to be known.
The ninth is declared to be the constituent part of ritual action (karmāṅga), and the tenth is remembered as pertaining to fate (daivika).
The eleventh is declared for journeys (yātrā), and the twelfth is considered for the purpose of nourishment (puṣṭi).

[300] Thus, this is intended merely to express the internal distinctions between the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites; it is not intended to establish them as entirely separate categories. For instance, in that context, the "obligatory" (*nitya*) refers to the daily *śrāddha*, while the "occasional" (*naimittika*) refers to the *ekoddiṣṭa*. To this effect, Pāraskara says:
"The *śrāddha* performed day after day is proclaimed as 'obligatory' (*nitya*);
however, when one is unable [to perform the full rite], it may be performed with water alone, omitting the *vaiśvadeva* offering."
"The *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha is called occasional (*naimittika*).
That too should be performed without [invoking] the gods; one should feed an odd number of twice-born [brahmins].

The *kāmya* is that performed for the sake of accomplishing a desired object. The *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is that performed on occasions such as the birth of a son or a marriage. *Sapiṇḍana* is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. The *pārvaṇa* is that performed at every lunar phase (*parvan*). The *goṣṭhī-śrāddha* is the śrāddha performed in a social gathering (*goṣṭhī*). Regarding this, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
The *kāmya* śrāddha is prescribed for the sake of accomplishing a desired object, and it is remembered as being performed like the *pārvaṇa*.
The *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is declared for occasions such as the birth of a son or a marriage.
A vessel for the arghya offering made of fresh butter and the rice-ball (piṇḍa) are scattered;
