that is indeed the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite performed with the vessels and rice-balls of the ancestors.
Because it occurs on every lunar festival (parvan), it is called pārvaṇa;
that śrāddha which is performed in a social gathering is called goṣṭhīśrāddha.
"For the sake of obtaining many learned men, for the sake of happiness, and for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of purification," it means that which is performed for the purpose of purification. On this point, Pracetas says:
"That feeding of Brāhmaṇas which is performed for the sake of purification..."

"For the sake of purification"—thus it is declared; that *śrāddha* is remembered as being like the *pārvaṇa*. "A limb of ritual action" (*karmāṅga*) refers to that performed at the beginning of a sacrifice and so forth. "Devotional" (*daivika*) refers to that performed with the gods in view. "The *śrāddha* of a journey" (*yātrā-śrāddha*) refers to that performed upon entering or departing. Regarding this, Pāraskara says:
"At the time of conception (*niṣeka*), at the *soma* sacrifice, and likewise at the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*)."
The Śrāddha performed at the Puṃsavana rite should be understood as a constituent part of that ritual, performed like a Vṛddhi-śrāddha.
That which is performed with reference to the gods is called *daivika*;
one should perform that with diligence on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) and other such occasions, just like the daily *śrāddha*.
"Indeed, when going to another country, one should perform that *śrāddha* with clarified butter (*sarpiṣā*);

it is declared to be for the sake of that journey, and likewise at the time of entry—of this there is no doubt. Here, the statement "it is an auxiliary part of the ritual act" (*karmāṅgam*) is intended to indicate that if it is not performed, there is a deficiency in the ritual. "With clarified butter" (*sarpiṣā*) means having clarified butter as the primary substance; for [if it were taken] according to its literal sense, satisfaction would be impossible through clarified butter alone.

Now, regarding the description of the location and the *śrāddha* rite: it should be performed in a place sloping toward the south, smeared with cow dung and other substances. Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"In a place sloping toward the south, or at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), or even in one's own home."
"One should perform the *śrāddha* with great care, provided it is accompanied by the purification of the ground and other such rites.

(ViDhPu 1.144.13) [304] "The ancestors are satisfied by what is given here on riverbanks, at sacred fords (*tīrthas*), on mountains, and on sandbanks—provided these places are indeed secluded. Thus it is said.
Vyāsa also says: "At Puṣkara, as well as at Mahodadhi, Prayāga, Kāśī, and Kurujāṅgala, a śrāddha, recitation, fire-oblations, and ascetic penances become inexhaustible."
Śaṅkha also says:
"On the banks of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, at Payoṣṇī and Amarakaṇṭaka,
on the banks of the Narmadā and Bāhudā, at Bhṛgutuṅga, and in the Himalayas."
"What is given at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, and likewise at Puṣkara, at Saṃnihatyā, and at Gayā, shall attain imperishability. Thus [it is said].
Also in the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa:
On the banks of a river or an ocean, in a lake, a cow-pen, or on a mountain;
on the bank of a river flowing to the sea, or at the confluence of a river and the ocean.
It is recommended at the confluence of two rivers, or near a Śālagrāma stone,
or at Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, or even Naimiṣa.
And especially at Śālagrāma, Gokarṇa, and Gayā—
whoever, endowed with devotion to the ancestors, performs a śrāddha in these sacred fields;
"The mortal who performs [the rite] according to rule is ordained as one who has fulfilled his duty. Bṛhaspati also says:
"The ancestors, fearing a fall into hell, long for sons."
"Whoever shall go to Gayā will deliver us."
He will perform the rite of releasing a bull and likewise carry out sacrifices and works of public utility;
in his old age he will protect [the family] and offer ancestral oblations every day.
"What is given at Gayā, on Dharmapṛṣṭha, in the assembly of Brahmā, and likewise at Gayāśīrṣa and the Vaṭa tree, is inexhaustible for the ancestors. Thus [it is said]. Viṣṇu also [states]:

At Gayāśīrṣa; at the Vaṭa tree; on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka; anywhere on the banks of the Narmadā; on the banks of the Yamunā; especially at the Gaṅgā; at Gaṅgādvāra; at Prayāga; at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean; at Kuśāvarta; at Bilvaka; on Mount Nīla; at Kanakhala; at Kubjāmra; at Bhṛgutuṅga; at Kedāra; [306] at Mahālaya; at Naḍantikā; at Sugandhā; at Śākambharī; at Phalgutīrtha; at Mahāgaṅgā; at Tāṇḍulikāśrama; at Kumāradhārā; at Prabhāsa; anywhere along the Sarasvatī; especially at the Naimiṣa forest; at Vārāṇasī; at Agastyāśrama; at Kaṇvāśrama; at the Kauśikī; on the banks of the Sarayū; at the confluence of the Śoṇa and the Jyotirathī; at Śrīparvata; at Kālodaka; at Uttaramānasa; at Vaḍavā; at Mataṅgavāpī; at Saptārṣa; at Viṣṇupada; in the region of Svargamārga; at the Godāvarī; at the Gomatī; at the Vetravatī; at the Vipāśā; at the Vitastā; on the banks of the Śatadrū; at the Candrabhāgā; at the Irāvatī; [307] on the banks of the Sindhu; at Pañcanada in the south; at Oujasa; and in other such sacred fords (tīrthas), among the best of rivers, at confluences, at sources, on sandbanks, at springs, in mountain groves, in forests and parks, and in houses smeared with cow-dung that are pleasing to the mind. Regarding this, there are also verses sung by the ancestors:
May that being be born in our family who would offer us a handful of water in rivers abounding with water, especially those that are cool.
"May there arise in our family some supreme among men who,
with a concentrated mind, shall offer us the śrāddha at the banyan tree of Gayāśīrṣa."
"One should desire many sons, so that even one among them might go to Gayā,
or perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or set free a dark-colored bull" (ViDh 85.4–7).
Furthermore, the measurement of Gayāśīrṣa is stated in the Ādipurāṇa:
The sacred field of Gayā extends for five krośas, while Gayāśiras is one krośa;
it lies to the west of the Mahānadī river as far as Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

[308] "From the northern end of the Brahma-pillar as far as the southern Mānasa, this is known as Gayāśiras, renowned throughout the three worlds. Thus [it is said]. Now, the times for the Śrāddha ceremony:

The times for *śrāddha* are the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the *aṣṭakā*s, and so forth. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says: "The new moon, the *aṣṭakā*s, an occasion of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), the dark fortnight, the two solstices (*ayanadvaya*), the availability of materials, the excellence of Brahmins, the equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), and the sun’s passage into a new zodiacal sign (*sūryasaṃkrama*)."
"Vyatīpāta, the shadow of the earth [eclipse], the eclipses of the moon and the sun, and a desire for the śrāddha—these are proclaimed as the times for śrāddha. (YDh 1.217–18).
That day on which the moon is not seen is the new moon (amāvāsyā). On that occasion, the śrāddha is obligatory. And so says Laugākṣi:
"A twice-born man whose father has died must certainly perform the *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*indukṣaya*),
every month, on the day of the lunar increase (*vṛddhi*), and also annually. The four *aṣṭakās* are the eighth days of the dark fortnights of the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa.
The Aṣṭakā rites are performed on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the two seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Śaunaka. In that regard, the *śrāddha* is obligatory. Regarding this, Pitāmaha says:

"On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), and on the *aṣṭakā* days, a learned man who does not perform the *śrāddha* becomes liable for penance."

*Vṛddhi* refers to the birth of a son and so forth; by this, a specific time characterized by such events is indicated. The *kṛṣṇapakṣa* is the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*). The two solstices (*ayana*) are the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) and the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*). *Dravya* refers to materials such as *kṛsara* (rice and peas) and meat. A *brāhmaṇa* is one endowed with Vedic learning and study. The time in which there is the attainment or acquisition of both of these is described as such. The equinoxes (*viṣuvat*) are the transits (*saṃkrāntī*) of the sun into Aries and Libra. The solar transit (*sūryasaṃkrama*) is the sun’s arrival at another zodiac sign from its current one. Although the solstices and equinoxes are already included by the term "solar transit" itself, their separate mention is for the purpose of indicating a superior fruit [of performing rites at those times]. *Vyatīpāta* is a specific astrological conjunction (*yoga*), or it may refer to the *mahāvyatīpāta*.
If Jupiter and Mars are situated in Leo, while the Sun is in Aries,
and the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) coincides with the Hasta nakṣatra, that is indeed a great Vyatīpāta yoga.
If the new moon occurs under the asterisms of Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, or Mūla,
and falls on a Sunday, it is called Vyatīpāta.

This is according to the statement of the elder Manu. *Nāgadaivata* refers to the asterism Āśleṣā; *mastaka* refers to Mṛgaśiras. The meaning is that when the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) falls on a Sunday and is conjoined with any one of the asterisms beginning with Śravaṇa, that is *vyatīpāta*. The definition of *gajacchāyā* is shown in another Smṛti:

"When the Moon is in the asterism presided over by the ancestors (Maghā) and the Sun is situated in Hasta, and the lunar day is that of Yama (the thirteenth), that indeed is proclaimed as *gajacchāyā*."

The Maghā constellation is presided over by the ancestors (pitṛdaivatyam). Haṃsa is the Sun. Kara is the Hasta constellation. Yāmyā is the lunar day (tithi) of the thirteenth. It is also stated in the Purāṇa:
“When the Sun is situated in the Hasta constellation and the thirteenth lunar day is conjoined with Maghā, that lunar day is named Vaivasvatī; it is the shadow of the elephant.”

Regarding the phrase "the eclipse of the moon and sun," *grahaṇa* means an occultation (*uparāga*). Here too, a specific time must be accepted as an integral part of the *śrāddha*. To this effect, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
"The gods are satisfied at the moment of contact (*sparśa*), likewise the ancestors;
humans [are satisfied] at the time of the middle (*madhya*), but the *rākṣasas* at the time of release (*mokṣa*)."

Regarding the phrase "a desire for the *śrāddha*," it means that it should be performed at the very moment one feels the longing for it. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), other times for the *śrāddha* are also included. For this very reason, Yama says:
"On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, or Māgha, one should satisfy three or five twice-born men, beginning with the ancestors; that [offering] of his is said to be inexhaustible."
Devala also says:
"The third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha joined with Rohiṇī,
and the thirteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya joined with Maghā."
Likewise, the ninth day of Kārttika conjoined with Śatabhiṣaj, as well as the new moon,
Gajacchāyā, the Vaidhṛti yoga, and the beginnings of the Yugas.
"These times have been specified as those which increase the satisfaction of the ancestors.
The beginnings of the Yugas are also times for *śrāddha*. These are shown in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"The third day of Vaiśākha and the ninth day of Kārttika..."
The fifteenth day of the month of Māgha and the thirteenth day of Nabhasya.
"For these are remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas, which cause what is given to become inexhaustible" (Matsya Purāṇa 17.4–5).
Also in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"The third day of the month of Vaiśākha, and that ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika..."
On the thirteenth and fifteenth days of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, and on the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha.

"A man who, being self-restrained, offers even water mixed with sesame seeds here to the ancestors, by him a Śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years; this is a secret, say the ancestors. (ViP 3.14.12–14)

The days of Manu and others are also times for *śrāddha*. Thus it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, the twelfth of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, and the third of the bright fortnights of Caitra and Bhādrapada."
The new moon of Phālguna, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa,
the tenth day of Āṣāḍha, and the seventh day of the month of Māgha.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, as well as the full moon of Āṣāḍha;
the full moons of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha, which are all bright.
"And these beginnings of the Manvantaras cause what has been given to become inexhaustible. (Matsya Purāṇa 17.6–9).
The lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā are the times for optional *śrāddha* rites. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"Heaven, progeny, vigor, heroism, as well as land and strength..."
Bestow upon me a son, preeminence, good fortune, prosperity, and auspicious leadership.
The turning of the wheel of sovereignty, as well as success in trade and other pursuits,
freedom from disease, fame, the absence of sorrow, and the supreme goal.
He who duly offers the śrāddha bestows wealth, the Vedas, success in medicine, base metals, cattle, goats and sheep, horses, and long life.
"From Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī, he shall obtain these desires. Thus [says Yājñavalkya]. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"By worshipping the ancestors under the asterism of Kṛttikā, a man attains heaven."
One desiring offspring should [beget] under Rohiṇī, while one should obtain vigor under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras).
Under Ārdrā one attains valor; under Punarvasu, land and the like;
under Puṣya, prosperity; and by worshipping the ancestors under Āśleṣā, one obtains excellent sons.
Under Maghā, one attains preeminence among kinsmen; under the two Phalgunīs, good fortune;
and under the Uttarās, one becomes disposed to giving and possessed of offspring.
A man who offers the śrāddha rite when the moon is in the hand (hasta) nakṣatra attains preeminence among the virtuous;
likewise, he shall obtain beautiful offspring when it is in the citrā nakṣatra.
Svāti bestows profit from trade; Viśākhā grants the desire for sons;
and those who perform rites under Anurādhā shall obtain the turning of the wheel of sovereignty.
[313] Under Jyeṣṭhā there is sovereignty over wealth; under Mūla, supreme health;
under Āṣāḍhā, the attainment of fame; and under the Uttarās, freedom from sorrow.
Under Śravaṇa one attains auspicious worlds; under Dhaniṣṭhā, great wealth;
under Abhijit, knowledge of the Vedas; and under Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), success as a physician.
One may obtain goats and sheep under Proṣṭhapadā, likewise a wife under Uttarā;
similarly, silver under Revatī, and horses under Aśvinī.

"Likewise, performing a *śrāddha* on the *bharaṇī* [nakṣatra] one obtains excellent longevity; therefore, the knower of reality should perform rites for specific desires under these lunar mansions. (MārkPur 33.8.16)

"Saumya" means having the Moon as its presiding deity; that is to say, Mṛgaśīrṣa. "Setting in motion the wheel" means the operation [of authority] everywhere without obstruction to one's command. "Abhijit" refers to the lunar mansion named Abhijit; thus says the Śruti: "Above the Āṣāḍhās and below Śroṇā. This, however, is a definition by piercing (vedha). "Success for the physician" is the attainment of the results of medicinal herbs. "Vāruṇa" is the lunar mansion Śatabhiṣaj. "Base metals" refers to tin, lead, and so forth. Viṣṇu also [says the same].

Heaven under Kṛttikā; offspring under Rohiṇī; spiritual luster under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras); success in ritual actions under Raudra (Ārdrā); land under Punarvasu; nourishment under Puṣya; fortune under Sārpa (Āśleṣā); all desires under Paitrya (Maghā); good fortune under the Phalgunīs; wealth under Āryamaṇa (Pūrvaphalgunī); preeminence among kinsmen under Hasta; handsome sons under Tvāṣṭra (Citrā); increase in trade under Svāti; gold under Viśākhā; friends under Maitra (Anurādhā); sovereignty under Śakra (Jyeṣṭhā); agriculture under Mūla; success in sea-voyages under Āpya (Pūrvāṣāḍhā); all desires under Śravaṇa; strength under Vāsava (Śatabhiṣaj); health under Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj); base metals under Āja (Pūrvabhādrapadā); a house under Āhirbudhnya (Uttarabhādrapadā); cattle under Pauṣṇa (Revatī); horses under Āśvina (Aśvinī); and life under Yāmya (Bharaṇī). Thus it is said. (ViDh 78.8–35)

The days of the week, beginning with Sunday, are also times for optional *śrāddha* ceremonies. Regarding this, Viṣṇu says: “One who constantly performs *śrāddha* on Sunday attains health; on Monday, good fortune; on Tuesday, victory in battle; on Wednesday, all desires; on Thursday, desired knowledge; on Friday, wealth; and on Saturday, long life” (ViDh 78.1–7). Also in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: “On Sunday, however, there is health;
on Monday, indeed good fortune; on Tuesday, victory everywhere; and on Wednesday, all desires.”
"One shall indeed obtain distinguished knowledge from a guru [under Jupiter], wealth from Venus,
and long life as well as very rare health under Saturn. Thus [it is said] in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* (1.2.20.16–17).
Therefore, O King, I shall describe to you the Śrāddhas performed for specific desires:
those for health, as well as for good fortune, victory in battle,
the fulfillment of all wishes, knowledge, wealth, and even long life.
“A man who always performs the *śrāddha* in this manner on the days beginning with Sunday attains these [results] in due order; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (ViP 1.142.30–32).
The lunar days (*tithis*) beginning with the first day (*pratipad*) are also times for optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddha*. Regarding this, Manu says:
By performing a śrāddha on the first lunar day (pratipad), one obtains handsome sons;
on the second, a daughter; and on the third, bards.
On the fourth day one obtains small animals; on the fifth, handsome sons;
on the sixth, one obtains a messenger; and on the seventh, one gains success in agriculture.
On the eighth day as well, the giver of a śrāddha always obtains trade;
on the ninth day, he obtains single-hoofed animals, and on the tenth day, many double-hoofed animals.
On the eleventh day, one obtains silver and sons who are eloquent in Vedic discourse;
on the twelfth day, however, one obtains gold, silver, base metals, and even forbidden goods.
On the thirteenth day, one attains preeminence among kinsmen; on the fourteenth day, one obtains good offspring;
and his ancestors who were slain by weapons in battle are gratified.
"One who performs the *śrāddha* on the fifteenth day attains all desires. Thus [says Manu]. Yājñavalkya also says:
"A daughter, those who seek daughters, cattle, small animals, and even sons..."
Gambling, agriculture, trade, as well as one-hoofed and two-hoofed animals;
The giver of the Śrāddha always obtains sons endowed with Vedic luster, gold, silver, and base metals, preeminence among kinsmen, and all his desires.
"Excluding one [day] among the days beginning with the Pratipad, [the offering] is given there for those who have indeed been slain by a weapon on the fourteenth day. (YDh 1.262–64)

The suitors for daughters are the sons-in-law. The giver of a *śrāddha* obtains these fruits in succession on the lunar days (*tithis*) beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight and ending with the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). For this very reason, Kātyāyana states: "On the first day, women of exceeding beauty; on the second, the birth of a daughter; on the third, horses; on the fourth, small livestock; on the fifth, sons; on the sixth, gambling; on the seventh, agriculture; on the eighth, trade; on the ninth, one-hoofed animals; on the tenth, cattle; on the eleventh, servants; on the twelfth, wealth, grain, and silver; on the thirteenth, preeminence among kinsmen and gold; on the fourteenth, young men die there, slain by weapons; on the new moon, everything. And this rule for performing the *śrāddha* on the lunar days beginning with the first of the dark fortnight applies to all dark fortnights (*aparapakṣas*), not merely to the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada. For this reason, Śaunaka says: "In the dark fortnight of Prauṣṭhapada, and likewise month after month. Āpastamba also [says the same].

"When performed on any day of the dark fortnight, one pleases the ancestors. However, due to the specific restriction of time for the performer, there is a distinction in the results: if it is performed on the first day, offspring consisting mostly of females are born; on the second, thieves; on the third, those endowed with Vedic luster (*brahmavarcas*); on the fourth, one possessing small livestock; on the fifth, males; [on the sixth], one has many children and does not die childless; on the seventh, one is habitually traveling; on the eighth, one is addicted to dice; on the ninth, success in agriculture; on the tenth, prosperity in trade; on the eleventh, iron, tin, and lead; on the twelfth, one possesses livestock; on the thirteenth, one has many sons, many friends, and handsome offspring, though they die young; on the fourteenth, success in weaponry; and on the fifteenth, prosperity. (ĀpDh 2.7.16.7–22)
Regarding the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, Mārkaṇḍeya states:
"When the sun has entered Virgo, for fifteen days,
the Śrāddha is prescribed there according to the very rite of the Pārvaṇa."
The first lunar day (pratipad) leads to the acquisition of wealth; the second bestows bipeds;
the third is for those seeking boons; and the fourth destroys enemies.
On the fifth day one attains prosperity, and on the sixth a man becomes worthy of worship;
on the fifth he gains the leadership of a host, and on the sixth, supreme intelligence.
On the ninth day, one obtains women; on the tenth, the fulfillment of all desires;
and on the eleventh, one devoted to ritual action attains all the Vedas.
On the twelfth day, the worshiper of the ancestors obtains gold,
progeny, intelligence, cattle, nourishment, independence, and supreme prosperity.
A man devoted to ancestral rites who performs a Śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day attains long life and sovereignty; of this there is no doubt.
He whose deceased ancestors were young men slain by weapons must perform [the rite] on the fourteenth day if he desires their prosperity.

"A man who, being pure, performs the *śrāddha* with food on the new moon day attains all desires and himself enjoys infinity. (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 33.1–8) When the sun has entered Virgo (*kanyā*), the entire fortnight beginning from the first day of the dark half of the month of Nabhasya is called the *mahālaya*. In that period, one should perform the *śrāddha* according to the *pārvaṇa* rite alone. Regarding this, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"The latter fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, during which the sun enters Virgo,
shall be known as Mahālaya, as well as by the name Gajacchāyā.
As for that which was stated by Śāṭhyāyani:
If the sixteen lunar days of the latter fortnight of the month of Nabhasya are conjoined with the Sun situated in Virgo, that time is [highly auspicious] for the performance of Śrāddha rites.

Thus, one should perform the *śrāddha* even on the additional day when there is an increase in the lunar days (*tithi*), and not only during the fifteen days; this is the intended meaning. Alternatively, the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya consists of sixteen days, including the first day (*pratipad*) of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja. This is because that [first day] may also be included within the dark fortnight, as there is no difference in its being a time when the moon has waned. Devala states: "The sixteen days which consist of the first day of the bright fortnight are also traditionally considered to be of the nature of the new moon (*darśa*), due to the lack of distinction in the moon's waning."

Now, an objection is raised: "In this view, what is the status of the statement, 'fifteen days'? It is replied: Just as the term "eight-potsherd" (*aṣṭākapāla*) is used for twelve potsherds, so too the mention of "fifteen days" regarding sixteen days will be a partial restatement (*avayutyānuvāda*). Alternatively, let there be an option (*vikalpa*) between the injunctions of fifteen days and sixteen days, like that of rice and barley (*vrīhi-yava*). Furthermore, the latter half of the month of *nabhasya* is said to be more excellent because it is conjoined with the sun being in Virgo; yet even in its absence, it remains excellent. Thus says Jābāli:
Even when the sun has entered Virgo, one should by all means perform the śrāddha;
the fifth fortnight of Āṣāḍha is highly recommended for rites dedicated to the ancestors.
By offering a śrāddha on the fifth day, one obtains sons, long life, health, incomparable sovereignty, as well as other desires.
[321] Thus says Bṛhanmanu as well:
"Taking Āṣāḍhī as the starting point, the ancestors, remaining distressed, desire food— and even water— every day during the fifth fortnight."
Therefore, one should give right there; given elsewhere, it is fruitless.
Taking the full moon of Āṣāḍha as the limit, that which is the fifth fortnight—

"In that regard, one should perform the *śrāddha*, whether or not the Sun is situated in Virgo. The superior excellence of this alternative view due to the Sun being in Virgo is shown in the *Ādipurāṇa*:
"Even in the other case, the *śrāddha* is praised when the Sun is in Virgo."
"One should especially perform [the rite] when the fifth month has entered the sign of Virgo.
Thus says Ślokagautama:
"Those sixteen days while the sun is in the sign of Virgo..."
"These are equal to sacrifices accompanied by complete and excellent sacrificial fees. Thus [says Śātātapa]. Śāṭhyāyani also says:
"The Sun situated in Virgo is auspicious, as is the fifth fortnight."
"The fortnight joined with the Sun in Virgo is said to be exceedingly meritorious.
This means that because the Sun is in conjunction with Virgo at its beginning, middle, or end—wherever that may be—the entire fortnight is meritorious. For this very reason, Kārṣṇājini says:
"Wherever the Sun enters Virgo—at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end [of the fortnight]..."

"That entire fortnight is meritorious for the sake of the sixteen *śrāddhas*. Thus it is said. If one is unable to perform the *śrāddha* from the first day (*pratipad*) until the new moon (*darśa*), one should perform the *śrāddha* according to one's capacity starting from the fifth day until the new moon, or from the eighth day until the new moon. Regarding this, Gautama says: "One should offer to the ancestors on the new moon day without a *śrāddha*; or on the days beginning with the fifth of the dark fortnight; or according to one's faith at any time" (GDh 15.1–3). Also, in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"In the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, one should perform the *śrāddha* day after day."
"Or [the fortnight] lessened by one-third, or indeed one-third, or even half.
Regarding this, in the view that the fortnight begins on the first lunar day (pratipad) and ends on the new moon (darśa), the days beginning with Nanda are not to be avoided. Thus said Kārṣṇājini:
"One should perform the Śrāddha rite day after day during the latter fortnight of the month of Nabhasya."
"Neither Nandā and the others should be avoided, nor indeed should the fourteenth day be avoided.
Now, one might object: "In this regard, [the rule] 'starting from the first lunar day, having omitted one [day], except for the fourteenth' (YDh 1.264)..."

If it be argued that this would contradict the statement of Yājñavalkya, we say no; for that statement is appropriately understood as referring to the view beginning with Pañcami (the fifth day). Otherwise, the statement of Kārṣṇājini would result in being purposeless. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says: “One should perform the Śrāddha in the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa). From the fourth day onwards, on whichever day it falls—provided it is after the seventh day and excluding the fourteenth—one should not let the dark fortnight pass even if one has only vegetables. Manu also says: “In the dark fortnight, starting from the tenth day, avoiding the fourteenth...”
"As these lunar days (tithis) are praised for the *śrāddha*, so are others not.

Even there, if one lacks the capacity, the householder should perform the *śrāddha* on any unprohibited lunar day—starting from the fifth day of the fifth fortnight up to the end of the immediately following five-day period—as circumstances permit. Regarding this, Yama says:
"When the Sun is in Leo (Haṃsa), during the rainy season, while the Sun is in Virgo (Kanyā), even if living at home with only vegetables..."
"One should offer [the śrāddha] within the interval of the two pentads on both sides.

Thus, if due to incapacity or other reasons the śrāddha is performed during the fifth pentad, one should continue offering the śrāddha as long as the sun remains in the zodiac sign of Virgo (kanyā). If it is not performed even then, it should be done until the appearance of Scorpio (vṛścika). Regarding this, Sumantu said:
"O Great King, as long as the sun remains in the zodiac sign of Virgo..."
"Therefore, from that time onwards, [the offering] should be given until Scorpio has arrived.
Thus it is said; and also in the Purāṇa:
"When the sun has entered Virgo, the ancestors indeed go toward their sons."
The entire city of the hungry ghosts is empty, extending as far as the sight of the scorpions.
Then, having failed to obtain the scorpion, the ancestors departed in despair;
after pronouncing a most terrible curse, they returned once more to their own abode.
If a householder does not perform the *śrāddha* rite when the sun has entered Virgo, how can he have wealth or sons? For he is tormented by the sighs of his ancestors.
"When Scorpio has passed, the ancestors, together with the deities, depart sighing after having uttered a most terrible curse.
Thus it is said; and also in the Ādi-purāṇa:
In the rainy season, Yama, having emptied his own city by releasing the deceased and the ancestors from the abode of Yama back into the world of men, departs.
Afflicted by hunger and confessing their own misdeeds,
they longed for milk-rice mixed with honey for the sake of their sons and grandsons.
Therefore, one should satisfy them there according to the prescribed rite with milk-rice mixed with honey,
clarified butter, and sesame seeds, as well as with cool water.
That man who obtains from another's house food merely the size of a mouthful,
or who sustains his own life by means of a mere alms-meal;
"Or he who nourishes his body by the sale of his own self—even he must perform the *śrāddha* with various well-accumulated materials. This is to be construed by supplying the words:

"having sent [the deceased] away from the abode of Yama and having made his own city empty, he causes the ancestors to dwell in the world of men. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the ancestors remain desiring milk-rice (*pāyasa*). Regarding those who are to be avoided in that context, Gārgya says:

"On the Nandā tithi, on a day of the Bhārgava [Venus], and on the thirteenth lunar day—on these three occasions of birth, a householder should not perform a Śrāddha, for fear of the loss of sons and wealth. Here, "trijanmani" means the birth asterism (janmanakṣatra) as well as the one preceding and the one following it. Vṛddhagārgya also says:

"But he who performs a *śrāddha* under the constellation of Prajāpati, or Pauṣṇa, or the Pitrya asterism, or likewise Bhārgava, his son perishes. Here, "Prajāpatya" is Rohiṇī; "Pauṣṇa" is Revatī; "Pitryarkṣa" is Maghā. Aṅgiras also says:
If a man performs a śrāddha on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one should know for certain that his eldest son will meet his death.
"For one performing a *śrāddha* during the *Maghā* [nakṣatra], the eldest son perishes.

In this regard, the prohibition of *śrāddha* on the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*) under the asterism of *Maghā* pertains specifically to a *śrāddha* intended solely for the class of ancestors (*pitṛvarga*). It is not, however, a prohibition of *śrāddha* in general.
Now, one might object: "A prohibition is only appropriate when there is a possibility of performing a *śrāddha* intended solely for the class of ancestors."

Wherever the ancestors (pitaras) are worshipped, there the maternal grandfathers (mātāmahas) must certainly be worshipped as well; it should be performed without distinction, for by failing to do so, one goes to hell.

Thus, because Dhaumya’s statement prohibits a *śrāddha* intended for a single class [of ancestors], there is no possibility [of its performance] at all; therefore, this restriction is not intended [by the author]. Do not say so. For even though the *smṛti* of Dhaumya exists, it prohibits the *śrāddha* for a single class which has been undertaken merely through delusion. It is just like the prohibition, "One should not eat *kalañja*," which forbids the eating of *kalañja* that has arisen from mere worldly desire (*rāga*). For this very reason, Kārṣṇājini says:
"One should not commence a *śrāddha* for a single class on the thirteenth lunar day."
"Those who are unsatisfied therein indeed harm his progeny.
There is also another Smṛti:
"One who has sons may desire a Śrāddha on the thirteenth day for the sake of his children's longevity."
"But one should not give [the śrāddha] to only one; rather, one should perform the pārvaṇa.

This means that he who has sons and desires the increase of their life-span should not offer the śrāddha to only one group (the paternal ancestors), but should instead perform the pārvaṇa rite intended for the group of maternal grandfathers as well. Therefore, the prohibition of the śrāddha on the thirteenth day of the month of Māgha when in conjunction with the Maghā nakṣatra refers only to offering it to a single group, and not to the śrāddha itself; for in that case, the śrāddha is highly commended. And so says Śaṅkha:
"When the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada has passed, [on] the thirteenth day joined with Maghā..."
Having reached [the proper time], the śrāddha must be performed with honey and milk-rice (pāyasa).
"The grandfathers, being always pleased by the *śrāddha*, bestow upon men desired offspring, fame, heaven, health, and likewise wealth. Thus [it is said in] the *Śaṅkhasmṛti* (14.6–7).
Also in the *Mahābhārata*:
"One who performs a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] shall become the most excellent among his kinsmen;
moreover, young men in his household will certainly not die prematurely.

In this regard, one should not perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) during a *śrāddha* on the Maghā-trayodaśī, because on that day, due to its being a *yugādi* (the beginning of a cosmic age), the offering of *piṇḍas* is prohibited. Thus says Pulastya:

"Likewise, on the two solstices (*ayana*), the two equinoxes (*viṣuva*), and on all the beginnings of the Yugas (*yugādi*), [the Śrāddha] is to be performed without the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍanirvapaṇa*).

The word "to be performed" (*kartavyam*) is to be supplied [from the context]. Even when [the moon is] conjoined with the Maghā constellation, there is no offering of rice-balls. And so it is stated in the *Ādipurāṇa*:

“O Bhārata, by fasting on the day of the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), by breaking the fast, and by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) during the Maghā asterism, the eldest son perishes. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the prohibition of performing a *śrāddha* on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) refers specifically to those who did not die by weapons; however, for those killed by an untimely death (*apamṛtyu*), the *śrāddha* must indeed be performed even on the fourteenth day. Regarding this, Marīci says:
"For those who have killed a Brāhmaṇa by means of poison, weapons, wild beasts, fire, or animals, the rite should be performed on the fourteenth day; for others, however, it is forbidden.
Thus [says] Pracetas as well.

"For those who have perished by climbing trees, [drowning in] iron and the like, lightning, water, poison, and so forth, or by [the attack of] clawed or fanged beasts, the fourteenth day is prescribed. Thus says Yājñavalkya as well.

"But for those who have been killed by a weapon, [the offering] is indeed given to them there. (YDh 1.264) Here, it is restricted that [the offering] is for those killed by weapons specifically on the fourteenth day; it does not mean, however, that it must be performed only on the fourteenth day. This being the case, the Mahālaya Śrāddha should be performed on other days as well for the sake of achieving the satisfaction of the grandfather and the rest, because the Mahālaya Śrāddha is prescribed as an *ekoddiṣṭa* on the fourteenth day, and therefore, through that [specific rite], the satisfaction of the grandfather and others would otherwise be absent. And Sumantu states that its nature is that of an *ekoddiṣṭa*:
"Even for a father who has attained equality [with the gods] but was slain by a weapon, the sons must perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on the fourteenth day during the *mahālaya*. [328]

The meaning is that for a father who has attained equality (*samatva*), whose *sapindīkaraṇa* has been performed, and who was killed by a weapon, an *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha must be performed by his sons on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) during the *mahālaya*. For one whose grandfather (*pitāmaha*) was also killed by a weapon or similar means, he must perform an *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha for both on the fourteenth day. And so says another Smṛti: "The rule of the *ekoddiṣṭa* applies to one or to two. This is the meaning: when one father is killed by a weapon or similar means, or when two—namely the father and grandfather—are killed by a weapon or similar means, the son must perform an *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha for each of them individually on the fourteenth day. For one whose father, grandfather, and great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) were all three killed by a weapon, he must perform the śrāddha on the fourteenth day according to the *pārvaṇa* rite itself; this is because of the specific mention in the rule "the rule of the *ekoddiṣṭa* applies to one or to two. This is the opinion of the authors of the *Candrikā* and *Aparārka*. The opinion of Devasvāmin is that even when all three—the father and the others—are killed by a weapon, an *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed separately for each of the three. Regarding this, it appears that Devasvāmin’s position is correct: since there is no direct scriptural injunction (*sākṣād-vidhāyaka-vacana*) for a *pārvaṇa* śrāddha when all three have been killed by a weapon, and since the statement "to one or to two" can be understood as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) [of three], only the three *ekoddiṣṭas* should be performed. On other days, however, for those killed by weapons and the like, the śrāddha must be performed according to the *pārvaṇa* rite alone. Therefore, Prajāpati says:
"During the transit [of the sun], during an eclipse, at the festival of the rains, and during the Mahālaya, one should offer three rice-balls (piṇḍas) here; so said Prajāpati.
Thus, the Mahālaya śrāddha for brothers, sisters, and others should be performed according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*. And so says Sumantu:
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, wherever [an offering] is given—
whether to a brother, a sister, a son, a husband, or a maternal uncle— [it is considered a śrāddha].
"For a friend or a teacher, the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha is prescribed, not the *pārvaṇa*.
Āpastamba also says:
"Those who die without sons—whether women or men—"
"And for them as well, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed, not the *pārvaṇa*. Here, "women" refers to sisters and others; "men" refers to brothers and others. Kātyāyana also states:
"For relatives, kinsmen, and the like, however, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is always [to be performed]."
Furthermore, as for those statements that prohibit the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite—such as Jātūkarṇya’s statement regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*:
"From this point onward, the *ekoddiṣṭa* should never be performed;
it is declared to end with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*," so says Mudgala.
Having crossed over the state of being a preta, he reaches the company of the ancestors;
yet, once a separate funeral ball (piṇḍa) has been offered, he falls away from the world of the ancestors.
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony, [the deceased] arises as separate;
but once separation has been effected, the *sapiṇḍatā* must be performed again.
Thus says Kārṣṇāgni as well.
"Therefore, after this point, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should never be performed;
for the deceased, this [rite] is inauspicious until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Thus says Yama as well.

"He who should offer a separate piṇḍa to a deceased person for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, becomes a destroyer of the ritual injunction and is born as a slayer of his ancestors. Thus it is said; and also in the Purāṇa:

"Wherever there is the offering of these [gifts] after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, there the wise man should perform the *śrāddha* according to the *pārvaṇa* rite and abandon the *ekoddiṣṭa*. All of these [rules] are to be understood as applying when the specific *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure prescribed for each case is absent. This *śrāddha*, however, if the primary time has passed due to birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or other such conditions, must be performed at the very first moment following the cessation of that impurity. Thus says Ṛṣyaśṛṅga:
"But when impurity (āśauca) arises during a Śrāddha intended for the ancestors,
the Śrāddha is offered to them once that period of impurity has passed.
As for the statement of Atri:
"If that day should be defiled by someone through birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or the like, one should perform it on the day following the *sūtaka*, or else on that very same day again. Thus it is said.

Two alternatives have been proposed: either immediately after the period of impurity (*sūtaka*), or in the next month, in that same fortnight, or on that same lunar day (*tithi*). Among these, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the first alternative. Furthermore, the alternative stating "on that very day" is established as referring to the *ekoddiṣṭa* monthly *śrāddha* prescribed for the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*) every month, in the event that an obstacle arises due to some cause other than *sūtaka*; this is done to avoid contradicting the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga. For this very reason, Devala says: "But when the *ekoddiṣṭa* has arrived, if an obstacle should arise..."
"One should diligently perform the śrāddha for him on any other day of that same lunar fortnight. Thus it is said.

"In another month immediately following" means on that lunar day, which is the anniversary of the death; the meaning is that one should perform the *śrāddha* in whichever fortnight—bright or dark—in which the person died, even if hindered by obstacles. However, when there is an obstacle caused by ritual impurity (*āśauca*), even the monthly *śrāddha* must be performed immediately after the period of impurity has ended, on the strength of the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga. Devasvāmin has also established this very distinction of cases: "This statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga refers to obstacles caused by ritual impurity. When the performance is obstructed for other reasons on that day, it refers to the statement from another Smṛti beginning with: 'But when the *ekoddiṣṭa* has arrived, if an obstacle arises... As for that which was stated by Vyāsa:
If an obstacle to the *śrāddha* arises midway due to a death or birth-impurity (*mṛtasūtake*),
some wise authorities maintain that one should perform it on the new moon day once purification has occurred.

[332] Thus: if, during the interval—that is, in the midst of the preparatory rites—before the commencement of the cooking, a death or birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) occurs, one should perform the *śrāddha* on the new moon day, or upon purification immediately following the period of impurity. This refers specifically to the monthly and annual *śrāddhas*. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"When the monthly or annual [śrāddha] has arrived, and a death or birth-impurity occurs in the interim, the wise declare that it should be performed upon purification or on the new moon day."

The mention of the new moon day (*darśa*) is intended as an illustration for both the eleventh days of the bright and dark fortnights. For this very reason, Marīci states: "When an obstacle to the *śrāddha* has arisen and the day of death is unknown, it should be performed on the eleventh day, especially during the dark fortnight."

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "On that Ekādaśī which falls in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), it should especially be performed," because for ancestral rites (pitṛkārya), the dark fortnight alone is specifically to be accepted. Furthermore, the primacy of the new moon (amāvāsyā) over even the dark Ekādaśī regarding ancestral rites is established by the maxim of the staff and the grain-offering (daṇḍāpūpanyāya). This is what is meant: the period immediately following the time of impurity (āśauca) is the very best [time for the rite] because of its proximity to the primary time; however, the time of the new moon is inferior to that because of its lack of proximity to the primary time. For this very reason, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says: "A gift should be given by one who has become pure on whichever lunar day (tithi) arrives."

"That lunar day (tithi) is to be observed for him, and never any other. Thus it is said. First, the *śrāddha* must be performed by one who is pure. In that regard, if due to impurity (*āśauca*) there is an absence of purity at the primary time, then the lunar day that follows and is obtained immediately after purification is to be accepted as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that rite. However, when there is no obstruction such as impurity, the primary time must not be bypassed out of laziness or similar reasons. As he himself says:
"The interruption of the lunar day must not be made arbitrarily, except in the case of impurity."
"The funeral ball (piṇḍa) and the śrāddha offering must be given; one must never allow the lineage to be interrupted. Thus it is said.

By the word *ca* (and), he includes the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire). Here, by the term *śrāddha*, only the satiation of the Brahmins is intended, because the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is mentioned separately. Regarding the injunction, “One should never cause an interruption,” the meaning is that if one is unable to perform the satiation of the Brahmins, one should at least perform the offering of the rice-balls; in no case should one cause an interruption in the worship of the ancestors. For this very reason, the *Nigama* states: “For one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the worship of the ancestors should be performed either with rice-balls alone or by feeding Brahmins. In this matter, there is a regulated option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*): when there is capacity, one should perform both the satiation of the Brahmins and the offering of the rice-balls; in the absence of such capacity, one should perform only the offering of the rice-balls. As for what was ordained by Hārīta—that when an obstacle to the *śrāddha* arises, an *ām-śrāddha* (a śrāddha with raw food) should be performed on the new moon day and other such occasions—[this applies to those who do not maintain the sacred fires].
"When there is an obstacle to the *śrāddha* for the twice-born, an *āma-śrāddha* is prescribed;

this applies to those fixed [rites] such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), except for the monthly and annual [rites]. (Hārīta Smṛti 21.13). "Monthly" means the monthly rite; "annual" means the annual rite. That [prescription] refers to cases where an obstacle is caused by the appearance of menses in the wife. Thus said Uśanas:

"One who is without a wife, one who is traveling abroad, and one whose wife is in her menses—these should not perform [the śrāddha] with cooked food; for them, raw food (āma) is prescribed. Thus [says Uśanas Smṛti 5.82]. Kātyāyana also says:
"In times of distress, when there is no fire, at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), while traveling abroad, upon the birth of a son,
or when one's wife is in her menses— one should perform an *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha with uncooked food). Thus says Vyāghrapāda as well.
"When a disruption of place and time regarding the *ārtava* (the period following menstruation) has arisen, the twice-born should perform an *āmaśrāddha*; indeed, a Śūdra should always do so.

Nor should it be thought that, upon considering the statements of Kātyāyana and Vyāghra, an *āmaśrāddha* would also apply to the monthly and annual rites; for by the specific statement, "except for the monthly and annual [rites]," it is understood that the *āmaśrāddha* pertains to occasions other than those. For this very reason, Marīci says:

"A twice-born man who is without a sacred fire, one who is traveling abroad, and one whose wife is in her menses—these should perform an *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha with uncooked food), but he should not do so on the anniversary of the death. This means that on the anniversary of the death, one should not perform that *śrāddha* with raw grain; rather, one should perform it with cooked food (*pakvānna*) alone. Laugākṣi also says:
"Even if his wife is menstruating, even if he is staying abroad, and even if he maintains no sacred fire,
he should perform the annual rite with food alone, or sometimes with gold or by name.
As for the prohibition of performing the *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death when the wife is menstruating, which is found in another *smṛti*:
When the anniversary of death has arrived, if his wife is in her menses, the śrāddha should not be performed then; it should be performed on the fifth day.

Thus, this is its subject matter: since the wife who is childless alone has the entitlement to perform the *śrāddha* on the anniversary of her husband’s death, when she herself happens to be in her menstrual period (*rajasvalā*), the *śrāddha* must not be performed on that day of death; rather, it should be performed on the fifth day. And so says Ślokagautama:
"But when the sonless wife has reached the annual anniversary of her husband’s death, if she should be in her menstrual period, she shall perform it on the fifth day. (ŚloGSm 5.14)
Also in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"A woman who has reached her menses becomes pure on the fourth day after bathing;
she becomes pure for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors on the fifth day."
Others, however, say:
"When the day for the *śrāddha* has arrived, if his wife is in her menses, the *śrāddha* should not be performed on that day; it should be performed on the fifth day. (ŚlGSm 5.19)

Having read this statement of Ślokagautama differently, they hold that since the entitlement to perform rites such as the *śrāddha* is heard to be shared with the wife, when she is defiled by the appearance of her menses, the entitlement ceases; thus, having passed the primary time, the *śrāddha* must be performed on the fifth day.
Now, an objection: "In this reading, would it not follow that even the *śrāddha* for the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and other such occasions must be postponed to the fifth day?"

It is not so; for by the statement of Hārīta, "In the event of an obstacle to the *śrāddha* of the twice-born," the use of raw grain (*āma*) is prescribed on the new moon day and other occasions to take the place of cooked food, just as *pūtīka* plants take the place of *soma*. If it is argued that the statement "on the day of the *śrāddha*" should be understood as having a scope distinct from the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), thereby remaining meaningful—[we reply: no.

This would be so if it were possible to state another subject matter; however, this is not the case. That the subject matter is the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) is understood precisely from the statement of another Smṛti: "When the day of death has arrived. Therefore, the *śrāddha* for the anniversary of death performed by one who has only a single wife must be performed at the very time when the obstacle consisting of the appearance of menstrual blood has ceased. But for one joined with another wife, since his entitlement (*adhikāra*) has not lapsed, it must be performed at the primary time itself. Whatever is logical in this regard should be accepted.
Now, regarding the examination of Brāhmaṇas at a *śrāddha*:
an examination of the Brāhmaṇas to be fed at the *śrāddha* must be performed. Concerning this, Yama says with reference to the *śrāddha*:
"One should examine the Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas even beforehand."
Those who have purified themselves from the defects arising from the body and have fulfilled their vows.
"One should examine from afar those Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas—whether they are liked or disliked—and at that time one must not treat them with contempt.

The word "previously" (pūrvam) means "before" [the invitation], as it implies the act of inviting. "Bodily defects" (śarīraprabhavā doṣāḥ) refer to leprosy, epilepsy, and so forth. "From afar" (dūrāt) means starting from the great-grandfather down to the Brāhmaṇa to be fed. Thus says Chāgaleya:

"One should perform every *śrāddha* with those endowed with the characteristics already described, possessed of learning, good conduct, and virtue, and renowned among the three classes of men. By "every," he means all *śrāddhas* consisting of both the *pārvaṇa* and the *ekoddiṣṭa* types. For this very reason, Manu also stated that a person attains preeminence through his father's status as a *śrotriya*.
He whose father is unlearned in the Vedas but whose son has mastered the Vedas,
or he whose son is unlearned in the Vedas but whose father has mastered the Vedas.
"One should know the elder of these two to be he whose father is a *śrotriya*. (MDh 3.136–37).
The Brāhmaṇas to be fed at a *śrāddha* have been indicated by Yājñavalkya:
"The foremost among all those learned in the Vedas is the *śrotriya*, the knower of Brahman who is young."
One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, one who is equal to an elder brother, one who knows the Trimadhu verses, and one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymns;

Those devoted to ritual action, those devoted to austerity, those who maintain the five fires, lifelong students, and those entirely dedicated to their father and mother—such Brāhmaṇas constitute the perfection of a Śrāddha. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.219–221)

[338] Thus: those who have mastered the recitation of all the Vedas, beginning with the *Ṛgveda*, without error; a *śrotriya*, one endowed with the study of the revealed scriptures (*śruta*); a knower of Brahman (*brahmavit*), one possessing knowledge of Brahman; a youth, being of middle age—and "youth" is a qualifying attribute for all [the following]; a knower of the meaning of the Veda, one possessing knowledge of Dharma; a *jyeṣṭhasāman*, referring to a specific *Sāman* chant and its associated vow—one who studies that [chant] by performing its vow is a *jyeṣṭhasāman*; a *trimadhu*, a portion of the *Ṛgveda* and its associated vow—one who studies that by performing its vow is a *trimadhu*; a *trisuparṇa*, a portion of the *Ṛg* and *Yajus* Vedas and its associated vow—one who studies that by performing its vow is a *trisuparṇika*; and Brāhmaṇas, not Kṣatriyas and so forth. The meaning is that these Brāhmaṇas, possessing the aforementioned characteristics, bring about the inexhaustible fruit of the *Śrāddha*. Bṛhaspati also says:
If one should feed but a single person at a śrāddha, one should feed a Chandoga there;
for in him the triad of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas is present.
One should wander the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves,
if one is to find even a single person who understands the syllables of the *sāman* chants for the sake of the ancestors.
"The father is satisfied by the *ṛc*, the grandfather by the *yajus*, and the great-grandfather by the *sāman*; the *chandoga* is even more [satisfied] than that. Thus says Śātātapa as well.
"He who feeds one learned in the Atharva Veda at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors—his fruit is indeed infinite and imperishable; such is the sacred revelation."
[339] Thus it is said. Yama also says:

"Those who have bathed after completing their Vedic studies and vows, who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and have mastered them, who are devoted to their own duty, peaceful, perform their ritual acts, and are ascetics."
"To them, when they are pleased, offerings to the gods (*havya*) and offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*) are presented. So too says Manu:
"Offerings to the gods and offerings to the ancestors must be given by donors only to one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*)."
That which is given to such a Brahmin who has attained Arhatship yields great fruit.
"One should feed even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or the ancestors;
one obtains abundant fruit [thereby], but not even from many who are ignorant of the mantras" (MDh 3.128–29).
Vasiṣṭha also says: "Ascetics or virtuous householders"—the word "should feed" is to be supplied. Also in the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*:

"One should cause [the food] to be given to the *śikhins*, to those dyed with minerals (*dhāturakta*), and to the *tridaṇḍins*. Here, *śikhins* are celibate students (*brahmacārin*). Those "dyed with minerals" are forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) who wear garments dyed with mineral pigments. *Tridaṇḍins* are ascetics (*yatayaḥ*) endowed with the three restraints (*daṇḍa*) of speech, body, and mind. Among these, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"He who, disregarding ascetics, should feed other twice-born [Brahmins]..."
"Knowing this, that which is offered in a village inhabited by such people goes to the Rākṣasas.
Also, in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"In the absence of meditating mendicants, one should feed a celibate student (*brahmacārin*)."
Even if these are not available, one should feed a neutral householder as well. Thus it is said.

For one who is indifferent is indeed unrelated. Therefore, Āpastamba says: “One should feed Brāhmaṇas who know the Veda, provided they are not related by birth, lineage, mantra, or pupilage” (ĀpDh 2.7.17.4). Those related by birth are maternal uncles and the like; those related by lineage are *sapiṇḍa* relatives; those related by mantra are Vedic teachers and the like; and those related by pupilage are students, teachers, and sub-instructors. The meaning is that one should feed Brāhmaṇas such as householders and others who are distinct from these types of relations. He also states that in a *śrāddha*, those such as those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) are distinguished recipients because they purify the row (*paṅktipāvana*).
Learn in full about those foremost of the twice-born who purify the row defiled by those unworthy of the company—
those best of the twice-born who are purifiers of the assembly.
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions of scripture,
and who are born of a lineage of Vedic scholars, should be known as the purifiers of the assembly.
One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas,
one whose lineage is descended from a daughter of a Brāhmaṇa, a Chāndoga, and one who sings the Jyeṣṭhasāman.

"One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, an expounder [of them], a celibate student (brahmacārī), a giver of a thousand, and one who has reached a hundred years of age—these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvana). Here, "born of a Brahma-gift" refers to the son of a woman wedded by the Brahma rite. "A giver of a thousand" means a giver of cows or gold. Yama also says:
Those who drink Soma, who are free from passion, knowers of dharma, and possessed of tranquil intellects;
those who observe vows, abide by their restraints, and approach their wives only during the proper season.
Even one who maintains the five fires, or one who studies the Yajurveda,
or a Bahvṛca (Rigvedin) who knows the Trisauparṇa, or one who knows the Trimadhu;
One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who is free from passion, a singer of the Chāndoga verses, a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāman,
and a student of the Atharvaśiras— all these are purifiers of the company at a meal.
Even a child who maintains the sacred fire, who is learned in logic, who knows the six Vedāṅgas,
who understands the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, and who is a reciter of the Dharma;
The son of one to whom a Brahman-gift was given, pure in disposition, a giver of thousands,
one who observes the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, truthful in speech, and a knower of the Purāṇas.
He was proficient in all branches of knowledge, tranquil, and free from impurity;
he was devoted to the worship of his guru, the Vedas, and the sacred fire, and was intent upon the pursuit of wisdom.
The wise one, ever liberated, having become Brahman, is the best of the twice-born;
he has no enemies and is not an enemy, for he is friendly and a knower of the Self.
A Snātaka should be constantly devoted to silent recitation, always fond of flowers and offerings;
he should be upright, gentle, patient, self-controlled, tranquil, firm in his vow of truth, and pure.
One who knows the Vedas, one who knows all the scriptures, one devoted to fasting,
a householder, a celibate student, and likewise one who is a knower of the four Vedas.

"Brahmins who have performed the ritual bath (*snāna*) after completing their Vedic studies and vows are purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*). Thus says Paiṭhīnasi: "Now, therefore, follow those who are purifiers of the assembly: one who has mastered the *Nāciketa* fire-altar, one who knows the three *Madhu* verses, one who knows the three *Suparṇa* verses, one who has fulfilled his vows, a Chāndoga (Sāmavedin), a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, one born in the lineage of a daughter given in marriage for religious purposes (*brahmadeyā*), one who has studied a thousand [verses] of the Veda, a knower of the four Vedas, one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one who studies the *Atharvaśiras*, one who maintains the five sacred fires (*pañcāgni*), and one who recites the Veda (*vedajapin*). Each one of these purifies the assembly, even if it is defiled by thousands [of other faults], when he is appointed to the head of the row."
Śaṅkha also says:
"Those who are descended from a *brahmadeya* grant, those who do not withhold a *brahmadeya* grant,
and those who are the masters of a *brahmadeya* grant— these Brahmins are purifiers of the assembly."
Those Brahmins who have mastered the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda, those who have also mastered the Sāmaveda, and those who study the Atharvaśiras— these are the purifiers of the assembly.

“The wise ascetic who is constantly devoted to yoga, for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal, who is habituated to meditation, is a learned Brāhmaṇa who purifies the row. (Śaṅkha Smṛti 13.6–8) Baudhāyana also says: “Those who know the *Trimadhu*, the *Triṇāciketa*, and the *Trisuparṇa*; those who maintain the five fires; those who know the six Vedāṅgas; those who know the *Triśīrṣaka*; and those who sing the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*—these are the purifiers of the row. (BDh 2.8.14.2) Hārīta also says:

Stability, being born of a lineage that has not mixed with those outside the Vedic tradition, and possessing ancestral descent (*ārṣeya*)—these are the qualities of family (*kulaguṇa*). The Veda, its auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*), the Dharma, knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātmavittva*), realized insight (*vijñāna*), and traditional memory (*smṛti*)—this is the sixfold sacred learning (*śruta*). Devotion to Brahmins, devotion to the gods and ancestors, equanimity, gentleness, not causing distress to others, lack of envy, absence of arrogance, freedom from harshness, friendliness, pleasant speech, gratitude, providing refuge, and tranquility—this is the thirteenfold character (*śīla*).
Forbearance, self-restraint, compassion, generosity, non-violence, and honoring the guru.
Purity, bathing, recitation, burnt offerings, austerity, and likewise the study of sacred texts.

"Truthfulness, contentment, firmness in vows, and the observance of minor vows—this is conduct (*vṛtta*) consisting of sixteen qualities. Therefore, those who are of noble birth, learned, possessed of good character, established in conduct, truthful, free from physical defects, and worthy of the *pāṅkteya* [invitation], as well as those who have studied the two Vedas on both sides, who have mastered the *triṇāciketa*, the *trisuparṇa*, the *trimadhu*, and the *triśīrṣaka*, who chant the *jyeṣṭhasāman*, who maintain the five fires, who know the six Vedāṅgas, who recite the *rudra-jāpya*, who are chaste (*ūrdhvaretas*), who approach their wives only during the proper season, and who know the reality (*tattva*)—these are the purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*). (Hārīta Smṛti 13.15–22)

"Stability" (*sthiti*) means the state of an uninterrupted continuity, that is, the state of having an uninterrupted experience of the Veda. Here, the word *vedi*—which denotes a specific location for placing the sacrificial oblation (*havis*)—indicates by implication (*lakṣaṇā*) the sacrifice (*yāga*) accomplished by that oblation. "Being of noble lineage" (*ārṣeyatva*) means being a knower of the sages who preside over one's ancestral line (*pravara*). "Dharma" refers to the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*). "Vijñāna" is proficiency in specialized sciences such as Vaiśeṣika and others. "Smṛti" is the non-forgetting of the Vedas and the śāstras. "The state of observing minor vows" (*upavratatva*) is the practice of eating only once a day (*ekabhakta*) on the tenth lunar day and other such occasions. An alternative rule (*anukalpa*) regarding this has been shown by Yājñavalkya: "A sister’s son, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a son-in-law, a sacrificer, a father-in-law, and a maternal uncle..."
"Those who have performed the Triṇāciketa rite, a daughter's son, a disciple, a relative by marriage, and kinsmen. (YDh 1.220).
For this very reason, Manu says:
"This should be known as a secondary rule (anukalpa), which has always been practiced by the virtuous."
One's maternal grandfather, maternal uncle, sister's son, father-in-law, and teacher.
"One should feed a daughter's son, the husband of a female Vaiśya, a kinsman, an officiating priest, and one for whom one performs sacrifices. (MDh 3.147–48)

The husband of a sister-in-law (*viṭpati*), a son-in-law, or a guest [is eligible]. As it was stated by Devasvāmin: “Others say that the husband of a sister-in-law or a guest [is meant]. Āpastamba also says: “In the absence of those possessing [excellent] qualities, even a uterine brother (*sodarya*) should be fed. By this, students (*antevāsinaḥ*) are explained. (ĀpDh 2.6.17.5–6). Baudhāyana also says: “In his absence, one who knows the secret doctrines (*rahasyavid*). The greatness of the *śrāddha* consists of the *ṛc*, *yajus*, and *sāman* verses; therefore, one should feed such a person even if he is a *sapiṇḍa*. (BDh 2.8.14.3–4). Also in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:

"One should honor with offerings to the gods (havya) and to the ancestors (kavya) the paternal uncle, the preceptor, the daughter's son, the officiating priest, the sister's son, the maternal uncle, the elders, guests, and kinsmen.

In this context, the officiating priest, the paternal uncle, and the uterine sapinda relatives are to be appointed in the place of the Viśvedevas; they are not to be placed in the position of the father and other ancestors. Thus says Atri:
A father, a grandfather, a brother, or a son who is a sapinda—these are not to offer arghya to one another; likewise, officiating priests are not to perform the śrāddha for each other.
"For these—officiating priests, sons, and so forth—are Brāhmaṇas of the same lineage;

they should be appointed at the Vaiśvadeva rite if they are more distinguished by their qualities. Thus, the student (*śiṣya*) is also included in the very place of the Vaiśvadeva, because Āpastamba extends the rule to the student by stating regarding the matter prescribed for a uterine brother: "By this, the resident pupils (*antevāsinaḥ*) are explained" (ĀpDh 2.7.17.6). As for the alternative procedure mentioned by Manu:
"One may, at will, honor a friend at a *śrāddha*, even if he is not worthy, but never an enemy;

for an oblation consumed by one who hates [the giver] becomes fruitless after death" (MDh 3.144). This [statement] does not intend to prescribe a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) directly; rather, it intends a secondary alternative to a secondary alternative, because [the author], having himself prohibited a friend with the words "one should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*" (MDh 3.144), subsequently permits that very friend with regretful words, saying "one may, at will, honor him. Vasiṣṭha also speaks of a secondary alternative to a secondary alternative.

"Kindness is the supreme dharma; whatever is given to one who asks should be given. But even to those who do not ask and are perishing, one should invite [them] by every possible means. Thus it is said.

Compassion (*ānṛśaṃsya*) is the supreme dharma. Therefore, one should invite those who do not beg—that is, those whose nature is not to ask—and who, for that very reason, are content even if they lack qualities, by using such means as will cause them to accept the invitation, provided there is no possibility of those who possess qualities serving as secondary alternatives (*anukalpa*). The meaning is that in the absence of those whose nature is not to beg, giving to one who begs—even if he lacks qualities—also constitutes a secondary alternative. When the primary alternative (*mukhyakalpa*) is possible, the secondary alternative should not be practiced. Thus says Manu:
"The master of the primary rule who acts according to a secondary rule—no fruit pertaining to the hereafter exists for that person of evil intellect. (MDh 11.30).
"Pertaining to the hereafter" means the fruit such as heaven and so forth belonging to a subsequent time. Also, in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*:
"There is no transgression against a Brāhmaṇa who is a fool and devoid of Vedic knowledge;
for one does not offer oblations into ashes while setting aside a blazing fire.
The phrase "devoid of Vedic knowledge" is intended as an indication of one who possesses no qualities whatsoever. For this very reason, it is stated in that same work:
There is never any fault in transgressing [the rules] regarding one who is devoid of merit;
however, for one whose fool is in his own house while a virtuous man remains far away, there is indeed a fault.
"It should be given to one endowed with virtues; there is no exception in the case of a fool.
As for that which has been stated in another Purāṇa:
"But he who, bypassing a Brāhmaṇa standing nearby—provided he is not an outcast (patita)—[gives to another, incurs sin]."
A fool who feeds one who is far away while neglecting a person nearby who is rich in virtues shall go to hell.
Therefore, one should honor him and contemplate his virtues;
O bird, one should consider only his birth, not his possession of virtues.
[348] But he who [neglects] a twice-born man who is nearby— one of noble birth, pleasant of speech,
whether a fool or a scholar, or even one destitute of livelihood— [commits a sin].
"A wise man should not likewise bypass one who is afflicted by poverty"—this refers to the daughter's son (*dauhitra*), the son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*), and others. For this very reason, Manu says:
"One should diligently feed even a daughter's son at a *śrāddha*, even if he is engaged in a religious vow" (MDh 3.234).

"Established in a vow" means established solely in a vow, that is to say, devoid of Vedic study and so forth. However, there is indeed a transgression if one bypasses those who are endowed with virtues and are nearby. And thus says the Purāṇa:
"O bird, by bypassing seven ancestors, seven descendants, and himself—these best of the twice-born—one would cause them to fall into hell."
Therefore, a wise man should not neglect his neighboring Brahmins,
nor any of his relatives, nor his daughter's son, nor the husband of his sister.
O Lord of Birds, O Lord of Cows, a man should especially not neglect his sister’s son, nor likewise his kinsman; even a wise man should not transgress against these.
"Having bypassed [the wise], one would go to the most terrible Raurava hell.

Here, the particle *api* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*. The intended meaning is: "Only by bypassing those who are not fools (the wise) would one go to hell; not by bypassing fools. The Brahmins who are to be avoided at a *śrāddha* have been shown by Yājñavalkya:
"One who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is one-eyed, and likewise one born of a remarried woman..."
One who has spilled his seed, one born from a vessel or a horn, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth.
One who teaches for wages, a eunuch, a defiler of virgins, one accused of a grave crime, a betrayer of friends, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, and a gambler; [349]

"One who abandons mother, father, or teacher; one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*; the son of a *vṛṣala*; the husband of a woman previously married to another; a thief; and one corrupt in action—these are censured. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.222–24)

A "sick person" (*rogī*) is one afflicted by sinful diseases such as insanity (*unmāda*). These have been shown by Devala: "Insanity, skin disease, consumption (*rājayakṣmā*), asthma, diabetes (*madhumeha*), fistula-in-ano (*bhagandara*), abdominal enlargement (*mahodara*), and urinary stones (*aśmarī*)—these are the eight sinful diseases. One whose limbs (*aṅga*) are deficient (*hīna*) or redundant (*atirikta*) is "one with deficient or redundant limbs" (*hīnātiriktāṅga*). One who does not see even with one eye is "one-eyed" (*kāṇa*); by this term, the deaf, the mute, and others are indicated. A "remarried woman" (*punarbhū*) is one who has married again; one born of her is a "paunarbhava. An "avakīrṇin" is one who has broken his vows. One who teaches for wages is a "paid teacher" (*bhṛtakādhyāpaka*). One who defiles a maiden with a false or true blemish is a "defiler of maidens" (*kanyādūṣī*). One accused of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) is an "accused person" (*abhiśastaka*). A "parivindaka" is a younger brother who marries before his elder brother. One who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* is a "consumer of a *kuṇḍa*'s food" (*kuṇḍāśī*); the word *kuṇḍa* also indicates a *golaka*. One who abandons prescribed duties is a "vṛṣala"; his son is a "son of a vṛṣala" (*vṛṣalātmaja*). The husband of a remarried woman is a "husband of one previously married to another" (*parapūrvāpati*). One who takes what is not given is a "thief" (*stena*). Those "corrupt in action" (*karmaduṣṭa*) are those possessed of conduct contrary to the scriptures. The meaning is that these are censured and must be excluded from the *śrāddha*. Manu also [says]:
[350] Those who are thieves, outcasts, or eunuchs, and those who follow the lifestyle of nihilists—
Manu has declared that such Brahmins are unworthy of offerings made to the gods or the ancestors.
One should not feed at a śrāddha those who have matted hair but do not study, nor those with shaggy hair, nor gamblers, nor those who officiate as priests for groups of people.
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers,
and those who live by trade— these should be avoided at offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
A servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth,
one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer;

One afflicted by consumption, a cattle-herder, one who marries before his elder brother, one who has been expelled from his caste, a hater of Brahmins, an elder brother whose younger brother has married before him, and one who belongs to a religious guild.
One who is of bad character, one who has broken his vow of chastity, the husband of a low-caste woman, the son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house a paramour resides.
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught for a fee,
one whose pupil is a Śūdra, one who is a teacher of a Śūdra, one who is corrupt in speech, and a Kuṇḍa and a Golaka.
One who has abandoned his mother, father, or teacher without cause;
and one who has entered into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial alliances.
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats from a vessel made of a skull, a seller of Soma,
one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger;
One who quarrels with his father, one who squints, and likewise a drunkard;
a squint is one whose gaze is oblique.
[351] One afflicted by a foul disease, one who is falsely accused, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids (or flavors).

One who makes bows and arrows, one who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried, a betrayer of friends, one who lives by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher to his own son.
One suffering from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one with leucoderma, as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and likewise a reviler of the Vedas— these should be avoided.
One who trains elephants, horses, or camels; one who lives by the stars;
one who raises birds; and likewise a teacher of warfare.
One who diverts watercourses, one who delights in obstructing them,
a builder of houses, a messenger, and likewise a planter of trees.
One who sports with dogs, one who lives by hawks, one who defiles a maiden, one who is cruel, one who subsists on the service of Śūdras, and one who performs sacrifices for groups (of people).
One devoid of proper conduct, a eunuch, one who is constantly a beggar,
one who lives by agriculture, and one who lives by a craft— all these are indeed censured by the virtuous.
A sheep-slaughterer, a buffalo-herder, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and one who carries out the dead— these must be avoided with great effort.

"A learned man who is the best among the twice-born should avoid these lowest of the twice-born, whose conduct is censurable and who are unworthy of sitting in the same row, in both [contexts]. (MDh 3.150–67)

In this context, the "thief" (stena) is intended to be one who steals property other than that belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, because one who steals such property is already included under the term "outcast" (patita). "Atheists" (nāstika) are those who believe that there is no action that yields results in the next world; "those who live by the livelihood of atheists" (nāstikavṛtti) are those whose means of subsistence depends upon them. A "jaṭila" is a religious student (brahmacārin). The term "not studying" (anadhīyānaḥ) is an epithet qualifying the *jaṭila*. Consequently, it is the religious student who does not study who is prohibited here, and not the religious student in general, for the latter is prescribed as a worthy recipient at a *śrāddha* rite in the rule: "The five fires and the religious student.
