[The text concludes with: "But all that is cooked on a fire is pure, O best of Brahmins, even if it is stale; there is no prohibition against it. [The text continues with: "However, one must avoid meat, fish, and vegetables that have turned sour, as well as those that are naturally sour, and all that is cooked on a fire if it has been left overnight. [The text concludes with: "But all that is cooked on a fire is pure, O best of Brahmins, even if it is stale; there is no prohibition against it. [The text continues with: "However, one must avoid meat, fish, and vegetables that have turned sour, as well as those that are naturally sour, and all that is cooked on a fire if it has been left overnight. [The text concludes with: "But all that is cooked on a fire is pure, O best of Brahmins, even if it is stale; there is no prohibition

"Excessively sour *śukta* is declared by the exponents of Brahman to be censurable. Thus, *śukta* is that substance which is not sour or only slightly sour, but becomes excessively sour after a lapse of time or through contact with another substance; it is not that which is naturally excessively sour. That which has been cooked over fire and kept overnight is called *paryuṣita*. The prohibition regarding *śukta* applies to cases other than curd and the like. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:
"Curd is fit for consumption among sour things, as is everything produced from curd."

"It is the established rule that food cooked on *ṛjīṣa* should be eaten with clarified butter. Thus it is said. *Ṛjīṣa* is heat without fire; [food] cooked by that is [permissible]. Sours or stale foods, when washed, may be eaten in times of distress. Regarding this, Yama says:
"A twice-born man should never eat sours as food."
They shall be washed and rendered free from defects, in accordance with the law for times of distress.
"Having washed lentils and black gram that have been combined [with other grains], as well as those that have become stale, one should indeed eat them after they have been sprinkled with water.
One should also not eat food that is corrupted by its source; and so says Yājñavalkya:
[The food] of misers, bound thieves, eunuchs, actors,
flute-players, those accused of crimes, usurers, courtesans, and those initiated into a guild;
[One should not accept gifts] from physicians, the sick, the angry, unchaste women, the intoxicated, and enemies;
nor from the cruel, the fierce, the outcaste, the vrātya, the hypocritical, or those who eat the remnants of others' food.
[The impurity lasts for one day] for those whose wives have no heroic husbands, for goldsmiths, for those who conquer their wives,
for village-priests, for sellers of weapons, for blacksmiths, for weavers, and for those who subsist by keeping dogs.
"[The food of] a cruel man, a king, a dyer, an ungrateful person, one who lives by slaughter, a washerman, a liquor-seller, and one who lives with a paramour in the same house" (YDh 1.161–65).
Here, *kadarya* means a greedy person. And likewise, another Smṛti states:
"He who, out of greed, causes suffering to himself, his religious duties, his children, his wife, and his parents and dependents—he is known as a miser (kadarya). Thus it is said.

"Bound" means fettered with chains. "Stage-player" refers to an actor. "Lute-player" refers to one who subsists by playing the lute. "Initiated" refers to one who has undergone the consecratory rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*); and for such a person, food is not to be eaten until the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal sacrificed to Agni and Soma is completed, according to the Vedic injunction: "As long as the sacrifice to Agni and Soma is not concluded, one must not eat in the house of the sacrificer. "Afflicted" means seized by a sinful disease. "Angry" means harboring intense internal resentment. "Intoxicated" means arrogant due to wealth and the like. "Cruel" means merciless. "Fierce" means one who inflicts suffering upon others. "Washer" refers to one who dyes clothes; "clothes-washer" refers to one who cleans clothes. The meaning is that the food of these individuals—beginning with the miserly and ending with the seller of *soma*, all of whom belong to the three higher castes—is not to be consumed. Yama also says:
One who lives by the wheel, a musician, a gambler, a thief,
a standard-bearer, one who lives off his wife, and those who teach or perform sacrifices for Śūdras.
"A potter, a painter, a usurer, and a seller of leather.

Here, "one who lives by wheels" means one who lives by carts; "a Gāndharva" means a singer; "a flag-bearer" means a seller of liquor; the others are well known. The meaning is that these are persons whose food should not be eaten. Āpastamba also says: "Only two of those in the stages of life (āśrama) are fit to be fed: the student and likewise the householder."
"The food of a *muni* shall be unfit for consumption, as shall that of all those who bear sectarian marks (*liṅgin*).
By the word *muni*, the ascetic (*yati*) and the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) are understood; "those who bear marks" refers to the Pāśupatas and others. Aṅgiras also says:
"The twice-born who eats the censured food of a Śūdra for six months..."
"While living he shall become a Śūdra, and upon death he is reborn as a dog. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 48).
As for that which was stated by Sumantu: "Milk products, barley meal, oil, and even oil-cake..."
One should eat cakes, O hero, and whatever else is prepared with milk.
Thus, as for that which is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"A Brahmin may accept the food of a Śūdra that has come to his house after sprinkling it with water," that refers to a situation of distress (āpad). For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"One should not eat the food of one who has abandoned the sacred fires, except in times of distress"—thus it is said. (YDh 1.160) "One who has abandoned the sacred fires" refers to a Śūdra.
Now, regarding meats that are to be avoided and those that are not, Manu states what among meats is to be avoided:
"All carnivorous birds, as well as those that dwell in villages."
One should also avoid single-hoofed animals that have not been specifically permitted, as well as the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird.
The kalaviṅka, the plava, the haṃsa, the cakrāhva, the village cock,
the sārasa, the rajjuvāla, the dātyūha, the parrot, and the maina.
Pecking birds, web-footed birds, the koyaṣṭi, birds that scratch with their claws, fish-eating aquatic birds, dog meat, and dried meat.
"The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail, fish-eaters, village pigs, and all kinds of fish" (MDh 5.11–14).

Carnivorous birds are vultures and the like. Village-dwelling birds are pigeons and the like. Unspecified refers to wild animals and birds whose specific species are unknown. Single-hoofed animals are horses and the like. The *ṭiṭṭibha* is a specific bird that utters harsh sounds. The *kalaviṅka* is the sparrow. The *plava* is the water-fowl (*jalakukkuṭa*). The *cakrāhva* is the ruddy sheldrake (*cakravāka*). The *sārasa* is the crane (*puṣkarāhva*). The *rajjuvālaka* is one whose tail resembles a rope. The *dātyūha* is the gallinule (*kālakaṇṭaka*). The *pratuda* is the hawk. The *jālapāda* is one whose feet have a web-like appearance. The *koyaṣṭi* is a specific bird. *Nakhaviṣkirās* are the chakora and other such birds. "Diving" refers to those who eat fish by diving; these are specific types of birds that consume fish after submerging themselves. *Śauna* is meat derived from a dog. *Vallūra* is dried meat. The *kākola* is the mountain crow. The *khañjarīṭa* is the wagtail (*khañjana*). By "fish-eaters," those who eat fish without diving are intended. *Viḍvarāhas* are village pigs. [388] Here, the prohibition regarding fish applies to species other than the *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍaka*, and so forth. For this very reason, it was stated by that same author:
"Rājīvas, siṃhatuṇḍas, and saśalkas in all respects.

(MDh 5.16) *Rājīvas* are fish with the color of a lotus; *siṃhatuṇḍas* are those with lion-like faces; *saśalkas* are those that possess scales—parts shaped like oyster shells—on their backs. The meaning is that these are all edible at a *śrāddha* ceremony as well as in one's daily meals. Devala also says: "The osprey, the *kurara*, the hawk, the vulture, the cock, and the crow..."
The cakora, the cuckoo, the rajjudālaka, the blue jay, and the water-fowl;
The pigeon and the dove are recorded as birds that are not to be eaten;
among the species of animals, the cow, the donkey, the camel, the horse, and the elephant are not to be eaten.
Lions, tigers, bears, and śarabhas; likewise, snakes and pythons;
as well as rats, mice, cats, mongooses, and village pigs.

"Dogs, jackals, wolves, leopards, baboons, and monkeys. Here, *kurara* means the osprey; *madgura* means the water-crow; the word *dvīpin* refers to a specific type of tiger; and *golāṅgūla* is a specific type of monkey. The mention of "monkeys" (*markaṭa*) is intended as an illustration for all five-toed animals (*pañcanakha*). For this very reason, Manu says: "Likewise, all five-toed animals" (MDh 5.47). The construction is "one should not eat [them]. In this context, the prohibition against eating five-toed animals applies to those other than the group of five beginning with the monitor lizard (*godhā*). Thus says Devala:
"Five five-nailed animals are declared by dharma to be edible; they are traditionally remembered as the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the hare, the porcupine, and the hedgehog. Thus [it is said].

The meaning of "the nature of things" (*dharmatā*) is that those [animals] obtained through purchase and so forth are to be eaten provided no violence has been committed. Nor is this an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), because the eating of them is already prompted by worldly desire. Nor is it a restrictive rule (*niyama*), because there is no possibility of its being otherwise. Therefore, only an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) remains: that those other than the five-clawed group of five—such as the monitor lizard and others—are not to be eaten. This being the case, by the force of this specific prohibition, it is understood that there is sin in eating their meat and not in eating others'. For this very reason, Manu said: "There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse."
"This is the way of beings; but abstention bears great fruit" (MDh 5.56).
For he himself has said:
"Meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings."
And the killing of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should avoid meat.
"Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and binding of embodied beings, one should desist from eating all kinds of meat. (MDh 5.48–49).
And as it has also been stated by Yājñavalkya:
"An evil-doer who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rule shall dwell in hell for as many days as there are hairs on the animal's body, like a thief. (YDh 1.180).

This refers to the consumption of meat preceded by the killing of living beings which is prohibited; it does not refer to the consumption of meat obtained through purchase and other such means, because the Smṛti texts enjoin the prohibition of meat specifically by way of censuring the slaughter of living beings. And as for that which was stated by Manu himself:
"By eating pure fruits and roots, and by consuming the food of sages, one does not obtain that fruit which is obtained from the total avoidance of meat" (MDh 5.54).

In this regard, the fact that the avoidance of meat is a means for attaining great fruit applies to cases other than those involving consecrated meat (prokṣita) and so forth. For this very reason, it was stated by that same author:

"One may eat meat that has been consecrated (*prokṣita*), or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas, or when enjoined according to the rule, or indeed when there is a danger to life" (MDh 5.27). "Consecrated" means meat remaining from a sacrifice; "at the desire of Brāhmaṇas" means out of consideration for the wish of Brāhmaṇas; "enjoined according to the rule" means invited to a *śrāddha* ceremony; and "when there is a danger to life" means due to hunger or due to disease—one may eat meat. Enough of this digression.
Now, regarding what is to be given to the invited Brahmins— namely, that which is to be given to those invited— Kātyāyana says: "Oil, anointment, bathing, and likewise the cleansing of the teeth."
"But on the following day, one should give to those whose hair and nails have been trimmed.

This means that one should provide the bath and the materials for bathing, as well as the tooth-stick and other implements for cleaning the teeth. This gift of oil and so forth pertains to occasions when the lunar days (*tithis*) are not prohibited. On prohibited lunar days, however, one should offer *āmalaka* fruit water as a substitute for sesame oil. Thus says Mārkaṇḍeya:
"When six *muhūrtas* of the day have passed, then [one should invite] those twice-born ones..."
"One should send messengers one by one, having given them water infused with *āmalaka* fruits.

This provision for giving *āmalaka* water also pertains to occasions other than the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), because another *smṛti* text prohibits bathing with *dhātrī* fruits on the new moon day: "One should not bathe with *dhātrī* fruits on the new moon day. A specific rule regarding the giving of oil and other items has been shown by Devala:
"Oil, unguents, bathing water, and various kinds of bath-powders..."
"One should give [the offerings] with vessels made of udumbara wood, beginning with those for the Viśvedevas.
In this context, "audumbara" refers to a copper vessel. As for that which was stated by Pracetas:
"One who eats at a śrāddha should not have his nails or beard cut."
Thus it is said; this refers to the prohibited lunar days. The materials to be prepared at the site of the *śrāddha* are declared in the *Purāṇa*:
"One should prepare there *kuśa* grasses with their roots intact and reaching to the base, barley, sesame seeds, seats (*bṛsī*), a bronze vessel, and water collected by pure persons."
"The vessels should be made of leaves, silver, or copper; there should be fuel-sticks, honey, flowers, incense, fragrant substances, and so forth, as well as a linen thread and a stirring-ladle.

Regarding this, *jarttila* sesame seeds are to be taken; in their absence, cultivated (*grāmya*) ones may be used. The definition of *jarttila* has been stated by Satyavrata: "Those which are black, small, and have a pungent taste are called *jarttila*. [Note: The original text contains a lacuna regarding the description of the *mekṣaṇa* (stirring-ladle), which is traditionally understood to be made of wood.]
"Jartila seeds are said to be black sesame growing wild in the forest.
Regarding their excellence, Āpastamba says:
"Those which have grown in the wilderness, as well as those produced without cultivation..."
"Indeed, sesame seeds are purifiers at a *śrāddha*; they are remembered as *jartila* [sesame].

For the purpose of seating the invited Brahmins, there is a seat (*āsana*) consisting of a grass mat (*bṛsī*). Regarding this, a specific rule has been stated by Manu: "One should provide a *kutapa* as a seat" (MDh 3.34). A *kutapa* is a woolen blanket (*kambala*) made from the hair of sheep and other animals originating from the country of Nepal. This is stated in another *smṛti*: "Midday, a sword-vessel, and likewise a Nepalese blanket..."
Silver, darbha grass, sesame seeds, cows, and the daughter's son is recorded as the eighth.

"They say that *pāpa* means 'contemptible'; because these eight cause torment (*tāpa*) for such [a person], they are therefore renowned as *kutapa*s. Vessels made of bell-metal, wood, silver, and copper should be prepared for the purpose of eating and for the *arghya* offering. In this context, however, only vessels made of *palāśa* leaves should be prepared for eating, and not vessels made of other leaves. Thus says Atri:
"One should not use vessels made of clay for the meals offered to the gods and the ancestors;
however, there should be no leaf-vessels for the meal except those made of *palāśa* leaves. Thus it is said.
For the purpose of the *arghya* offering, other leaf-vessels are not prohibited. Therefore, Baijavāpa says:
In the rite of Śrāddha, the vessels for the Arghya offering may be made of Khadira or Udumbara wood, or they may even be made of stone or clay; likewise, leaf-cups may also be used.
[393] Thus it is said. Regarding the flowers to be prepared for this occasion, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* shows them as follows:
"White *sumanas* flowers are best, as are lotuses and water-lilies (*utpala*), and whatever others there may be, provided they are endowed with fragrance and beauty. Thus it is said.
Also in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"All varieties of jasmine, white pūthikā flowers, all water-born blossoms, and the campaka should be offered."

As for that which was stated by the descendant of Aṅgiras: "Neither *jātī* flowers nor plantain leaves [are suitable]," Kratu also said: "The *jātī* flower was born in the lineage of the Asuras during the primordial creation;
by the mere sight of it, the ancestors departed in despair."

Thus, in this context, the prohibition of *jātī* flowers is optional. Regarding that, the flowers to be avoided have been stated by Matsya: "The lotus (*padma*), the *bilva*, the *arka*, the *dhattūra*, the *pāribhadra*, and the *aṭarūṣaka*—these should not be offered in rites for the ancestors, nor should sheep's milk. (MatPu 15.37–38)

The *pāribhadra*, the *mandāra*, the *āṭarūṣa*, the *vāsaka*, and even the *śaṅkha*— flowers that are pungent-smelling, odorless, grown from trees at a *caitya*, and those that are red in color— should be avoided. (ŚaṅSm 13.14)

[394] Thus it is said. Here, the prohibition regarding red-colored flowers refers to those other than those produced in water. For this very reason, it was stated by that same author: "Those produced in water should be offered, especially even if they are red" (ŚaṅSm 13.15). Viṣṇu also says: "One should avoid flowers with a pungent odor, those without fragrance, and those born of thorny plants, even if they are red; one should offer white flowers that are fragrant, even if they are born of thorny plants" (ViDh 79.5–6). The substances for incense are also shown in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
"Incense should be offered, such as *guggulu*, as well as that produced from the heartwood of sandalwood;
likewise *agaru* with camphor, *turuṣka*, and cinnamon bark. (ViDhPu 2.141.14).
*Turuṣka* is the *śallakī* tree; *tvak* is the bark of the clove tree (*lavaṅga*). *Marīci* is also [to be included].

Regarding both sandalwood and agalloch, as well as *tamāla*, *uśīra*, and *padmaka*—thus Viṣṇu has stated that these are substances to be avoided for incense: "And everything produced from living beings is not for the purpose of incense" (ViDh 79.9). "Produced from living beings" refers to musk and the like. "Sandalwood, saffron, camphor, agalloch, and *padmaka* are for the purpose of anointing" (ViDh 79.11). Regarding the oily substance for the lamp, Marīci says:
"The lamp should be made from ghee or sesame oil, but not from any other substance."

And here, the prohibition of other substances refers to substances consisting of fat (*vasā*) and marrow (*medas*), but not to oils such as safflower oil (*kausumbha*). For this very reason, Śaṅkha says:
"A lamp should be offered with ghee, or else with the juices of other medicinal herbs;
one should carefully avoid a lamp produced from fat or marrow. (ŚaṅSm 13.16)
The provision of linen thread pertains to the case where cloth is unavailable. When possible, linen cloth should be provided. For this very reason, another Smṛti states:
"He who gives these at Śrāddhas—silk, linen, cotton, fine silk (dukūla), and unwashed cloth—attains abundant desires" (Vāyu Purāṇa 2.18.37).

*Kauśeya* is that which is produced from threads originating in the cocoon of silkworms. *Kṣauma* is that which arises from threads produced from the bark of the flax plant (*atasī*). *Dukūla* refers to fine cloth. *Ahata* is defined as follows:
"That which is slightly washed, new, white, with its fringes intact, and not yet worn—one should know that to be *ahata*, purifying in all rites. (396)

Alternatively, having prepared the materials beginning with the garment and ending with the *darbha* grass and the stirring-stick (*mekṣaṇa*), he should bathe and put on a white garment. Thus says the Smṛti:
"One who has bathed becomes entitled to perform rites for the gods and the ancestors."
"One who performs a *śrāddha* should wear white garments. Thus it is said.
Now, regarding what is to be done immediately after bathing, Yama says: "Then,
having bathed, one should rise with palms joined in reverence toward those who have returned."

"One should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) in due order. This means that, having said "Welcome" with palms joined in reverence, one should offer water for washing the feet and water for sipping in sequence, for the purpose of purifying the exhaustion caused by the journey. Immediately thereafter, two mandalas should be prepared in the courtyard of the house. And so says the Matsya Purāṇa: "... on the ground in front of the residence..."
"In a mandala smeared with cow dung and [prepared] with cow urine" (MatP 16.27–28).
The ellipsis to be supplied is that the mandala is to be made with cow urine mixed with cow dung. Regarding this, Śambhu states the specific detail:
"The northern side should slope toward the north, and the southern side should slope toward the south."

One should make the northern Vaiśvadeva circle slope toward the north, and the southern Pitrya circle slope toward the south. From the time of drawing the circles until the completion of the Śrāddha, the Vaiśvadeva rite must be performed clockwise by one wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*). The Pitrya rite must be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) and with the hands in the *apasavya* position. Thus says Manu:

"With the sacred thread over the right shoulder, properly in the *apasavya* manner, unwearied, and with *darbha* grass in hand, the Pitrya rite should be performed according to rule until its conclusion. (MDh 3.279)
Regarding this very point, Kātyāyana states another distinction:
"One should always cause the right knee to touch the ground when attending upon the gods; one should likewise cause the other knee to touch the ground when attending upon the ancestors. (KSm 1.2.5)
Śātātapa also says: "One should face north for the gods, but face south for the ancestors. Baudhāyana also says the same.
"The circumambulation for the gods is clockwise, while for the ancestors it is counter-clockwise;
for the gods, the *darbha* grass blades are straight, and for the ancestors, they are traditionally held to be doubled.
Thus [it is said]. Śambhu states what is to be done immediately after the drawing of the mandala:
In the north, the wise man should place unbroken kuśa grass with its tips pointing east; in the south, he should place kuśa grass with its tips pointing south, together with sesame seeds.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:

"Having worshipped that [liṅga] with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) together with flowers, while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), one should wash the feet of the Brahmins, saluting them again and again. (MatPu 16.28–29)

The meaning is that one should first worship the northern mandala with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), and afterwards worship the southern mandala. One should perform the washing of the feet for the Brahmins beginning with the deities. For this very reason, the *Brahmanirukta* states:
"One should first employ the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the water of honor (*arghya*) for the deities;
one should offer the water for the feet with the mantra 'śanno devī'."
The offering of water for the feet (*pādya*) and other items should be performed preceded by the utterance of the name and lineage (*gotra*). This is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"The name and lineage of the ancestors are the means by which they receive the offerings to gods (*havya*) and ancestors (*kavya*)" (MatPu 19.4).
Sumantu states what is to be done after the washing of the feet:
With darbha grass in hand, having sipped water twice, wearing light garments, and with his senses subdued,
he should sit in an enclosed, pure place smeared with cow dung.
On a site sloping toward the south, he should cause those who have properly sipped water, who are self-restrained and pure,
to sit upon separate seats provided with *darbha* grass.
[399] Thus. "In secluded places" means in places that are not in contact with one another. Manu also says:
"When separate seats covered with sacred grass have been prepared, he should cause those Brahmins, who have properly sipped water, to sit down. (MDh 3.208)

The manner of seating has been shown by Yama: "Touching the seat with his left hand and clasping the Brāhmaṇa with his right hand, and having said, 'Be seated,' he should cause him to sit. Also in the *Dharma* [text]:
"Then, touching the knees, having seated the gods and then the ancestors, he should cause them to sit upon their seats with all the *vyāhṛtis*. (ViDh 1.141.20)
In the Ādipurāṇa as well:
"One should first seat two Brahmins facing east before the others;
with the mantra 'śanno devī', one should cause the water for washing the feet (pādya) to be offered."
"Three Brahmins facing north [should always be seated] for the ancestors," so it is said. Yājñavalkya also states:
"Two for the gods facing east, three for the ancestors facing north, or even one for each."

"Regarding the maternal grandfathers as well, it is thus; or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). (YDh 1.228) The phrase "regarding the maternal grandfathers as well, it is thus" is an extension (*atideśa*) of the rules concerning number and direction. With the intention that the Vaiśvadeva rite—pertaining to the purpose of both types of *śrāddhas*—should be performed either by repetition or by a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), it is stated that "or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed by way of a single ritual procedure. For this very reason, Marīci says: "Likewise, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfathers is accompanied by the Vaiśvadeva."
"Or, endowed with devotion, one should perform the *tantra* ritual for the Viśvedevas.

Here, because the performance of the *vaiśvadevika* rite is prescribed as a *tantra* (common procedure) for both types of *śrāddha*, it follows that it is subject to both a single procedural injunction (*ekaprayogavidhi*) and distinct procedural injunctions (*bhinnaprayogavidhi*). Consequently, it is understood that it serves to accomplish the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of a single qualification (*ekādhikāra*) and the *apūrva* of distinct qualifications (*bhinnādhikāra*).
Now, the rules regarding the Brahmins:
The rules for Brahmins once seated are shown in another Smṛti:
"All of them, with sacred grass (pavitra) in their hands and observing a vow of silence,
should avoid touching one another who are defiled by the remains of food (ucchiṣṭa)."
And the state of silence refers to matters other than discourse concerning Brahman; for this very reason, Yama says:
"They should engage in discourses concerning Brahman, for this is desired by the ancestors."
Now, regarding the eligibility of ascetics (*yati*) and students (*brahmacārin*) to be fed:

even when the Brahmins have already been seated, if an ascetic or a student arrives, he too must be fed at the *śrāddha*. To this effect, Yama says: "A mendicant or a student who has arrived for the purpose of eating..."
When they have sat down, he should arrive and feed him as well, according to his desire.
Thus it is said. Chāgaleya also states:
"One should honor an ascetic and a celibate student even at the time of a Śrāddha;
such a person delivers from sin the Brahmins, as well as his ancestors and the host of his maternal kin."
Manu also says:
"A Brahmin or even a mendicant who has arrived for the purpose of a meal,
one should honor according to one's ability, with the permission of the Brahmins" (MDh 3.243).
Now, regarding the duties to be performed immediately after the Brahmins have been seated, it is stated in the Purāṇa:
"Having meditated upon Gayā at the site of the Śrāddha, and having meditated upon the Lord Gadādhara..."
"And having paid homage to those two, one should then proceed with the *śrāddha*.
This means that one should ask the seated Brahmins, "I shall perform the *śrāddha*. For this very reason, it is stated in that same [text]:
"Having placed both hands level, situated between the knees..."
"Having sat down with humility, he should question all those best of the twice-born.
Being permitted by them with the words "Do so," he should recite three times the mantra: "To the deities and to the ancestors... This is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"To the deities, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis..."
Salutation to Svadhā, salutation to Svāhā; let there be constant salutation, salutation indeed.
"One should always recite [the mantra] three times at the beginning and at the end of the *śrāddha*.

Immediately thereafter, one should scatter sesame seeds in all directions. This is stated in the *Nigama*: "One should scatter sesame seeds with [the mantra] 'apahatā asurāḥ'. Having scattered the sesame seeds, one should offer a seat of *darbha* grass. This is stated in the *Purāṇa*:
"Being told by them, 'Do so,' he should then offer a seat of *darbha* grass."
The offering of a seat of *darbha* grass should be performed by first pouring water into the hand of the Brahmin. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states:
"Having given water for washing the hands, one should also give *kuśa* grass for the purpose of a seat" (YDh 1.229).
The meaning is that one should place the *kuśa* grass intended for the seat upon the seats. This has been stated in the Purāṇa:
"One should offer a seat on the seat, either on the left or even on the right.

This option—either "on the left" or "even on the right"—is to be understood as being determined by the context of offering seats to Brahmins for the sake of the ancestors (*pitṛ*) or for the sake of the gods (*deva*). For this very reason, it is stated in that same [text]:
"In rites for the ancestors, indeed on the left; in rites for the gods, on the right."

Regarding the specific rule for offering seats during rites for the gods (*daiva-karma*), it is stated in the *Kāṭhaka*: "For the gods, the *darbha* grass is with barley. Having offered the seat, one should invite them again. On this, the author of the *Saṃgraha* says: "Then, having again offered water, one should invite them, saying: 'May the moment be made auspicious for the gods (*daive kṣaṇaḥ kriyatām*). Then the Brahmin should say: 'Om, so be it (*om tathā*). The performer should say again: 'May you receive [it] (*prāpnotu bhavān*). The Brahmin should reply again: 'I shall receive it (*prāpnuvāni*). And the invitation must be performed by taking the hand [of the guest] without the thumb. This is stated in the *Purāṇa*."
"Having taken [the hand] excluding the thumb, one should summon the Viśvedevas.
This means that, having grasped the hand with the thumb excluded and having invited them, one should summon the Viśvedevas. Yama states the procedure for the invocation:
"Then, with barley in his hand, he should inform the gods regarding the invocation."
Being authorized, one should invoke [the Viśvedevas] with the verse beginning "viśvedevāsaḥ."

"Having recited the mantra *viśvedevāḥ śṛṇuta*, one should then scatter unbroken rice grains (*akṣatān*) clockwise with the mantra *oṣadhayaḥ*. 'Clockwise' means that one should scatter—that is, place—the unbroken rice grains starting from the right foot up to the head. The ten Viśvedevas have been shown by Bṛhaspati as follows:
Kratu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kāla, and likewise Kāma; Dhuni and Rocana, and also Purūravas.
"And Ārdrava—these ten are proclaimed as the Viśvedevas.
Among them, the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava are to be invoked here, because this is a *pārvaṇa* śrāddha. For this very reason, Śaṅkha states:
"In the *iṣṭi* śrāddha, Kratu and Dakṣa are to be celebrated in the rite for the Viśvedevas."
Satyavasu [are the two] at the Nāndīmukha rite, and Dhuni and Rocana at the Kāmya rite.
"Purūravas and Ārdrava are declared for the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha]; for the *naimittika*, one should likewise recite Kāla and Kāma in all cases. Thus it is said.
The *iṣṭi-śrāddha* is the śrāddha that is an auxiliary part of a ritual (*karmāṅga-śrāddha*). And that has been demonstrated by Pāraskara.

"At the time of impregnation (*niṣeka*), during the *soma* ceremony, likewise at the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), and at the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the *śrāddha* should be known as a constituent part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*), performed like an occasion of prosperity (*vṛddhi*). By the phrase "like an occasion of prosperity," it is understood that the *śrāddha* as a constituent of the ritual is distinct from the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. The *nāndīmukha* is the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. Its nature is described by Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:

"The *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is prescribed for occasions such as the birth of a son and marriage. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), sacraments such as the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) and the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*) are included; however, the rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the male-impregnation rite (*puṃsavana*), and the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) are not included, because the *śrāddha* performed on those occasions is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the ritual itself. The *kāmya* [śrāddha] is that which is conditioned by the desire for a specific fruit. The *pārvaṇa* is the *śrāddha* performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). The *naimittika* is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Now, one might object:

"However, that *śrāddha* which is performed for a single person (*ekoddiṣṭa*) is called occasional (*naimittika*). Since the word "occasional" is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in reference to the *ekoddiṣṭa*, how can it be applied to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*? True; nevertheless, because of the statement "that too must be performed without [offerings to] the gods," the *ekoddiṣṭa* is devoid of the deities. Consequently, since there is no possibility of including the Viśvedevas known as Kāma and Kāla, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*—which is associated with the *ekoddiṣṭa*—is expressed by the term "occasional" through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Now, regarding the offering of the *arghya* and so forth:
having invoked the Viśvedevas, one should perform the placement of the *arghya* vessel and other rites. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"Then, having scattered barley grains into the vessel containing the *pavitra* grass..."
"Having sprinkled water with the mantra *śanno devīr*, one should likewise offer barley grains with the mantra *yavo ‘si*. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Having first offered a seat, one should worship the Viśvedevas with barley and flowers."
"One should fill a pair of vessels after placing *darbha* grass as a purifier. Thus [it is said]. Pracetas also says:
"One should pour the *arghya* water for each individual Brahmin into a vessel."

"Having recited 'Thou art barley' (yavo 'si) over the barley grains, [the vessel] should be well-honored with perfumes and flowers. Thus it is said. The *arghya* vessels are made of gold, silver, and so forth. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "In any one of the vessels made of gold, silver, udumbara wood, rhinoceros horn, or precious stones; or in whatever [vessels] are available; or even in leaf-cups. The meaning is: or in those made of metal, such as bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and the like. A silver vessel is employed for the ancestral rites (*pitrya*), but not for the divine rites (*daiva*). Regarding this, Matsya says concerning the silver vessel: "Since it was produced from the eye of Śiva, it is therefore dear to the ancestors."
"That which is inauspicious should be diligently avoided in rites for the gods. (MatPurāṇa 17.23).
An *arghya* offering and a purifier (*pavitraka*) should be prepared separately for each vessel. As it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"Having placed two sticks in each of the vessels for the gods, one should pour milk [into them]."
Regarding the procedure for the *pavitraka* (purificatory blades), Yogi-Yājñavalkya states:
"With the mantra 'You two are purifiers' (*pavitre sthaḥ*), one should prepare two *pavitra*s made of *kuśa* grass,
cut from within a clump of *darbha*, consisting of *kauśa* fibers, and measuring a span (*prādeśa*) in length."
"Kuśacchinna" means that which is cut after having placed a *kuśa* blade in between. For this very reason, Yajñapārśva says:
"Having placed a medicinal herb between the thumb and the finger, one should cut a *pavitra* of the measure of a span (*prādeśa*), dedicated to Viṣṇu."

"Not with a fingernail, nor with wood, nor with iron, nor from an earthen vessel. Immediately following this, one should place the *arghya* vessel near the Brahmins for the sake of the deity, using the mantra "Svāhārghyā. And so says Gārgya: "One should utter 'Svāhā' in the ritual of the *homa* for the gods."

It is understood from the context itself that when the rite of offering the *arghya* to the gods has arrived, one should recite the mantra “*svāhārghyā*” in order to set down the vessel. Having placed the *arghya* vessel, one should give the *arghya* into the hand of the Brahmin. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
“With the mantra ‘*yā divyāḥ*...’, one should pour the *arghya* into their hands.
(YDh 1.231). Gargya states a specific rule regarding the giving of the *arghya*:
"Having placed the *pavitra* in his hand and worshipped him, one should offer the *arghya*.

Here, the plural number in "in the hands" (*hasteṣu*) is not intended to be significant, as it must conform to the singular number used in the opening statement. Immediately after that, fragrances and other offerings should be given preceded by water. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"Having offered water, fragrance, garlands, incense, and a lamp... (YDh 1.231).

The offering of perfumes and so forth is also indicative of clothing (*ācchādana*), since the latter is included therein. Having thus performed the worship for the *vaiśvadeva* ancestors—beginning with the seat and ending with clothing—according to the method of sequential performance (*kāṇḍānusamaya*), one should perform the worship for the paternal ancestors, beginning with the seat and ending with clothing, while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) and moving counter-clockwise (*apradakṣiṇam*). Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, one should perform the rite for the ancestors counter-clockwise" (YDh 1.232).

Now, an objection is raised: in rites for the gods (*daiva*) and rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), it is logical that even the constituent items (*padārtha*), beginning with the seating and ending with the covering, should be performed according to the *padārthānusamaya* (item-by-item sequence), and not according to the *kāṇḍānusamaya* (section-by-section sequence). For in the *padārthānusamaya*, there is proximity to the principal act (*pradhāna*) for all those items, as well as uniformity; otherwise, a disparity would arise where some items have proximity to the principal act while others do not.

True. Regarding the items such as the seats and so forth, it is precisely the *kāṇḍānusamaya* (performance of all items for one recipient before moving to the next) that is accepted on the strength of the scriptural injunction. This scriptural basis is found because the ritual for the worship of the ancestors (*pitṛ-arcanavidhi*) is prescribed immediately after the section on the items for the Vaiśvadeva deities, beginning with the words: "Then, having placed [the offerings] in the apasavya manner. He himself describes the manner of giving the seats and other items:

"Having given double-folded *kuśa* grass together with the verse 'uśantas tvā,' and having invoked [the ancestors], being permitted by them, he should then recite: 'May they come to us' (*āyāntu naḥ*)."
The purposes served by barley should be performed with sesame seeds; one should perform the rites for the guest-offering (arghya) and so forth as previously described.

Having offered the *arghya* water and having placed their remnants in a vessel according to the rule, he turns the vessel face down below with the words, "Thou art the seat for the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ sthānam asi*). (YDh 1.233–35)

One should provide double-folded *kuśa* grass mixed with sesame seeds for the purpose of seats. As it is stated in the *Kāṭhaka*: “For the ancestors, [offer] double-folded [grass] with sesame. One should offer water both before and after the giving of the seats. Thus says Āśvalāyana: “Having offered water; having given the seat of double-folded *darbha* grass; having offered water” (*ĀśGṛ* 4.7.5–7). Having granted the invitation (*kṣaṇa*) as before by saying, “May the invitation be made for the *śrāddha*,” and having asked the Brahmins, “I shall invoke the ancestors,” and being permitted by them with the words, “Invoke [them],” one should invoke them with the mantra “*uśantas tvā*. Then, scattering sesame seeds from the head down to the right foot with the mantra “*namo vaḥ pitaraḥ*,” one should pay homage with the mantra “*āyāntu naḥ pitaraḥ*. Thus says Pracetas.
"From the head down to the feet, [one should recite] 'Obeisance to you' in the rite for the ancestors. Thus it is said.
The subsequent duty after the ritual attendance (upasthāna) is stated in the Purāṇa:
"One should properly and completely recite the mantra beginning with 'May they come to us' (āyāntu naḥ)."
For the sake of protecting the ancestral sacrifice, he went three times in every direction.
One should scatter sesame seeds while reciting the mantra beginning with "apahatāḥ."

[409] Thus. One should perform the rites from the *arghya* offering up to the covering of the vessels as previously described. Regarding the specific procedure for the placement of the *arghya* vessels and so forth, Viṣṇu has shown: "One should pour water into three *camasa* cups, which have their tips pointing south and are arranged ending toward the south, with the mantra *śanno devīr abhiṣṭaye*" (ViDh 73.12). This is the meaning: on *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, having placed three *camasa* cups—serving as *arghya* vessels—with purifiers (*pavitra*) placed inside them and arranged so that they end toward the south, one should pour water into each vessel individually with the mantra *śanno devīr abhiṣṭaye*. Śaunaka also says: "Having poured water into the vessels covered with *darbha*, he scatters sesame seeds over the water consecrated with the mantra *śanno devīr abhiṣṭaye*: 'Thou art sesame, whose deity is Soma; thou art created by the gods at the Gosava sacrifice. Offered by the ancients, do thou, through the *svadhā* offering, gratify these Pitṛs and these worlds for us; *svadhā*! Homage! And in this matter, whether there is an invitation of multiple Brahmins for each of the three ancestors—the father and the others—or even if all three ancestors are invited by a single Brahmin, there are exactly three *arghya* vessels, not according to the number of Brahmins. For this very reason, Baijavāpa says:

"Having strewn [the sesame seeds], the knower of dharma should prepare exactly three vessels for the ancestors, whether there be one or many Brāhmaṇas, according to the rule. The meaning of "having strewn" is having scattered sesame seeds into the water for the *arghya* offerings. And the *arghya-pavitra* (the purificatory ring) should be made in an odd number; this is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"In the *pārvaṇa* rite, there should be three sticks (*śalākā*) for each of the vessels of the ancestors.
[410] After scattering the sesame seeds, one should scatter perfumes and flowers. This is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Those [vessels] should be worshipped according to the scriptures with perfumes and flowers as the *arghya* offerings."

The meaning is that those waters which are worthy of the *arghya* offering should be honored with perfumes (*gandha*) and other such items. Śaunaka states what must be done immediately thereafter: “Intending to cause them to accept [the water], [he says] ‘Svadhā-arghya’. The meaning is that, intending to have the Brāhmaṇas accept those waters, he should set them down with the mantra “Svadhā-arghya. Then, after the *pavitra* blades have been placed [on the hands], he should offer the *arghya* water preceded by water with the mantra “yā divyā” (those divine...). And so Paiṭhīnasi says: “Then, having first given *darbha* grass into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas, preceded by water, he gives the *arghya* water preceded by water, saying ‘yā divyā... and ‘This is your *arghya* water, O So-and-so,’ and having touched water; he does exactly the same for the other two. Regarding this, Dharma states a specific rule: “Having lifted the vessel with both hands with the words ‘yā divyā āpaḥ,’ and having taken up the name and *gotra*, he should give the *arghya* into the hand that holds the *pavitra*. As for the plural number in the word “hasteṣu” (in the hands) in Paiṭhīnasi’s statement, that refers to the view where the number of Brāhmaṇas is prescribed as three each for [each ancestor]. This is because the use of the plural in the phrase “having first given *darbha* grass into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas” occurs specifically in the context of honoring the Brāhmaṇas intended for the ancestors (*pitṛ*). Otherwise, there would be no separate injunction for honoring the Brāhmaṇas intended for the grandfather and great-grandfather in the words “exactly the same for the other two. Having thus given the *arghya*, one should collect the remnants (*saṃsrava*) of those *arghya* waters—the drops trickling from the Brāhmaṇas' hands—into the vessel, and then, holding that vessel inverted (face down) with the words “Thou art the place for the ancestors,” he should place it on the ground. Baijavāpa states what must be done immediately after inverting the vessel.
"Having placed *kuśa* grass upon that [seat], one should offer—beginning with the deities (*daivapūrvakam*)—scent, flowers, incense, a lamp, a garment, and a sacred thread.

Thus, this "beginning with the deities" refers to the *padārthānusamaya* (sequential performance of individual items), which is an alternative to the *kāṇḍānusamaya* (sequential performance of groups of items) mentioned by Yājñavalkya; therefore, there is no contradiction.
Now, regarding the *agnaukaraṇa*: having thus honored the Brahmins with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the rite known as *agnaukaraṇa*. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"Having offered perfumes and seasonal flowers to the Brahmins..."
"And thereafter, one should offer incense into the fire in the proper sequence. Thus [it is said].
Yājñavalkya describes the method for the *agnaukaraṇa* rite:
"Intending to perform the *agnaukaraṇa*, he takes food soaked in clarified butter and asks [the Brahmins' permission]."
Being thus authorized with the words "Perform [the rite]," he should offer oblations into the fire as in the Pitṛyajña.
"Being composed, one should offer the remnants of the oblation into vessels, especially those made of silver, as they may be obtained. (YDh 1.236–67)

Intending to offer food soaked in clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into the fire, one should take the food and ask the Brāhmaṇas, "I shall offer it into the fire. By the word "clarified butter," vegetables and the like are excluded. Then, being permitted by them with the words "Do so," one should perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* rite according to its prescribed procedure: having brought about the presence [of the ancestors] and having taken a portion with the *mekṣaṇa* spoon, one should sacrifice into the fire with the mantra, "Svadhā! Adoration to Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs; Svadhā! Adoration to Agni, the bearer of the *kavya* offerings. Then, having sacrificed the *mekṣaṇa* itself, one should place the remainder of the offering into the vessels for the father and others as they are available, but not into the vessels used for the *vaiśvadeva* offering. This has been stated in the Purāṇa.
"One should offer the remainder of the *agnaukaraṇa* into the Vaiśvadeva [portion]. Thus it is said.

One should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* (the offering into the fire) either with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) or over the left shoulder (*upavītī*). Since its archetype, the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, possesses both types of characteristics—being both divine and ancestral—and thus allows for an option between these two modes, it is understood that this option between *prācīnāvītī* and *upavītī* applies to its modification, the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation as well. In this matter, the specific rule should be observed according to one's own *Śākhā*. Furthermore, the *agnaukaraṇa* should be performed in the *vivāha-agni* (wedding fire) because it is of the nature of a *Smārta* rite. However, when the *aupāsana-agni* is absent due to having performed a *sarvādhāna* (comprehensive consecration), one should offer the oblation in the *dakṣiṇāgni*; and in the absence of that, in the common (*laukika*) fire. Thus says the *Vāyupurāṇa*:

"Having brought the *dakṣiṇāgni* with effort for the purpose of the *homa*, or even the common (*laukika*) fire for the sake of the fire-ritual, one should offer oblations for the successful completion of the rite. (Vāyu Purāṇa 2.13.52–53).

Here, "for the sake of the fire" means for the purpose of accomplishing the duties pertaining to the *aupāsana* fire. In the absence of the *dakṣiṇāgni*, the *homa* should be performed in the hand. And so it is stated in another *smṛti*:

"A twice-born man who maintains a sacred fire (*sāgnika*) should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* (the offering into the fire) either in the hand or in the fire. Here, "one who maintains a sacred fire" refers to one who has established the fires through the *sarvādhāna* rite. The meaning is that in the absence of the *dakṣiṇāgni*, he should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* either in his hand or in a common (*laukika*) fire. However, when even one who has established the fires through the *ardhādhāna* rite is without a sacred fire, he should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* in the *aupāsana* fire. In its absence, [he may do so] in the hand of a twice-born man or in water. Thus says Mārkaṇḍeya:
"But one who has not established the sacred fires, in the absence of the *aupāsana* fire, [should offer] in a twice-born man or in water."

By the word "ca" (and), one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) by means of the half-ritual (*ardhādhāna*) is included. It should be understood that the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) takes place in the water when the *śrāddha* is performed near water. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says in the Viṣṇudharmottara: "That which was prescribed by Mārkaṇḍeya for [the offering] in water—when the *śrāddha* is to be performed near water, that rule is to be known as applicable."

As for that which was stated by Manu: "In the absence of fire, however, one should offer [the oblation] directly into the hand of a Brahmin" (MDh 3.212), that refers to the case of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). Jātūkarṇya says this:
"In the absence of fire, however, one should give into the right hand of the Brāhmaṇa.

The absence of fire is traditionally held to last as long as one has not found a wife. Thus, even when the fire is present, in the case of the four types of Śrāddhas beginning with the *kāmya*, the oblation (*homa*) is to be offered into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa alone. Regarding this, the authors of the Gṛhyasūtras say:
The Anvaṣṭakya rite is performed on the day before [the Aṣṭakā], the Pārvaṇa rite is performed month by month,
the Kāmya rite on an auspicious occasion, the Aṣṭamī rite on the eighth lunar day, and the Ekoddiṣṭa rite is the eighth.
"In the first four [rites], for those who maintain the sacred fires, the oblation is prescribed to be offered into the fire;
in the latter four, it should be placed into the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors."

The *aṣṭakā* Śrāddhas are prescribed by the rule: “The eighth days (*aṣṭamī*) of the four dark fortnights (*aparapakṣa*) of the winter and cool seasons are the *aṣṭakās*. Among these, the Śrāddha performed on the ninth day (*navamī*) following the *aṣṭakā* Śrāddhas is called the *anvaṣṭakā*. The Śrāddha performed on the preceding day, the seventh (*saptamī*), is indicated by the term “on the preceding day” (*pūrvedyuḥ*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The monthly Śrāddha performed during the dark fortnight is expressed by the phrase “month after month” (*māsi māsi*). The *pārvaṇa* Śrāddha, which serves as the archetype for all Śrāddhas, is the Śrāddha on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). The *kāmya* Śrāddha is that performed with a desire for specific fruits such as sons. The *ābhyudayika* Śrāddha is expressed by the term “auspicious occasion” (*abhyudaya*). The Śrāddha known as the *aṣṭakā* is expressed by the term “on the eighth day” (*aṣṭamyām*). By the term *ekoddiṣṭa*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is indicated through figurative indication, because the *ekoddiṣṭa* form also exists within the *asapiṇḍīkaraṇa* (pre-*sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*) rites. Among these, in the first four, those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) perform the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation into the fire itself; in the latter ones, for those with fires, it is performed into the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors. Regarding the oblation into the hand (*pāṇi-homa*), a specific rule has been shown by Kātyāyana.

"In the rite for the ancestors, having offered into the hand of the one who is at the head of the row according to the mantra, without fire, he should silently pour [the offering] into the vessels of the others.
As for that which was stated by Yama:

Regarding the statement, "In the event of an impediment regarding the gods, the twice-born who does not maintain a sacred fire shall perform the *agnaukaraṇa* [offering] into the fire," a systematic arrangement by way of option (*vikalpa*) should be understood therein. Even in the case where the offering is made into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the gods, one should still deposit the remnants only into the vessels of the Brāhmaṇas representing the ancestors. For this very reason, the *Vāyupurāṇa* states:
"Having offered into the hand of the one representing the gods, he who does not maintain a sacred fire should present the remnant to those representing the ancestors."
"For the Viśvedevas are not traditionally remembered by those who follow the Purāṇas as partakers of the remnants.

Regarding what must be done when the oblation is offered into the hand, Śaunaka says: "If one has no sacred fire, having taken the first portion [of food], one should ask, 'I shall perform the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation in you yourselves,' as before; they should reply, 'So be it. This is the meaning: having taken the first portion of food soaked in clarified butter, and having asked as before, "I shall perform the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation in you yourselves," and being permitted by them with "So be it," one should offer the oblation. Yama also states: "In that case, the oblation should be performed in the hand of the deity-representative (the Brahmin) just like the *agnaukaraṇa*."
"Having spread the *paryasta-darbhas*, for he [the fire] is indeed equal to fire.

Here, *paryasta-darbhās* refers to the *darbha* grass suitable for the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*). By mentioning the hand of the deity (the guest), the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the ancestors is also implied, since the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*) is prescribed as an option in both cases. Regarding the use of the food offered upon the palm of the hand, the author of the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* says:
"That which is given upon the palm of the hand, and whatever else has been prepared..."
One should enjoy [the offering] through a state of oneness; no state of separation exists.
[416] "The foolish first eat the food given upon the palm of the hand;
by that the ancestors are satisfied, and they do not receive the remaining food. Thus it is said.

When the *homa* is performed into the hand of the officiant (*daivavipra*), then for the sake of both the *śrāddha* for the ancestors (*pitṛ*) and the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*), it should be performed only once; for even though there is a difference in the *vaiśvadeva* offerings, the locus of the action (*adhikaraṇakāraka*) is common in that case. When the *homa* is performed into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the ancestors (*pitryabrāhmaṇa*), then it must be performed separately even into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa representing the maternal grandfather, because even though the *tantra* (ritual procedure) for the *vaiśvadeva* is the same, the locus of the action is not common in that case. And so says Kātyāyana:
"Even when there is a difference regarding the maternal grandfather, one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) should perform [the *homa*] in that very place."

The meaning is that, in the event of a division of the Vaiśvadeva rite or when performed as a single collective rite (*tantra*), one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) should perform the *homa* offering into the hand of the maternal grandfather’s Brahmin as well. One should wash the vessels twice. Accordingly, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states:
"Having washed the hands, vessels, and so forth, afterwards with water according to the rule, one should pour the washing-water mixed with sesame seeds into pure [water] along with *darbha* grass."

"Rubbed with the hand, [such as] a bowl, etc. (hastena nirmṛṣṭaṃ pātrādi) is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ). By the word "etc. (ādi), items for holding ghee and so forth are included.

Now, as for the serving: when the vessels have been thus washed, the performer, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), should place the remains of the oblation into the vessels for the ancestors and then serve the prepared items. And so Śaunaka says:
"Having offered into the fire, he should immediately thereafter place the remainder into the vessels for the ancestors."
Having offered [the food], one should perform the serving with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya).

[417] Thus. The phrase "with the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (apasavyena) connects with the offering of the remnants of the oblation (hutaśeṣanivedana), but not with the act of serving the food. For this very reason, Kārṣṇājini says: "The ancestral rite (pitrya-kṛtya) must be performed especially with the sacred thread over the right shoulder;
everything except the giving of food is thus for the maternal grandfathers as well. Thus it is said.
The manner of serving the food has been shown by Manu: "Having himself taken the vessel containing the food with both hands,
he should slowly set it down near the Brahmins while meditating on the ancestors" (MDh 3.224).

The vessel filled with food for the purpose of serving should be placed near the Brahmin’s eating-vessel; this is the "increase of food" by means of food. Because of the word "himself," serving [the food] personally is the primary rule. For this very reason, the *Vāyu Purāṇa* states:
"In serving [the food] himself, the infinity of the fruit is proclaimed.
As for that which is stated in the same work:
Indeed, serving food for the satisfaction of the ancestors is highly commended when performed by one's wife,
since it is recorded in the Smṛtis that the ancestors, gods, and humans are accompanied by women.
Thus, this should be understood as being in comparison with others. The serving [of food] must also be performed by a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*). And so says Nārāyaṇa:
"Whatever substance, whatever purifying item, whatever is intended for the ancestors, and whatever brings happiness—this is to be given to the twice-born with the hand of a wife of the same caste."
[418] Thus; "with the hand" means with both hands. To this effect, the *Matsya-purāṇa* states:

"Having taken [the food] with both hands, one should serve it. (MatPu 17.28) Even with the hand, it should not be given directly; rather, it should be done by means of a ladle or similar utensil. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"But those oily substances, salts, condiments, and so forth, which are given with the hand, do not reach the giver; the eater partakes of sin. (VaDh 14.31).
Also in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:

"One should not serve food at *śrāddhas* with an impure hand, nor with only one hand, nor without *kuśa* grass, nor indeed with an iron vessel. Thus it is said; "with an iron vessel" means one should certainly not serve with a vessel made of iron. When it is asked what vessels are recommended for serving, Viṣṇu states: "For the offering of ghee and other substances, metallic vessels, vessels of rhinoceros horn (*khaḍga*), and vessels of *phalgu* wood are recommended. And on this point there is a verse concerning the ancestors (*pitṛs*)."
"Whatever is given with a ladle made of gold or silver, or of udumbara wood, or even with a ladle made of phalgu wood, becomes inexhaustible. (ViDh 79.22–24).

"With a *khaḍga*" means with a ladle or similar utensil made from the horn of the *khaḍga* deer. "With a *phalgupātra*" means with a ladle or similar utensil made from the wood of the tree known as *kākaudumbarikā*. Manu also mentions other items that should be used for serving food:
Various kinds of food and drink, roots and fruits,
as well as savory meats and fragrant beverages.
"Having brought all that [food] forward, being very composed and restrained, he should serve it slowly, extolling all its qualities. Thus [says Manu, MDh 3.227–28]. Śaunaka also says:
Having brought all the cooked food and presented it individually,
one should begin the serving according to the prescribed rite, starting with the deities.

[420] Thus, having placed everything prepared into the vessels, one should perform the consecration of the vessels (*pātrābhimantraṇa*). Regarding this, Pracetas says: "Having given all that has been prepared, one should touch the vessel and recite [the mantra]. Yājñavalkya states a specific rule for this:
"Having given the food, one should perform the consecration of the vessel with the words 'The earth is the vessel.
Having done so, one should place the thumb of the twice-born into the food with the words 'This is Viṣṇu'. (YDh 1.138)
Atri states what must be done immediately thereafter:

"One should declare with one's hand, over the food and other items that have been released, 'This is food,' and then one should utter 'Svāhā' to effect the withdrawal of [the food] from one's own possession."
"Having uttered the names connected with the lineage and the ancestral line, saying 'This food is for you, Svadhā!', one should withdraw one's own sense of self-existence. Thus it is said.

The meaning is as follows: after pronouncing the words "to the Viśve Devas" with reference to the deity, one should then pronounce "this food. Thereafter, one should pronounce the mantra "svāhā. Then, one should effect the renunciation of ownership by saying "not mine. Subsequently, having designated the deity by first pronouncing the relationship, the lineage (*gotra*), and the name according to the order beginning with the ancestors, and having pointed out the substance to be offered by saying "this food," one should pronounce the mantra "svadhā," which indicates the giving of the *kavya* (offering to ancestors), and effect the renunciation of ownership by saying "not mine. Laghu-Yama states the subsequent duty:
"Whatever may be deficient in food, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in mantra, one should say, 'May all be without flaw,' and then diligently cause [the guests] to eat. Thus [it is said].
Pracetās states what must be done immediately after saying, "May there be no flaw":

"Having given the *āpośāna* [water for sipping], one should then recite the *Sāvitrī* three times, as well as the triplet beginning with 'madhuvātā' and likewise that triplet beginning with 'madhu'. The meaning of the fourth quarter [of the verse] is that the word 'madhu' is to be repeated three times. One should recite the *Sāvitrī* together with the *Vyāhṛtis*. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"Having recited the Gāyatrī with the Vyahṛtis and the triplet beginning with 'madhuvātā,' they should eat while remaining silent, speaking only as much as is necessary. (YDh 1.239).
Regarding the phrase "as is comfortable" (*yathāsukham*), the word "juṣadhvam" (enjoy) is to be supplied. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
"Having been told, 'Enjoy [the food],' they, holding their vessels properly and observing silence, should eat after the *apośāna* rite. Thus it is said.
The eater at a *śrāddha* should not offer a *bali* offering. For this very reason, Atri states:
Whether one gives or does not give, if anyone should cast an offering upon the ground,
that food goes forth fruitlessly, having been met by the ancestors who are left in despair.

[422] Thus. Kātyāyana states what must be performed immediately after the commencement of the meal: “While they are eating, one should recite the *gāyatrī* preceded by the *vyāhṛtis*, together with the *praṇava*, once or thrice; as well as the *rakṣoghnī* verses, the *pitrya* mantras, the *puruṣasūkta*, the *apratiratha*, and other purificatory hymns. Manu also says:

“At the ancestral rite (*pitrya*), one should cause them to hear their own Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), as well as the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*), narratives (*ākhyāna*), histories (*itihāsa*), the *purāṇas*, and the *khilas*. (MDh 3.232)
In this context, the recitation of the *sūkta* must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*). For this very reason, Jamadagni states:

"The entire *śrāddha* ceremony should be performed according to rule with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), except for the recitation of the *sūkta* hymns and the dismissal of the Brahmins."
Now, regarding the rules for the giver and the eater:
Vṛddha-Śātātapa states the rule for the giver and the eater:
"He who does not give what has been requested and prepared for the sake of the śrāddha..."
But the miserly person of dull intellect does not obtain the fruit of the śrāddha.
"One should request what is needed from that which has been prepared for the sake of the *śrāddha*.
If a twice-born man does not request it, he is a fool; he would be a slayer of his ancestors.
Now, [one might object]:
If a Brahmin devoid of knowledge begs from a donor, his ancestors become angry with both the giver and the eater; of this there is no doubt.
Thus,
by performing the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance, one is liberated from that karma.
Therefore, a wise person should neither give, nor beg, nor cause [another] to give.

If it be argued that the *Vāyu Purāṇa* and the *Smṛti* would thus be in contradiction, it is not so; for both are justified by having as their scope things that have not been specifically intended [for such use]. Even regarding an object that has been intended, Śaṅkha and Likhita prohibit giving or accepting it if it is excessively excessive: "One should not give what is excessively excessive; one should not accept it. The *Nigama* states the manner of prohibiting an unintended object:
"In a *śrāddha*, one should never offer food, drink, and so forth directly from the mouth."

"Because it is undesirable, or because there are many [requests], one should ward them off with a hand gesture. This "warding off" is intended as an illustration for refusing a request as well, since there is no difference in the breaking of silence whether the request is made verbally or otherwise. Having said, "I shall give the object you desire," one must not fail to give it. And so says Yama:
"As long as there is sacrificial food available, and as long as it is desired, it should be given."
"The ancestors eat only so long as I do not say, 'I give.
Thus, the rules for the donor at the time of feeding are shown in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"One should never shed tears, nor should one utter improper speech."
One should not gaze at those who are eating, nor should one harbor envy.
"A wise man should always perform the *śrāddha* with a one-pointed mind, neither dejected, nor angry, nor with a distracted mind. Thus [it is said].
Sumantu states the rules for those who eat:
"Free from anger, one should eat flavors properly, whatever pleases each person; their meal should continue until satiety, and there should be no leaving of food behind out of desire.
Thus it is said in the Nigama as well.
"They should eat in silence, without looking around, and without lifting the bowl," so says Baudhāyana; also:
"The twice-born who eats while standing with one foot treading upon the other, except in an emergency..."
"He should not feed such a person at a *śrāddha*; the ancestors depart disappointed. Thus [says Manu]. Pracetas also says:
"Having sipped the *āpośāna* water, one should eat what has been placed in the vessel, provided it is not censurable."
"One should not allow the restlessness of any of the senses, nor of the hands and feet. Thus [says] Manu as well:
"All food should be very hot; and they should eat while restraining their speech."
"And the twice-born, when asked by the donor, shall not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial food" (MDh 3.236).

Regarding the phrase "and they shall eat," the particle *eva* is intended to show that even if there is mutual contact through negligence, the eating does not cease. For this very reason, Śaṅkha says:
"But while eating in the row at a śrāddha, if a Brāhmaṇa should touch another Brāhmaṇa..."
"Having eaten that food and abandoned it [by spitting], one should recite the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times. Thus [it is said]. Again, that same [text] states:
"He who speaks with a *huṃ* sound, or who enumerates the virtues [of the food] from his hand..."
One should lift the vessel from the ground, or release it with the hand.
He eats with his feet raised up, or with his loincloth outside, or with his hands above his knees;
or he eats without using his thumb, or makes a noise with his mouth.
Or, having drawn up again the water and so forth remaining after being drunk, he may drink it;
or, having eaten half of a sweetmeat or fruit, he may eat more.
"Or one may blow upon the food with the mouth, or spit even into the vessel;
eating in this manner at a *śrāddha*, a twice-born man destroys the rite and goes to a low state.

"With feet raised" (*prauḍhapādaḥ*) means having the feet placed upon a seat or similar support. "With the outer garment outside" (*bahiḥkakṣaḥ*) means having both armpits exposed by the outer garment. Śaṅkha states the rule for the donor:
One should not inquire about salt and other such items while those engaged in a *śrāddha* are eating;
for if one does so inquire, the ancestors depart as if they were left with remnants—of this there is no doubt.
"The arm of the giver indeed falls, and the tongue of the eater is split asunder. Thus [it is said].
Pracetās also stated other rules for the eater:
"While eating, one should never touch the food with the left hand."
One should not touch one's feet, head, or bladder with the foot, nor should one touch a vessel with the foot.
A wise person should never eat his food until it is completely finished,
except in the case of curd, milk, honey, or roasted barley flour.

[426] Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the statement of Jamadagni, “They should not censure [the food], nor should they leave any remainder,” for that refers to the subject of leaving a large remainder. For this very reason, he himself stated: “However, a small amount should be set aside, because it is to be given as a portion to those who died before receiving the sacraments. And Manu declares that the status of being the portion of those who died before receiving the sacraments and so forth belongs to the leavings: “The leavings shall be the portion for those who died before receiving the sacraments, for those who have abandoned [their kin], and for women of the family; as well as the *vikira* scattered during the rites. (MDh 3.245)
When the Brahmins have thus eaten according to the rule, Pracetas states what must be done:
"Having ascertained that they are satisfied, one should take food mixed with sesame seeds and recite [mantras] as before.

"As before" means one should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis and the Madhumatī verses. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "Having recited the Gāyatrī, the Madhumatīs, and 'madhu, madhu, madhu,' he asks, 'Are you satisfied? After the question, Vyāsa says:

When asked, "Are you satisfied? they should reply, "We are satisfied. Now, Manu states what is to be done immediately following the feeding of the Brahmins: [The verse continues: "Then, having sprinkled water around [the food], he should offer the *svadhā* oblation; thereafter, he should dismiss the Brahmins with the words, 'May you be satisfied. [Manu 3.254–256] "Then, having sprinkled water around [the food], he should offer the *svadhā* oblation; thereafter, he should dismiss the Brahmins with the words, 'May you be satisfied. Having said this, and when they have replied, 'We are satisfied,' he should say, 'May there be *svadhā*! and they should respond, 'May there be *svadhā*! [Manu 3.257] "Then, having circumambulated them from left to right, he should bid them farewell with the word 'Go! and, having prostrated himself, he should follow them for some distance. [Manu 3.258] "Having thus completed the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) according to the rules, he should feed his own family, and then he may eat what remains of the offering. [Manu 3.259] "He who eats without first performing the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) is a thief of the ancestors' food; and he who performs the ancestral rite without having first fed his dependents is a thief of the guests' food. [Manu 3.260] "The ancestors remain satisfied for a month by the food of one who eats the remnants of the ancestral offering after first feeding his dependents. [Manu 3.261] "But those who eat the food of one who has not first fed his dependents eat, in fact, nothing but sin, for that food is not fit to be consumed. [Manu 3.262] "One should not give food to a guest who has not been invited, nor to one who comes at an improper time; for such a person is called a 'thief of the sacrifice' (*yajñacaura*). [Manu 3.263] "If a Brahmin arrives seeking food at the time of the ancestral rite, one should, after consulting the Brahmins, provide him with a portion of the food intended for the ancestors. [Manu 3.264] "One should not offer the ancestral oblation (*svadhā*) while the guest is present; for the guest is the very embodiment of the *svadhā* itself. [Manu 3.265] "Even if a guest is hungry, one should not offer him the ancestral food; rather, one should satisfy him with other food, and then offer the ancestral oblation. [Manu 3.266] "If a Brahmin arrives at the time of the ancestral rite, one should honor him with the same respect as the ancestors themselves. [Manu 3.267] "Whether he has come by chance or was previously invited, one should not turn away a Brahmin who has arrived at the time of the ancestral rite. [Manu 3.268] "If a Brahmin arrives at the time of the ancestral rite, he should be honored with the same respect as the ancestors themselves, even if he is a stranger. [Manu 3.269] "One should not ask a Brahmin who has arrived at the time of the ancestral rite about his lineage or his conduct. [Manu 3.270] "Even if his lineage and conduct are unknown, or if he is a man of great learning, one should honor him at the ancestral rite as if he were a direct descendant of one's ancestors. [Manu 3.271] "One should not ask a Brahmin who has arrived at the time of the ancestral rite about his lineage or his conduct; for the ancestors themselves do not know the origins of such a guest.
