[Manu 3.295] "One should not ask a Brahmin who has arrived at the time of
[427] “Having gathered various kinds of food and sprinkled them with water, one should scatter the *vikira* on the ground in front of those who have eaten.

(MDh 3.244) That which contains various types of condiments is called *sārvavarṇika*. Regarding this, Pracetas states a specific rule: “One should cast it on the ground with the mantra ‘ye agnayaḥ...’. Having offered the *vikira*, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). For this very reason, Marīci says:

"Having offered the *vikira* at the *śrāddha* rites, if one does not perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) due to a lapse of intellect, his ancestors shall remain eaters of leftovers for six months.
Immediately thereafter, one should offer water for the purpose of rinsing the mouth (*gaṇḍūṣa*). And so says the statement of Madālasa:
"In the same way, one should give water once each for the purpose of sipping," so it is said. (MāPu 31.53)

One should first offer water for the washing of hands and for sipping (*ācamana*) to the Brahmins invited for the ancestors (*paitṛka*). Regarding this, Viṣṇu says: “One should first give water for sipping to those facing north, and then to those facing east. Then, having sprinkled the site of the *śrāddha* with the mantra ‘suprokṣitam,’ one who holds *darbha* grass in his hand should perform everything. (ViDh 73.25). The meaning is that, having first given water for the washing of hands and for sipping to the Brahmins of the paternal line, and subsequently having given it to the single Brahmin of the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should then sprinkle the site of the *śrāddha* with the mantra ‘prokṣitam’ and, holding *darbha* grass in hand, perform all the subsequent ritual acts.
Now follows the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*); one should then perform the offering of the rice-balls. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having taken all the food together with sesame seeds, facing the south..."

"One should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) near the remains of the meal, according to the ritual of the Pitṛyajña. (YDh 1.242) The meaning of this is as follows: having taken all the food cooked for the Brahmins and mixed with sesame seeds, one should form balls and offer those rice-balls near the remains of the meal according to the procedure of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. This should be understood to apply when there is no cooking of the *caru* (sacrificial porridge). However, when there is the presence of cooked *caru*, then one should take all the food together with the remainder of the *caru* left over from the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) and offer the rice-balls in the vicinity of the fire. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Having made three pindas from that remainder of the sacrificial food, being composed, he should offer them according to the very rite for water-libations, facing the south. (MDh 3.215).
Atri describes the nature of the *ucchiṣṭasaṃdhi*:
"Three *aratnis* in front of the place where the ancestors' seats are located is the place for depositing the leavings; however, it is not in the immediate vicinity of the seat for the leavings.
The phrase "in three *aratnis*" is intended to indicate a nearby location that is free from contact with the leavings. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:

"Having left a space of one *aratni*, one should cause the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to be offered there, so that no drops reach those who are performing the ritual sipping (*upaspṛśatām*). Thus [it is said].
Manu states the time for the offering of the rice-balls:
"Some perform the offering of the rice-balls even beforehand," so it is said. (MDh 3.261)

Some desire the offering of the *piṇḍas* (rice balls) either before the meal, after the worship (*arcana*), or after the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire). Others, however, desire the offering of the *piṇḍas* after the meal—either before the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) or after the dismissal of the Brahmins; this is understood from the phrase "some [desire it]. The offering of the *piṇḍas* before the meal is prescribed for those inauspicious *śrāddhas* performed prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. In auspicious *śrāddhas*, such as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and others, the offering of the *piṇḍas* occurs only afterwards. As Laugākṣi said:
"In non-praiseworthy sacrifices, the offering of the *piṇḍas* and their rinsing (*avanejana*) should be performed first;

but in a praiseworthy meal, one should prepare them only afterwards. Thus, according to different Vedic schools (*śākhā*), there are established positions that the offering of the *piṇḍas* may take place either before the sipping of water (*ācamana*), or after it, or even after the dismissal of the Brahmins. And so it is stated in another Smṛti:

"Regarding the offering of the funeral ball (piṇḍa) which has been prescribed by the sages for different times, a wise man should perform it according to the tradition of his own Vedic school, wherever that may be."

In this regard, for those belonging to the *Āśvalāyana* branch (*śākhā*), there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the two alternatives—either before or after the sipping of water (*ācamana*)—since both are equally valid. Thus says Āśvalāyana: “One should place the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) after the guests have eaten and have sipped water; according to some, when they have sipped water” (*ĀśGṛ* 4.8.12–13). In whichever branch a specific time is not heard, one should adopt the alternative of offering the rice-balls after the sipping of water for the sake of ease in performance. The procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the offering of the rice-balls is set forth in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
With his right and left hands, the twice-born man should perform the scraping;
thereafter, he should perform the rubbing, remaining unwearied in the rite of the śrāddha.
“Breaking, pounding, and likewise the act of scraping—the twice-born should scrape the earth with either a *vajra* or *kuśa* grass.

Here, “breaking” (*khaṇḍana*) means the cutting of *kuśa* grass and the like; “pounding” (*peṣaṇa*) means rubbing the ground. By the word *vajra*, the wooden sacrificial sword (*sphya*) is meant. And the mantra for scraping has been shown by Kātyāyana: “Having scraped it, [one recites] ‘apahatāḥ’ (the spirits are struck down). Immediately thereafter, one should sprinkle it, because of the traditional teaching of Āśvalāyana: “having sprinkled it. There, one should spread *kuśa* grass. This is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
"And one should scatter *kuśa* grass there with the tips pointing toward the south. Then, one should perform the *avanejana* (sprinkling). Regarding this, Sumantu says:
"O [Name], sprinkle yourself!"—addressing each individual person in turn.
"One should perform the washing three times with each hand. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that, having addressed the father and others by their names and *gotras* with the word "O [Name]," one should perform the pouring of water—the ritual washing (*avanejana*)—three times for each person using the right hand alone. Regarding this, Āśvalāyana has stated a different mantra for the washing: "Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), one should lead the line three times with water, saying 'May the ancestors be purified' (*śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*)," and so forth; this is not contradictory, as such arrangements are established according to the differences between Vedic schools (*śākhā*). The mantras for the offering of the rice balls (*piṇḍa*) have been shown by Kātyāyana: "O [Name], this is for you," and some say one should follow the four mantras beginning with "ye ca tvām atra. Having addressed them as "O [Name]"—that is, "O [Name] of such-and-such *gotra*, [Name] Śarman"—one should offer the rice ball with the mantra "This is for you" (*etat te*). Some say one should offer the rice ball with the mantra "ye ca tvām atra. Furthermore, the offering of the rice ball must be performed while bending the left knee; this is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*.
"A wise man, devoted to the ancestors, should offer three balls of rice mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, having placed his left knee upon the ground" (Vāyu Purāṇa 2.13.22).
Thus [it is said]. Manu states what is to be done immediately after the offering of the rice balls:

"Having offered the rice-balls to the ancestors according to the rule while being self-restrained, he should wipe that hand on those *darbha* grasses for the sake of those who partake of the smearing. (MDh 3.216)

In this regard, the mantra was shown by Viṣṇu: “O ancestors, rejoice here; rain down according to your respective portions. This refers to the rubbing of the hands at the roots of the *darbha* grass. Kātyāyana states what must be done immediately thereafter: “Having said, ‘O ancestors,’ while facing north, one turns back until the exhaustion [of breath] and mutters, ‘The ancestors have rejoiced’” (Viṣṇusmṛti 7.22). One should remain facing north until the exhaustion resulting from the pressure of the breath during *prāṇāyāma*. Then, without exhaling, one should turn around and mentally mutter the mantra “The ancestors have rejoiced,” and only then exhale. A specific detail regarding this is shown in the *Karmapradīpa*.
Some declare that the turning is counter-clockwise, ending toward the north;
Gautama, Śāṇḍilya, and Śāṇḍilyāyana, however, hold it to be clockwise.

"Having restrained the breath and drawn it in, meditating upon the ancestors as is appropriate, and performing the recitation while turning [the breath] by that same means, one should then release the vital breaths. (KSm 2.17.21–22)

After the consecration with the mantra "They have rejoiced" (*amīmadanta*), Viṣṇu [433] states: "Having consecrated with 'They have rejoiced' and having smelled the remainder, one should pour out water over the *piṇḍas* as before with 'May the ancestors be purified' (*śundhantāṃ pitaraḥ*). Then, one should give the ointment with 'O so-and-so, anoint yourself' (*asāv abhyaṅkṣva*), and the collyrium with 'O so-and-so, apply [collyrium]' (*asāv aṅkṣva*). Then, in the absence of a garment, one should offer a fringe or wool; [with the words] 'This is your clothing, O ancestors' (*etad vaḥ pitaro vāsaḥ*), and 'Do not take away anything else, O ancestors' (*mānotonyat pitaraḥ yuṅgdhvam*). Following that, Vyāghra says: "One should present perfumes, flowers, incense, and a lamp."
"O ancestors, this garment is for you; having given the fringe [of the cloth] separately to each," thus [it is said].
After the worship, the Matsya Purāṇa states:
"Whatever food, whether hard or soft, is cooked in the house that is not forbidden..."
"And one should never eat without having offered [the food] at the base of the *piṇḍas*. (MatPurāṇa 17.36).
Immediately after that, Bṛhaspati says:
"But without having worshipped [them], one should pour out a vessel of water over them."

Immediately after, Viṣṇu states: "Then one should pay homage to them with the verse beginning 'Homage to you, O fathers,' and so forth, ending with the three-verse hymn 'Manonvāhuvā saha'; then one should move those rice-balls with the verse 'Depart, O fathers'. (ViDh 73.27).
This refers to the ritual duties to be performed immediately following the offering of the rice-balls.

Āśvalāyana states the subsequent rite: "One should approach the fire with [the mantra], 'O Agni, you who eat our offerings with hymns...'; [one approaches] the *agnaukaraṇa* fire, the *gārhapatya* fire, [and the fire with the mantra] 'That which is the intermediate space, the earth... The meaning is that one should pour water once into each of the hands of the Brahmins. This is to be understood as applying to the procedure where the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) occurs before the sipping of water (*ācamana*). However, in the procedure where the offering of the rice-balls occurs after they have sipped water, one should sip water, offer the rice-balls, and then pour water once into each of the Brahmins' hands. Kuśa grass should also be given. This is also stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
"When they have sipped water, one should offer water along with flowers and barley.

Here, the mention of "barley" is intended as an indicator for *tila* (sesame seeds). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to further aggregate the offering of water. Since their purpose has been fulfilled, once those [flowers, barley, etc. have been discarded in some clean place, one should again offer water and so forth. Thus says Matsya:
"When they have sipped water, one should again offer water, flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and water. (MatPu 16.47)
He himself states what must be done immediately thereafter:
"Having given the blessing, the wise man, facing east, should receive [the response] from the twice-born;
when the twice-born have replied, 'May the ancestors be non-terrible,' he should say, 'So be it.'"
"May our lineage likewise increase," he said; and they replied to him again, "May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny."
“May our faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.
“May these blessings be true, may they be true,” they said again. (MatPurāṇa 17.53–55) Now follows the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*).
Immediately after, having performed the stirring of the vessel (*pātracālana*), one should perform the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*). For this very reason, Nārāyaṇa says:
"Those twice-born who pronounce a blessing without having stirred that vessel—their ancestors depart as they came, having uttered a curse and being left without hope."
Jātūkarṇya states the specific rule regarding the shifting of the vessels:
"In a Śrāddha, one should shift the vessels oneself, or a disciple, or a son;
never by women, nor by a child, nor by one of a different caste under any circumstances."

Pāraskara describes the manner of pronouncing the benediction (*svastivācana*): "‘Blessing, O Blessed One! Speak it!’—this is the recitation. Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), the performer should say to the hand of the one representing the Viśvedevas: "O Blessed One, say ‘Blessing’ to the Viśvedevas known as Purūravas and Ārdrava. The Brahmin should then reply, "Blessing. The same procedure applies to the hands of the Brahmins representing the ancestors. Yājñavalkya states the subsequent rite: "Then one should cause the blessing to be pronounced and likewise offer the water for imperishability (*akṣayyodaka*). (YDh 1.243)
[436] Thus; the meaning is that one should offer water into the hand of the Brāhmaṇa, saying, "May it be inexhaustible. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"Immediately thereafter, water should be offered for the ancestors by their name and lineage;
the twice-born should say to the Brāhmaṇas, 'May this be inexhaustible. Thus.
The construction is made by supplying the word "hasteṣu" (in the hands).
Now, regarding the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*): immediately after [the rite], one should give the sacrificial fee. Manu says:
"One should perform the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*) and likewise the offering of imperishable water (*akṣayyodaka*)."
One should give [the offering] with sesame seeds, pronouncing the name and lineage, and provide a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability.
One should give cows, land, gold, garments, and excellent beds—
whatever is desired by the Brahmins— for the sake of oneself and one's father.
"Free from stinginess regarding wealth, he should act so as to please the ancestors.

Regarding this, Pāraskara states a specific rule: "One should give gold to the Viśvedevas and silver to the ancestors; furthermore, one should give other things such as a cow and a black antelope skin, as much as possible, to the Brahmins seated in a single row during the Śrāddha rite."
"Solid food and soft food should be given equally, but the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to [the guest's] merit.

The phrase "according to [merit]" means in accordance with the degree of learning and virtue of the invited brāhmaṇas. The giving of the sacrificial fee on behalf of the deceased should be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī). For this very reason, Jamadagni says:
"In that case too, it should be done with the sacred thread over the right shoulder; for the venerable Matsya is my authority."

Regarding the phrase "even there, even in the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)," as for what was stated by that same author— "all ritual action is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), except for the giving of the sacrificial fee"—
that should be understood to apply to the alternative where the sacrificial fee is given specifically for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa. And that alternative has been shown by Devala.
"Then one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born who have sipped water.
He [the same author] states the sequence for giving the dakṣiṇā intended for the Brāhmaṇas:
"One should give the dakṣiṇā first to the Brāhmaṇas representing the ancestors, and then to the two [representing the gods]."

The meaning is "of the two Brahmins for the Vaiśvadeva rite. Here, because of the co-occurrence with the term *pitṛviprebhyaḥ* ("to the Brahmins of the ancestors"), the genitive case is used in the sense of the dative. Immediately thereafter, Yājñavalkya states:
"Having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his ability, he should utter the word *svadhā*.
Being permitted [by the Brahmins] with the words 'Let it be spoken,' he should say, 'Let the *svadhā* be uttered for the ancestors.'"
When they have said, "Let there be *svadhā*," one should then pour water on the ground;
and when this has been spoken by the brahmins, one should mutter: "May the Viśvedevas be pleased."
"May our donors increase, as well as our Vedic knowledge and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
Having spoken thus and having uttered pleasant words, he should prostrate and ask for forgiveness;
then, being pleased, he should dismiss them, starting with the ancestors, saying "Vāja-vāje" (Success in every sacrifice). Thus.
Now, regarding the eating of the middle piṇḍa: immediately thereafter, one desiring a son should give the middle piṇḍa to his wife. Thus says the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"One desiring offspring should give the middle piṇḍa to his wife, preceded by the recitation of the mantra. (VāyPu 2.14.31)

The meaning is "the middle ball of rice. Its procedure is as follows: there, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he should place the middle ball of rice into the joined palms of his wife with the mantra: "I cause thee to consume the essence of the waters and the plants; conceive a fetus created by the beings. The mantra for its consumption has been shown by Matsya: "O ancestors, bestow within [her] a fetus that increases the lineage" (MatPu 16.54). Manu also says:
Then, the devoted wife, faithful to her husband and intent on the worship of the ancestors,
desiring a son, should properly eat the middle *piṇḍa*.
"One should obtain a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence, wealthy, possessed of offspring, righteous, and likewise virtuous" (MDh 3.262–63).
Thus it is said. He [Manu] himself states the unfitness for the offering of the *piṇḍa*:

"One should not offer the funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) into the hollowed palms [of the recipient] when he is one who has not yet reached youth, one who is aged, one who is pregnant, one afflicted by disease, or even one whose son and wife are young. Regarding the disposal of the *piṇḍa* in cases such as the absence of the wife, Bṛhaspati says:
"If the wife has gone to another country, or is pregnant, or likewise ill,
then that [animal] may be eaten by an old bull or a goat.
Āpastamba also mentions another method of disposal:
If the wife is abroad, or if she is impure from eating leftovers, or if she is dead, or if she is wicked and unfaithful— what becomes of that funeral cake?
"One standing in water, facing south, should cause the ball [of rice] to go into the sky;
for the sky is the station of the ancestors, as is the southern direction.
As for that which was stated by Devala:
Then, once the rite has been completed, immediately thereafter,
a Brāhmaṇa, fire, a goat, or a cow should consume those rice-balls, or he should cast them into water.
Thus, that [rule] refers to the absence of a desire for a son. At a *tīrtha-śrāddha*, the *piṇḍas* are to be cast directly into the water. As it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"At a *tīrtha-śrāddha*, one who is composed should always cast the *piṇḍas* into the *tīrtha*;
facing south, for that is proclaimed to be the direction of the ancestors. (ViDhPu 1.141.8)
[440] Now, regarding the cleaning of remnants:
immediately thereafter, one should clean up the remnants. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"One should cast [the water] among the Brahmins and wipe away the remnants of the twice-born" (YDh 1.257).

This is the meaning: one should not wipe away the remnants before the dismissal of the Brahmins; rather, it is only after they have been dismissed and the disposal of the *piṇḍas* has been performed. As for that which was stated by Vyāsa:
"One should not wipe away the remnants until the sun has set."
Thus it is; and as Vasiṣṭha has stated:
"In a Śrāddha, the remnants of the food must not be removed until the end of the day;
for the offerings of *svadhā* continue to drip, and those who have not yet performed their water-libations drink them. (VaDh 11.21)
This refers to the case where another house is available. For this very reason, Pracetas says:
"Surrounded by his circle of servants, he should eat the remains of the *kavya* together with those born of his own *gotra*;
until the time of the *śrāddha* at evening, he should not clear away the leavings of the twice-born."
Then the sacrificer should eat himself;
after the cleaning of the remnants, having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite, he should eat the remaining food together with the Brāhmaṇas. And so says the Matsya Purāṇa:
"And then, at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva, [he should eat] along with his servants, sons, and kinsmen."
"One should eat everything enjoyed by the ancestors, accompanied by guests. (MatPurāṇa 16.55).
When the Vaiśvadeva and other rites are performed after the Śrāddha has been completed, they should be done using the remains of that very [Śrāddha] meal. To this effect, Paiṭhīnasi says:
"Having performed the Śrāddha according to the rules, one should then perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites from that [remnant]."
“Then one should go for alms and likewise give *dhantakāra* (betel-nut) and so forth.

By the word “and so forth,” the daily *śrāddha* (*nityaśrāddha*) is included. “Then” means from the remains of the food prepared for the ancestors. The daily *śrāddha* may be performed with a separate cooking. For this very reason, Mārkaṇḍeya, referring to that, says: “Others say it may be done with a separate cooking. In this regard, even the daily *śrāddha* is not mandatory. He himself states this: “Some men desire the daily rite for the ancestors.”
"Likewise for the ancestors; one should perform the remainder as previously described.
As for that which was stated by Laugākṣi:
"One should prepare the cooked food for the sake of the ancestors and likewise for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva."
The Vaiśvadeva rite is not for the sake of the ancestors, nor is the Darśa rite for the sake of the Viśvedevas.

Thus, this refers to the *śrāddha* performed by one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), because for such a person, the *vaiśvadeva* rite has been prescribed by that very same authority even prior to the *śrāddha*: "Having completed the rites at the end of the fortnight and the *vaiśvadeva*,
the wise one who maintains the fires should then perform the *piṇḍayajña*, and after that, the *anvāhāryaka*."
The rite at the end of the fortnight is the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*). The *anvāhāryaka* is the *darśa* ancestral offering (*śrāddha*). As for the statement from the *Purāṇa*:

"If the daily fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed at the beginning of the *śrāddha* and other rites, the gods do not accept the *havya* (oblation to the gods), nor do the ancestors accept the *kavya* (oblation to the ancestors)."

Thus, this [rule] should be understood as applying when one performs the *vaiśvadeva* rite from the food prepared for the ancestors (*pitṛpāka*). For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi states: "He who performs the *vaiśvadeva* by taking [food] out from the ancestral offering—his *śrāddha* becomes *āsura* (demonic) and does not reach the ancestors."

When the Vaiśvadeva rite is performed either immediately after the *agnaukaraṇa* offering or after the scattering of the food (*vikiraṇa*), it must likewise be performed from a separate cooking. This is because the fault incurred by performing the Vaiśvadeva from the remnants of that [Śrāddha] meal is the same here as well. Furthermore, the performance of the Vaiśvadeva after the *agnaukaraṇa* is prescribed in another Smṛti: "One should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblations into the fire before the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas; it is traditionally taught that one should perform the *bhūtayajña* and other rites after having completed the Śrāddha."

Whether the Vaiśvadeva offering is performed from the remnants of the ancestral oblation (*pitṛpāka*) or from a separate cooking, in both cases the meal must be eaten from the remnants of the ancestral oblation alone. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"Having circumambulated [the fire] clockwise, one should eat what has been partaken of by the ancestors" (YDh 1.249).
However, if there are no remnants of the ancestral oblation, one must certainly eat even after preparing a separate cooking, because fasting is prohibited. And so says Devala:
"However, if a Brahmin who has performed a *śrāddha* never eats thereafter,
the gods do not accept the *havya* offerings, nor do the ancestors accept the *kavya* offerings.

Since eating the remnants of the *pitr-śrāddha* is obligatory, for this very reason, a substitute for the meal is prescribed in the Smṛtis when one observes the mandatory fast on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) and other such occasions.

"When fasting is obligatory and a *śrāddha* occurs as an occasional (*naimittika*) duty, one should then observe the fast after smelling the food consumed by the ancestors. Thus, the rule regarding eating the food consumed by the ancestors pertains only to the permissive view. For this very reason, Śātātapa says:
"Immediately thereafter, the wise man, being well-composed and acting according to the rules, should eat the remaining food that has been permitted, together with those he holds dear.
Thus Bṛhaspati states the rule for both the giver and the eater following the meal.
"The performer of the śrāddha, together with those participating in the śrāddha, should observe celibacy during that night;
otherwise, both of them would go to hell.
Thus it is stated also in the Matsya Purāṇa.

One who performs a śrāddha and one who eats at a śrāddha should avoid all of the following: eating again, traveling, riding in a vehicle, physical exertion, sexual intercourse, and [eating] after the śrāddha meal.
"Self-study of the Vedas, quarreling, and sleeping during the day according to one's own will.
Thus [it is said]. Yama states a specific rule for those eating at a *śrāddha*:
"Eating again, traveling on a journey, carrying a load, physical exertion, and sexual intercourse..."
"One who has eaten at a *śrāddha* should avoid these eight: the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), receiving gifts (*pratigraha*), and the fire-oblation (*homa*).

This prohibition regarding the twilight prayers and the oblation applies to one who has not performed the penance; however, once the penance has been performed, he should certainly perform them. For this very reason, the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* states:
"A twice-born man who has eaten at a *śrāddha* should drink water ten times while reciting the *gāyatrī*."

"Then one should perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), recite prayers, and also offer oblations. Thus, according to the method described, one who is unable to perform the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] should perform the śrāddha by means of the rite of formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). This is stated in another Smṛti:
"When one is unable to perform the constituent parts of the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña)..."

"He should perform only the *saṃkalpa-śrāddha*, devoid of the *argha* and other [ritual elements]. This is the meaning: he who abandons the sacred fire out of laziness is a "fire-abandoner" (*tyaktāgni*). He has no entitlement to perform the *śrāddha*. Rather, it is for one who possesses the fire and is distinct from the fire-abandoners. Furthermore, the entitlement of the *vidhura* (the widower) and others is stated even for the *śrāddha* characterized by the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*). Since the *śrāddha* must necessarily be performed by an entitled person who has not abandoned the fire, therefore, one who is unable to follow the extensive *pārvaṇa* procedure should perform it according to the *saṃkalpa* method. He himself has stated the definition of the *saṃkalpa* method: [The text continues with the ritual procedure.]
"But when one makes the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should not perform the filling of the vessel;
there should be no invocation (āvāhana) or the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), and one should not cause the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to be given.
Thus, the rice-ball for the leavings (ucchiṣṭapiṇḍa) is not to be offered.
But when one does not perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the *śrāddha*, the filling of the vessel and the scattering of food (*vikiro*) must be offered.
Thus, from another Smṛti.

Now, the annual *śrāddha* (pratyābdika-śrāddha) is to be performed in this manner on the new moon day (*darśa*), as the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* has already been described. Next, its derivative form, the annual *śrāddha*, is defined. Regarding this, Laugākṣi says:
"One whose father has died must certainly perform the *śrāddha* himself."
"In the mother's [death] anniversary, month by month, and likewise every year during her waxing [period]," so it is said.
Regarding the procedure for that, Jātūkarṇya states:
"A son should perform [the rite] for his father who has joined the group of ancestors (pitṛgaṇa) according to the *pārvaṇa* method."

"The eternal rule should be understood as applying every year and every month. Thus it is said. One who has been incorporated into the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite belongs to the group of ancestors (*pitṛgaṇa*). For him, one should perform the annual and monthly *śrāddha* according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure. Jamadagni also says:
"Having attained the status of being a *sapiṇḍa*, the legitimate son (*aurasa*) shall perform the rite according to the rule."
One should perform the śrāddha for one's mother and father on the anniversary of their death according to the rules for the new-moon śrāddha.
[446] Thus it is said.
But surely—by the extension of the rule from the *darśa* sacrifice, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfathers would also follow as a consequence?
This is not a fault, because in the annual (*pratyābdika*) rite, the six *piṇḍas* have been excluded. And so says Kātyāyana:

"Excluding the *karṣū-samanvita* [rite], the annual rite (*pratyābdika*), and the sixteenth *śrāddha*, there shall be six rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) in the remaining cases; such is the settled rule. (KSm 3.24.14). Here, "accompanied by the *karṣū*" refers to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. As for that which was stated by Yama:

"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, every year on the anniversary of death, the sons must separately perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* for their mother and father. And as for that which was stated by Vyāsa concerning the anniversary of death:

"If a man performs the *pārvaṇa* rite while abandoning the *ekoddiṣṭa*, one should know that it is as if unperformed, and he becomes a slayer of his ancestors. Here, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the *pārvaṇa* and the *ekoddiṣṭa*. Even so, the determination is made according to the practice of the elders (*vṛddhācāra*). For those who died on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) or during the fortnight of the deceased (*pretapakṣa*), the *pārvaṇa* is mandatory. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:
"But for one whose [death] occurs on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) or again during the fortnight of the ancestors (pretapakṣa), the pārvaṇa rite must be performed for him; never the ekoddiṣṭa.
For an ascetic (yati), however, there is never an ekoddiṣṭa; rather, in all cases, it is exclusively the pārvaṇa. And so says Pracetas:
"Merely by taking up the staff, an ascetic does not immediately become a *preta*;
therefore, his *pārvaṇa* rite must always be performed by his son.
Regarding this, some propose an alternative arrangement between the *pārvaṇa* and the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites.
Every year, he and his son born of the wife shall perform the rite according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure alone; the other ten sons shall perform the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
[447] Thus, according to the statement of Jātūkarṇya.
That is incorrect, for it is said:
"The ekoddiṣṭa rite must be performed by the legitimate son on the anniversary of the day of death."
But after the sapindikarana rite, the ancestral offering for one's mother and father shall be performed according to the parvana method.

This is because it contradicts the statement of Paiṭhīnasi. As for the statement of Jātūkarṇya, however, it remains consistent even if it refers to the Akṣayyatṛtīyā and other rites to be performed every year on occasions other than the anniversary of death (kṣayāha). Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Sumantu:
"A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires should perform the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha according to the rules;
a wise man who does not maintain the fires should perform the Ekoddiṣṭa on the day of death for his parents."
Thus it has been said; however, that is incorrect, for:
"But those Brahmins who maintain many sacred fires, as well as those who maintain only one sacred fire—for them, after the *sapiṇḍana* rite, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is prescribed, not the *pārvaṇa*."
Thus, because the *Ekoddiṣṭa* rite is prescribed even for one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) in another Smṛti, Yājñavalkya states the definition of the *Ekoddiṣṭa*:
"The *Ekoddiṣṭa* is devoid of [offerings to] the gods; it has a single *arghya* offering and a single *pavitra*;
it is indeed without the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and the pouring of oblations into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and it is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*)."
"At the point where [the water] is offered as inexhaustible, one should say 'May you be dismissed' during the dismissal of the Brahmins;
one should say 'May you be pleased,' and they should reply, 'We are indeed pleased. (YDh 1.251–52)

Kātyāyana also says: "Now, regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa*: there is one vessel, one *arghya* offering, and one *piṇḍa*; there is no invocation (*āvāhana*), no offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and no Viśvedevas here. The question regarding satisfaction is 'Is it well-eaten? (*svaditam*); the response is 'It is very well-eaten' (*susvaditam*). At the place for the *akṣayya* water, one says 'May it remain present' (*upatiṣṭhatām*); at the dismissal, one says 'May you be delighted' (*abhiramyatām*), and the other replies 'We are delighted' (*abhiratāḥ smaḥ*). And that *ekoddiṣṭa* is of three kinds: the new (*nava*), the mixed-new (*navamiśra*), and the old (*purāṇa*). Among these, the *nava-śrāddha* is prescribed from the first day up to the eleventh day. Thus says Aṅgiras:
"On the first day, the third day, the fifth, or even the seventh;
and on the ninth and the eleventh—this is called the *navaśrāddha*. Thus says Vasiṣṭha as well.
The nine *śrāddhas* should be performed on the seventh day, the third day, the first day, and likewise the ninth;
as well as on the eleventh and the fifth days—thus there are six.
"Some hold that there are only five [days]; if the ninth is omitted, one should perform it on the eleventh day—thus the authors of the Smṛtis know.
Regarding this, Śivasvāmin has shown the systematic arrangement of these two positions.

"The followers of the Āśvalāyana branch say there are nine *navaśrāddhas*, while the Āpastambas say there are six; for the Taittirīyas, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*). A specific rule for Vaiśyas and others is shown in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*.
The great seers say that there are nine and seven funeral rites (śrāddhas) for Vaiśyas and Kṣatriyas respectively in sequence; however, for the first and last of the castes, they say there are six.

[449] Thus: the *māsika* (monthly) rite mixed with the *navaśrāddha* (ninefold funeral rites) should be performed after the six *navaśrāddhas*. Accordingly, Āśvalāyana states: "The *navamiśra* follows the six. The *purāṇa* (ancient/regular) rites, such as the annual anniversary (*pratyābdika*), should be performed after the *māsikas*. For this very reason, Hārīta, having prescribed the penance for the two *māsikas* in sequence within the *Prāyaścittakāṇḍa*, subsequently refers to the later *śrāddha* by the term *purāṇa* and prescribes the penance:
"A *cāndrāyaṇa* for a *navaśrāddha*; a *prājāpatya* for a *māsika*."

"But in the Purāṇas, a one-day penance is prescribed. (Hārīta Smṛti 21.17). Now, regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*: since the *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites have been described, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, which possesses the nature of both, is now explained. Regarding this, Laugākṣi says:
"Having performed the sixteen *śrāddhas*, one should perform the *sapiṇḍana*. Thus it is said.
The sixteen *śrāddhas* have been shown by Jātūkarṇya:
"The twelve monthly [śrāddhas], as well as the first and the sixth-month [śrāddhas]."

"The Traipakṣika, the Ābdika, and so forth—these are the sixteen Śrāddhas. Here, the terms *ādya-ṣāṇmāsika* and *ābdika* refer respectively to the *ūna-māsika*, the *ūna-ṣāṇmāsika*, and the *ūna-ābdika*. The time for the twelve monthly Śrāddhas has been shown by Yājñavalkya:
"On the day of death, however, it should be performed every month for a year."
"And likewise every year, the first [rite] on the eleventh day.

(YDh 1.256) For one year—that is, for the duration of a year—a *śrāddha* must be performed month by month on the anniversary of death. After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, it must be performed every year on the anniversary of death. However, the first monthly rite (*māsika*) must be performed on the eleventh day. Gālava states the timing for the "deficient six-month" (*ūna-ṣāṇmāsika*) and other rites: "The deficient six-month rite is on the sixth month; the deficient monthly rite is indeed on the half-month."
"In the case of a *taipakṣika* [intercalary month], it should occur within three fortnights; likewise, in the twelfth year, it is deficient by one year.
Thus says Ślokagautama as well:
"When [the lunar month] is deficient by one, two, or three days, or even deficient by a third part [of a day]."
"Gautama states that one should perform the *śrāddha* rites for the deficient monthly anniversary (*ūnābdika*) and so forth. (ŚloGSm 3.27).
Gobhila states the alternative timings for the deficient monthly rite (*ūnamāsika*):
"The deficient monthly rite should take place on the twelfth day after death, or at the end of the first month."
Gārgya states the times to be avoided for deficient śrāddhas:
"On a Nandā tithi, on a Saturday, on the fourteenth lunar day, and during the Tripuṣkara yoga,
a householder should not perform an ūna-śrāddha, lest there be loss of sons and wealth."
Marīci also says: "In Dvipuṣkara, on the Nandās, on Sinīvālī, on the day of Bhṛgu,
on the fourteenth lunar day, and in Kṛttikā during Tripuṣkara— these are not deficient [in merit]."

The conjunction of three specific lunar days (*tithi*), weekdays (*vāra*), and asterisms (*nakṣatra*) is called *tripuṣkara*. The conjunction of two is *dvipuṣkara*. What are these specific ones? The auspicious lunar days are the second, seventh, and twelfth; the weekdays are Sunday, Tuesday, and Saturday; and the asterisms are Punarvasu, Uttaraphalgunī, Viśākhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvābhādrapadā.

Having thus performed these sixteen *śrāddhas*, one should then perform the *sapiṇḍana*. Regarding its timing, Atri says: "Now, as for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*: when a year has passed, or on the twelfth day. Kātyāyana also says: "Now, as for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*: when a year has passed, or after three fortnights, or on whatever day an auspicious occasion (*vṛddhi*) occurs. Baudhāyana also says: "Now, when a year has passed, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed; or after three fortnights, or in the third month, or in the sixth, or in the eleventh, or on the twelfth day. Thus, eight times have been proclaimed: the eleventh day, the twelfth day, the third fortnight, the third month, the sixth month, the eleventh month, the end of the year, and the arrival of an auspicious event. Regarding the specific application among these, Hārīta states:

"But if the new moon that precedes the tenth day from the anniversary of death should occur, the son who maintains the sacred fires must indeed perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on that [new moon]. (Hārīta Smṛti 20.19) The meaning is: "starting from the day following the anniversary of death. Kārṣṇājini also says:

"A son who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite as before; if it occurs after ten nights have passed, it should be on the new moon day (*kuhū*) following the anniversary of the year. Thus it is said.

Since the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* must necessarily be performed by those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), and since that sacrifice cannot take place without the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed on the eleventh day if the new moon occurs. Regarding the necessity of performing the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, it is heard in scripture: "On the new moon day, in the afternoon, they perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Gālava has shown the impossibility of performing the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*: "Once the deceased has attained the status of an ancestor through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *pitṛyajña* for one who maintains the sacred fires proceeds on the *sinīvālī* (new moon) day."

But upon the arrival of the *darśa* (new moon), one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgni*) should perform the *sapiṇḍana* on the twelfth day. This is stated in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*: "O King, if the sacrificer possesses the sacred fires while the deceased lacks them, the sons should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the twelfth day."
Gobhila also says:
"But when the performer possesses the sacred fires while the deceased is without them,
then the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa should be performed by the sons on the twelfth day."

In the third alternative, when the deceased possesses the sacred fires (*sāgnitva*), the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite must be performed. Regarding this, Sumantu says: "If the deceased was one who maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and the performer [of the rite] is without such fires, one should perform his *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* in the third fortnight."

[453] Thus: "When both [the performer and the deceased] possess the sacred fires, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed on the twelfth day. When the performer possesses the sacred fires, or when the deceased (the father) also possesses the sacred fires, then the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the father should be performed on the twelfth day. So it is said.

When both [the sacrificer and the deceased] are without sacred fires (*anagni*), seven times—the beginning of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) and so forth—are optionally prescribed as the times for the performance. This has been stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "The sacrificer who is without fire should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the deceased who maintained no sacred fires, O bull of the Bharatas, when the full year has elapsed."

"On the twelfth day, or the sixth, or the three-fortnightly [period], or at the end of three months, or even on the eleventh day of the month, an auspicious occasion should be present. Among these seven times, the twelfth day is the most recommended. Thus said Vyāghra.

"Because family customs are infinite, because the lifespan of men is subject to decay, and because the body is impermanent, the twelve-day period is recommended. All of this refers to the members of the three twice-born castes (*traivarṇika*). For a *śūdra*, however, the twelve-day period alone is fixed. Therefore, Viṣṇu states, following the rule that "the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed": [text continues].
"For it is declared that for Śūdras, [the rites] on the twelfth day are to be performed, excluding the recitation of mantras.

When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed before the completion of a year—having already performed the sixteen *śrāddhas* on the eleventh day and so forth—then the monthly *māsika* and other rites must be repeated at their respective times. Regarding this, Gobhila says:
"For one whose *sapiṇḍatā* is ordained before a year has passed..."
"One should perform those sixteen *śrāddhas* again according to rule.

"According to rule" means by the method appropriate to the occasion, whether by the *ekoddiṣṭa* or the *pārvaṇa* rite. Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi says: "Before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should perform the sixteen *śrāddhas*."
One should perform all of those rites according to the procedure for the Ekoddiṣṭa.

"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, whenever one performs [the annual rites], then one should always perform them again in the same manner as one performed them for each year. And this repetition applies only to those [rites] occurring after [the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*], not to those occurring before it. Regarding this, Kārṣṇājini says:

"Wherever the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed within a year, thereafter the monthly rites (*māsika*) shall be performed at their proper times. Thus, after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, when there is the arrival of an occasion for increase (*vṛddhi*) regarding those rites to be repeated, such as the monthly rites and so forth, they must be postponed again. Regarding this, Śāṭhyāyani says:
"Even those [rites] performed by anticipation prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* are again postponed,
because of the prohibition against performing them subsequent to a *vṛddhi* (prosperity) rite.
And this prohibition was stated by Kātyāyana:
"Having completed the *vṛddhi-tantra*, one should not perform the monthly rites.
Regarding the secondary time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says:
"If the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha has not been performed at the prescribed time..."
"One should perform it under the asterisms of Ārdrā, Hasta, Rohiṇī, or Anurādhā.
Regarding the procedure for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, Yājñavalkya says:
"One should prepare four vessels joined with scented water and sesame seeds."
For the sake of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).

"By means of the two verses beginning with *ye samānāḥ*, one should perform the remainder as previously described. (YDh 1.256, 254). Kātyāyana also states: "Then, when the year is complete, having filled four vessels with sesame seeds, scents, and water—three for the ancestors and one for the deceased—one pours the vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors while reciting the two verses beginning with *ye samānāḥ*. By this, the rite for the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is explained. When the father dies while the grandfather is still living, then the father’s *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed together with the great-grandfather and the others. This has been stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:

"When the father has died and the grandfather still exists, three rice-balls (piṇḍas) must be offered by him, beginning with the great-grandfather. Regarding this, some do not even accept that there is *sāpiṇḍya* (the sapinda relationship) in such a case.

"Furthermore, for those who have died out of the natural order [of seniority], the *sapiṇḍana* rite must not be performed," according to this statement. Others, however, consider the scope of this statement to exclude the mother, father, and husband; they cite the following passage from the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is prescribed even for those who have died out of the natural order."
Whether it be the mother, the father, or the husband—this is the rule recorded in the tradition.

[456] Thus it is said. In this matter, the settled rule is to be observed according to the practice of the elders. The *sapiṇḍya* for the mother must be performed together with the paternal grandmother and the other female ancestors. To this effect, Śaṅkha says:
"How should the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the mother be performed by her sons?
It is traditionally taught that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is to be done together with the paternal grandmother and the others."
Yama states the alternative for one whose father has died:
"A son whose father is living should perform the *sapiṇḍana* with his grandmother;
however, a son whose father has died [should do so] with his father or with his paternal grandmother."
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) should perform the sapinda rite for his mother together with his maternal grandfather and the others. Thus says Baudhāyana:
"In the first pinda, the son of an appointed daughter should designate his mother;
in the second, her father; and in the third, his paternal grandfather."
In the case of *anvārohaṇa* (the wife following her husband onto the funeral pyre), however, *sāpiṇḍya* with the husband alone is certain. Thus said Śātātapa:
"She who dies having followed her lord is entitled to share in the *piṇḍa* with him, even while dwelling in heaven, until the dissolution of all beings."
Yama also says:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a woman must be performed by her husband alone;
for even while alive, she attained oneness with him through mantras, oblations, and vows."

Here, the word "oneness" (*aikya*) is intended to exclude options such as the paternal grandmother and so forth; it is not intended to exclude the three ancestors. This is because the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite takes the form of both the *pārvaṇa* and the *ekoddiṣṭa*. All of this should be understood to apply to marriages such as the *brāhma* and others. However, in the case of the *āsura* and other types of marriage, there is a fourfold option. Regarding that, Śātātapa states the three alternatives: "In the *āsura* and other forms of marriage, the *sapiṇḍana* for women of the various castes may be performed with her mother, her paternal grandmother, or her mother-in-law. [457]
Sumantu states the fourth position:
"The father should be joined with the paternal grandfather by his sons after a full year has passed;
likewise, the mother with the maternal grandfather—so said the blessed Śiva."
Regarding the rule for the *gotra* in the case of the mother’s *sāpiṇḍya*, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"In the case of marriages such as the Brāhma and others, whatever maiden has been wedded,
the performance of her *piṇḍa* and water offerings must be done by means of the husband’s *gotra*."
"One who knows the Dharma [should perform the rites] for those born of Āsura and other such marriages according to the mother's paternal lineage (pitṛgotra). Thus says Laugākṣi:
"The offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water-rites for the mother should be performed according to the lineage of the maternal grandfather."
"The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) should perform [the rite]; thus said Prajāpati. Thus Paiṭhīnasi shows the sapinda relationship of the wife:
"But when a woman dies without a son, the husband shall perform the sapindana."
"Her *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should take place together with her mother-in-law and the others.
Regarding the *sapiṇḍya* of the husband, Laugākṣi says:
"In the absence of all [male relatives], the wives themselves [perform] for their husbands without mantras."
"They should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and thereafter the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha]. Sumantu also says:
"If the deceased has departed without a son, and there is no performer of the śrāddha rite..."
"In that case, the wife also should perform the *sāpiṇḍya* as well as the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha].
As for another Smṛti text which states:
"For one who has died without a son, one should not perform the *sapiṇḍatā* at all..."
Impurity, water libations, and the piṇḍa offering should be performed as the ekoddiṣṭa rite, not the pārvaṇa rite.
For those men or women who die childless,
because the *sapiṇḍana* rite is absent for them, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is prescribed and not the *pārvaṇa*.
Thus, this [text] should be explained as being intent upon praising the rule for procreating a son. Uśanas prohibits *sāpiṇḍya* for ascetics:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite should not be performed for them by sons and others;
simply by the taking up of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), the state of being a *preta* does not arise at all."
"One should never perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for ascetics (*yatins*);
rather, for them, the *pārvaṇa* rite is prescribed on the eleventh day.
Thus, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, which possesses a dual nature, has been described.
Now, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *pārvaṇa* rite, is described.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states:
"In this manner, proceeding in a clockwise direction, one [should worship] the *nāndīmukha* ancestors at a rite of prosperity (*vṛddhi*)."
"One should sacrifice; the ritual should be performed with balls made of barley mixed with curd and jujube fruits.
Thus, the meaning is "just as in the *pārvaṇa* rite. And so it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"In the case of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), the wise man should always worship the *nāndīmukha* ancestors."

"But the specific [details] have been accomplished; the remainder shall be as in the *pārvaṇa* rite" (ViDhPu 1.142.15). By the phrase "as in the *pārvaṇa*," the invocation (*āvāhana*), the designation of the three ancestors (*tripuruṣoddeśa*), and so forth are extended by analogy (*atideśa*). However, this specific detail has been established: that the ancestors are designated as "those with the *nāndīmukha* name. And this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the clockwise circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇāvṛt*), the jujube fruits (*badara*), the curd (*dadhi*), and other such specific features mentioned by Yājñavalkya, as well as others. Those specific features have been shown by Kātyāyana.

In the *ābhyudayika* śrāddha, the ritual procedure is performed clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*). There is an exclusion of mantras dedicated to the ancestors (*pitrya*). The *darbha* grass blades are straight. Barley (*yava*) serves the purpose of sesame seeds (*tila*). The question regarding satisfaction is "Is it well-prepared? (*susaṃpannam*). The response is "It is well-prepared" (*susaṃpannam*). The funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) are mixed with curd, jujube fruits (*badara*), and unhusked rice grains (*akṣata*). He asks: "Shall I invoke the *nāndīmukha* ancestors? At the place where the word "imperishable" (*akṣaya*) would normally occur, he says: "May the *nāndīmukha* ancestors be pleased. He asks: "Shall I honor the *nāndīmukha* ancestors? With the formula, "May the *nāndīmukha* fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers be pleased," he should offer the *svadhā*. He should feed an even number of guests. Thus it is said.
Pracetas also says:
"The Śrāddha for the mothers should come first, followed immediately by that for the fathers;
then for the maternal grandfathers—these three Śrāddhas are prescribed for the Vṛddhi ceremony."
"One should not recite the ancestral *japya*, nor should one cause meat to be offered there.
Facing east, with the *devatīrtha*, one should quickly perform the cleansing of the site.
Here, the ellipsis "one should perform the offering of the *piṇḍas* and so forth" is to be supplied. For this very reason, Pracetas says:
One should not perform the *apasavya* rite, nor should one fail to circumambulate clockwise;
just as one should worship the gods, so too should one serve the ancestors during the ancestral rites (*vṛddhi*).
"One should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) facing east during a rite for prosperity (vṛddhi), using the left hand while remaining silent.
Regarding the specific details of offering the piṇḍas, Vasiṣṭha says:
"Facing east, using the *devatīrtha* [part of the hand], upon kuśa grass whose tips point eastward..."
"Having given the rice-balls (piṇḍas), one should not turn the alms-bowl face down.
Thus, one should not offer the rice-balls in the vicinity of the leavings;
nor should one, while facing downward, offer the rice-balls during the rite for the ancestors (vṛddhi-śrāddha) after having invoked them by name.

This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Śātātapa. Furthermore, the utterance of the name occurs only at the first *piṇḍa*, not at the second. Thus it is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata: "One should offer the *piṇḍas* individually—one by name and the next silently. This means that for each individual [deceased], two *piṇḍas* are offered; among them, the first is to be given with the name and the second silently. In the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the offering of *piṇḍas* is optional. Accordingly, the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa states:
"O lord of men, one may perform the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) or one may not;
O mighty-armed one, this depends on observing the family customs during the *vṛddhiśrāddha*.
Regarding the occasions for the *vṛddhiśrāddha*, Laugākṣi says:

"The Nāndī-śrāddha is prescribed for the first-fruits feast, the tonsure ceremony, the godāna rite, the Soma sacrifice, the Saṃsava, the ritual bath, the establishment of the sacred fires, and marriage. Thus says Kārṣṇājini as well.
At the marriages of daughters and sons, at the entry into a new house,
at the naming ceremony of children, and likewise at the tonsure ceremony and other such rites;
"And at the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), as well as upon seeing the face of a son or other [offspring],
the self-controlled householder should worship the Nāndīmukha ancestors.
Thus says Vṛddhagārgya as well.

"One should perform the Vṛddhi-śrāddha at the installation of the sacred fires, at consecrations and the like, for sacrifices and works of public utility, during a woman’s fertile period, and likewise upon entering a stage of life. Now follows the determination of those who perform the śrāddha.
Thus, the *śrāddhas* have been described. Now, their performer is being described. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"The *śrāddha* for a deceased father must be diligently offered by his sons, as well as by kinsmen, relatives, friends, disciples, officiating priests, servants, and family chaplains."

In the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well: "O King, the son, the grandson, or the great-grandson, or likewise the lineage of a brother, or even the lineage of a *sapiṇḍa*, becomes eligible to perform the rites. (ViPu 3.13.30)
Regarding this, Śaṅkha distinguishes between the primary and secondary options:
"The offering of rice balls and the water-rite must be performed by the son for his father;
in the absence of a son, it shall be performed by the wife; and in the absence of a wife, by the uterine brother."
Also in the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*:
"The son should perform the *śrāddha* for his father; in his absence, the wife;
then the heir to the wealth, the daughter’s son, and then the brother and his son."
"The brother born of the same womb shall perform the cremation and other rites for his brother, as shall the son of that [brother];
likewise the brother not born of the same womb, and in his absence, the son of that [brother].

By the word "son" (*putra*), both primary and secondary sons are included. In the absence of all of them, the grandson (*pautra*) shall perform [the rites]. In his absence, however, it is the wife (*patnī*). For this very reason, Bṛhaspati has stated the equality of the grandson with the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*).
"The grandson and the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) both cause the attainment of heaven;
they are declared to be equal in regard to inheritance and the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
One should not, however, suspect an option of equality between the two on this account alone.

"A grandfather who has a son need not perform [the rite] through his grandson," according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Kātyāyana. The sequence "but in the absence of a wife, the uterine brother" is to be understood as applying to the case where the wife is the heir to the inheritance; otherwise, whoever is the heir to the inheritance shall perform [the rite]. For this very reason, Viṣṇu and Āpastamba state: "He who takes the wealth is the giver of the *piṇḍa*" (ViSm 15.40). A son should offer the *piṇḍa* even in the absence of paternal wealth; in his absence, a *sapiṇḍa* should offer it; and in the absence of a *sapiṇḍa*, those such as the *samānodaka* relatives should perform it. Thus says the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
In the absence of a son, the sapinda relatives shall perform it; in their absence, the samānodaka relatives;
or those who are the mother’s sapindas, or those who are the mother’s samānodakas.
The son of a daughter who has no sons should properly perform this rite for his maternal grandfather;
likewise, the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should do so for his maternal grandfather.
In the absence of all these, women shall perform [the rite] for their own husbands without mantras;
and in their absence, the king shall cause it to be performed by means of that person's estate.
"All the rites, beginning with cremation, should be performed correctly by men of that same class for all castes, since the king is the kinsman of everyone. (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 30.19–23).

The rule that "in the absence of all [others], women should perform [the rites]" refers specifically to women married through the Āsura and other such forms of marriage. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the rule stating "in the absence of a son, the wife [should perform the rites]," because such a woman lacks the status of a *patnī* (wife/partner in ritual). For this very reason, Śātātapa prohibits her from having the status of a *patnī*.
But a woman who has been purchased with money is not called a wife;
she is not for rites to the gods nor for rites to the ancestors—the wise know her to be a slave.

[464] Thus, Parāśara, in the Viṣṇupurāṇa, demonstrates the established authority of sons and others regarding the rites categorized as prior, intermediate, and posterior: "The rites are of three kinds—those called prior, those called intermediate, and likewise those called posterior. Listen to me concerning their distinctions."

Those rites which are prescribed to be performed during the interval between the cremation and the tenth day are considered the "former" (pūrva); those performed month by month are the "middle" (madhyama), known as the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
When a deceased person has attained the status of a *pitṛ* following the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,
those ancestral rites (*pitryāḥ kriyāḥ*) which are performed thereafter are designated as the "later" rites, O King.
But by the father’s and mother’s sapindas, as well as by those who share the same water (samānodaka),
by those included in their respective groups, or by the king who takes away the wealth;

"The initial rites and the intermediate ones, O best of men, should be performed by the sons and others, while the subsequent rites should be performed by the daughters' sons or their sons. (ViP 3.13.34–38) The meaning is that the initial and intermediate rites must be performed by those beginning with the *sapiṇḍas* and ending with the king; however, the subsequent rites must be performed by those beginning with the sons and ending with the lineage of brothers, and by those beginning with the daughters' sons (*dauhitras*), but not by those beginning with the *sapiṇḍas* and ending with the king. Even an *aurasa* son who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*) shall perform the rites such as cremation. Regarding this, Sumantu says:

"One who has lost his father must certainly perform the *śrāddha*, whether he is established in a vow (*vratastha*) or not established in a vow (*avratastha*), even if he should be alone. Here, "not established in a vow" refers to one who is uninitiated (*anupanīta*). Regarding this, Vṛddhamanu says:
"Even one who has not been initiated, if he is the only son, should perform the *śrāddha*;
he should offer the oblation for the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*) into the hand of a Brahmin.
Regarding this, a specific rule has been shown by Pracetas:
"But one whose tonsure has been performed should offer water and the funeral cake (piṇḍa), and should employ the utterance 'svadhā', yet he should not cause the Veda to be recited.
The meaning is that he should perform these for both parents. And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
"But one who has had the tonsure ceremony performed but has not yet received the initiatory rites (anupeta) should perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) for his parents;
he may utter the word *svadhā*, but he must not pronounce the syllables of the Veda.
As for that which was stated by Manu:
"For no ritual act whatsoever is prescribed for him prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass;

nor should he utter the Veda, except for the offering of the *svadhā* [funeral] libations"—this refers to the case of one whose *cūḍā* ceremony has been performed in the rainy season. And so says Sumantu:
"Even one who has not been initiated should perform the *paitṛmedhika* rites with the recitation of mantras,
provided he has had his tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) performed and is three years of age.
Now follows the determination of eligibility for the *śrāddha* offerings for maternal grandfathers and others.
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"A twice-born man should satisfy his paternal ancestors and maternal grandfathers with the Śrāddha rite;
thus he becomes free from debt to his ancestors, and they go to the world of Brahmā."
[466] Thus. The plural number in the term "mātāmahānām" (of the maternal grandfathers) is intended to include the mother’s paternal grandfather and great-grandfather as well. And so Pulastya says:
"Starting from the mother’s father, three are recorded as maternal grandfathers;
their daughters' sons should perform the *śrāddha* for them just as they do for their own fathers."

The *mātāmaha-śrāddha* (ancestral rite for maternal grandfathers) is also obligatory, just like the *pitṛ-śrāddha*, because it is recorded in the legal tradition (*smṛti*) that there is sin (*pratyavāya*) incurred by its non-performance. This has been stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"He who performs the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] solely for the sake of his paternal ancestors, but does not perform it for his maternal grandfathers, is born as a slayer of his ancestors."
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga also says:
"Where the fathers are honored, there the maternal grandfathers must certainly be honored as well; it must be done without distinction, for by failing to do so, one goes to hell."
In some instances, Kātyāyana excludes the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* [the ancestral rite for maternal grandfathers], stating:

"Excepting that which is accompanied by the *karṣū* (the sacrificial pit), as well as the sixteenth *śrāddha* and the annual (*pratyābdika*) rite, there shall be six *piṇḍas* in the remaining cases; such is the settled rule. (KSm 3.24.14)

The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha is accompanied by the *karṣū* (the sacrificial pit). The mention of the "sixteen" [śrāddhas] is intended as an illustration for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites. Regarding the sequence of śrāddhas in the case of a mass death, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says:
"If there should be a simultaneous death of several *sapiṇḍas*, one should perform the śrāddha according to that order, having considered the proximity of their relationships."

In this context, the relative proximity of the relationship among the wife and other *sapiṇḍas* should be understood as follows: the relationship between husband and wife is immediate, because it has a single common referent and lacks any intervening step. However, the relationship of a son is more remote, because its cognition is delayed by the fact that he is defined by reference to both parents. The relationship of a brother is even more remote than that, because it is mediated by the fact that he is born from the father. One should infer other cases in the same manner. Regarding the simultaneous death of the wife and the two parents, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says: "Of the wife, the son, his son, his brother, and his grandson..."
If there is a simultaneous death of both the daughter-in-law and mother-in-law, or of both parents;
"One should perform the *sāpiṇḍya* [relationship] within ten years, beginning with the mother and father.
His son is the "son's son" (*putraputra*). His grandson is the "brother's son" (*bhrātṛtanaya*). As for that which was stated by Devala:
"The body of one whose parents have died shall be impure."
Neither for the gods nor for the ancestors [should one perform rites] until the year is complete.

Thus, this refers to *sapiṇḍa* relatives other than those previously mentioned, such as the wife and so forth. For this very reason, Laugākṣi says: "In the event of the death of a great guru, one should perform the funeral rites for others even before a year has passed, but one should omit the *śrāddha*."

The funeral rites (*pretakāryāṇi*), beginning with cremation and ending with the first *śrāddha*, are intended here; for there is a specific traditional rule stating: "Even one who is impure may perform the first *śrāddha* on the eleventh day. The word "one" (*ekam*) means "other [than the daily rites]. Regarding the simultaneous death of both parents, Devala says:

[468] "Upon the death of both parents, the sons shall perform the rites for both; likewise when others follow in succession, or even in the case of a simultaneous death (saṅghātamaraṇa). According to this, when there is a simultaneous death of both parents through *sahagamana* (following in death), or when the mother follows [the father] in death, or even when they die on different days, one should perform the respective rites on the twelfth day (*dvādaśāha*). However, when others and the two parents die simultaneously, one should not perform them at their respective times, but rather only after three fortnights (*tripakṣa*). To this effect, Laugākṣi says:
If, on a single day, one's wife, son, grandson, mother, her sons,
and both parents should all die together;

"One should perform the first [rite] in the eleventh month, but the *sapiṇḍana* in the third fortnight. Thus it is said. Even in the case of a collective death (*saṅghātamaraṇa*) without following one's parents, or in the case of a mother dying on another day without following her [father], one should perform the *sapiṇḍana* for the mother in the third fortnight. And so Devala says:
"When there is death on the same day for both parents, but the other [parent] dies on another day..."

"The *sapiṇḍana* should take place after three fortnights, except in the case of death while traveling. Thus, even if the two *śrāddhas* for the mother and father coincide in time due to fate, one should perform the father’s *śrāddha* first. Regarding this, Kārṣṇājini says:
"When the *śrāddhas* for both parents arrive simultaneously—whether on a new moon day or when the food has become stale..."
"A son should perform [the rites] beginning with those for his father, except where there is a lack of proximity or fitness.

The meaning is that, "except" (*anyatra*)—that is, in cases other than those involving his mother or paternal uncle—he should perform them provided there is a fitness regarding the proximity of the relationship.
As for that which was stated by Pracetas:

"One should never perform two *śrāddhas* on the same day. This rule applies to a case where, when one *śrāddha* is being performed, another is accomplished by way of *prasaṅga* (incidental inclusion) due to the identity of the deity; for example, the incidental accomplishment of the daily (*nitya*) *śrāddha* by means of the new-moon (*amāvāsyā*) *śrāddha*, or the accomplishment of the *darśa* *śrāddha* by means of the *yugādi* *śrāddha*. Regarding the case where the death days of both parents coincide, a specific rule has been stated by Laugākṣi concerning the performance of the *anvāhārya* (monthly ancestral rite).
"On the day of death, the offering of the *piṇḍas* should be performed separately in brief;

however, the *navaśrāddha* for a husband and wife occurs only when she follows him in death (*anvārohaṇa*). Thus, the offering of the *piṇḍas*, which is the *śrāddha*, should be performed separately—meaning without the co-wife—by means of a single preparation of food and so forth. One should perform the *navaśrāddha* in the same manner. Another *Smṛti* text also states:
"Having ascended the same funeral pyre, two spouses have met their death;
one should perform the *śrāddha* separately, and likewise offer rice (*odana*) separately for each.

When several mothers ascend the same funeral pyre, if the cooking and other rites are performed as a single unit, one should first perform the rite for the father, then immediately for the [biological] mother, and thereafter for the others in order of seniority, beginning with the eldest. Thus says Bhṛgu:
If many, or even two, have died at the same time,
one may perform the cooking by a single ritual procedure (tantra), but one should perform the Śrāddha offerings separately for each.

"In the case of a conjunction [of deaths], this is the sequence: first for the one who died previously, then at the very least for the second, and then for the third. Here, "the first" refers to the primary father; "the second" refers to the mother, who is inferior to him; and "the third" refers to the most junior relative, who is even more inferior than her—this is the meaning. Regarding the conjunction of the *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, Jābāli says:

"If both the *ekoddiṣṭa* and the *pārvaṇa* should occur at one time, having first performed the *pārvaṇa*, one should then perform the *ekoddiṣṭa*. Thus it is said. When multiple occasions for a *śrāddha* coincide, one should perform the *śrāddha* according to the sequence of those occasions. And so says Kātyāyana:
"Two or many occasions for rites may arise on a single day;
the occasional rites (naimittika) should be performed according to the sequence in which the occasions arise.

Although it is not proper to perform two *śrāddhas* dedicated to the same deity on one day—since by performing one, the purpose of the other is also accomplished through *prasaṅga* (incidental fulfillment)—nevertheless, occasional rites must be performed even if they are numerous, by virtue of the force of the scriptural injunction. Thus says Jābāli:
"Having performed a *śrāddha* for that very person, one should not perform another *śrāddha* on that same day;

however, an occasional (*naimittika*) rite must be performed whenever its specific occasion arises. Thus, when a mandatory (*nitya*) and an optional (*kāmya*) rite directed toward the same deity coincide, the fulfillment of the mandatory requirement is achieved through the performance of the optional one alone. This has been stated in the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*:
Through the ritual of the optional [rite], the ritual of the obligatory rite of ancestral offerings (śrāddha) is accomplished.
Thus [it is said].

That chapter which, while not abandoning the collection of rules regarding impurity (*āśauca*), explains them through its own application, and wherein the *śrāddha* rite for those who have assumed a body is declared as the ground for prosperity—
may that *Tāttīrya* chapter, known by those who discern what is external and internal, be the dispeller of my distress.
Thus, this Lord of Mantras, Mādhava, who possesses independent majesty, provides this exposition.

Thus ends the third chapter of the Mādhavīyā, the commentary on the Pārāśara-smṛti, composed by the minister Mādhava, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the Great King of Kings, Supreme Lord, promoter of the Vedic path. || 3 ||
